artigo.texto: BYD Builds Out European Charging and Storage Networks While Deliveries Slide Published on 10/20/2026 at 05:10 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD is betting that infrastructure and after-sales muscle can do what a busy product calendar alone has not: revive momentum in a stock that has spent the year under pressure. The Chinese group unveiled a two-pronged expansion on Tuesday, pairing a European fast-charging buildout with a global service network for its battery storage business, even as its sales figures point the other way. On the storage side, the BYD Energy Storage unit announced a worldwide customer service network for its battery systems. The structure takes in nine operations and maintenance centres and leans on more than 200 field engineers, with additional branches slated for South Africa and Bulgaria in 2027. Over 100 research and development specialists are tied into the network, a push aimed at giving commercial clients technical support long after installation and shoring up confidence in the reliability of BYD's storage solutions. Charging, Staffing and a Paris Flagship The vehicle business is moving on a similar scale in Europe. At the Paris Motor Show, BYD presented new models and core technologies alongside its Denza brand, including the seven-seat ATTO 8 flagship SUV and the second generation of its Blade battery. To drive uptake of its own fast-charging technology, the company said it will install 3,000 fast-charging stations across Europe by the end of 2027. Headcount on the continent is set to follow. Deputy chairwoman Stella Li told Bloomberg that the European workforce will soon pass the 10,000 mark, with roughly 40,000 employees planned in the region by 2030. The ATTO 8 itself packs a 115 kilowatt-hour second-generation Blade battery, delivers up to 653 kilometres of WLTP range and comes with fast-charging capability. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? At home, BYD introduced the Da Han electric flagship sedan, built on a 1,000-volt architecture with up to 1,008 kilometres of CLTC range. The entry-level variant is priced at 235,900 Yuan. The domestic line-up is being refreshed at a brisk clip: the second generation of the compact Seagull EV was due to launch in China on Tuesday, according to media reports, arriving as a larger five-seater with a more powerful electric motor, though official prices were not yet available at launch. Safety Nod and Battery Share International ambitions got a lift from Europe's safety tester. The SHARK DMO plug-in hybrid pickup received the top five-star rating from Euro NCAP in mid-October. In energy storage deployment, data from the China Automotive Battery Innovation Alliance showed BYD installed 18.29 gigawatt-hours of traction batteries in China in September, a market share of 21.09%. Deliveries Retreat as Q3 Looms The product offensive has yet to show through in volumes. BYD delivered 463,561 new-energy vehicles in September, 180,700 of them exported. Over the first nine months of 2026, sales totalled 3,131,576 vehicles, down 3.94% from the same period a year earlier. Investors will get a clearer read on the financial impact shortly. The company has called a board meeting for 29 October 2026 to review unaudited results for the third quarter and the first nine months of the year. The shares have reflected the softer sales momentum. BYD closed yesterday's session at EUR 8.30, leaving the stock just 3.3% above its 52-week low. In today's trading it slipped 0.1% to EUR 8.33, extending its loss since the turn of the year to 22%. The upcoming quarterly report should shed light on how margins and profitability are holding up in an intensifying battle for market share. artigo.texto: The next decade of battery materials growth is likely to be shaped as much by regulation as by vehicle demand. According to IndexBox, the market for life cycle safe battery production chemicals is expected to keep expanding through 2035, supported by tougher compliance expectations in Europe and by automakers pressing suppliers to clean up their sourcing.The forecast points to a structural shift in how battery inputs are bought, processed and documented. Rather than treating chemicals as a narrow procurement item, cell makers and their upstream suppliers are increasingly being asked to prove that the materials used in production can stand up to scrutiny across the full value chain. That includes traceability, environmental controls and adherence to rules that are becoming more demanding as battery manufacturing scales up.Regulation is now a commercial driverThe most immediate catalyst is the European Union's battery regulatory framework, which has pushed sustainability and disclosure from the margins into the centre of industrial planning. For chemical suppliers, the compliance burden is no longer limited to product quality and pricing. Buyers are now looking for evidence that inputs align with life cycle safety requirements, a trend that is likely to influence sourcing decisions well beyond Europe.IndexBox said the market outlook is being reinforced by automaker supply chain mandates, which are adding another layer of pressure on suppliers. As carmakers seek to de-risk their battery ecosystems, chemical vendors are being pushed to meet tighter standards on safety, documentation and consistency. In practice, that can favour larger suppliers with better process control, audit readiness and the ability to serve multiple geographies from a single compliance framework.Gigafactory expansion is widening the addressable marketAt the same time, the build-out of gigafactories is expanding the volume of chemicals needed for battery production. Every new cell plant adds demand not only for core active materials but also for a range of supporting chemicals used in manufacturing, treatment and quality assurance. As capacity rises, so does the need for suppliers that can deliver at industrial scale without compromising on regulatory standards.This creates a dual effect. On one hand, scale-up increases volumes and opens the door to larger contracts. On the other, it raises the bar for operational discipline, because any compliance lapse can ripple quickly through high-volume battery supply chains. That dynamic is likely to reward producers that can combine capacity, consistency and documentation in a sector where procurement decisions increasingly carry reputational as well as technical risk.What the forecast means for chemical makersFor chemical companies serving the battery industry, the opportunity is not simply about selling more product. The market is moving toward a model in which compliance credentials, product stewardship and supply chain transparency are part of the offer itself. Suppliers that can demonstrate life cycle safety may find themselves better positioned as preferred vendors to battery makers and automakers alike.The wider implication is that battery chemicals are becoming a strategic layer in the energy transition, not just a supporting input. As governments tighten standards and manufacturers expand capacity, the market is likely to favour players that can adapt quickly to documentation-heavy procurement and cross-border regulatory demands.IndexBox's outlook suggests that this is still an early stage of a longer cycle. Through 2035, the combination of battery regulation, automotive sourcing rules and gigafactory investment is expected to keep the market on an upward path, with compliance increasingly tied to commercial competitiveness. For suppliers, the message is clear: growth will depend not only on chemistry, but also on the ability to prove that every step of production is safe, traceable and fit for the next generation of battery manufacturing. - Policy & Regulation - 3 min Read Battery chemical suppliers eye compliance-led growth through 2035 IndexBox expects the market for life cycle safe battery production chemicals to grow through 2035 as EU battery rules and automaker sourcing mandates reshape procurement. Gigafactory expansion is adding demand, but suppliers will need stronger compliance, traceability and documentation to win contracts. - Published On Oct 19, 2026 at 12:46 PM IST

artigo.texto: Pitt County planning staff is scheduled to present an assessment of the county’s existing data center ordinance as the commissioners weigh implementing a moratorium on the facilities. The presentation will take place during the Pitt County Board of Commissioners’ 6 p.m. meeting today at the county office building, 1717 W. Fifth St. Residents have lobbied the commissioners to establish a moratorium in an effort to prevent data centers from locating facilities in the unincorporated areas of the county. In order to adopt a moratorium, the board needs to identify a deficiency in its current regulations that it wants to fix, officials have said during previous discussions. Along with the presentation, planning staff wants input from the commissioners on their concerns, potential impacts or regulatory issues that weren’t addressed in the evaluation. If the board proceeds with the moratorium, it will have to hold a public hearing. Staff is proposing the hearing be held at the board’s Nov. 16 meeting. Zoning amendment The board also is set to hold a public hearing on a request to amend the county’s zoning ordinance so the use “Outdoor Farm and Construction Equipment Auction” can be added as a permitted use. The county planning board in September said it was consistent with the county’s Comprehensive Land Use Plan but recommended it only be allowed as a conditional use in the rural agricultural zoning district. This would require the planning board and board of commissioners to hold public hearings on the request before making a decision. Planning staff recommends it be a permit by right in the rural agricultural zoning district, which only requires staff approval. Other actions State Reps. Gloristine Brown and Tim Reeder will present the commissioners with a $250,000 grant. The commissioners’ agenda did not indicate what grant program made the award or how the money will be used. The board is scheduled to adopt a proclamation recognizing October as Domestic Violence Awareness Month. A representative of Inspire Placemaking Collective, a consultant working with the county to develop a unified development ordinance, is scheduled to provide an overview of the project, which is expected to take 14-18 months to complete.

artigo.texto: Those pushing for a statewide moratorium on data center development worked to amplify their case during a rally on the steps of the courthouse in Leesburg. Organized by the Piedmont Environmental Council, the hour-long event was attended by about 100 supporters who heard comments from residents whose lives have been impacted by data centers and power lines and from state legislators supporting plans to halt work on new projects until new regulations to limit those impacts can be established. The event was held a week after Sen. Russet Perry (D-31) submitted a bill for the upcoming General Assembly session that would impose a three-year state moratorium and just days before a Board of Supervisors vote on plans to slow review of projects in Loudoun County. Jared Mummert is leading the data center reform campaign for the PEC. “For more than 26 years, data centers have been a part of life here in Loudoun, and there is no community that understands and has seen the transition of this industry like us,” he said in kicking off the rally. “We have seen this industry turn from smaller centers closer to office parks … and they have transitioned into energy-guzzling, grid-destabilizing, water-consuming, ear-ringing, air-polluting, skyrocketing electric bill giants that they are today. And they're ugly, absolutely.” “Loudoun has 233 data centers, with 100 more on the way, and there are hundreds of others across the state. Today, from the data center capital of the world, we say enough is enough,” Mummert said. Speakers included Ashley Warmerling, a Lovettsville area resident leading the fight against the Valley North transmission line; Victor Block, the HOA president working to limit the impact of new transmission lines on his Loudoun Valley Estates neighborhood; Gregory Pirio, a Sterling resident who raised concerns about the health impacts of a natural gas power plant feeding a data center in his community; Sarina Virmani, a Riverside High School student working to help young people have a greater voice in community issues; and attorney Phillip Thompson, a member of the Loudoun NAACP who said a moratorium is needed to protect the public’s health and safety. Perry and Del. John McAuliff (D-30) said they will continue to make better regulations of data centers a top priority. “When I first ran for office last year, I channeled, or I tried to channel the best I could, that anger and that frustration into the first race ever fully focused on data centers, and we won—with your help, we won,” McAuliff said. “This year, you've shown up at public hearings, raised your concerns, and asked whether anybody is listening while project after project continues to move forward. No more. Because of your voice, our leaders in Richmond, governors, senators, congressmen from around the country are all racing to show how much they're going to do about data centers because of the work that you all have done.” McAuliff said history was made last year when the General Assembly imposed the first restrictions on dirty diesel generators and the first zoning rules on data centers. “No one had ever done that before until you spoke up,” he said. McAuliff laid out a five-point plan for additional work to better protect the region. That includes ending the use of dirty diesel generators for all existing data centers, banning data centers in low groundwater areas and on farmland, making existing data centers pay for “every dime” of their energy and infrastructure need, protecting homes and farms from transmission lines and fully compensate those impacted, and imposing a moratorium on new data center development across the commonwealth. “You have done your part by showing up today, making your voices heard time and time again. It is now our responsibility to take those concerns and turn them into actions,” McAuliff said. “Don't stop speaking up. Don't stop organizing. … We have already sent an unmistakable message, which is that we demand better and we will win.” Perry said that when she first went to Richmond three years ago, the state senators who were concerned about the impacts of data centers could fit inside a Honda Civic. But that has changed. “[There were] three of us, three of 40. It was worse than apathy,” she said. “Just last year, Governor Youngkin stood before the General Assembly and delivered his State of the Commonwealth address. And what he said was he wanted Virginia to be the data center capital of the world, and the room jumped to its feet, including people who represent Loudoun County. Rest assured, I was not clapping, and I certainly was not standing. But things have changed, and you all are all the reasons.” State leaders are increasingly raising concerns about higher electric bills, groundwater depletion, the loss of farmland and community impacts of data centers and transmission lines. “Legislators from across the commonwealth are slowly, too slowly, but starting to join and see what you all have been saying for so long,” Perry said. “Virginia does not exist to be a pass-through state for corporate greed. We do not exist to swallow massive high-voltage lines and bail out bad corporate math. And we will not be quieted. We will not sit down, and we will not let anyone sacrifice our quality of life for their bottom line.” Perry said her bill, SB 843, would create a three-year pause that would give state leaders time to develop better rules for the scale, design and location of data centers. “That's three years to stop and think, three years to build a real statewide plan for where these facilities go, how they're powered, and who pays for them. Three years to protect our water, our farmland, and our historic places, and three years to make sure our communities finally have a seat at the table,” Perry said. artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Google aposta em data center com energia limpa, mas especialistas questionam custos da expansão elétrica Publicado 19/10/2026 • 12:20 | Atualizado há 19 horas KEY POINTS Foto: AFP Google propõe data center de 780 MW em Minnesota para ampliar o uso de energia limpa, especialistas questionam os custos e a expansão. Se há algo com que a maioria dos americanos parece concordar é que não quer um data center no próprio quintal. Uma pesquisa da Gallup realizada em março constatou que 71% dos americanos se opõem à construção de um data center em sua região. Entre as principais preocupações está o consumo de energia. Metade dos americanos entrevistados pelo Pew Research Center em julho e agosto afirmou que os data centers seriam predominantemente prejudiciais ao meio ambiente e aos custos de energia das famílias. Agora, o Google aposta que um enorme data center voltado à inteligência artificial pode ajudar a financiar uma rede elétrica mais limpa e confiável. O acordo proposto com a Xcel Energy acrescentaria uma capacidade de geração de energia e armazenamento em baterias superior à que o data center deverá consumir. Pelo acordo, o Google ajudaria a pagar pela capacidade adicional e continuaria arcando com os custos mesmo que não utilizasse toda a energia disponível. Leia também: Google terá uma nova fonte de energia; conheça o projeto de US$ 4 bilhões Pine Island, em Minnesota, é uma pequena cidade com cerca de 4 mil habitantes, localizada a uma hora a sudeste de Minneapolis. O Google espera que seu projeto de data center de 780 megawatts fortaleça o relacionamento com a comunidade local e ajude a empresa a cumprir a meta de operar com energia livre de carbono 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana, até 2030. O Google, cuja divisão de computação em nuvem sustenta sua própria inteligência artificial Gemini e gerou quase US$ 25 bilhões em receita no segundo trimestre, alta de 82% em relação ao mesmo período do ano anterior, afirma ter encontrado um modelo para desenvolver esse tipo de projeto de maneira adequada. A empresa planeja financiar a adição de 1.400 megawatts de energia eólica, 200 megawatts de energia solar e 300 megawatts de armazenamento em baterias à rede da Xcel. Essa capacidade adicional supera a potência do próprio data center. Segundo o Google, isso ocorre porque as fontes eólica e solar não geram energia continuamente. A Xcel Energy afirmou que a nova eletricidade atenderá a todos os consumidores da região, e não apenas ao Google. A concessionária também disse que as melhorias contribuirão para ampliar o fornecimento de energia livre de carbono na rede local. O acordo proposto entre Google e Xcel inclui cobranças mínimas por demanda e taxas de saída. Segundo o Google, essas cláusulas manterão a empresa responsável pelos custos da infraestrutura construída para atendê-la, mesmo que o crescimento da inteligência artificial perca força. O Google pagará por pelo menos 75% da capacidade contratada, mesmo que utilize menos energia. Caso encerre o contrato antecipadamente, poderá ter de pagar o equivalente a até oito anos dessas cobranças mínimas por demanda. “Ninguém quer realizar uma grande expansão e depois não ter para onde direcionar essa energia nem quem pague por ela”, afirmou Amanda Rome, vice-presidente executiva e diretora de relacionamento com clientes da Xcel Energy. “É para isso que servem essas proteções.” O acordo entre Google e Xcel Energy ainda depende da aprovação da Comissão de Serviços Públicos de Minnesota. Leia também: Chefe do Google DeepMind alerta para novos riscos de segurança envolvendo I.A. Novos data centers responderão pela maior parte do aumento projetado da demanda por eletricidade na próxima década, segundo a North American Electric Reliability Corporation, organização reguladora sem fins lucrativos. O Departamento de Energia dos Estados Unidos, durante o governo do presidente Joe Biden, informou que mais de 70% das linhas de transmissão e dos transformadores elétricos do país tinham pelo menos 25 anos. O órgão também concluiu que as alternativas mais baratas para atender à demanda futura exigiriam mais que dobrar a capacidade do sistema nacional de transmissão até 2050. Isso reduziria a necessidade de construir – e financiar – novos equipamentos de geração e transmissão. “Se o crescimento da carga elétrica desejado pelos data centers fosse acomodado na rede existente, as tarifas de todos cairiam bastante”, disse Shah. Isso ocorre porque a rede elétrica existente tem custos fixos elevados, relacionados à infraestrutura já instalada, como usinas, linhas de transmissão e subestações. Quando um novo consumidor entra na rede e assume uma parcela significativa desses custos, as contas dos demais usuários podem diminuir. “Então, a verdadeira questão é: por que as empresas não estão construindo data centers de 25 megawatts? artigo.texto: Swiss company FlexBase has begun construction on the world's largest underground energy storage facility based on a redox flow battery. The facility is being built in Laufenburg, canton of Aargau, on a site known as the "Star of Laufenburg"—a historic hub of the European energy grid, reports swissinfo. Construction of the Laufenburg Technology Center began in the spring of 2025. In addition to battery storage, it will include a water-cooled data center powered by artificial intelligence, office space, and laboratories. To accommodate the battery's key components, a pit approximately 27 meters deep and longer than two football fields is being excavated. Once operational, the storage capacity will exceed 2,1 GWh and its output will exceed 1,2 GW—comparable to the Leibstadt nuclear power plant, located in the same canton. The project is based on vanadium flow battery technology developed by Invinity Energy Systems. Unlike lithium-ion batteries, redox batteries store energy in large reservoirs of liquid electrolytes and are fire-resistant and do not degrade over many years of use. According to calculations, the accumulated energy will be sufficient to supply 210 000 households with uninterrupted power for 24 hours. The facility's capacity will significantly exceed that of the current largest operating redox storage facility—China's Xinhua Ushi project, with a capacity of 700 MWh. The facility is scheduled to be commissioned in 2029. The project is being implemented with private funding, without government participation, and is estimated to cost between 1 and 5 billion Swiss francs (1,2 USD and 6,2 billion USD). The project is expected to create approximately 300 jobs in the region.

artigo.texto: MELBOURNE, Australia, Oct. 20, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Fox ESS, a global leader in renewable energy solutions, has introduced Power Cube, an all-in-one residential energy storage system combining the inverter and batteries in a sleek, stackable design. Engineered for simpler, faster installation, it helps Australian households manage their energy needs today while allowing flexibility for the future. The launch follows SunWiz's announcement that Fox ESS ranked No. 1 in Australia for installed energy storage capacity in H1 2026, reinforcing the company's strong position in the market. By integrating essential components into one compact system, Power Cube streamlines installation and can help reduce installation time and costs. Its modular EQ5500 batteries offer storage capacities from 10.92 kWh to 49.14 kWh across two to nine modules, allowing homeowners to choose a system that suits their household energy needs. "Power Cube has been designed with the Australian market in mind," said Brooks Richard, Managing Director of APAC & Middle East at Fox ESS. "It delivers superior round-trip efficiency and a flexible range of capacities that align well with Australian household energy needs and available battery rebate tiers. Just as importantly, its integrated design simplifies installation, helping installers deliver a complete energy storage solution with greater ease." artigo.texto: POWERGRID Invites Bids for 187.5 MW/750 MWh Battery Storage Project 19 Oct 2026 2 Min Read CW Team Share Power Grid Corporation of India (POWERGRID) has invited online bids for developing a 187.5 MW/750 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) in Telangana. The project is intended to strengthen grid stability and support the integration of renewable energy into the electricity network. Designated as Package TS-BESS-01, the project carries Tender Reference Number CC/T/W-BESS/DOM/A02/26/14098. The proposed BESS will provide 187.5 MW of power capacity and 750 MWh of energy storage, equivalent to 4 hours of storage at full output. The tender is being conducted through the Tariff Based Competitive Bidding (TBCB) route and is classified as a power and energy project works contract. Eligible companies can access the tender documents through POWERGRID’s PRANIT Portal using RFX Number 5002005732, subject to the stated technical, financial and pre-qualification requirements. The participation fee has been fixed at Rs. 25,000, while the tender value and earnest money deposit (EMD) are listed as zero on the portal. Bidders are required to review the official documents for eligibility conditions, technical specifications, commercial requirements and other instructions before submitting their offers. The tender schedule set October 12, 2026, at 7:50 PM as the start of document sales and soft copy bid submissions. Document sales will close on October 17 at 11:55 PM, while bids must be submitted by October 19 at 11:00 AM and are scheduled to be opened at 11:30 AM the same day. The tender is being managed by Satyam Gupta, Engineer (CS), from POWERGRID’s corporate office in Gurugram, Haryana. The project will add flexible storage capacity that can absorb electricity when supply is available and discharge it during periods of higher demand or lower renewable generation, supporting grid balancing and the wider integration of solar and wind power. artigo.texto: Powering the AI Boom: What Electrical Engineers and Contractors Need to Know About Microgrids, BESS, and BYOP Already registered? Click here to log in. A certificate of attendance will be offered. Data center construction is colliding with a power bottleneck. Interconnection queues now stretch past five years in major markets, and developers are responding with microgrids, battery energy storage systems, and bring-your-own-power strategies that push more electrical infrastructure inside the fence line. For engineers and contractors working on these projects, that shift changes what conduit specification looks like, and raises new questions around grounding, fire code compliance, and installation at scale. Join Matt Fredericks, VP of Sales and Marketing at Champion Fiberglass®, for a practical look at how these power strategies are reshaping underground electrical infrastructure. Drawing on real project data and current code requirements, Matt will walk through what's driving these builds, where conduit decisions carry the most risk, and what tools are available to help your team plan with confidence. What you'll learn: - How microgrids, BESS, and BYOP strategies are changing data center power delivery, and what's driving developers toward each approach - The specific conduit challenges each strategy introduces, from fault resistance to fire resistance requirements - How grounding and bonding work with nonmetallic conduit systems - Specification guidance for medium-voltage duct banks and multi-circuit runs - Lessons from real data center installations, including common field pitfalls to avoid - How tools like BIM modeling and the Champ Pull® calculator can streamline design and installation Speaker Sponsored by:

artigo.texto: [SMM PV Flash] Times Digital Wins Commissioning and O&M Contract for 1.2 GW Solar Project in Saudi Arabia Times Digital Holdings’ subsidiary, through Concord New Energy’s O&M technology arm, has won the commissioning and operations and maintenance technical services contract for Saudi Arabia’s 1.2 GW Al Masa’a (MAS) solar PV project, per SMM understanding and public information. The project is Times Digital’s first market-oriented overseas benchmark project, marking the formal export of its new-energy technical service capabilities. MAS is located in Ha’il province, about 590 km north of Riyadh, and is a key independent power producer project under Round 5 of Saudi Arabia’s National Renewable Energy Program, developed by a consortium of EDF, SPIC Yellow River Hydropower and Saudi SAPCO. The project is scheduled to begin pre-energization commissioning on November 15 and achieve partial grid connection by the end of November; once fully operational, it is expected to generate 4.4 billion kWh annually. Times Digital’s domestic new-energy O&M service portfolio has exceeded 34 GW.

artigo.texto: BYD Pairs European Luxury Push With 3,000 Chargers as Shares Languish Near Yearly Low Published on 10/20/2026 at 03:31 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD is betting that premium badges and its own charging infrastructure can lift its fortunes in Europe, even as its share price continues to sag. At the Paris Motor Show, the Chinese group rolled out its Denza marque with a technology-led pitch for what it calls intelligent luxury — a direct challenge to Europe's established premium names. The display came alongside the seven-seat ATTO 8 flagship SUV and the second generation of its Blade battery. Charging is central to the pitch. BYD plans to build 3,000 fast-charging stations across Europe by the end of 2027, a move aimed at winning drivers over to its rapid-charging technology. The company is also scaling up its local footprint: deputy chairwoman Stella Li told Bloomberg that European headcount will soon pass 10,000, with roughly 40,000 employees targeted in the region by 2030. A Two-Pronged Expansion The European push runs in parallel with a broader build-out beyond vehicle sales. BYD Energy Storage announced a global after-sales service network for battery storage systems, built around nine operations and maintenance centres and more than 200 field engineers. Additional sites in South Africa and Bulgaria are slated for 2027, and over 100 R&D specialists are tied into the network — a signal that BYD intends to stay close to commercial customers long after installation. At home, the group keeps widening its lineup. The Da Han EV, a new flagship sedan for the Dynasty range, launched on 13 October with a 1,000-volt architecture and a CLTC range of up to 1,008 kilometres; the entry version is priced at 235,900 yuan. BYD also introduced the second generation of its Seagull compact EV in China, according to media reports, shoring up its volume base. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? September Sales and a Hybrid Trade Deal Those model launches land in a testing market. BYD's September 2026 production and sales report showed 463,561 vehicles sold and 463,864 built during the month. Sales through September reached 3,131,576 units, down 3.9% on the same period a year earlier. Trade policy adds another variable. BYD has reportedly backed an agreement between China and the European Union on hybrid vehicle trade, though Reuters noted that such a deal — by capping exports of Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid models — could create headwinds for manufacturers. Details on how the arrangement would work in practice have not been disclosed. Investors Stay on the Sidelines The market has yet to be moved by the operational announcements. The stock closed Monday at EUR 8.30, down 0.5%, and slipped a further 0.1% to EUR 8.33 in today's session. That leaves the shares down 22% since the start of the year and well below the 52-week high of EUR 12.30 touched in mid-April. A nearer-term catalyst is on the calendar: the supervisory board meets on 29 October 2026 to review third-quarter results. For now, BYD is sticking to its strategy of putting technological innovation and higher-margin segments such as Denza at the forefront of its international drive. artigo.texto: Texas residents promised a state-ordered freeze on data center permits are instead watching approvals advance and public comment deadlines tick down. Nearly a month after Gov. Greg Abbott directed the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to pause issuing permits for data center projects on Sept. 12, the advocacy group said the agency had issued several water-related authorizations and continued reviewing air permit applications. Residents trying to understand what the pause actually stopped were advised by agency’s own staff to treat public comment as active, the group said. Communities struggling to link corporate names to construction sites face mounting confusion as state agencies continue issuing permits despite a promised freeze. That confusion plagues residents near Lufkin, where investigative reporting previously uncovered a web of separate corporate entities handling the proposed Amp Z development's air permits, land deals and political backing. The newspaper later found that a TCEQ reviewer asked whether the proposed power plant’s emissions could be lowered enough to avoid a more extensive federal pollution review, further minimizing’s the areas where residents can voice concerns. “The TCEQ’s own data indicates that it’s business as usual for data centers,” said Kathryn Guerra, director of Public Citizen’s TCEQ Watchdog Campaign. “Affected communities were promised a freeze. Instead, they’re getting another reason to distrust the TCEQ and ineffective attempts to govern by press release.” Public Citizen released its findings the same day the TCEQ was due to update Abbott’s office on its compliance with his directive. When the governor announced the pause through a late September directive, he formally called for state reviews of data centers before making permitting decisions. “Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects,” Abbott said in the announcement. Public Citizen identified 16 permit actions that came after Abbott’s directive, including seven new construction stormwater authorizations, one amended stormwater authorization and an industrial wastewater permit renewal. Stormwater authorizations were cited as examples of approvals that were issued after Abbott’s announcements by Guerra. Those authorizations allow stormwater discharges from construction sites. Public Citizen identified seven counties, with approvals dated from Sept. 22 through Oct. 13. Following the nonprofit’s investigation, Guerra said Public Citizen has not yet approached the governor’s office about its findings, which it began compiling late last week. Abbott’s directive followed months of pressure over the industry’s demands on electricity, water and rural communities. Some Republican leaders even crossed party lines, such as Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller, who called for a temporary moratorium on new hyperscale data center developments, arguing that Texas needed to assess the effects on infrastructure and agriculture before the state could allow the rapid expansion to continue. Notably, Abbott’s September audit of data centers seeking to connect to the electric grid and subsequent pause on environmental permits has not accounted for facilities that plan to generate their own electricity, allowing them to proceed without relying on the grid-connection, The Texas Tribune reported. A separate Tribune analysis published Monday found Abbott had received about $9 million since July 2025 from donors with direct or indirect ties to data centers, representing about 13% of his fundraising during that period. Abbott’s campaign spokesman Eduardo Leal defended the governor’s position to the Tribune, saying his priorities remained on protecting the grid, requiring data centers to cover their costs and preventing disruption to communities. But for people living near the proposed facilities, the immediate concern is whether the promise of a pause could cause them to miss their opportunity to respond and voice their opinion. Public Citizen said the TCEQ mailed notices Sept. 22 for three major source air permit applications involving power facilities near Abilene and in Hill County. The notice for the Nexus project in Hubbard has a public comment deadline of Friday, Oct. 23, according to the group’s review. Guerra said a senior agency staff member told Public Citizen that residents should treat the deadline as active. Public Citizen asked commissioners Oct. 7 to clarify the situation or withdraw the notices, she said. Without state clarification on whether public comment periods remain active, residents are left scrambling to meet deadlines while navigating contradictory signals from Austin. The group also argued that people are being asked to comment on permit applications without truly knowing or being able to access the findings of the state’s review. When asked whether the Sept. 22 mailing dates could have simply been a reflection of notices that may have been prepared before the directive, Guerra acknowledged that possibility. But she said subsequent steps in the public participation portion have only continued. For Linda Polley of Save Hill County, residents also are still seeing work continue on the ground. Trucks traveling the roads with loads, cranes working, large piles of dirt and walls going up are what can be found at the Nexus construction site. Polley said nighttime lighting is visible even from her home 15 miles away. “What exactly did you pause?” Polley asked about Abbott, urging the governor to explain what communities should expect as the state’s review proceeds. In Caldwell County, resident Claudia Hollern said neighbors began examining and monitoring permits as they learned that proposed data centers would rely on large power-generating facilities to be built nearby. She described residents trying to follow applications filed under company names they did not initially recognize which had residents following one piece of infrastructure which led to another. artigo.texto: In 2027, Chinese manufacturers only won half of the Dutch residential energy storage market. On September 23, Sungrow announced that its latest all-in-one residential energy storage system, PowerHarbor, has been officially launched for sale in Europe, with the Netherlands selected as its first stop. Product image of PowerHarbor. Image source: Sungrow Why the Netherlands, instead of familiar major residential storage markets like Germany? Because in just over two months, Dutch households will "have no choice but to buy home batteries". Around 3 million households in the Netherlands have installed solar panels on their rooftops. For more than two decades, they have been enjoying a favorable policy: Excess electricity generated during the day is fed into the grid; when there is a shortage of power at night, they draw electricity back from the grid. They can store as much as they take out, with almost no handling fees charged. The grid acts like a free power bank. On January 1, 2027, this free power bank will be taken away. Going forward, for each kilowatt-hour of electricity fed into the grid during the day, the law only guarantees a return of just over 40 euro cents; but buying one kilowatt-hour of electricity at night costs around 1.9 euros. After deducting various fees charged by power companies, the electricity fed to the grid by many households is almost given away for free. The most cost-effective solution is to install a residential storage battery at home: store the excess electricity during the day for self-use at night. Therefore, Dutch research institute Dutch New Energy Research forecasts that the new installed capacity of residential energy storage in the country will skyrocket from 0.86 GWh in 2025 to 4.5 GWh in 2027. A 5.2-fold increase in just two years. By that time, based on the average price of around 470 euros/kWh for residential batteries in the Netherlands in 2025, the 4.5 GWh of new capacity in 2027 corresponds to a hardware market of approximately 2.1 billion euros, or 160 billion RMB. This scale ranks third in Europe, only smaller than that of Germany and Italy. Chinese manufacturers have already taken the lead in this business. According to information from New Energy Industrialist, the two best-selling residential storage brands in the Netherlands at present, Votai and Sungrow Power Supply's residential storage brand Sinexcel, are both from China. Now, Sungrow is also entering the market. But when these Chinese-made batteries are actually installed in the basements of Dutch households, a deeper business reality emerges: the delivery of hardware is only the beginning. When to charge the battery, when to discharge it, and who to sell the excess electricity to at a high price — these issues that determine profit margins are not decided by Chinese manufacturers. The right to set these rules is held by local Dutch power companies. For example, an enterprise called Frank Energie does not manufacture a single battery itself, but it remotely manages more than 14,000 household batteries made by other manufacturers on the cloud every day. This is a bit like Didi: it does not manufacture a single car, but decides where the car goes and how much to charge for each order. Selling batteries is certainly profitable, but it is a highly competitive one-off transaction; those who hold the scheduling rights earn a steady stream of "toll fees" over time. In the feast of European energy transition, Chinese manufacturers, with their exceptional manufacturing capabilities, have won the first half of the "hardware selling" game. But the truly lucrative, compound-return second half of the energy storage business, as well as the other half of the large profits, are still firmly in the hands of those who send electricity bills to Dutch households every month. 01 In 2027, why do people have to buy batteries By the end of 2024, around 3 million households in the Netherlands had installed photovoltaic systems. For more than two decades, almost none of these households needed batteries. The reason is a policy implemented in 2004 called net metering. Excess electricity generated during the day is fed into the grid, which can be offset 1:1 when the household uses electricity. The grid is equivalent to a free power bank, where users can store as much as they take out without paying any handling fees. This "power bank" can no longer sustain the operation. There are too many photovoltaic systems installed, and at noon in summer, there is so much excess electricity that there is nowhere to send it. In June 2025, the Dutch wholesale electricity price dropped below zero for 127 hours, which means that power generators had to pay others to take their electricity, and still could not sell it. But power companies still have to record accounts for photovoltaic users at a retail price of more than 1 euro per kWh. Part of this loss-making business is ultimately passed on to neighbors who have not installed photovoltaic systems. Before the legislation was finalized, power companies took action first. Since the end of 2023, they have successively charged a "feed-in feedback fee" to photovoltaic users: the more electricity users send to the grid, the more fees they have to pay. According to a three-year fixed contract from a large power company in December 2025, if a household sends 2400 kWh of electricity to the grid every year, it has to pay more than 400 euros in feedback fees alone, equivalent to more than 3000 RMB. Users even have to pay extra to send electricity to the grid, and Dutch photovoltaic users have experienced the cost of doing good deeds in advance. The government also wants to reform the policy, but the process has been full of twists and turns. The gradual phase-out plan was rejected by the upper house of parliament in February 2024. artigo.texto: Pilot production system underway Commercialization targeted for late next year SK Nexilis, the copper foil unit backed by SKC's secondary battery investment arm, announced Tuesday it has successfully developed "high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil" technology, a key material for next-generation batteries. The technology applies a specialized carbon coating to the surface of copper foil to suppress the volumetric expansion of silicon anode materials, improving electrode stability. It addresses a growing industry trend of increasing silicon content in anodes to boost energy density — a shift that makes maintaining strong adhesion between the anode material and the copper foil increasingly critical. The newly developed copper foil is also compatible with dry electrode processing, a next-generation battery manufacturing method drawing growing attention in the industry. SKC expects strong demand from that segment as well, given that adhesion between electrode materials and copper foil is equally critical in dry-process applications. To prepare for full-scale mass production, SK Nexilis is building a pilot production system for the high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil. The company is currently verifying process stability and plans to secure the technology needed for mass production, targeting commercialization in the second half of 2027. "The development of this high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil is a result of our efforts to respond to technological shifts in the next-generation battery market — including the expansion of high-silicon-content anode materials and the introduction of dry electrode processing," a company official said. "We will proceed with commercialization optimization without delay, while continuing to develop new technologies to strengthen our competitiveness in the next-generation battery materials market." klee@heraldcorp.com

It plans to build a charging network using its self-developed flash-charging technology and also launched premium electric vehicles equipped with its second-generation BYD Blade Battery. The strategy is to expand its business model overseas, combining electric vehicle sales with batteries and charging infrastructure. BYD said on the 19th that it announced plans to build a flash-charging network in Indonesia on the 14th and launched the new D9 and Z9GT from its premium brand Denza. This is the first time BYD’s flash-charging technology has entered an overseas market. BYD plans to first install flash chargers at 10 Denza showrooms in Indonesia so customers can try them out, and to gradually expand the public charging network starting at year-end. The flash charger is distinguished by its integration with an energy storage system (ESS). BYD was the first in the world to apply a T-shaped suspended design. It also improved convenience by introducing a “Zero Gravity” charger that reduces the burden of the charging cable’s weight, and a Plug and Charge function that enables charging authentication and payment simply by connecting the vehicle. Alongside expanding its charging infrastructure, BYD also strengthened its new-car lineup. The new Denza D9, a luxury multipurpose vehicle (MPV), is the first model to feature the second-generation BYD Blade Battery and flash-charging technology. It targets families and business customers with improved driving range, powertrain performance and ride comfort. The Denza Z9GT, launched alongside it, is a luxury electric vehicle combining high-performance driving with intelligent control technology, built on a dedicated e3 platform. BYD aims to expand its foothold in Indonesia’s premium eco-friendly vehicle market with the two models. Liu Xueliang, vice president of BYD Group and general manager of its Asia-Pacific Automotive Business Unit, said, “BYD’s technological innovation has gone beyond simply making and selling cars.” He added, “I believe technological innovation can create greater value for society and bring the benefits of advanced technology to more people.” [email protected] Kim Dong-ho Reporter

artigo.texto: Region forging master key for next industrial revolution, proving that whoever can best store electricity holds future of power For a long time, electricity has been a unique energy commodity, with production and consumption happening almost simultaneously. You use it the moment it is generated. But today, as solar and wind power have become China's largest sources of installed capacity, energy storage is quietly building "warehouses" for the power grid. These massive facilities store surplus green electricity during the day and deliver it to factories, shopping malls and millions of households at night. This time-shifting magic has found its grandest stage in North China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region. Driven by the massive deployment of new-type battery facilities designed to support its vast wind and solar power bases, Inner Mongolia has overtaken California to become the world's largest energy storage region. READ MORE: China takes lead in global power storage As of the end of 2025, the region's cumulative installed capacity of new-type energy storage exceeded 25 million kilowatts, ranking first in the nation. Under the blueprint of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30), this figure is projected to break the 50 million kW mark, cementing the region's role as the most critical power "reservoir" for the country's renewable mega-bases in the Gobi Desert and other arid areas. The sheer scale of this deployment has triggered a profound industrial metamorphosis. In the past, Inner Mongolia's vast Gobi Desert served merely as an application ground for energy storage, with complete sets of equipment largely purchased from manufacturing clusters in China's eastern provinces. Today, the narrative has shifted from isolated breakthroughs to a multi-city synergy. Hohhot, Baotou and Ordos are firing on all cylinders, forming a differentiated energy storage equipment manufacturing cluster. This has created a new paradigm of "desert application plus multicity collaborative smart manufacturing" — a concentrated reflection of the region's upgrading new energy industry chain. Each city brings a unique strength to the table, but the regional capital, Hohhot, stands out for its specialized focus on system integration and custom solutions engineered for extreme environments. Operating at the forefront of grid resilience, Hohhot's manufacturing sector produces energy storage equipment uniquely designed to withstand the severe cold and punishing sandstorms characteristic of the northern frontiers. While Baotou boasts the most comprehensive industrial chain and Ordos combines equipment manufacturing with ultra-large application scenarios at sites like Envision's zero-carbon industrial park, Hohhot's tailored approach to hostile climate operations ensures these massive systems remain reliable year-round. "Deploying gigawatt-scale battery facilities in the Gobi Desert is fundamentally different from installing systems in temperate coastal plains," said Lin Boqiang, head of the China Institute for Studies in Energy Policy at Xiamen University. "Extreme sub-zero winters can degrade battery performance and discharge efficiency by double digits, while seasonal sandstorms pose severe risks to thermal management and air filtration systems." Hohhot's focus on hostile-climate customization addresses the industry's biggest operational bottleneck — ensuring that massive desert storage parks don't just get built, but actually run safely and reliably 365 days a year, he said. Inner Mongolia's regional triumph mirrors a broader national strategy. Entering 2026, the strategic importance of new-type energy storage has reached unprecedented heights. For the first time, it has been listed among the nation's six emerging pillar industries for the 15th Five-Year Plan. The China New Energy Storage Development Report 2026, released recently by the National Energy Administration, said China's cumulative installed capacity of new-type storage had reached 136 million kW/351 million kilowatt-hours by the end of 2025, representing a year-on-year surge of 84.3 percent. Accounting for roughly 50 percent of the global total, new-type energy storage has surpassed pumped-hydro storage to become China's largest regulating resource, it said. Yet, after years of rapid expansion, the fundamental logic of the industry is evolving. Experts agree that the sector has bid farewell to the era of simple policy-driven scale expansion. "The industry has formally entered a new phase characterized by market-oriented selection, value priority and a focus on quality," said Dai Hongcai, director of the new energy institute at the State Grid Energy Research Institute. While the "forced pairing" of storage with renewable projects drove early growth, future expansion will rely on sustainable business models. The market is also demanding longer duration capabilities. While the average storage duration was around 2.5 hours at the end of 2025, four-hour storage has now become the mainstream, and eight-hour long-duration storage is moving from demonstration to commercial application. This shift ensures that "giant power banks" don't just respond quickly, but can actually sustain the grid through the entire evening peak. As the technology matures, the application boundaries of energy storage are expanding far beyond the traditional power grid. A new and highly lucrative frontier has emerged: the intersection of energy storage and artificial intelligence computing power. In the era of AI large models, a massive global "compute-power race" has sparked acute anxiety over electricity consumption. A single 10,000-GPU computing cluster can consume roughly 100 million kWh of electricity annually. While tech giants in the West are resorting to isolated gas turbines or small nuclear plants to power their AI ambitions, China is leveraging its robust wind, solar and storage ecosystems to pioneer a "compute-power and electricity synergy" model. Full disclosures below. This is the latest investigation in Hunterbrook Media’s series on the poisoning of American communities. For decades, polluters have released toxins across the U.S. We've built a nationwide database to expose harm to communities and ecosystems, then hold accountable those responsible. After reporting from Illinois, Nebraska, California, Texas, Louisiana, New Mexico, Indiana, and Virginia, this investigation takes us to Hawaii. Hunterbrook Media has also investigated environmental damage spanning from Namibia to Argentina to Peru. Please email ideas@hntrbrk.com if you suspect pollution or poisoning in your community. In 2025, Digital Realty spent $120 million to purchase a 97-acre parcel of land that was once part of Fort Gillem, a former United States Army post in Forest Park, Georgia. The company, one of the world’s largest real estate investment trusts, is constructing a massive data center complex on the site, returning valuable land to a “productive, tax-generating use,” as its executives put it. But the land came with a historical burden. From 1941 until around 1980 the Army dumped everything from gas masks and medical waste to solvents and sewage sludge on this parcel in the northwest corner of the former army base that now houses a maze of warehouses, including a Kroger distribution center and an Amazon delivery station. There’s quite a bit of environmental issues with the site,” a Digital Realty asset manager said at a meeting with county officials in 2025. “Tons and tons and tons of — physical tons — of trash and environmental hazards.” An investigation by Hunterbrook found that the hazards unearthed included military waste that was still combustible. Meanwhile, residents in neighboring communities are reporting cracks on their walls from explosive blasting on the site and say their questions about environmental and health threats stemming from Digital Realty’s Fort Gillem project are being ignored. The company plans to spend $3 billion on this project, and the first phase is expected to open in early 2028. But a document filed with the Georgia Environmental Protection Division suggests construction may surface some surprises. In December 2025, the company encountered white phosphorus on the property, which “reacted when exposed to air and exhibited a dense white smoke,” according to a letter an environmental consultant sent on behalf of Digital Realty to Georgia EPD. The company asked the Army for guidance and contacted the local police department, which sent a bomb squad to inspect and sample the material. The letter states that the white phosphorus was found in an area on the western side of the property that’s going to be under the planned data center. “Upon completion of the Property’s redevelopment, the area of concern will be encapsulated with a concrete building foundation,” the letter states. “At this time, the size of the area of concern is not known but is not anticipated to be larger than 100-feet by 100-feet by 8-feet deep based on grading already completed at the Property.” The material has since been removed, a Digital Realty spokesperson told Hunterbrook in an email. “Trained professionals carefully excavated the 100-foot by 100-foot by 8-foot area in accordance with an approved work plan, using appropriate equipment and personal protective equipment to identify any additional material containing white phosphorus,” the spokesperson wrote. “The excavation recovered five 30-gallon steel drums of material containing white phosphorus, far less than could have been encountered across the full area. The drums were then transported under a hazardous waste manifest to a permitted treatment, storage, and disposal facility.” The company also said that “work in the area where the material was initially discovered was stopped immediately upon the discovery of the material” and that “there were no reported injuries.” No other munitions and explosives of concern have been encountered since the white phosphorus discovery, according to Digital Realty. A Georgia EPD spokesperson confirmed the temporary work stoppage in the area where white phosphorus was found and that Digital Realty was in the process of removing the material in February, when EPD representatives visited the site. White phosphorus is used in artillery shells, rockets, and grenades to create dense smoke screens, provide battlefield illumination, mark targets, or act as an incendiary weapon. The use of white phosphorus weapons in civilian areas has been considered a war crime by human rights organizations like Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International. Its presence at the Digital Realty construction site “is assumed to be associated with historical Army disposal operations,” according to the letter to the Georgia EPD. “Measures are in place to protect construction workers, future occupants, and the public throughout remediation and development activities,” the Digital Realty spokesperson told Hunterbrook. Toxic Land Is Data Center Boom’s Next Frontier The frenzied AI build-out has turned Digital Realty into a digital infrastructure colossus. According to its website, Digital Realty operates more than 300 data centers worldwide. It counts Oracle, IBM, Meta, AT&T, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and Morgan Stanley among its customers. Amid the scramble to feed AI’s seemingly endless need for compute, other companies besides Digital Realty have resorted to building data centers on contaminated land. TeraWulf is developing the former Century Aluminum smelter site in Hawesville, Kentucky, into a more than $4 billion data center campus, with Anthropic as its tenant. artigo.texto: A $200 million loan, a carbon-credit market, and a Rayong industrial platform aim to cut energy costs, draw in private capital, and create jobs, officials say. Thailand’s Ministry of Finance and the World Bank Group have unveiled a suite of initiatives designed to finance clean energy, build a credible carbon market, and crowd in private investment, as the 2026 IMF-World Bank Annual Meetings drew to a close in Bangkok. Deputy Prime Minister and Finance Minister Ekniti Nitithanprapas and World Bank Group President Ajay Banga announced the measures on Saturday (October 17) under the theme "Low Carbon Cities and Energy Security: Building Systems at Scale, Mobilising Private Capital, Creating Jobs". At the heart of the plan is the Low Carbon Cities and Carbon Market Development Project (LCC). The initiative aims to facilitate transparent, verifiable carbon-credit transactions aligned with international standards, supporting Thailand's commitments under the Paris Agreement and its national net-zero targets. To kick-start the project, the World Bank is providing a $200 million loan to the Export-Import Bank of Thailand (EXIM Thailand), backed by a sovereign guarantee from the Ministry of Finance. The funds will enable energy service companies (ESCOs) to invest in clean energy and energy efficiency across public-sector assets, preparing both public and private sectors for evolving market standards. Ekniti also highlighted a $2.4 million World Bank grant under the Partnership for Market Implementation, alongside contributions from Krung Thai Bank (KTB), to establish the framework for a just transition. KTB will play a central role in aggregating, verifying, and monetising greenhouse gas emission reductions to connect credits with domestic and international buyers. The strategy spans three main pillars of cooperation: • Business Transition: KTB and the Department of Climate Change and Environment (DCCE) will develop financial tools to help small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) transition to low-carbon technologies while supporting affected workers. • Carbon-Credit Market: KTB will aggregate credits, while the Stock Exchange of Thailand (SET) establishes a transparent auction and price-discovery mechanism. Prospective buyers including Grab, ACEIS Electric and Power, DriverAI, and Thai Airways have expressed interest. All credits must complete formal validation and verification prior to sale. • Industrial Investment: PTT, KTB, and the DCCE will create blended-finance mechanisms for the I-SPARK low-carbon industrial platform in the Map Ta Phut–Rayong area, aiming to mobilise private capital for speciality, bio-based, and circular industries. Ekniti stressed that development finance must be measured by outcomes rather than capital raised. Over time, he noted, robust carbon markets and accessible green financing should reduce Thailand's reliance on government subsidies and tax incentives. He acknowledged that the government must deliver clear regulatory frameworks and bankable projects to accelerate scale. "Success should be measured by whether we can bring down energy costs, make industry more competitive, and create better jobs. That should be the legacy of the Annual Meetings 2026," Ekniti said, requesting further guarantee support from the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). Commending Thailand for its exceptional hospitality throughout the summit, Banga emphasised that the success of the carbon framework hinges entirely on credibility. "Without trust and credibility, nothing would happen," Banga noted, pointing to the partnership between the SET, the Securities and Exchange Commission, and KTB as the "secret sauce" that will attract private investors. Banga outlined three key advantages of the initiative: 1. Cost Savings: Energy efficiency reduces utility bills for businesses, cities, and households, freeing up public funds for schools, roads, and services while creating local maintenance jobs. 2. Private Capital Integration: Government budgets alone cannot fund modern infrastructure. "There is not enough public money to do these kinds of things," Banga said, stressing that private capital is essential to scale impact. 3. Market Continuity: A thriving commercial ecosystem ensures businesses continue investing in urban sustainability without permanent reliance on public funding. According to government officials, the initiatives align with a broader strategy to use finance as a tool for economic restructuring. By addressing market constraints and establishing reliable financial data, the public sector aims to de-risk green investments for institutional capital.

artigo.texto: US solid-state battery maker QuantumScape, backed by Volkswagen and Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, is working with a South Korean equipment supplier. The development could expand the role of Korean companies beyond conventional lithium-ion batteries into the next-generation battery market. According to industry sources on Oct. 20, Mplus has developed assembly equipment for QuantumScape’s solid-state batteries and is conducting validation for mass production. QuantumScape completed its Eagle Line pilot production facility at its headquarters in San Jose, California, in February. The company is currently increasing sample production of its first commercial product, the QSE-5, at the facility. The uptime of key production equipment has exceeded 90%. Uptime refers to the proportion of available operating time during which equipment functions normally. “Among US solid-state and lithium-metal battery startups, QuantumScape has one of the most developed production infrastructures, including dry rooms,” an industry official said. “Because next-generation battery manufacturing processes differ among companies and mass-production viability has yet to be fully demonstrated, commercialization will depend on how quickly manufacturers can achieve sufficient production speeds and yields.” QuantumScape is supplying samples to Volkswagen’s battery subsidiary PowerCo and other companies to evaluate battery performance and practical applications. It has jointly developed next-generation batteries with Volkswagen since 2012 and has received more than $300 million in cumulative investment from the automaker. Volkswagen invested in QuantumScape to secure next-generation battery technology that could improve electric vehicle driving range and safety. Solid-state batteries replace the liquid electrolyte used in conventional lithium-ion batteries with a solid material. By eliminating flammable organic solvent-based liquid electrolytes, they reduce fire risks. They can also accommodate more energy within the same volume by reducing the components and space required to ensure internal battery safety. The core of QuantumScape’s technology is its proprietary ceramic separator. Conventional lithium-ion batteries use a porous separator between the cathode and anode, along with a liquid electrolyte that allows lithium ions to move between them. QuantumScape’s ceramic separator prevents direct contact between the electrodes while allowing lithium ions to pass through. The company has partnered with Corning and Murata to mass-produce the ceramic separators. Another distinguishing feature is its anode-free architecture. Instead of mixing and coating anode active materials such as graphite, the design uses only an anode current collector, reducing associated material and production costs. In QuantumScape’s manufacturing process, ceramic separators are laminated onto copper foil used as the anode current collector after the cathode electrode process. Cathodes are then attached to both sides to form individual units called monocells. The monocells are subsequently immersed in and removed from a solution containing catholyte, a liquid electrolyte that facilitates lithium-ion movement between cathode active materials. Multiple monocells are stacked to complete a battery cell. After packaging, QuantumScape simplifies the formation process, which stabilizes battery performance through initial charging and discharging, to reduce production time and costs. Beyond expanding its own manufacturing facilities, QuantumScape is pursuing a licensing business that would allow other companies to use its battery manufacturing technology. It has signed a technology licensing agreement with PowerCo covering battery production capacity of up to 85 GWh. QuantumScape is also considering outsourcing production line operations to external companies. It is reportedly holding related discussions with South Korean battery manufacturers. If its manufacturing technology expands to external production facilities, Mplus could secure additional equipment orders, having developed machinery tailored to QuantumScape’s processes. Mplus has secured equipment technologies required for QuantumScape’s battery manufacturing process. As with conventional lithium-ion batteries, the process involves notching, which cuts electrodes to specified dimensions; stacking, which layers multiple electrodes; and packaging, which encloses the cells in external materials. Mplus can supply a complete range of assembly equipment for these processes, as well as specialized high-temperature and high-pressure equipment required for solid-state battery production. Mplus has also diversified its customer base. SK On accounted for more than 80% of its revenue in 2022, but that share fell to approximately 22% in 2025, while other customers’ combined contribution rose to nearly half of revenue. The company has expanded its order base among US and European battery manufacturers. It recently supplied equipment for producing prismatic batteries for defense applications to a European battery company, believed to be France’s Saft. Mplus is pursuing additional orders and is reportedly close to signing a new contract. “We cannot confirm specific details concerning our customers,” an Mplus official said. “We intend to drive earnings growth by securing overseas customers and expanding new orders.” Mplus had an order backlog of 63.1 billion won at the end of the second quarter of 2026.

artigo.texto: LS Electric has signed a contract worth approximately 170 billion won to supply switchgear for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers operated by a major US technology company. The company has secured supply volumes for 2027 and is negotiating additional orders for 2028, along with other power equipment. LS Electric announced on Oct. 19 that it had signed a long-term agreement (LTA) worth $125.23 million to supply power distribution solutions for North American data centers. The customer was not identified because of a confidentiality agreement. The contract covers a two-year period from 2027 to 2028. The announced contract value represents deliveries scheduled for 2027, while the volume for 2028 will be determined through further negotiations with the customer. The products covered by the agreement are 38-kilovolt (kV) high-voltage switchgear systems. Switchgear distributes incoming high-voltage electricity to equipment throughout a data center and protects facilities in the event of electrical faults. LS Electric is also discussing additional supplies of low-voltage switchgear, distribution transformers and high-voltage ring main units (RMUs). The company is expanding its US operations through LS Electric Utah in Cedar City, Utah, and its Bastrop Campus in Texas. It has established local capabilities covering sales, engineering, manufacturing and services to meet demand from North American data center customers. “We will expand supplies of high-value-added power equipment for data centers to secure a stable revenue base and improve profitability,” an LS Electric official said.

artigo.texto: 'SOL Solid State Battery&Silicon Anode Materials' Ranks No. 1 Among Equity ETFs in Three-Month Returns Three-month return of 22.76% Shinhan Asset Management said on Oct. 19 that its SOL Solid State Battery&Silicon Anode Materials ETF, which invests in key companies in next-generation batteries, including solid-state batteries, ranked first among Korea-listed equity ETFs in three-month returns. According to the Korea Exchange on Oct. 16, the ETF posted a return of 22.76% over the past three months, the highest among Korea-listed equity ETFs, excluding leveraged and inverse ETFs. As gains in the semiconductor sector have slowed, secondary battery ETFs have ranked among the top performers, highlighting a divergence between sectors. The SOL Solid State Battery&Silicon Anode Materials ETF, in particular, posted strong returns even among secondary battery ETFs, outperforming the KOSPI by more than 39 percentage points over the same period; the index recorded a return of -16.90%. The secondary battery sector has recently emerged from a prolonged correction triggered by slowing electric vehicle demand and is securing new growth drivers. Rising demand for energy storage systems (ESS) as AI data centers expand is improving battery companies' earnings, while expectations for the commercialization of next-generation technologies, including solid-state batteries and silicon anode materials, are also growing. ESS is emerging as a key growth driver reshaping the structure of the secondary battery industry. The importance of stable power supply and energy storage is increasing as AI data centers' power demand rises and renewable energy generation expands. Progress toward commercializing solid-state batteries is also encouraging. Samsung SDI is pursuing technology development and collaboration with customers with the goal of mass-producing solid-state batteries in 2027, while domestic materials companies are working to secure production capacity for key raw materials. The government also plans to provide about KRW 400 billion in research and development support for next-generation batteries over five years starting in 2027. The SOL Solid State Battery&Silicon Anode Materials ETF responds to these industry shifts by concentrating its investments in key companies involved in solid-state batteries and silicon anode materials. Its major holdings include Samsung SDI, which is working toward mass production of solid-state batteries; LG Energy Solution, a key ESS company; EcoPro BM, a solid-state battery cathode material company; Isu Specialty Chemical, a company involved in lithium sulfide; LOTTE Energy Materials, a battery materials company; and Daejoo Electronic Materials, a silicon anode material company. artigo.texto: SK On Holds Future Technology Institute Symposium to Share Next-Generation Battery Research Achievements Research Team Wins Grand Prize for Improving LFP Cathode Manufacturing Process More Than 300 Research Projects Submitted Across Six Battery Fields Sharing Research Achievements and Strengthening Technological Competitiveness SK On said on October 18 that it had held the 2nd Future Technology Institute Symposium to share research achievements in next-generation battery technologies. The event was held for two days starting October 14 at SK On's Future Technology Institute in Yuseong-gu, Daejeon. Attendees included SK On President Lee Yongwook and Future Technology Institute Director Park Gisu. Under the theme "The Future We Create," the symposium featured more than 300 research projects across six fields: battery processes, cells, systems, materials, next-generation technologies, and platforms, about 15% more than last year. This year's grand prize went to a research team that developed a process to replace expensive carbon nanotube (CNT) paste used in manufacturing lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cathodes with powder. CNTs are a material used as a conductive additive to facilitate the movement of electrons within battery electrodes. The team was recognized for uniformly dispersing CNT powder in cathode materials to achieve performance on par with existing processes while improving cost competitiveness. SK On plans to review the technology's application in actual production processes. Research on the design of electrodes for large-area pouch-type lithium-metal batteries received the top excellence award, while research on developing a model to predict capacity degradation and internal resistance based on battery charging, discharging, and storage conditions received an excellence award. The event also featured a technology exhibition showcasing key research projects. In his keynote address, Yonsei University Professor Lee Yongmin introduced the current state and outlook of digital twin technology, which recreates actual battery designs in a virtual space to analyze their performance and condition. SK On plans to make the symposium a regular event to promote knowledge exchange and research collaboration among its employees and strengthen its competitiveness in next-generation battery technologies. artigo.texto: SK Nexilis Develops Carbon-Coated Copper Foil for Next-Generation Batteries Improves Adhesion to Silicon Anode Materials to Prevent Electrode Delamination Also Suitable for Dry Electrode Processes Commercialization Targeted for the Second Half of 2027 SK Nexilis, the investment vehicle for SKC's copper foil business for secondary batteries, has developed copper foil for next-generation batteries that improves adhesion to silicon anode materials. The technology can extend battery life, improve safety, and be applied to dry electrode processes. Commercialization is targeted for the second half of 2027. SK Nexilis said on October 20 that it had successfully developed “high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil,” a technology that coats the surface of copper foil with a special carbon material. The technology increases adhesion between copper foil and anode materials, helping suppress electrode delamination caused by the expansion of silicon anode materials. This is expected to improve the structural stability of electrodes and enhance battery life and safety. Recently, the battery industry has been increasing the silicon content of anode materials to boost energy density. However, silicon expands in volume during charging and discharging, making it important to ensure strong adhesion between copper foil and anode materials. The newly developed copper foil can also be used in dry electrode processes, which can reduce battery manufacturing costs and energy consumption. SK Nexilis said the material has strong potential for use in dry processes, where adhesion between electrode materials and copper foil is also important. SK Nexilis is currently validating process stability and plans to secure mass-production technology after establishing a pilot production system.
