artigo.texto: Protests against widespread state corruption have flooded the Philippines in recent weeks, putting pressure on the leadership of a country that for years has been one of the United States’ closest military and commercial allies in Southeast Asia. The domestic turmoil threatens to shake up the U.S.-Philippines partnership, particularly given that American-funded data center projects under President Donald Trump’s Pax Silica initiative are among the targets of the protesters’ rage. On September 21, 2026, President Ferdinand Marcos — whose national trust rating sits at just 28% — put the presidential palace under lockdown in anticipation of mass protests, as more than 17,000 police officers were deployed and tens of thousands of protestors marched through Manila to demand change in the face of the country's largest corruption scandal in years. The scandal revolves around more than $9 billion worth of proposed flood-control infrastructure projects, intended for construction since Marcos took office in 2022. The projects were designed to improve infrastructure like drainage and flood control systems to mitigate the effects of typhoons common in the Philippines. These projects are under legal investigation for being of poor quality or having never been built at all. The investigation into the matter has led to the arrest of former Philippines House Speaker Martin Romualdez, a cousin and formerly close ally of Marcos, on a $118 million plunder charge. Romualdez is only one of a number of officials currently detained under suspicion of pocketing money from the project, with Interior Secretary Ombudsman Remulla alleging that co-conspirators attempted to hide the money through the purchase of houses or Romualdez’s $1 million donation to Harvard University. Another layer of controversy involves the impeachment trial of sitting Vice President Sara Duterte. A major point of contention occurred on day 34 of the trial, when it was revealed that over 30 undeclared accounts showed Duterte’s net worth to be over $3 million — almost 15 times more than her declared net worth of $209,000. The public backlash and corruption-induced chaos currently surrounding the Philippines could affect relations with the U.S. at a time when the United States is trying to counterbalance China’s expansive aims in the South China Sea. The military alliance between the United States and the Philippines dates back to the 1951 Mutual Defense Treaty, which ensures mutual protection in the event of a foreign armed attack. This pact was preceded by the 1947 Military Bases Agreement, an executive order granting the U.S. 20 years of renewable access to bases in the Philippines, and later reinforced by the 2014 Enhanced Defense Cooperation Agreement, which currently provides the U.S. rotational access to nine military bases in the archipelago. This continued relationship has established the Philippines as a crucial node in Washington’s foreign policy strategy in regard to China. Although the number of stationed U.S. troops has remained at a few hundred since the 1990s, U.S. military activity has increased, as evidenced by the fact that U.S. troops made up more than 10,000 of the 17,000 personnel from seven countries that participated in the Balikatan military exercises this May. Congress has also authorized up to $2.5 billion in foreign military financing for the Philippines, and up to $1 billion in loans for military sales, for fiscal year 2026. This is the highest amount that the U.S. has given to the Philippines, an increase of $500 million from the prior year. Outside of military investment, the Philippines has also emerged as an increasingly important ally for economic collaboration. The United States has shown intense interest in the Luzon Economic Corridor (LEC), a trilateral infrastructure and technology initiative by the U.S., Japan, and the Philippines. The plan invests in the construction of infrastructure across Luzon island. The scale is large relative to current investment: the Philippines received $7.8 billion in net foreign direct investment in 2025, while Luzon alone attracted over $20 billion in projects at a September investor forum. Though the project is still mostly aspirational, Marcos is largely in favor of it, having told a crowd of investors at the forum to turn LEC “from a shared vision into concrete investments and projects.” “The United States is all-in on the Luzon Economic Corridor because it's good for the Philippines and good for America," stated Lee Lipton, Washington’s ambassador to the Philippines, in response. The U.S. private sector is also supportive of the initiative, with over fifty American companies reported to be engaged in investment opportunities in the LEC, according to the Subic Bay Metropolitan Authority. Despite the apparent enthusiasm from both governments, the court of public opinion seems skeptical of the initiative, particularly because of one aspect of the LEC: the proposed Pax Silica technology center in the industry hub of New Clark City, estimated to attract between $40 and $70 billion in investment and create nearly 200,000 new jobs. During city-wide protests throughout Manila on September 21, protestors held signs attacking U.S.-backed data center projects, which are a part of the Pax Silica initiative, as a major source of grievance with Marcos' government. Pax Silica, which aims to pursue similar initiatives across more than 20 other countries, has sparked worry from many Filipinos over the risks of heavy water usage, high electricity demands, and overdependence on foreign technology and capital. "[Pax Silica] threatens to permanently lock the Philippines into having the highest power rates not just in Southeast Asia but in all of Asia,” stated the Makabayan Bloc, a left-wing Filipino party that, although it lacks much representation in the country’s government, has a strong grassroots presence, and has often led anti-U.S. sentiment across the country. artigo.texto: The Xiaomi 18 Series is officially on its way, following its initial debut in China on September 23, 2026. Xiaomi 18 Series Launch in India: The Xiaomi 18 Series is officially on its way, following its initial debut in China on September 23, 2026. The upcoming flagship lineup introduces massive upgrades, including world-first 2nm mobile chipsets, dual 200MP camera systems, and revolutionary high-capacity silicon-anode batteries. Here is everything you need to know about what to expect from the India launch. While the series is already live in China, prominent industry insiders tip the Xiaomi 18 Series to launch in India by December 2026, matching the late-winter shopping rush. This represents an earlier launch cycle compared to previous generations, which typically arrived in India around March. The official launch events are expected to take place in the standard late-afternoon window (around 4:00 PM IST). India will likely receive the Xiaomi 18 Pro initially, while the standard Xiaomi 18 might follow in March or April 2027, and the top-tier Xiaomi 18 Pro Max might remain heavily limited or exclusive to global/China distributions. Thanks to a new 32% silicon-anode composition, Xiaomi has packed a massive 7,000mAh battery into the Pro model without adding bulk to the body. The chassis features a premium glass-metal build protected by Xiaomi Dragon Crystal Glass 3.0. Extreme Leica Optics: Developed alongside Leica, the Pro variant boasts two massive 200MP sensors. The main lens uses a 1/1.28-inch Light Hunter 960 sensor for extreme low-light clarity, complemented by a 200MP periscope zoom lens capable of 3.2x optical telephoto macro shots. Hardware Privacy Display: Taking inspiration from secure display technologies, the 18 Pro series features a hardware-integrated privacy shield functionality, preventing side-angle snooping on your screen when you are in public areas. Next-Gen Connectivity: The devices are fully equipped for future network standards, integrating Ultra-Wideband (UWB) tracking, 5G-Advanced (5G-A), Wi-Fi 7, and Bluetooth 6.0. The series introduces the world’s first mobile platforms built on an ultra-dense 2nm architecture. Xiaomi 18 & 18 Pro: Equipped with the core Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 chipset, featuring Qualcomm's 4th-generation custom Oryon CPU architecture that hits clock speeds up to a massive 5.0GHz. Xiaomi 18 Pro Max: This top-tier model breaks away with the unthrottled Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 SoC, designed specifically to handle multi-stream 8K AI video processing and massive local generative AI large language models smoothly. All models support 100W HyperCharge wired charging (with the charging block included in the box), 50W wireless charging, and a powerful 27W reverse wireless charging capability to top up accessories or other phones on the go.

artigo.texto: OpenWorld Signs Term Sheet to Finance Solar-Powered, Distributed AI Computing Network Initially Integrated with Residential Battery Storage with Tokenized Financing Program of up to $1 Billion LAKE MARY, Fla., Oct 15, 2026 - (ACN Newswire) - OpenWorld, Inc. ("OpenWorld" or the "Company") (NASDAQ: OPNW), an innovation company advancing global real-world asset ("RWA") tokenization, today announced that it has entered into a non-binding term sheet with Meridian to establish a tokenized financing program of up to $1 billion to fund the purchase and deployment of a distributed AI computing network powered by on-site solar energy and residential battery storage. Under the term sheet, OpenWorld will serve as advisor, structuring agent and services provider for the program, and its OpenWorld Enterprise platform will finance and operate the orchestration of the network. The news follows recent OpenWorld tokenized financing announcements, including a proposed transaction to transform BeyondAI's industrial AI intellectual property rights into financeable collateral on OpenWorld's tokenization platform. Key Highlights - Meridian founded by Josh Raffaelli: Raffaelli was involved early in Tesla, Solar City, and SpaceX while at DFJ and Silver Lake. - Up to $1 billion in tokenized financing: OpenWorld structures and administers the tokenized financing program on OpenWorld Enterprise. Residential battery storage, solar panels and AI computing equipment form the asset base of the structure. - Meridian's role: Meridian holds purchase rights to Powerwall residential battery storage systems for the program and will own the storage assets within the structure. - AI inference without new data centers: AI providers pay to run trained models on the network with no new centralized data-center sites, no additional grid interconnections and no water-based cooling. The program is intended to supply capacity to one or more leading AI inference providers. - Initial deployment of 10,000 homes: Compute nodes at participating homes, with larger installations at local schools, hospitals and local commercial campuses. - Hosts get paid: Homeowners receive monthly hosting payments and lower-cost electricity, with household energy needs taking priority over computing workloads. Commercial hosts receive a share of site revenue and backup power. - Timeline: Initial installations scheduled to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026; first commercial site targeted for the first quarter of 2027. "Access to power is a major constraint on the growth of AI infrastructure," said Matt Shaw, CEO and Chairman of OpenWorld. "By bringing computing equipment to homes and commercial properties through solar generation and battery storage, we can build AI capacity closer to the power source instead of waiting years for a grid connection. Our term sheet with Meridian brings together the tokenization, financing and operating capabilities needed to develop this network at scale, and it shows what OpenWorld Enterprise is built to do: turn real-world assets into financeable, on-chain infrastructure." "Residential battery storage is the foundation of this program," said Josh Raffaelli, founder of Meridian and clean energy investor. "OpenWorld will help us finance the equipment, turning solar generation and battery storage at participating properties into infrastructure that can serve growing demand for AI computing." Solving the Power Problem in AI Infrastructure Access to power is a growing constraint on AI infrastructure. New data centers face lengthy grid interconnection timelines, local opposition and significant water demands. The planned network of home-hosted, distributed AI inference computing would place compute nodes at participating homes and larger installations at local schools, hospitals and commercial campuses, each powered by on-site solar generation and battery storage. AI providers would pay to use this computing capacity for inference, the process of running trained AI models, without requiring new centralized data-center sites, additional grid connections or water-based cooling. Participating homeowners would receive monthly hosting payments and lower-cost electricity, with household energy needs taking priority over computing workloads. Commercial hosts would receive a share of site revenue and backup power. How the Program Works Meridian, a privately held Delaware limited liability company, holds purchase rights to residential Tesla Powerwall battery storage systems for the program. The program's initial deployment is planned for 10,000 homes. Under the term sheet, OpenWorld will serve as advisor, structuring agent and services provider for the financing program. OpenWorld will establish and administer the tokenized financing structure on its OpenWorld Enterprise platform. The financing would support Meridian's purchase of residential battery storage systems, as well as the purchase by OpenWorld or a subsidiary of solar panels and associated AI computing equipment, all of which will be used within the structure. OpenWorld is also developing an integrated system to support each installation. The OpenWorld Enterprise platform will monitor equipment performance and provide investors with reporting on the underlying assets. The program is intended to supply computing capacity to one or more leading AI inference providers. Test installations are scheduled to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026, with the first commercial site targeted for the first quarter of 2027. Non-Binding Agreement The Term Sheet is non-binding, except for the provisions expressly stated to be binding, and the proposed transaction remains subject to the completion of confirmatory due diligence, negotiation and execution of definitive documentation, satisfaction of applicable conditions and completion of the contemplated transaction. artigo.texto: Israel wants an AI data center boom. Its power grid may not be ready The Electricity Authority is preparing new rules for connecting energy-intensive facilities as data centers could account for 20% of national electricity consumption by 2030. Industry figures say transmission bottlenecks, gas dependence and national security concerns make local computing infrastructure both a challenge and a strategic necessity. During the August 2025 heat wave, Israel broke its electricity consumption record four days in a row. The new peak of 17,282 megawatts was 10% higher than the previous record, set just two years earlier. Israel’s current electricity generation capacity stands at approximately 18,800 megawatts. Despite the strain on the system, the Electricity Authority is expected to publish a regulatory framework today for connecting data centers to the grid. The move would allow more energy-intensive facilities to connect to an electricity system already operating close to its limits during periods of peak demand. According to the Authority’s load forecast, data centers could account for up to 20% of Israel’s electricity consumption by 2030. In July, the Electricity Authority halted approvals for applications to build data centers in Israel. The framework expected today is intended as a compromise, allowing construction to proceed while limiting the strain on the country’s infrastructure. Under the proposed rules, each data center would be capped at 200 megawatts of power consumption, roughly equivalent to the electricity demand of a mid-sized Israeli city such as Rehovot or Holon. According to estimates, as many as 15 facilities could be built at the maximum capacity of 200 megawatts. The proposed cap would apply to half of the 100 connection requests submitted to Noga, Israel’s electricity system operator. According to sources in the electricity sector, generation itself will be a challenge. “Electricity generation will be a problem. We see how hard it is to build a power plant in Israel, and how much politicians try to avoid decisions like that,” they said. The transmission grid, however, poses an even greater constraint, according to the sources. “There are problems in the transmission grid in the center of the country, and so it’s actually in the periphery that the risk is an opportunity. In the Negev there is renewable energy; instead of transmitting the electricity north, you can route it to data centers.” The challenge is not only how much electricity data centers consume, but also when they consume it. “Usually, there’s a kind of balance in electricity consumption: work zones and offices during the day, and residential areas in the evening. But data centers run 24/7 and raise the base load on the system, meaning several power plants need to run without stopping,” the sources said. Heavy electricity demand would also increase consumption of natural gas from Israel’s reservoirs. According to the Energy Ministry, those reserves could be depleted in less than 20 years, and greater reliance on gas-fired generation would also increase air pollution. Why, then, do data centers need to be built in Israel? Why not rely on facilities overseas, as Israeli companies and institutions do today? “The world is in the midst of a technological arms race, in which countries and giant corporations are investing hundreds of billions of dollars in building the computing infrastructure that will determine the balance of power in the global economy in the coming decades,” Shelly Lanzman, a partner and chair of the advisory board at NED, a company specializing in building and developing data centers and the former CEO of Microsoft Israel, told Calcalist. “Already today it’s clear that the scope of computing power, its strength and its availability will be decisive factors in the ability of countries to develop technologies and preserve a competitive advantage,” she said. In this context, Lanzman argues, data centers should be treated as national infrastructure on a par with power plants, airports and communications networks. “For Israel, whose economic and security standing relies to a large extent on technological superiority, this is a national interest of the first order.” National security is another argument for operating data centers locally. Government agencies and other organizations handling sensitive information, including the Shin Bet, the Mossad, the military and hospitals, increasingly rely on advanced AI and data systems. These organizations handle information with significant security or privacy implications, making local storage an important part of protecting it. Operational independence and continuity of service are also concerns. About a year ago, Microsoft restricted Unit 8200’s access to some of its cloud services after determining that the unit had violated the company’s terms of use. The decision followed reports that the service had been used to collect information on and track Palestinians, including by storing recordings of millions of their phone calls. Beyond security, a strong domestic data center industry could give Israeli entrepreneurs an advantage when launching startups and help attract international companies. Access to computing infrastructure is becoming an increasingly important consideration for businesses developing and deploying AI. “The global race is already creating growing competition for critical resources, from electricity supply and advanced chips to computing equipment, land and investment capital,” Lanzman added.

artigo.texto: Israel caps new data centers at 200 megawatts as demand overwhelms power grid The Electricity Authority will allocate an additional 1,000 megawatts to large data centers, bringing approved and planned capacity to about 3,000 megawatts. That would equal roughly 20% of projected national electricity consumption in 2030. After lengthy deliberations, the Electricity Authority published the main points of its new rules for connecting large data centers to Israel’s electricity grid on Sunday evening. As previously reported by Calcalist, the rules will cap the capacity of a new data center at 200 megawatts. The Authority will allocate an additional 1,000 megawatts to large data centers. Combined with approximately 2,000 megawatts in connections already approved, this would bring the total to around 3,000 megawatts, equivalent to about 20% of Israel’s projected electricity consumption in 2030. According to the Authority, the policy will make Israel “one of the world’s leaders in the rate of server farms relative to consumption.” The new rules became necessary after Noga, the company responsible for managing Israel’s electricity system, received requests to connect data centers with a combined capacity of 27,000 megawatts, roughly three times the country’s current average electricity consumption. In response to the surge in demand, the Electricity Authority issued a temporary order freezing responses to data center connection requests. To prevent developers from reserving grid capacity through projects with little chance of being built, or trading in connection approvals, the Authority will require developers to provide guarantees of NIS 2 million per megawatt of requested connection capacity, alongside additional conditions. The rules will also require backup mechanisms that allow data centers to be disconnected from the grid during periods of extreme demand. A 200-megawatt data center consumes electricity on a scale comparable to that of a mid-sized Israeli city, and construction costs are estimated at more than NIS 4 billion. The full decision is expected to be published in the coming days for a three-week public consultation. The Authority will consider the comments received and may make changes before the rules take effect. The decision would allow electricity consumption to grow as Israel attracts more data center investment, but it comes amid warnings that natural gas prices, and consequently electricity prices, could rise. A deal to supply natural gas involving NewMed and Ratio, partners in the Leviathan reservoir, collapsed. Last June, Israel Electric Corporation legal adviser Gershon Berkovitz warned that gas prices could increase. He also raised concerns about competition in the domestic market, warning that the problems could reach “the point of failure to meet the state’s energy needs.” While the new rules will restrict access to the grid for additional data centers and prevent the construction of some proposed megaprojects, including facilities with capacities of 500 megawatts and even 1,100 megawatts for which requests have already been submitted to Noga, limiting new connections will not eliminate the need for more electricity. Israel will still need to expand its generation capacity to meet growing demand from data centers and the wider economy.

artigo.texto: Near Arlington, Oregon, a 29,950-acre proposal combines 500 MW each of wind and solar with 4,000-MWh battery storage The Columbia River plateau desert of Eastern Washington lying above the Columbia River basin is an expansive area that is mostly windy, where rangeland stretches to the horizon beyond the small city of Arlington, Oregon, which has only 500 people living there. It would be hard for most Americans to locate it on a map. But it has drawn attention of energy experts and planners. An application is under consideration by the state regulators that proposes installing two kinds of renewable energy generation devices, along with a battery system large enough to overturn the assumptions about power grid reliability in the Pacific Northwest region. Remote Oregon plateau at heart of green energy gamble Arlington lies within the rain shadow of the Columbia River Basin – an area defined by high desert, created by the forces of wind, volcanic basalt, and hundreds of years of ranching and wheat farming. Arlington has some of the most consistent winds in the Pacific Northwest, as well as high-intensity summer solar radiation that few coastal areas can equal. The combination of natural features and existing power line routes in the area makes it increasingly attractive for renewable energy development. A developer filed a Notice of Intent with the Oregon Department of Energy on August 4, 2026, to pursue a site certificate for the Big River Renewable Energy Project. For perspective on the size of 29,950 acres, the urban land use in all of Portland occupies about 90,000 acres. This project alone would take up one-third of that space. This is no small project, but an extensive alteration of agricultural land visible from miles away. The Big River Renewable Energy Project proposal A developer filed a Notice of Intent with the Oregon Department of Energy on August 4, 2026, to pursue a site certificate for the Big River Renewable Energy Project. The Notice of Intent is the initial formal step in Oregon’s process of siting a facility and is not an approval in any way. There are four components to this proposal. A 500 MW wind turbine portion will place turbines on the plateau. Another 500 MW solar generation portion will overlay photovoltaic generation on the same footprint — co-location allowing wind and solar generation to share land and other infrastructure. Both will be supported by a 4,000 MWh battery energy storage system, able to store excess generation and dispatch it to the grid during peak times. Public comments can be submitted between August 7, 2026, and September 25, 2026, according to the Oregon Department of Energy – Big River. Why co-location of wind, solar, and storage is significant Wind energy and solar energy have often been referred to as intermittent forms of energy, but the generation patterns for these two in the Columbia Basin region are complementary. While wind blows the hardest at night and during the winter period, solar energy peaks at midday during the summer period. By combining both wind and solar energy together, the generation pattern becomes less intermittent. The addition of a 4,000 MWh battery system makes the entire process even better, as the battery takes care of the surplus generated during peak generation periods. The surplus energy is then used during the evening peak consumption times and when there are periods of cloudy weather without any wind blowing. The total 1,000 MW generating capacity will be enough to power hundreds of thousands of Pacific Northwest households. Grid operators have increasingly favored co-located hybrid projects because they reduce transmission congestion by delivering more usable power through a single interconnection point, improving overall capacity factors. Process review and role of the public in Oregon In Oregon, large energy projects need to get a Site Certificate from the Department of Energy before they can start construction. This process is purposely designed as such. The NOI phase, where Big River finds itself now, sets off environmental scoping, interagency coordination, and public participation. Submitting an NOI does not mean getting approval to build. An informational public hearing was held on August 20, 2026, and was available online and offline. The deadline for comments is set for September 25, 2026. Comments usually revolve around land use compatibility, effects on wildlife and habitats, landscape visual quality, water resources, and transmission corridor issues, given the size of the project. The future of Big River — and the energy situation in Oregon Once the comment period for the NOI is over, the developer will be required to file an application for site cacertificate. This application should respond to any issues identified during the public comment period and must meet all requirements of the Oregon Siting Standards. The project’s trajectory matters well beyond Arlington. Oregon has set ambitious clean energy targets, and the Pacific Northwest grid increasingly needs firm, dispatchable renewable power to replace retiring fossil fuel generation. A hybrid facility of this scale — if approved — would demonstrate that large co-located projects are viable in the American West, potentially accelerating similar proposals elsewhere. If it meets significant opposition or regulatory obstacles, that outcome would be equally instructive. For now, the project’s future remains genuinely open, shaped by the technical record, agency review, and the voices of people who live and work on that high desert plateau. Kelly is an experienced writer with 15 years of experience exploring the big stories that shape our world, from tech breakthroughs and space exploration to climate, energy, and the fascinating quirks of science. She has a talent for turning complex ideas into sharp, memorable insights that stay with readers long after they’ve finished reading.

artigo.texto: Tech CATL Unveils Five-Minute Battery Swapping for Electric Trucks, Targets 2,000 Stations by 2027 CATL introduces new electric-truck batteries and plans thousands of rapid-swapping stations. Chinese battery manufacturer CATL has unveiled a new generation of batteries for heavy-duty electric trucks and expanded its battery-swapping technology, offering a system designed to replace depleted truck batteries in approximately five minutes. The announcement marks another step in China’s efforts to electrify freight transportation, an industry traditionally dependent on diesel-powered vehicles. The new Tianxing II battery platform includes different configurations for commercial vehicles, while the company’s Qiji battery-swapping system is designed to reduce the time trucks spend waiting to replenish energy. According to Reuters, CATL is targeting 900 heavy-truck battery-swapping stations by the end of 2026, expanding to 2,000 stations in 2027 and eventually building a network of 10,000. The company’s plans reflect the growing importance of battery replacement technology as manufacturers seek to overcome some of the main obstacles to electric freight transportation, including charging times, battery weight, operating costs and infrastructure availability. How the Five-Minute Battery Swapping System Works Unlike conventional electric trucks that must remain connected to a charger while their batteries recharge, CATL’s system allows a vehicle to enter a specialized station where an automated mechanism removes its depleted battery and installs a charged replacement. The process is designed to take approximately five minutes, allowing drivers to resume operations without waiting for the original battery to recharge. CATL’s Qiji system uses standardized battery modules intended to work across compatible heavy-duty vehicle models. The battery-swapping approach can also separate battery ownership from vehicle ownership. Freight operators may be able to purchase or lease a truck without paying the full upfront cost of its battery, depending on the commercial arrangement. In an earlier company announcement, CATL said its standardized Qiji battery-swapping system could support a wide range of commercial trucks, with compatible designs developed alongside multiple vehicle manufacturers. The company says battery swapping can improve fleet efficiency, particularly for long-distance transportation, ports, mining operations and logistics services where vehicle downtime carries substantial costs. New Batteries Designed for Longer Truck Journeys The Tianxing II platform introduces batteries intended for different heavy-truck operating conditions. Its long-range configuration includes a battery pack with a capacity of 760 kilowatt-hours, which CATL says can support more than 600 kilometres of driving range under specified conditions. The company has also developed lighter battery configurations and chassis-mounted designs aimed at improving vehicle efficiency and preserving cargo capacity. CATL says its new standardized battery-swapping modules contain 52% fewer components and cost approximately 15% less than previous designs. These figures represent company-reported technical improvements. Actual vehicle range, battery performance and operating savings will depend on driving conditions, vehicle weight, climate, electricity prices and the availability of compatible swapping stations. CATL Plans Thousands of Battery-Swapping Stations CATL’s expansion strategy goes beyond developing new batteries. The company plans to establish a nationwide network of heavy-duty truck battery-swapping stations along China’s major freight transportation routes. Its current targets include 900 stations by the end of 2026 and 2,000 by 2027, followed by a longer-term ambition to reach 10,000 locations. The new goals build on earlier infrastructure investments. In May 2025, CATL announced an extensive battery-swapping network intended to connect major freight corridors across China. The company’s strategy includes standardized battery modules, partnerships with commercial vehicle manufacturers and infrastructure development along important highways and industrial routes. CATL has also expanded cooperation with logistics companies. In July 2026, the battery manufacturer announced an agreement with J&T Express to support battery-swapping solutions for more than 5,000 heavy-duty trucks. The collaboration illustrates how the technology could be integrated into large commercial fleets that operate on predictable schedules and transportation routes. China Pushes to Reduce Diesel Dependence The expansion comes as China accelerates efforts to replace diesel-powered heavy trucks with electric alternatives. Heavy commercial vehicles consume substantial amounts of fuel and contribute to transportation-related emissions, making freight electrification an important part of China’s energy transition. A separate Reuters report outlined China’s plans to increase electric vehicles to 40% of new heavy-truck sales by 2030. Battery swapping could help support those ambitions by addressing operational challenges associated with charging large commercial batteries. For freight operators, the potential advantages include shorter stops, more predictable vehicle scheduling and reduced exposure to changes in diesel prices. However, large-scale adoption will require substantial infrastructure investment, reliable electricity supplies, standardized equipment and commercially viable agreements between manufacturers, energy providers and transport companies. Technology Could Influence Global Freight Transportation CATL is also seeking to expand its electric-truck technology beyond China. The company has announced a preliminary collaboration with DHL Group to explore environmentally sustainable freight corridors in Europe using electric trucks. artigo.texto: Award-winning technologies focus on LFP manufacturing efficiency, lithium-metal electrodes and battery performance prediction South Korean battery manufacturer SK On is accelerating research into cost-efficient lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries and next-generation lithium-metal technologies as it seeks to strengthen its competitiveness in the global battery market. The company announced on October 18 that it held its second Future Technology Institute Research Conference on October 14–15 at its R&D center in Daejeon, South Korea. Under the theme "Creating Our Future," the event brought together SK On President Lee Yong-wook, Future Technology Institute head Park Ki-soo and company researchers to share technological achievements and explore opportunities for collaboration. More than 300 research projects were submitted across six areas, including battery manufacturing processes, cells, systems, materials, next-generation technologies and platforms. The number of submissions increased approximately 15% from the previous year. LFP Manufacturing Innovation Takes Top Research Award The conference's grand prize went to a research team that developed a manufacturing process capable of replacing costly carbon nanotube (CNT) paste with CNT powder in LFP battery cathode production. CNTs are conductive materials that facilitate electron movement within battery electrodes. The research team developed a method to distribute CNT powder evenly throughout cathode materials, achieving performance comparable to conventional paste-based processes while improving cost competitiveness. SK On plans to evaluate the technology for potential application in commercial battery manufacturing. The development is particularly relevant as battery manufacturers seek to improve the economics of LFP batteries, which are increasingly used in electric vehicles and energy storage systems. Other award-winning projects included the design of large-format pouch-type lithium-metal battery electrodes and a predictive model for battery capacity degradation and internal resistance under different charging, discharging and storage conditions. The research projects were evaluated through a blind review process based on relevance, differentiation, contribution, originality and practical applicability. Digital Twin Technology Supports Next-Generation Battery Research The conference also featured a technology exhibition where researchers presented their projects, exchanged technical insights and participated in on-site evaluations. In a keynote presentation, Professor Lee Yong-min of Yonsei University discussed the current state and future prospects of digital twin technology in battery development. Digital twins create virtual representations of physical battery systems, enabling researchers to analyze performance and operating conditions through simulation. The technology could help improve development efficiency and support more accurate performance predictions. SK On plans to make the research conference a regular event to encourage knowledge sharing, strengthen collaboration and connect research achievements with practical product and manufacturing technologies. "The Future Technology Institute Research Conference is an important platform where our employees' challenges and research achievements contribute directly to SK On's technological competitiveness," said Lee Yong-wook, President of SK On. "We will continue to foster a research-driven culture and pursue technological innovation to lead the next-generation battery market," he added. The company aims to build on these research initiatives to strengthen its technology portfolio and manufacturing capabilities as competition intensifies across the global battery industry.

artigo.texto: SK Nexilis, an investment company of SKC in the copper foil business for secondary batteries, said Tuesday that it has successfully developed 'high-bonding carbon-coated copper foil' technology, which is considered a core material for next-generation batteries. High-bonding carbon-coated copper foil is a product that applies special carbon to the surface of the copper foil to enhance adhesion with the anode material. It is characterized by suppressing the 'delamination phenomenon,' where silicon anode materials expand during charging and discharging processes, causing them to separate from the copper foil, thereby improving the structural stability of the electrode. The company explained that this can also contribute to enhancing battery lifespan and safety. SK Nexilis developed the related technology in line with the trend in the battery industry to increase the silicon content of anode materials to boost energy density. While silicon can store more lithium ions than conventional graphite, its significant volume change during charging and discharging processes is cited as a drawback. This is why adhesion between the anode material and copper foil becomes increasingly important as the silicon content rises. High-bonding carbon-coated copper foil can also be applied to dry electrode processes, which are gaining attention as a manufacturing method for next-generation batteries. Unlike conventional wet processes that use liquid solvents, dry electrode processes can reduce steps such as drying, thereby lowering manufacturing costs and energy consumption. However, since it is crucial to stably bond electrode materials with copper foil, the utilization of high-adhesion copper foil is expected to expand. SK Nexilis plans to build a pilot production system for high-bonding carbon-coated copper foil ahead of full-scale Yangsan. The company is currently verifying process stability and aims to commercialize in the second half of next year after securing Yangsan technology. An official from SK Nexilis said, "We will proceed with commercialization optimization work without any issues while strengthening our competitiveness in the next-generation battery materials market through continuous technological development."

artigo.texto: Desvendando o potencial dos créditos de carbono florestal. (Baoquangngai.vn) - Com aproximadamente 826.000 hectares de floresta, Quang Ngai possui um potencial significativo para o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono. A província está finalizando a coleta de dados, implementando projetos-piloto e explorando gradualmente o valor econômico das florestas, criando recursos adicionais para a proteção e o desenvolvimento florestal. Quang Ngai possui atualmente cerca de 826.000 hectares de floresta, incluindo aproximadamente 604.000 hectares de floresta natural e cerca de 222.000 hectares de floresta plantada. Com sua vasta área e diversidade de tipos e condições florestais, a província tem muitas oportunidades para pesquisar e implementar atividades que visem reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa e desenvolver créditos de carbono florestal. Segundo o Instituto de Ciências Florestais do Vietnã, o potencial de carbono florestal de Quang Ngai pode ser explorado por meio de diversas soluções, tais como: proteção de florestas naturais, limitação do desmatamento e da degradação florestal, restauração e enriquecimento de florestas degradadas, melhoria da qualidade de florestas plantadas, conversão de pequenas florestas madeireiras em grandes florestas madeireiras, extensão do ciclo de negócios de florestas plantadas, manejo florestal sustentável, desenvolvimento de árvores dispersas e modelos agroflorestais. Essas atividades contribuem para a melhoria da qualidade florestal, a redução das emissões ou o aumento da capacidade de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono. Segundo o Sr. Nguyen Van Nam, chefe do Departamento Provincial de Proteção Florestal, com base em cálculos orientados pelo Departamento de Silvicultura e Proteção Florestal, as florestas da província absorvem e armazenam aproximadamente 2 milhões de toneladas de carbono anualmente, o equivalente a cerca de 2 milhões de créditos. Atualmente, a província está implementando o Programa de Redução de Emissões para as regiões Centro-Sul e Planalto Central, no âmbito da iniciativa LEAF, que deverá receber aproximadamente 1,13 milhão de créditos de carbono. Esses dados indicam que a província possui um potencial significativo para o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono florestal. No entanto, a quantidade estimada de carbono absorvida e armazenada pelas florestas não corresponde necessariamente ao número de créditos que foram reconhecidos e são elegíveis para negociação. Para gerar valor econômico , os programas e projetos devem atender aos requisitos estipulados em relação aos métodos de cálculo, normas aplicáveis, medição, avaliação e verificação de resultados. A província de Quang Ngai está pesquisando o desenvolvimento de carbono florestal com o objetivo de reduzir as emissões de gases de efeito estufa e desenvolver projetos-piloto. Isso inclui o manejo e a proteção florestal sustentável, a prevenção de incêndios florestais e o manejo adequado da vegetação durante o reflorestamento, contribuindo para limitar os riscos de emissão, proteger os recursos florestais e fornecer uma base para avaliar os resultados da redução de emissões e considerar o acesso ao apoio de organizações não governamentais e empresas internacionais. Os resultados dos projetos devem ser avaliados, analisados, verificados e submetidos à autoridade competente para consideração e reconhecimento antes de participarem de transações no mercado de carbono, conforme regulamentado. Essas duas abordagens vinculam a proteção florestal ao objetivo de reduzir as emissões e gerar recursos financeiros adicionais. No entanto, para traduzir o potencial em valor tangível, é necessário demonstrar os resultados da redução de emissões, da manutenção da qualidade florestal e da conformidade com os padrões de cada programa e projeto. Criação de uma plataforma para o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono florestal. Os dados sobre a área, o estado e as características de cada tipo de floresta são a base para determinar os estoques de carbono, monitorar as mudanças nos recursos e avaliar os resultados da implementação do projeto. Portanto, a coleta completa de dados florestais é uma das tarefas importantes para Quang Ngai, a fim de criar as condições necessárias para o desenvolvimento de créditos de carbono. O Departamento de Agricultura e Meio Ambiente está atualmente realizando um levantamento e inventário florestal, conforme orientação do Ministério da Agricultura e Meio Ambiente e do Comitê Popular Provincial. Os resultados do inventário devem ser publicados em 2027. O Sr. Nguyen Van Nam afirmou que os dados de levantamento e inventário ajudam a determinar as reservas de carbono, avaliar o potencial de cada área e selecionar métodos adequados às características de cada tipo de floresta. Isso também serve como base para o desenvolvimento e avaliação da viabilidade de projetos de carbono florestal. Paralelamente ao trabalho de inventário, Quang Ngai está coordenando com o Instituto de Ciências Florestais do Vietnã o desenvolvimento de projetos-piloto de carbono florestal na Dak To Forestry Company Limited, na Kon Ray Forestry Company Limited e no Conselho de Gestão Florestal de Proteção de Dak Ha. Essas áreas foram selecionadas com base no tamanho da área florestal, na extensão da floresta e na diversidade de tipos e condições florestais. Essa característica facilita a avaliação da aplicabilidade dos métodos de determinação de carbono em diferentes condições florestais. artigo.texto: San Antonio is considering stricter regulations on data center development to address concerns about electricity use, water consumption, air quality, and neighborhood impact, with proposals requiring varying levels of City Council approval and community engagement. Public hearings are scheduled in October to decide on potential changes to the approval process for new data centers. - Data centers require significant electricity, cooling, and backup power, raising concerns amid rapid expansion in San Antonio. - Three regulatory proposals range from permitting data centers with specific requirements to requiring individual City Council approval and additional safeguards. - Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones proposes a 1,000-foot setback, advance community notice, neighborhood meetings, and green space replacement. - Council members are divided between ensuring resident input and maintaining economic development incentives. - Public hearings by the Zoning Commission and City Council are scheduled for October 20 and 29, respectively, allowing resident participation. San Antonio Moves Toward Tougher Data Center Restrictions as Residents Raise Concerns Over Water, Power and Neighborhoods San Antonio is moving closer to imposing stricter regulations on data centers as city leaders debate how to balance economic development with growing concerns about electricity consumption, water use, air quality and the impact of large industrial facilities on surrounding neighborhoods. The debate could change how data centers are approved throughout the city, potentially requiring developers to obtain City Council authorization before constructing new facilities. A public hearing before the Zoning Commission is scheduled for October 20, followed by an anticipated City Council vote October 29. Growing Industry Brings Growing Concerns Data centers house computer servers and other equipment supporting cloud computing, artificial intelligence and digital services. Their operations can require substantial electricity, cooling infrastructure and backup power systems. San Antonio has become an attractive market for developers because of available land, energy infrastructure and access to natural resources. However, the rapid expansion has raised questions about whether existing zoning regulations adequately protect residents. District 6 Councilman Ric Galvan has been among those pushing for stronger oversight, particularly as data center development expands across the city’s West Side. Galvan introduced a council consideration request last year calling for a comprehensive review of the industry’s impact on infrastructure and natural resources. “The residents of San Antonio deserve to have a say in where and how data centers are built in our city,” Galvan said in an October 15 statement. Three Proposals Could Reshape Development City officials are considering three approaches to regulating future facilities. One proposal would permit data centers in designated commercial and industrial districts if developers meet specific requirements, without requiring individual City Council approval. A second proposal would require developers to obtain specific use authorization, allowing council members to evaluate each project and providing opportunities for public comment. Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones has introduced a third approach combining individual council approval with additional safeguards. Her proposal includes a 1,000-foot setback, advance notice to affected communities, neighborhood engagement meetings and requirements to replace twice the green space eliminated during construction. The proposals also address concerns involving noise, lighting, emergency planning and environmental protections. Economic Growth Versus Neighborhood Protections Council members remain divided over how far the restrictions should go. Some argue that requiring individual approval for every facility would provide accountability and give residents a meaningful voice in decisions affecting their neighborhoods. Others warn that overly restrictive requirements could discourage investment and limit opportunities for economic development. Data centers could also generate additional revenue for municipally owned CPS Energy, potentially increasing funds transferred to the city. The central question is whether those economic benefits outweigh the demands placed on public infrastructure and surrounding communities. Residents Have Opportunity to Weigh In The Zoning Commission will consider the proposals October 20, with City Council expected to take up the issue October 29. Both meetings will provide opportunities for public participation. The outcome could determine whether data centers continue receiving approval under established zoning rules or face greater scrutiny from elected officials and residents. For communities already experiencing rapid development, the decision may establish how much influence neighborhoods have over the industry’s future expansion.

artigo.texto: How Long Was The First Samsung Galaxy Phone's Battery Life? The Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra offers about 16 hours of battery life on average, with some users reporting more than a day's worth of use. That's a solid battery life, but it took a lot of advancements and ingenuity to get here. To see how far battery technology has come, look back at the first device to bear the Galaxy name. Launched in 2009, the Samsung Galaxy I7500 was the first ever series release. It came with a 1,500 mAh removable battery and a quoted talk time of 9 hours and 20 minutes over a 2G connection, and 6 hours and 10 minutes over 3G. CNET reported it would barely last a day without recharging. Compared to the S26 Ultra's stats, of up to 52 hours of continuous talk time on a single charge, 6 to 9 hours doesn't seem like much. Yet, against some of the year's most popular phones, the Galaxy I7500 was about average. iPhone 3GS offered 5 hours of talk time via 3G, 12 hours via 2G. Meanwhile, the Samsung Eternity, another popular Samsung model, delivered up to 5 hours of talk time — though CNET stretched that further in testing — and the Nokia E52 could get up to 8 hours of talk time. However, even in 2009, devices weren't quite as feature-rich as what you might get today. Apple's iPhone and Samsung's earliest Galaxy models were a big step toward the modern smartphones we have now, crammed with extra hardware and functionality. Though it covers only 2013 to 2016, PhoneArena's study of battery improvements also shows how far we've come. The Samsung S and Note lines saw several battery upgrades in those years. Charging times improved significantly, too It's easy to get caught up in capacity improvements, which are, admittedly, a core part of any device's battery life. The bigger the battery, the longer it lasts, for the most part. However, another aspect of today's phone batteries makes a huge difference for convenience and performance: charging times. If your phone has a huge battery but takes forever to charge, that'll slow you down quite a bit throughout the day. You'll need to plug it in and wait for it to replenish, maybe for an inordinate amount of time. Of course, fast charging and high-power ports have changed that big time in something like the Galaxy S26 Ultra, which can charge to full in under an hour despite its 5,000 mAh battery. Many additional phones today have batteries the same size or larger. The original Galaxy, the I7500, would take about 2 to 3 hours to charge. That's nearly double what the S26 Ultra takes, but more importantly, its battery is less than half the size. Phones today can charge much larger batteries much faster. The PhoneArena battery study also shows battery charging times improving significantly between 2013 and 2016, decreasing exponentially. Fast forward to today, the Galaxy S26 also supports faster wireless charging, so you no longer need a cable for a quick battery boost. That was absolutely unheard of in 2009. Look at us go.

artigo.texto: Funding Strains, Power Shortages and Local Opposition Hit Projects, Squeezing Chip Demand At Least 47 Large Data Center Projects in the United States In the United States, the world’s largest artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure market, at least 47 large-scale data center projects have faced disruptions this year alone. Concerns are rising that cracks are forming in the U.S. AI infrastructure boom, estimated to be worth $10 trillion, due to a combination of practical issues such as worsening corporate financial conditions, power shortages, and opposition from local residents. On Oct. 18 (local time), the Financial Times (FT) cited data from regulatory intelligence firm RegLayer, reporting that at least 47 data center development projects in the U.S. have been delayed, withdrawn, or halted this year. RegLayer explained, “We surveyed primarily large-scale worksites, and the figures were compiled conservatively.” Recently, investment bank (IB) Bernstein also estimated that only 35% of the data center construction projects currently planned in the U.S. are feasible. Funding shortages are cited as the primary cause of the successive disruptions in AI infrastructure projects in the U.S. Concerns have grown over the structure in which new operators take out loans to bear massive costs for purchasing GPUs and securing sites. In particular, the controversy intensified recently as the corporate bond yield of AI infrastructure company CoreWeave surged to the 15% level. CoreWeave is a so-called ‘neocloud’ company that operates a business of buying Nvidia AI chips to build data centers and then leasing the infrastructure to tech companies. The FT stated, “The overheating of infrastructure competition among companies has turned the overall AI industry into a ‘Wild West’,” adding, “Interest rate hikes and the bond market slump are threatening the ambitions of AI infrastructure companies.” The increasingly severe power shortage and opposition from local residents, who have begun to perceive data centers as undesirable facilities, are also stumbling blocks. Big tech company Oracle notified the developer of the 2.45GW (gigawatt) ‘Project Jupiter’ underway in New Mexico of force majeure last month in preparation for disruptions in securing power. The intent is to delay rent payments if the set schedule is not met. PJM, the largest power grid operator in the US, recently decided to halt a previously planned special auction for 15 years’ worth of power for data centers to respond to the AI-driven power shortage. According to the FT’s own survey results, it was found that more than 1,000 communities in the US have attempted to introduce temporary halts or restrictive measures related to AI infrastructure development this year. Concerns over AI infrastructure companies are emerging in various parts of the market beyond the US. It is reported that Nscale, a British neocloud company, is also pursuing an initial public offering (IPO) with a corporate value of about $30 billion, but is facing difficulties as investors’ expectations are much lower than this. Bloomberg reported that due to the recently deteriorated industry conditions, some investors view Nscale’s corporate value at $16 billion to $19 billion. Previously, Australian AI infrastructure company Firmus also withdrew its IPO plan, which had been pursued at a scale of about $5 billion. It is pointed out that such crises for AI infrastructure companies could ultimately affect the earnings of semiconductor manufacturers. This is because if infrastructure companies increasingly struggle to secure investment funds and construction plans are consequently delayed, they may delay or reduce orders for semiconductor chips to be used in data centers. In fact, the stock prices of domestic memory companies such as Samsung Electronics and SK hynix have continued to show weakness recently. This is due to worsened investor sentiment caused by concerns over U.S. interest rate hikes and the pace adjustment of AI infrastructure. Bloomberg stated, “As borrowing costs rise and uncertainty about the long-term profitability of AI technology grows, investor sentiment regarding overall AI infrastructure, including server companies and semiconductor manufacturers, has deteriorated.”

artigo.texto: Two-Year LTA Covers 2027 Supply of High-Voltage Switchgear LS Electric has accelerated its push into the North American data center market after winning power infrastructure supply rights worth 170.0 billion won ($125.80 million) from a major U.S. tech company. LS Electric said on Oct. 19 that it signed a contract to supply power distribution solutions for data centers in North America. The agreement was structured as a long-term agreement, or LTA, running for two years from 2027 to 2028. The order value of 170.0 billion won ($125.80 million) corresponds to the volume scheduled for supply in 2027, while the scale of the 2028 business is to be finalized through additional consultations later. The main product to be supplied is 38kV-class high-voltage switchgear. The equipment serves as core infrastructure that stably distributes high-voltage electricity entering data centers and protects facilities when abnormalities occur in the power system. Given the nature of artificial intelligence, or AI, data centers, which must continuously receive large-scale electricity around the clock, product reliability and quality acted as key indicators in the contract. LS Electric is seeking to expand beyond this high-voltage switchgear supply. It is understood to be holding additional discussions on supplying other customized high-end power equipment for data centers, including low-voltage switchgear, distribution transformers, and ring main units, or RMUs. The latest result is seen as reflecting the effectiveness of the company’s strategy of strengthening its local response system in the United States. LS Electric has established bases at LS Electric Utah in Cedar City, Utah, and the Bastrop Campus in Texas. Through these operations, it has built a locally completed value chain that handles the full process on site, from sales and design to production, commissioning, and service, enabling it to respond quickly to customer demands. An LS Electric official explained that trust built through world-class technological capabilities and project execution experience led to the long-term contract. The company said it plans to further strengthen a stable revenue base and improve profitability by increasing supplies of high-value-added products for data centers in the future.

artigo.texto: Memphis leaders are set to consider a contentious plan Tuesday to pause new data center developments for up to a year — two weeks after a meeting on the issue led to protests, calls to police and a fist fight at City Hall. The moratorium vote comes more than two years after some communities in Memphis got a new life courtesy of trillionaire Elon Musk, as his artificial intelligence company moved in amid a local effort to make the city a hotspot for advanced technology. But the effort ended up angering residents as the company installed dozens of gas-powered turbines, known to produce a cocktail of toxic pollutants. A surge of new data center construction to fuel the booming AI industry is escalating public resentment and fear of both the energy-sucking infrastructure and AI itself in the US, roiling communities from coast to coast and transforming localized energy debates into a high-stakes, multi-million-dollar battleground for the 2026 midterm elections. At an early October council meeting in Memphis — a city used to fighting for clean air as the home to more than a dozen polluting facilities — fierce opposition was on full display. More than 100 people filed into the chamber to hear about the moratorium, bearing witness to clashes between anti-data center protesters and council members, and between the city officials themselves. Two women were also restrained in the lobby as they swung fists at each other. All eyes will be on City Hall as it considers the moratorium, which, if passed, would put a temporary pause on new data centers and on the expansion of existing ones, as well as develop a study committee to establish regulations. It would not shutter data centers already operating legally in Memphis, nor smaller data usages at facilities like hospitals and universities. Here’s what we know: How Memphis got here An abandoned factory in southwest Memphis got a makeover in June 2024, as the AI company owned by the world’s richest man, now called SpaceXAI, worked to turn the building into the “world’s largest supercomputer.” Dubbed “Colossus,” the data center was hailed by Musk at the time as the “most powerful AI training system in the world,” and the company’s website heralded plans for a second facility in the area to quickly follow. For some residents in the southwest Memphis suburb of Boxtown, a historic, majority Black and economically disadvantaged community that has long endured industrial pollution, the new gas-powered turbines represented yet another threat to their health. About 10 miles to the east in Southaven, Mississippi, more SpaceXAI turbines would chug to life at the new site of Colossus 2 — which fuels its Grok AI chatbot. CNN has reached out to SpaceXAI for comment. The NAACP filed a federal lawsuit against SpaceXAI in April of this year under the Clean Air Act, alleging it was operating dozens of unpermitted turbines in Southaven. The Department of Justice has since urged the court to throw out the lawsuit, saying the Grok AI chatbot was “critical” to national security. The case remains active, though tied up in appeals. The data centers have also caused a myriad of disruptions to daily life in Memphis, including relentless noise pollution and physical vibrations from the centers as described in a noise complaint filed by residents; concerns of dangerous emissions from the turbines brought by state officials; and an offer from SpaceXAI to buy Southaven residents’ homes in exchange for not signing onto a class action lawsuit against it. But it was at an August meeting — where the moratorium passed its first reading — that Memphis City Council Member JB Smiley Jr. said he proposed the measure to temporarily halt new data center builds after learning Musk’s company was planning a data center expansion in the city from a post on social media. “Not only did the council not know about the expansion of the data center, the community residents did not know,” Smiley said at the meeting. “I was intentional about bringing this ordinance because I think the people deserve an opportunity to voice their concerns; I think the council deserves to be treated with respect by the folks who are pushing these data centers in our community.” An earlier council meeting on data centers devolved into chaos Members of the Memphis City Council voted on whether to delay making a decision on the moratorium for two weeks at an October 6 meeting. When the effort to delay passed 7-5, the chamber erupted. “Officers, we need to clear it out,” council Chairwoman Jana Swearengen-Washington said from the podium as observers began shouting. As people rose from their seats in the chamber and a woman shouted chants into a megaphone speaker, the chairwoman repeatedly slammed her gavel, saying, “Get that f**king bullhorn!” A livestream of the meeting showed dozens of protesters gathering at the front of the room, fists in the air as they chanted above the council members’ shouts to stop, yelling, “Ain’t no power like the power of the people ‘cause the power of the people fight back!” before the livestream went dark. Councilwoman Yolanda Cooper-Sutton clashed with members of the crowd, according to CNN affiliate WMC, as she told one attendee, “You pipe down baby, I clap back.” She also lashed out at Smiley, who voted against postponing the vote on his moratorium, shouting that he “confuse(s) the people over and over,” as she was ushered out of the room by staffers. In the lobby of the building, a fist fight broke out between two women, WMC reported. Memphis police were called to the disturbance at City Hall, but according to WMC, a department spokesperson said no one was harmed or detained. Days after the chaotic meeting, Memphis Mayor Paul Young issued an executive order to establish a 90-day study “to develop clear, actionable recommendations for regulating large and hyperscale data centers in Memphis.” “The study will proceed concurrently with the Memphis City Council’s ongoing consideration of data cente

artigo.texto: AI Data Centers Snap Up Optical Fiber, Spot Prices Soar 5x Year-on-Year, Shortage Could Persist Through 2028 The AI data center (AIDC) construction boom is pushing optical fiber from a supporting role into the spotlight. TrendForce's latest communications industry research estimates that the global optical fiber supply-demand gap will reach 180 million fiber-kilometers in 2026. The supply crunch is directly reflected in pricing, with spot prices for finished optical fiber up 2.8 to more than 5 times compared with 2025, and the tight conditions are expected to last at least through 2028. The research notes that global optical fiber supply began tightening at the end of 2025, driven primarily by the massive new demand created by AI data center-related applications. There is no slack left on the supply side: global optical fiber capacity utilization is projected to rise to 92% in 2026, inventory levels have been compressed from four months in 2024 to just one month, and some major manufacturers' order books are already filled through the first quarter of 2027 — meaning existing capacity is running near full. Expanding capacity is not something that happens overnight. Optical fiber preform expansion involves the installation of deposition equipment and process setup, requiring roughly 18 to 24 months from planning to production. Even if manufacturers launch expansion plans now, new supply will take time to come online, making it difficult to effectively ease the shortage in the near term. Demand remains robust. The research estimates global optical fiber demand at 577 million fiber-kilometers in 2026, with growth driven mainly by data center construction, which accounts for roughly 18% to 20% of total demand and is expected to rise further to 30% to 35% in 2027. In addition to large Cloud Service Providers continuing to expand AI data centers, chipmakers and telecom operators are also investing in related infrastructure, driving optical fiber consumption for data center interconnect and high-capacity backbone networks. The supply-demand imbalance is already reflected in spot quotes across optical fiber product categories. Broken down by application, bend-insensitive fiber used for cabling inside data centers has seen the steepest increase, with average prices in 2026 more than 5x higher than in 2025. AI backbone fiber used for data center interconnect and high-capacity backbone networks has risen about 2.8x year-on-year. Mainstream fiber for telecom services has also climbed about 3.7x. Note: Year-on-year increases reflect the change in 2026 average prices versus 2025 average prices. Faced with persistently tightening supply, telecom operators' procurement strategies have clearly shifted. The previous model centered on short-term purchasing is gradually giving way to long-term contracts that lock in resources in advance. For example, Verizon and Corning signed a multi-year supply agreement in September 2026, planning to secure more than 129 million fiber-kilometers (about 80 million miles) of high-density optical fiber and connectivity solutions between 2027 and 2032. In addition to supporting broadband buildouts, the fiber will be used for high-capacity backbone networks connecting AI data centers. The nature of this tightness differs from past telecom buildout cycles. The research argues that the root of this shortage is the continuous expansion of new AI data center-related demand, rather than a cyclical rebound in traditional telecom capital spending. With supply unable to ramp up quickly in the short term and demand growing steadily, it will become increasingly common for telecom operators and large infrastructure players to lock in optical fiber resources through long-term contracts in advance. For the industry chain, optical fiber's shift from a buyer's market to a seller's market means upstream preform and fiber manufacturers have significantly strengthened their pricing power, along with extended order visibility. Conversely, telecom carriers and data center operators face rising construction costs, making procurement timing and cost control increasingly important. The market's focus has shifted from "is there demand" to "can we get the material" — and the pace at which optical fiber supply chain capacity comes online will be a key indicator for tracking AI infrastructure progress over the next two years.

artigo.texto: SK On Develops CNT Powder Process to Cut LFP Costs, Wins Top Prize at Future Technology Institute Conference SK On has developed a new process that can lower the manufacturing cost of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery cathodes. The technology replaces the expensive carbon nanotube (CNT) paste previously used with a powder form while maintaining equivalent performance, and the company plans to review its applicability to actual mass production processes. The research achievement was selected as the grand prize winner at the "2nd Future Technology Institute Academic Conference" held over two days starting October 14 at the Future Technology Institute in Yuseong-gu, Daejeon. This year's event was held under the theme "The Future We Create," with SK On President Lee Yong-wook and Future Technology Institute Director Park Ki-soo in attendance. A total of approximately 300 research projects were submitted across six categories: battery process, cell, system, materials, next-generation technology, and platform. This represents an increase of about 15% compared to last year. Award winners were selected through a blind review process based on five criteria: topic relevance, research differentiation, contribution to outcomes, creativity, and practicality. The grand prize-winning research team secured technology to uniformly disperse CNT powder into cathode materials. CNT serves as a conductive agent that facilitates electron movement within battery electrodes. The use of powder form was highly evaluated for its potential to replace the relatively expensive paste process and reduce manufacturing costs. SK On plans to review whether the technology can be applied to actual production processes. The top excellence award went to a research team that developed electrode design technology for large-area pouch-type lithium-metal batteries. The excellence award was given to a team that developed a model predicting capacity degradation and internal resistance based on repeated battery charge-discharge cycles and storage conditions. The conference also featured a technology exhibition showcasing key research achievements. Researchers directly explained their technologies and conducted Q&A sessions, with the exhibition operated through on-site voting by members to evaluate the technologies. The keynote speech was delivered by Professor Lee Yong-min of Yonsei University. He introduced the current status and outlook of digital twin technology, which implements actual battery designs in virtual space to analyze performance and condition. In the subsequent Q&A session, he exchanged views on battery technology with SK On members and discussed the latest trends in industry-academia collaboration. Strengthening LFP Battery Price Competitiveness SK On's process development aligns with the growing importance of LFP battery price competitiveness in the global battery market. While LFP batteries have lower energy density than nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) batteries, they are cheaper to produce and offer higher thermal stability, driving rapid demand growth alongside the expansion of electric vehicle adoption. With Chinese battery manufacturers leading the LFP market, South Korean companies are also making all-out efforts to secure cost-reduction technologies. The process of replacing CNT paste with powder carries significant meaning in this price competition. Paste form offers the advantage of easy dispersion but contains solvents, making it more expensive with higher storage and transportation costs. Converting to powder form can simultaneously reduce material and logistics costs while maintaining the same performance. However, the technical difficulty of uniformly dispersing powder is high, making it a key question whether the research team's achievement can translate into actual mass production. The top excellence award for lithium-metal battery electrode design technology is also noteworthy. Lithium-metal batteries are considered a next-generation technology that can significantly increase energy density by replacing the graphite anode of conventional lithium-ion batteries with lithium metal. Electrode design for large-area pouch-type cells is one of the key challenges for commercialization. Institutionalizing as a Platform for Sharing Research Achievements SK On plans to make the academic conference a regular event to expand technical exchange and collaboration among researchers. The company views a systematic structure for sharing and evaluating internal research achievements as a foundation for enhancing next-generation battery technology competitiveness. President Lee Yong-wook said, "The Future Technology Institute Academic Conference, now in its second year, is an important venue where our members' challenges and research achievements translate into SK On's technology competitiveness. We will further spread a research-centric culture and continue technological innovation to lead the next-generation battery market." SK On currently operates production bases in the U.S. states of Georgia and Kentucky, as well as Hungary and China, while simultaneously preparing for LFP battery mass production and developing next-generation technologies such as lithium-metal and solid-state batteries. How quickly the research achievements from this conference can be applied to actual products and processes will serve as a test of the company's future technology competitiveness.
