artigo.texto: Shinhan Asset Management's SOL All-Solid-State Battery ETF Ranks No. 1 Among South Korean Equity ETFs With 22.76% Three-Month Return Shinhan Asset Management's "SOL All-Solid-State Battery & Silicon Anode" exchange-traded fund (ETF) has posted the highest return among South Korean-listed equity ETFs over the past three months. As of the 16th of this month, the product's three-month return stood at 22.76%, ranking first among South Korean-listed equity ETFs excluding leveraged and inverse products. That is 39.66 percentage points ahead of the KOSPI's -16.90% over the same period. The ETF concentrates investments in key companies tied to all-solid-state batteries and silicon anodes. All-solid-state batteries replace conventional liquid electrolytes with solid materials to boost safety and energy density, and expectations for their commercialization have recently been rising. Major holdings include Samsung SDI, which is pursuing mass production of all-solid-state batteries; LG Energy Solution, a key energy storage system (ESS) player; EcoPro BM, an all-solid-state cathode materials company; ISU Specialty Chemical, a lithium sulfide-related company; battery materials company Lotte Energy Materials; and silicon anode company Daejoo Electronic Materials. The portfolio is built around next-generation battery technology advancement and industrial structural change rather than short-term shifts in electric vehicle demand. The secondary battery sector has recently been shaking off a prolonged correction driven by slowing electric vehicle demand and securing new growth drivers. Rising ESS demand from the spread of artificial intelligence (AI) data centers is translating into improved earnings at battery companies, and investment sentiment is recovering as expectations build for commercialization of next-generation technologies such as all-solid-state batteries and silicon anodes. The fact that secondary battery-related ETFs have ranked among the top performers while the South Korean semiconductor sector's rally has stalled is seen in the same light. ESS is emerging as a key growth driver reshaping a secondary battery industry that had been centered on electric vehicles. As power demand from AI data centers grows and renewable energy generation expands, the importance of stable power supply and energy storage has increased. LG Energy Solution posted preliminary third-quarter operating profit of 756 billion won (approximately $566.2 million), topping market expectations. The company's earnings recovery is attributed to expansion of its North American ESS business and conversion of production facilities. The fact that commercialization timelines for next-generation batteries are taking concrete shape is also working in favor of investment sentiment. Samsung SDI is pursuing technology development and cooperation with customers with the goal of mass-producing all-solid-state batteries in 2027. South Korean materials companies are also moving to secure production capacity for key raw materials, and the South Korean government plans to support next-generation battery research and development worth about 400 billion won (approximately $299.6 million) over five years starting in 2027. All-solid-state batteries are expected to see their applications broaden beyond electric vehicles to humanoid robots and the aerospace sector. Kim Jung-hyun, head of Shinhan Asset Management's ETF business group, said, "The secondary battery industry is securing a new demand base through ESS, and growth drivers are diversifying as commercialization of next-generation technologies such as all-solid-state batteries and silicon anodes becomes visible." He added, "Going forward, earnings recovery through ESS and competitiveness in next-generation technologies such as all-solid-state batteries will be key factors determining corporate value."

artigo.texto: South Korea's LS Electric Signs approximately $125 Million AI Data Center Power Distribution Deal with U.S. Big Tech South Korea's LS Electric (010120) has signed a long-term supply agreement (LTA) worth approximately 169 billion won (approximately $126.8 million) with a U.S. Big Tech company for power distribution solutions for artificial intelligence (AI) data centers. As AI infrastructure expansion drives a clear shift in power equipment procurement from short-term orders to long-term volume commitments, analysts say the company has secured a bridgehead to broaden its supply range from high-voltage switchgear to high-end product lines. LS Electric said in a regulatory filing on the 19th that it had signed a $125.23 million (~169 billion won) contract to supply power distribution solutions for North American data centers. The contract runs for two years from 2027 to 2028, and the order value corresponds to volumes scheduled for delivery in 2027. The 2028 supply volume will be finalized through additional negotiations with the company. The main supply item is 38kV-class high-voltage switchgear. This equipment distributes extra-high-voltage power coming from outside at appropriate levels to each computing facility inside the data center and cuts off circuits when abnormal currents such as leakage or short circuits occur, protecting critical servers. In AI data centers where large-scale computation runs around the clock, continuity of power quality and equipment reliability determine operational success, and analysts say demand for high-reliability distribution equipment is bound to grow structurally. Global Big Tech companies have recently favored long-term supply agreements to secure stable power solutions for AI data center construction. As data center construction demand grows rapidly, the view that power equipment supply contracts themselves will be reorganized around long-term deals is gaining traction. Some skeptics argue that returns on AI infrastructure investment may be short-lived, but large-scale data center expansion continues on the judgment that AI will become fundamental infrastructure going forward. Building on this contract, LS Electric is also negotiating additional supply of data center-tailored power equipment such as low-voltage switchgear, distribution-class transformers, and RMUs (high-voltage gas-insulated load break switches). The goal is to expand its supply scope from a single high-voltage switchgear item to data center power infrastructure overall. The company is also strengthening its local North American response system. Centered on LS Electric Utah in Cedar City, Utah, and the Bastrop Campus in Texas, it has built a value chain that completes sales, design, production, and service locally, supplying products tailored to each customer's needs. The strategy is seen as aimed at reducing tariff and logistics risks while improving delivery responsiveness. An LS Electric official said, "Our world-class data center solution technology and the trust built through executing customized projects led to this long-term supply agreement," adding, "We will continue to expand supply of high-value-added products for data centers to secure a stable revenue base and maximize profitability." The deal is significant in that it is a case of North American AI data center-driven demand for power equipment translating into long-term results for a South Korean manufacturer, and could lead to expanded exports of adjacent product groups such as transformers and circuit breakers. However, since the contract value is limited to the 2027 portion and 2028 volumes remain undetermined, actual revenue recognition is expected to depend on the outcome of further negotiations and data center construction schedules.

artigo.texto: Li Xiang on "making cars doesn't mean making batteries": Li Auto aims to be the automaker that understands batteries best On October 19, Li Xiang, chairman and CEO of Li Auto (02015.HK), posted on social media to lay out the industry value of automakers developing core battery technology in-house. He argued that ultra-large-scale industries need "two legs advancing alternately"—one being specialized suppliers with a deep understanding of the product, the other being OEMs that delve deeply into core technologies. "The world needs both battery companies that best understand smart electric vehicles and smart EV companies that best understand batteries," Li wrote. He did not name names directly, but the remarks were widely interpreted as a response to earlier comments by Ni Jun, chief manufacturing officer of CATL (300750.SZ). In mid-to-late September, asked about automakers developing their own batteries at CATL's "Global Quality Open Month" event, Ni said: "Making cars doesn't mean making batteries. You still need professionals to do professional things." He also noted that how far a car can go and how long it lasts "is not determined by the best cell, but by the worst one." This time Li did not maintain a confrontational stance. He stressed that partner battery suppliers remain partners, and that which steps to do in-house and which to do with partners are choices made at different stages, with only one criterion—which approach is better for users. He also said Li Auto will hold an electric technology launch event on October 20 to announce its latest technological progress. This was not the first time Li has spoken publicly about the in-house development route. On September 28, he published a long post responding to discussion about "de-CATL-ization," saying zero-sum thinking is not how Li Auto defines its in-house strategy, and describing CATL as Li Auto's "comrade-in-arms." "Self-developed and self-manufactured PACK, self-developed cells with contract manufacturing" Li Auto sums up its battery approach as "self-developed and self-manufactured PACK, self-developed cells with contract manufacturing": Li Auto leads cell design and R&D, production is contracted to battery makers such as Sunwoda (300207.SZ) and CALB (03931.HK), while the battery pack, BMS and thermal management are developed and manufactured in-house by Li Auto. Capital-level ties are already in place. On September 4, Sunwoda announced that Li Auto had injected 2.65 billion yuan (approximately $396.6 million) into Sunwoda Power for an 8.79% stake; Li Auto and its affiliates hold a combined ~11.17%, making it the second-largest shareholder of Sunwoda Power. Business registration information shows that Shandong Li Auto Battery Technology Co., Ltd. was recently registered in Xuecheng District, Zaozhuang City, Shandong Province, with registered capital of 10 million yuan (approximately $1.5 million), wholly owned by Beijing Li Auto Co., Ltd., with a business scope focused on battery components and energy recovery systems. In October 2025, Li Auto had also set up a joint venture with Sunwoda Power, Shandong Li Auto Battery Co., Ltd., with registered capital of 300 million yuan (approximately $44.9 million), each holding 50%. The pace of battery deployment is accelerating in tandem. The L8, L6 and i8 already use self-developed batteries; new-generation MEGA models ordered through the Li Auto app from September 7 switch to self-developed 5C ternary lithium batteries, with deliveries expected to begin in November; the i9 launched in mid-September still uses CATL 5C batteries in its first batch; and the 2026 i6 to be launched in the fourth quarter will carry both self-developed 5C batteries and Li Auto's self-developed Mach chip, with plans to no longer offer a CATL version. Note: The above deployment plans are compiled from public reports; specific configurations are subject to Li Auto's official announcements. System integration innovation becomes the focus of competition and cooperation On cooperation models, Li Auto takes an open approach. Li Auto President Ma Donghui said in an earlier interview that as sales grow and capacity demand rises, the company very much wants to work with leading battery makers, but the prerequisite is that underlying data must be connected. He noted that OEMs do not think only from the perspective of battery components, but instead consider the battery together with all electrical components, thermal management and control systems of the vehicle, designing collaboratively from the vehicle architecture. This points to a shift in the innovation path for power batteries: as OEMs become more deeply involved in battery R&D, the industry's innovation focus may move from the performance of a single component to system integration innovation between the battery and the vehicle. For battery companies, this means the competitive dimension extends from cell metrics to data interfaces, thermal management and vehicle integration capability; for automakers, a model of parallel in-house development and contract manufacturing allows them to hold core definition rights while avoiding heavy-asset investment. In his latest post, Li reiterated that walking on two legs is not one company's choice but the entire industry's, and the progress it drives ultimately benefits users. He also warned that if the industry relies on only one leg for a long time, hopping on one foot is hard to sustain over long distances, and companies can easily fall into scale competition while the performance, quality, safety and lifespan that users truly care about stall in place. Notably, the pace of Li Auto's in-house battery push is rising in step with its supply chain bargaining power. From injecting capital into Sunwoda Power to setting up a battery technology company, and now to the gradual switch of mainstream models to self-developed cells, Li Auto is turning batteries from a purchased part into a defining component. artigo.texto: BYD Exports '9-Minute Charging' Ecosystem to Indonesia, Putting Hyundai Motor and South Korean Batteries on the Back Foot in Southeast Asia China's BYD has moved into overseas markets by building an ultra-fast charging network in Indonesia that can charge an electric-vehicle battery in nine minutes. Under an "ecosystem export" model that bundles finished vehicles, batteries and charging infrastructure into a single package, the push is increasing pressure on Hyundai Motor and Kia, which trail China in both charging speed and infrastructure, as well as on South Korea's three major battery makers. BYD said on Oct. 19 that it unveiled plans on Oct. 14 in Jakarta to build a flash-charging network of up to 1,500 kW and simultaneously introduced the new D9 and Z9GT from Denza, its premium brand. The project marks the first time BYD's ultra-fast charging technology has been deployed outside China. According to the company, the flash chargers combine an energy storage system (ESS) and are the world's first to use a T-shaped suspended design that reduces the weight burden of the charging cable. They also feature plug-and-charge functionality, with authentication and payment completed simply by connecting the vehicle. BYD plans to install chargers first at 10 Denza showrooms to create customer touchpoints, then gradually expand to public charging networks starting at the end of the year. The network will be open to vehicles of all brands, but top speeds will be available only on cars equipped with compatible batteries. Charging performance reaches 70% from a 10% state of charge in five minutes and 97% in nine minutes. The second-generation Blade Battery underpinning this is a lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery that BYD first unveiled in China in March, with energy density 5% higher than the first generation. Even at minus 30 degrees Celsius, it charges from 20% to 97% in 12 minutes. The Z9GT equipped with this battery claims a driving range of 1,036 kilometers. The new D9, a luxury multi-purpose vehicle (MPV), is the first model to apply both the second-generation Blade Battery and flash-charging technology. Indonesia is the testing ground for the packaged market entry BYD is pushing. Since entering the market in 2024, BYD has sold Chinese-made finished vehicles while receiving duty-free import benefits in exchange for committing to invest in a local plant. When the local production obligation began in 2026-2027, BYD completed a plant in Subang, West Java (annual capacity of up to 150,000 units) on the third of last month and halted finished-vehicle imports. It plans to sell down remaining inventory and then replace imports with locally produced vehicles. BYD and Denza are said to have captured 40% of Indonesia's local EV market within two years of entry. However, the pace of building overseas charging networks is slower than originally planned. In June, the company outlined a plan to build 3,000 stations in Europe by the end of this year, but at this month's Paris Motor Show the target was revised to 100 by year-end and 3,000 by the end of 2027 — effectively a one-year delay. The gap with South Korean competitors is evident in the numbers. Hyundai Motor's Ioniq 5 and Kia's EV6 take about 18 minutes to charge from 10% to 80% on 350 kW chargers — more than three times the speed BYD is touting, on a simple comparison. There is also a gap in exporting charging ecosystems. Hyundai Motor and Kia, through Ionna — a U.S. charging joint venture founded by eight automakers — expanded their U.S. charging sites from 90 at the start of this year to more than 200 by mid-October. Another 80 are under construction, with a goal of 30,000 fast chargers by 2030. But because Ionna is a consortium jointly funded by multiple companies, its structure differs from BYD-style vertical integration, in which a single company sells batteries, vehicles and chargers together. In Indonesia, Chinese capital continues to flow into battery value-chain investment. A consortium including affiliates of China's CATL has launched an integrated project worth about $6 billion (approximately 8 trillion won) spanning nickel mining through battery production and recycling. The LG Energy Solution consortium, by contrast, withdrew last year from an 11 trillion won (approximately $8.3 billion) battery value-chain project. The Indonesian government is bringing in new Chinese investors to carry the follow-up project forward. Chinese dominance is also clear in global market share. According to SNE Research, in terms of global EV battery usage from January to August this year, CATL held 39.4% and BYD 15.1%, with seven Chinese companies combined accounting for 73.3%. LG Energy Solution held third place at 8.1%, but that was down 1.5 percentage points from a year earlier. Analysts say that while South Korea's three battery makers are preparing to mass-produce LFP batteries, China has already entered an ultra-fast charging race built on LFP. "China has moved beyond competing on battery performance to a stage where it sells the charging experience itself," a battery industry official said. "With South Korea's structure, in which finished vehicles, batteries and charging infrastructure operate separately, we could lose emerging markets like Southeast Asia first." Stella Li, BYD Group's executive vice president and CEO of its Asia-Pacific auto business, said, "BYD's technological innovation has gone beyond simply making and selling cars," adding, "We believe technological innovation can create greater value for society and bring the benefits of advanced technology to more people." The market is watching the project as a variable that could reshape competition in Southeast Asia's EV market. artigo.texto: Chinese EV and Battery Makers Build 26 Plants in Europe, Sidestepping Tariffs for Duty-Free Market Grab Chinese EV and battery companies are rapidly expanding local production bases across Europe, effectively sidestepping tariff barriers. The number of Chinese-owned EV and battery plants either under construction or already operating in Europe has reached 26. Chinese companies have shifted away from the strategy of manufacturing cheaply at home and exporting, instead building factories directly in Europe to sell tariff-free. In Szeged, southern Hungary, BYD—China's top EV maker—is building a factory on a 3 million square meter site, roughly the size of Seoul's Yeouido district. Once completed by the end of this year, BYD will become the first Chinese passenger EV company to be fully exempt from the European Union's 27% tariff. CATL, the world's largest battery maker, has built its largest battery plant outside China in Debrecen, Hungary. The facility, backed by a €7.3 billion (approximately $8.2 billion) investment, has an annual production capacity of 100 gigawatt-hours (GWh). The first of three planned plants began operations earlier this month, with European automakers including Mercedes-Benz having placed advance orders covering several years of output. Jin Liang, CATL's Debrecen plant manager, said: "Given the lower skill levels of workers in Europe, we have set a higher automation rate than in China. We plan to re-export this system to China soon, as it represents our most advanced facilities to date." CATL chose European production to avoid EU tariff and regulatory uncertainty. Unlike the United States, the EU does not outright block Chinese battery makers from entering, but it is preparing to introduce the Industrial Acceleration Act (IAA), which provides incentives to companies producing within Europe. EVs must be assembled in the EU and source more than 70% of components—excluding batteries—from within the region to qualify for subsidies. "This will serve as a base that eliminates uncertainties such as future EU export restrictions or tariff hikes," he said. "CATL will make in Europe, work for Europe, and become a member of Europe." Europe's Battery Self-Sufficiency Ambitions Collapse The intensifying Chinese offensive comes against the backdrop of Europe's own battery industry collapse. Northvolt, once hailed as "Europe's battery hope," filed for bankruptcy in March last year after failing to withstand production disruptions and funding shortages. Its core assets—the Swedish plant and R&D facilities—were transferred to U.S. battery company Lyten in February this year. ACC, a battery joint venture co-invested by Stellantis, Mercedes-Benz, and TotalEnergies, has also scrapped plans to build plants in Germany and Italy. Europe's "battery self-sufficiency" vision has effectively crumbled. European automakers are also struggling with the EV transition. Volkswagen Group's operating margin fell to 3.8% in the first half of this year, its worst performance since COVID-19. The company has begun cutting approximately 100,000 jobs and reducing vehicle lineup and production capacity. Stellantis and Ford are handing over some of their European production facilities to Chinese companies. Kilian Csaba, president of the Hungarian Automobile Association, said: "After Europe's manufacturing industry, including automobiles, collapsed, Chinese companies are rapidly filling the void. This will pose a major threat to South Korean companies as well." Why Hungary Became the Chosen Hub CATL selected Hungary as its European base due to geographic advantages. Key materials and components can be sourced from Hungary, Poland, and other nearby countries, while proximity to automotive plants in Germany and elsewhere reduces logistics costs. The Debrecen region has a dense battery value chain, including South Korea's EcoPro BM cathode material plant and China's Semcorp separator plant. In northwestern Hungary, Solus Advanced Materials operates a battery copper foil plant and Soulbrain runs an electrolyte facility. Expanding the scope to nearby Poland, Belgium's Umicore also operates a cathode material plant. Kaderják Péter, president of the Hungarian Battery Industry Association, explained: "With environmental regulations tightening across Europe recently, obtaining permits for new battery plants has become more difficult. Companies that have already secured or are preparing facilities will hold a clear advantage." China's Accelerating Encroachment on the European Market The number of Chinese battery companies building or operating plants in Europe has reached 14. Gotion plans to establish plants totaling 50 GWh in Spain and Slovakia in partnership with Volkswagen. EVE Energy has begun operating a 28 GWh battery plant in Hungary. The total battery cell plant capacity Chinese companies plan to operate in Europe reaches 282.8 GWh—far exceeding the 160 GWh European production capacity of South Korea's three major battery makers. The European battery market landscape has shifted dramatically. In the January-August period this year, the top seven Chinese companies held a 67.8% share of the European market, surging 26.8 percentage points from 41.0% in 2023. Over the same period, South Korea's three major battery makers saw their share halve from 55.6% to 28.7%. Chinese companies are expanding not only production bases but also R&D and design centers across Europe. Geely Group has established centers in Frankfurt, Germany and Gothenburg, Sweden; BYD in Budapest, Hungary; and XPeng and Xiaomi in Munich, Germany—all vying for European talent. Note: Chinese companies are pursuing or operating a total of 26 EV and battery plants in Europe.

artigo.texto: Uncertain carbon credit revenues in agriculture are making it difficult to assess how much projects can earn beyond their core business activities. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, deputy head of Agribank’s Steering Committee for Environmental, Social, and Governance, highlighted these constraints and more at VIR’s seminar on credit policy and the carbon market last week in Hanoi. She said financing arrangements needed to reflect project viability, repayment capacity, and the timing of expected returns. “Carbon credit revenue can supplement project returns, but it cannot be treated as a reliable source of repayment before the conditions for generating and selling those credits are established,” said Ha. Vietnam’s shift towards lower-emission production is creating funding needs beyond equipment and technology. Businesses must also pay for project preparation, environmental monitoring, and changes to production processes, while ensuring that investments generate sufficient returns to service debt. “The domestic carbon market remains at an early stage, making the commercial contribution of carbon credits dependent on project readiness and market development,” she added. Vietnam has continued to develop the regulatory framework for emissions reduction and carbon market activities, including plans for a domestic carbon exchange and rules governing international carbon credit transactions. Greenhouse gas inventory requirements have also expanded. The number of covered facilities rose from 1,912 in 2022 to 2,441 in September 2026. Criteria have also been expanded for identifying green projects, including circular economy activities. However, meeting environmental requirements does not in itself make a project commercially viable or eligible for bank financing. Businesses may still need feasibility studies, technical assessments, environmental monitoring systems, and agreements covering production, purchasing, and the distribution of financial benefits. In agriculture and rural development, low-emission rice cultivation, livestock waste treatment, sustainable forestry, and biomass utilisation require funding at different stages of the value chain. Financing must account for the needs of farmers, cooperatives, and processors, as well as seasonal production cycles, market access and operating costs. Across the value chain Green projects require funding at several stages, from feasibility studies and environmental assessments to equipment, working capital, monitoring, and compliance. For small producers, the cost of preparing a project can be a barrier before any return is generated. Once operations begin, maintenance and verification add to expenditure, while purchasing and processing businesses need capital to handle agricultural output. For that reason, Ha emphasised the need to align financing with project costs and cash flow cycles. In agriculture, adopting new cultivation methods can increase expenses before additional income materialises, while seasonal production and delays between delivery and payment can put pressure on borrowers’ liquidity. “Financing arrangements need to reflect the costs incurred at each stage of a project, the timing of expected cash flows and the borrower’s repayment capacity,” Ha said. Commercial loans can finance equipment and working capital where credible repayment sources exist, while technical assistance, concessional funding, and guarantees may help cover project preparation costs or address specific risks. The source of repayment is particularly important for projects that expect to earn carbon credit revenue. Reduced energy and material consumption can lower operating costs directly, but income from carbon credits depends on project eligibility, verification, buyer demand, and payment terms. “Businesses cannot treat carbon credit revenue in the same way as savings from reduced energy or material consumption. Income from credits depends on whether emissions reductions can be verified and the credits sold,” she added. Agribank’s existing agricultural lending provides a channel for financing investment in lower-emission production, according to Ha. By mid-2026, the bank’s assets exceeded $108 billion, deposits surpassed $100 billion and outstanding loans topped $80 billion. At the end of August, lending to agriculture, farmers, and rural areas exceeded $53.6 billion, equivalent to 64.7 per cent of total outstanding loans. She also outlined the bank’s reach among smaller borrowers. As of July 31, Agribank’s more than 58,000 lending groups comprised over 910,000 members, with total loans exceeding $8.64 billion. “These established lending relationships could provide a route to identifying farmers and cooperatives seeking to invest in resource efficiency or emissions reduction. However, such projects would still need to meet the bank’s lending requirements, including those relating to project readiness and repayment capacity,” Ha shared. Agribank’s green credit programmes provide further funding channels. Its green credit portfolio stood at nearly $1.2 billion at the end of March. For the year, the bank has allocated $120 million to a programme targeting individual customers and $2 billion to clean and high-tech agriculture. It also operates a programme worth at least $1.2 billion to support production, processing, and consumption under the Mekong Delta’s one-million-hectare project for high-quality, low-emission rice cultivation. The rice initiative illustrates the need to coordinate financing across the agricultural supply chain. Farmers may require seasonal loans to adopt new cultivation methods, while cooperatives need equipment and working capital to coordinate production and collect data. Technical partners can provide training and support environmental measurement, while processors need funds to purchase and handle the crop. “Financing needs to be considered across the value chain, from production and data collection to purchasing and processing,” Ha said. artigo.texto: The global data center fire detection and suppression market is projected to more than double in value by 2035 as operators respond to higher rack densities, lithium-ion battery hazards and tighter restrictions on clean agents, according to a new report from DC Market Insights. The market, valued at $4.47 billion in 2025, is forecast to reach $10.35 billion by 2035, representing a compound annual growth rate of 8.75%, the report said. Annual data center capacity additions of about 12 GW are expected to support approximately $2.95 billion in new-build fire protection spending. Demand is being driven by hyperscale, colocation, enterprise and edge facilities that are adding denser computing infrastructure to support artificial intelligence and other high-performance workloads. Lithium-ion uninterruptible power supply and rack battery deployments are also changing detection and suppression requirements. Because thermal runaway develops differently from a conventional electrical fire, operators are placing greater emphasis on off-gas sensing, localized protection and revised response strategies in areas with large stored-energy inventories. At the same time, restrictions on some PFAS- and HFC-based products are tightening the clean-agent supply environment and increasing interest in water mist, hybrid and alternative clean-agent systems. DC Market Insights projects the water mist and hybrid suppression segment will reach $1.14 billion by 2035. “Fire protection is becoming more specialized as data centers combine higher energy density with batteries, liquid cooling and more complex electrical infrastructure,” said Amit Jain, senior consultant for ICT and emerging technologies at DC Market Insights and author of the report. “Operators are reassessing where clean agents still make sense, how early off-gas detection can reduce battery risk and how water-based systems can protect high-value equipment without creating unacceptable downtime. That makes codes, testing and lifecycle maintenance as important as the initial suppression hardware.” North America accounted for 40% of the market’s value in 2025, followed by Asia-Pacific at 28% and Europe at 23.5%. The Middle East and Africa represented 4.3%, while Latin America accounted for 4.2%. The report said regional performance reflects differences in hyperscale investment, AI adoption, installed data center capacity, power availability, supply chains and the pace of new construction and retrofit projects. Inspection, testing and maintenance services are expected to reach $2.66 billion by 2035, giving fire protection providers a recurring revenue opportunity beyond equipment sales. Companies profiled in the report include Johnson Controls, Honeywell, Siemens Smart Infrastructure, Minimax Viking Group, Halma, Hochiki, Fike, Victaulic, Wagner Group, Securiton, Firetrace International and APi Group. Recent developments cited include Johnson Controls’ August 2026 launch of Simplex Incident Manager and Autocall Fire Site Administrator workstations for large facilities, with support for as many as 250,000 devices. The report also noted FM’s July 2026 revision of Data Sheet 5-32, which advised against clean-agent systems for rack-mounted lithium-ion battery units above 20 kWh.

For energy sector decision-makers, selecting a bankable battery cell supplier requires evaluating proven delivery capacity alongside product readiness. Broad shipment rankings provide a starting point, but they seldom address a crucial question: which supplier offers the right cell design for 2-hour, 4-hour, or long-duration 8-hour storage? Using SMM’s full-year 2025 ranking together with InfoLink’s full-year 2025 and H1 2026 shipment data, this comparison focuses on five manufacturers that repeatedly appear in the leading utility-scale group: CATL, HiTHIUM, EVE Energy, BYD, and CALB. Each company is benchmarked by strategic focus, cell-to-system fit, product readiness, and global delivery. It provides a practical reference for comparing leading battery cell manufacturers and matching their cell platforms to specific utility-scale BESS duration requirements. How to Evaluate Battery Cell Manufacturers for Energy Storage Projects? Shipment rankings reflect volume, not project fit. Project developers, EPCs, system integrators, and procurement teams should evaluate suppliers across four core dimensions. 1. Strategic Focus and Application Coverage Identify whether a company follows a dual-track EV-and-BESS model or focuses entirely on storage. This helps indicate how directly its product roadmap addresses stationary cycling, storage duration, and system-integration requirements. 2. Cell Portfolio and Duration Match Check C-rate, cycle profile, voltage, and duration compatibility. The industry transition from 314Ah to 500Ah+ and kAh-class cells aims to optimize Balance of Plant (BOP) and reduce Levelized Cost of Storage (LCOS) via higher density—gains that must be verified at the system level. 3. Product Evidence and Commercialization Separate product announcements from commercial shipments. Review applicable IEC 62619 compliance documentation, UL 9540A thermal-runaway test reports, and UL 9540 system certification where required. Independent technical due diligence by firms such as DNV or Black & Veatch can support lender and insurer review but does not by itself establish bankability. 4. Manufacturing and Global Delivery Review manufacturing consistency, committed capacity, project references, regional logistics, local field support, and warranty execution over the project lifecycle. InfoLink’s H1 2025 utility-scale report also placed CATL and HiTHIUM in the top two, with CALB and EVE Energy tied for third. - Rise of Pure-Play Storage Specialists: Positions within the leading group continue to rotate. HiTHIUM moved from third in SMM’s 2024 total-shipment ranking to second in 2025, illustrating the growing market presence of manufacturers focused specifically on stationary energy storage. - H1 2026 Ranking Dynamics: InfoLink’s H1 2026 total-shipment ranking retained CATL, HiTHIUM, EVE Energy, BYD, and CALB as the top five. In the utility-scale segment, the order was CATL, HiTHIUM, BYD, CALB, and EVE Energy. artigo.texto: Líderes de pensamento Estamos buscando no lugar errado para resolver o desafio da sustentabilidade dos data centers de IA? Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google Cadeias de suprimentos mais inteligentes podem ser a chave para reduzir o impacto ambiental da expansão da IA Líderes em sustentabilidade de todo o mundo debatem o paradoxo da IA. De um lado, a pegada ambiental da IA está aumentando. Do outro, a IA está ajudando ativamente a resolver alguns dos problemas de sustentabilidade mais desafiadores do mundo real. Os benefícios da IA não se limitam ao aumento da produtividade nas empresas ou à automação de processos; são muito mais amplos e têm consequências mais significativas. Quando aplicada à pesquisa científica, à saúde e aos sistemas de energia, a IA tem o poder e o potencial de salvar vidas. Aplicadas aos desafios da sustentabilidade, suas capacidades de previsão e otimização podem reduzir o desperdício, o consumo de energia e as emissões. A Agência Internacional de Energia (IEA) estima que, se as aplicações atuais de IA para processos industriais fossem adotadas em todo o setor, somente a economia de energia superaria o consumo total atual de energia do México. Embora não possamos fechar os olhos para a atual pegada ambiental da IA e do ecossistema de data centers, também não podemos ignorar o impacto significativo e as promessas que essa tecnologia oferece. Abandonar a IA agora nos impediria de aproveitar todos os seus benefícios. No entanto, para concretizar seu potencial, precisamos desenvolver a infraestrutura física que a sustenta e encontrar maneiras de fazer isso de forma sustentável. Até agora, as discussões sobre sustentabilidade e IA têm se concentrado, em grande medida, nos data centers. Mas, para reduzir de forma significativa a pegada ambiental da IA, também precisamos olhar para além das paredes dos data centers e acompanhar o percurso dos materiais, equipamentos e componentes de hardware ao longo das etapas anteriores da cadeia. Uma das formas mais eficazes de reduzir a pegada ambiental da IA é otimizar as cadeias de suprimentos globais que sustentam a infraestrutura de IA. A verdadeira pegada ambiental da IA também inclui as cadeias de suprimentos Em muitos aspectos, é compreensível que as discussões sobre o impacto ambiental da IA se concentrem atualmente nos data centers. Hoje, as cargas de trabalho de IA representam cerca de 20% do uso dos data centers. Prevê-se que esse percentual dobre, chegando a 40% até 2030. A IA exige enorme capacidade computacional, que, por sua vez, requer grandes quantidades de eletricidade para funcionar e de água para resfriar os sistemas. A IEA informa que um data center típico dedicado à IA pode consumir tanta eletricidade quanto 100.000 residências. Algumas das mentes mais brilhantes em sustentabilidade, design e infraestrutura defendem a adoção em larga escala de energia renovável para abastecer data centers, práticas de construção sustentável em todas as instalações e inovações em resfriamento que usem pouca água. Essas questões são fundamentais, mas abordam apenas parte do problema. As mudanças devem começar pela otimização das cadeias de suprimentos com o uso de IA. A pegada ambiental da IA começa muito antes de um data center entrar em operação. O data center é o ponto final de milhares de cadeias de suprimentos extensas, responsáveis pela produção e pelo transporte de semicondutores, servidores, equipamentos de rede, transformadores, equipamentos de manobra e proteção elétrica, sistemas de resfriamento, aço e concreto. As cadeias de suprimentos desses produtos abrangem vários fornecedores em redes globais. Esse sistema costuma ficar de fora das discussões sobre sustentabilidade da IA. No entanto, essas cadeias de suprimentos representam uma parcela significativa da pegada ambiental total da IA e devem ser otimizadas para reduzir o desperdício e as emissões. Como cadeias de suprimentos sustentáveis, impulsionadas por IA, reduzem o impacto ambiental dos data centers Uma análise de 2026 de 112 estudos revisados por pares, publicada na revista Cogent Engineering, constatou que a IA pode desempenhar um papel transformador na otimização das cadeias de suprimentos, aprimorando seus processos, o compartilhamento de informações e a transparência. Veja como a otimização das cadeias de suprimentos com IA reduz o impacto ambiental da IA: - Fabricação mais eficiente: Quando aplicada à fabricação, a IA pode ajudar a reduzir o desperdício ao otimizar o consumo de energia, identificar problemas nos equipamentos que causam impactos na sustentabilidade e revelar processos ineficientes. Na cadeia de suprimentos da infraestrutura de IA, esses ganhos de eficiência são especialmente importantes, pois os produtos fabricados — incluindo servidores, sistemas de resfriamento, equipamentos elétricos e semicondutores — exigem muitos recursos e energia para serem produzidos e, muitas vezes, dependem da extração de minerais críticos, segundo a BSR (Business for Social Responsibility). A manutenção dos equipamentos computacionais exige a substituição frequente de servidores e hardware de IA a cada dois a três anos. Por isso, otimizar a fabricação dos produtos nas etapas anteriores da cadeia é uma das maiores oportunidades para reduzir o impacto ambiental geral dos data centers. - Melhor coordenação para transportar equipamentos com menos desperdício de recursos: Depois de fabricado o hardware, é hora de transportá-lo até o local de construção do data center. A IA pode ajudar a reduzir deslocamentos desnecessários e o consumo de recursos, facilitando a consolidação de cargas, o planejamento do transporte e a otimização de rotas. A Agência de Proteção Ambiental dos EUA confirmou que esse é um aspecto fundamental para melhorar a sustentabilidade das cadeias de suprimentos. - Melhor visibilidade e planejamento de cenários: Com os avanços da IA em visibilidade, previsão e planejamento de cenários, as empresas não precisam acumular estoques exce

artigo.texto: A few weeks ago, the famed investor Steve Eisman warned that the companies driving the AI boom were using the same financial shenanigans that once brought down Enron in what is still regarded as one of the greatest financial frauds ever. Eisman has credibility when it comes to anticipating economic disasters. As one of the handful of investors who saw the 2008 financial crisis coming, he made an estimated $1 billion betting that the market would collapse. In Michael Lewis’s book The Big Short, and the subsequent movie, Eisman is one of the heroes. Eisman now has a popular Substack as well as a YouTube channel with some 224,000 subscribers. “What I find disturbing is some of the off-balance-sheet financing [vehicles] I thought had gone the way of the dodo bird after the Enron and post-GFC (Great Financial Crisis) debacles,” he told his viewers last month. “Are we going to do this all over again?” Michael Burry is another hero of The Big Short. An early AI bear, he closed his hedge fund last November because his bearish views were not, as he acknowledged at the time, “in sync with the market.” He has since started a Substack called Cassandra Unchained, which has over 300,000 subscribers. But he has never stopped viewing the financing of the AI build-out as a house of cards. Like Eisman, he has been relentlessly pointing out various AI-related financing techniques that are, unquestionably, reminiscent of Enron and the 2008 financial crisis. “History is repeating,” he posted ominously in mid-August. “Time to read this one again or for the first time,” he added, referring to The Smartest Guys in the Room, the 2003 book about the Enron debacle.

artigo.texto: Microsoft has withdrawn from the UK’s largest AI data center project in Loughton, Essex over concerns about electricity supplies. Nscale, a British vertically integrated, full-stack AI infrastructure and neocloud company remains committed to the facility’s development which was announced in 2025, and originally expected to be completed in 2027. The project was backed by the UK government as a major part of its plans to expand the UK’s artificial intelligence infrastructure. Microsoft had been expected to fund a supercomputer at the site and act as its anchor customer. Its withdrawal leaves Nscale without an official public customer for the Essex facility. The setback follows reports that electricity supply problems would delay the project’s connection to the national grid as reported by the BBC. “We remain committed to both the Loughton project and the UK and we are exploring alternative power sources for the site, in addition to other expansion sites in the UK,” Nscale told the BBC. “Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term. This unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts.” Microsoft declined to comment on the partnership termination. Nscale is also reportedly preparing for a potential New York stock market listing this year, with a possible valuation of £ 26 billion (US$ 35 billion). Delays to major projects and the loss of a significant customer could complicate those plans. Microsoft’s withdrawal could create further uncertainty around Nscale’s expansion plans and attract greater investor scrutiny ahead of its planned US initial public offer (IPO) on the New York stock market listing according to the Guardian. The two companies continue to work together on projects in Norway, Portugal and the United States. The withdrawal raises questions about the project’s delivery and Nscale’s wider expansion plans, supported by Nvidia, is among the businesses selected to support the government’s ambition to establish domestic AI computing capacity.

artigo.texto: Batam and Bintan’s widespread outage last Monday was not due to the operational testing of a data center, according to President Director of PT PLN Batam Kwin Fo as quoted by a local daily. “The widespread blackout that occurred on Monday (12/10) on Batam and Bintan islands had nothing to do with a data center. The information that there is testing or commissioning for data center operations, and it requires a lot of power, is not true at all,” Kwin reportedly told reporters in Batam yesterday, after news that the outage was linked to a data center testing was widely circulated in the community. He added that the data center in question is still under development and is not expected to be fully operational in the near future. And if it does start operating, the operational capacity would not exceed 10 per cent of the total capacity of the data center, Kwin said. The data center was not named. PLN Batam is Batam’s electricity utility, a subsidiary of Indonesia’s state-owned electricity company, PT PLN (Persero). Its full name is PT Pelayanan Listrik Nasional Batam; and it supplies electricity in Batam and surrounding areas. Kwin Fo emphasized that Batam’s long-term electricity supply for data centers has been catered for in PLN Batam’s planning. “We do not have a deficit or a shortage of supply. Our power reserves are still around almost 20 percent. Batam’s electricity load is targeted to increase from around 930 MW to more than 1,000 MW. Therefore, we estimate that by the end of 2027, the supply capacity will reach 1,200 to 1,300 MW,” he said. Currently, Batam’s electricity system has a supply capacity of 930MW, with a load of around 780 MW. Thus, the power reserve is still around 20 percent. The growth of electricity demand in Batam has exceeded 15 per cent, much higher than the 3-4 per cent growth of national electricity consumption. “We estimate that in the 2027-2032 range, the load will increase by around 300-400 MW. There is a growth of about 30 percent. To meet the demand, PLN Batam is taking steps to add additional power such as building a new Gas Power Plant (PLTG) and a new Solar Power Plant (PLTS),” he said. Additionally, PLN Batam plans to use a Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) or a battery-based energy storage system to support Batam-Bintan electricity. It takes only nnoseconds or milliseconds for the battery to release power which is much faster than a conventional plant such as coal-fired steam power plants (PLTU), Kwin Fo added.

artigo.texto: Support WBUR How some AI researchers skip big data centers by thinking small "Hey, Ava." Ava, a wheeled white pillar with a camera and screen docked in a Tufts University lab hallway, responded with a two-tone bleep. Mattias Scheutz, director of the school's Human-Robot Interaction Lab, continued his request. "I'm wondering if you could take me to the elevators," he said. "Heading there," the robot said from some hidden speaker. And the experimental pylon started to move. Scheutz said he imagines a future where robots like Ava do many things big and small, from search-and-rescue missions to washing dishes. With recent advances in artificial intelligence, he said, that vision feels closer than ever. Scheutz is one player in a cast of Boston-area researchers and engineers using AI to build robots that can adapt to changes in their physical surroundings. And the tech solution they’re harnessing doesn’t rely on data centers. Popular chatbots like Claude and ChatGPT are powered by models trained on enormous amounts of information, which means spending billions on vast data centers that can take more power and water than entire cities. Instead, roboticists like Scheutz are thinking small. They’re designing AI systems compact enough to fit on a single computer chip. Robots powered with these small AI models can make decisions quickly. And because the chips are installed in the robots, there's no need to send signals to and from data centers for processing. That means the robots can run AI without an internet connection. On its journey to the elevators, Ava encountered a student sitting at a desk in its path. The robot stoped and stuttered: It’d never seen this obstacle before. “That's not in its map,” Scheutz explained. “So now it has to plan around it.” Within seconds, Ava skirted around the desk and continued onward. By making that little adjustment, Scheutz said Ava accomplished a key challenge in robotics; it navigated what’s known as a “dynamic obstacle.” The robot tackled this task with a type of AI called a neurosymbolic model. The model allows the robot to execute tasks and recognize patterns in its environment, which allows Ava to move in response to unfamiliar situations. Models like this reduce the most energy-intensive aspect of AI: training. To create the large language model GPT-4, for example, MIT Technology Review cited an estimate that Open AI used as much energy as San Francisco consumes in three days. And small AI models have another energy-saving bonus. Since they don’t need data centers to operate, they bypass the energy costs of running hefty cooling systems and thousands of servers at once. The Tufts team loaded its neurosymbolic model onto a robotic arm and tested it against a larger AI model. The researchers asked both systems to tackle a block stacking puzzle. The results, which they presented at an international robotics conference this year, showed the neurosymbolic model was more accurate and required 100 times less energy to train, compared to the larger AI. “Who doesn't want a model that's more capable given the same data or a model that's as capable but requires less data?” asked Helen Lu, a Ph.D candidate and co-author of the Tufts study. Other companies are working on their own versions of small, energy-efficient AI. “We want to find the most intelligent model per watt,” said Alexander Amini, chief science officer at Liquid AI, an MIT spinoff company. Amini said the startup’s strategy runs counter to most big AI companies, which focus on creating intelligence “at all costs.” By honing in on smallness instead, Liquid AI can run its models on any device with a computer chip. Like the chips in your car. The company has partnered with Mercedes-Benz in North America, and Amini envisions cars that respond to conversational prompts like, “My back hurts.” "And the car is intelligent enough to reason about those statements and start to, let's say, turn on the seat heater, turn on the massager,” he said. A potential downside is that limited training may create AI models with less intelligence, and less usefulness, than large AI. But Liquid AI’s cofounder, Daniela Rus, argues there’s plenty of room for both. “It is important to keep in mind that not all AI problems require cloud-level intelligence,” said Rus, who directs MIT’s Computer Science and AI Laboratory. A lot of what users ask AI chatbots are relatively simple queries that can be answered without “extreme Ph.D-level knowledge,” according to Amini. Big AI — the type of model that can both do astrophysics and write a book report — isn’t going away. But Rus and Amini are betting that not every task, or every robot, needs that. This story is part of Awaiting Data, a special series from the New England News Collaborative.

artigo.texto: O início dos testes do primeiro sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) integrado a uma usina solar no Brasil, autorizado pela Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel), representa um marco para a evolução do setor elétrico nacional. Instalado na usina solar Sol de Brotas 7, da Statkraft, na Bahia, o projeto combina geração fotovoltaica e armazenamento de energia, abrindo caminho para novos modelos de operação, maior flexibilidade da rede e uma gestão mais eficiente dos ativos renováveis. + NOTÍCIAS NO GRUPO NM DO WHATSAPP Para a Voltxs Energia, o avanço demonstra que o armazenamento deixa de ser apenas uma tecnologia promissora e passa a integrar as estratégias de desenvolvimento dos empreendimentos renováveis. À medida que a participação das fontes solar e eólica cresce na matriz elétrica brasileira, aumenta também a necessidade de soluções capazes de conferir maior previsibilidade, flexibilidade e eficiência à operação desses ativos. “O início desse projeto representa um passo importante para a maturidade do mercado brasileiro de armazenamento de energia. O BESS deixa de ser apenas um tema de planejamento e passa a ser validado na prática como um componente estratégico para a operação dos ativos renováveis. A combinação entre geração fotovoltaica e armazenamento amplia as possibilidades de gestão da energia produzida e prepara o setor para uma matriz cada vez mais dinâmica”, afirma Matheus Ivanoski Teixeira, Diretor de Operações (COO) da Voltxs Energia. Armazenamento passa a integrar a estratégia dos ativos (bateria) Os sistemas BESS permitem armazenar a energia gerada em momentos de maior produção e disponibilizá-la quando houver necessidade operacional ou maior demanda do sistema elétrico. Na avaliação da Voltxs, o principal ganho está na integração entre geração, armazenamento e gestão inteligente dos ativos. “Quando analisamos um projeto híbrido, não estamos falando apenas da instalação de baterias. O grande diferencial está na capacidade de integrar geração, armazenamento e inteligência operacional para extrair mais eficiência dos ativos. Essa visão tende a se tornar cada vez mais relevante para investidores, operadores e proprietários de usinas”, explica Teixeira. Segundo o executivo, os primeiros projetos em operação terão papel fundamental para fornecer dados reais sobre desempenho, dimensionamento, custos, retorno econômico e aplicações do armazenamento em diferentes cenários. Mercado entra em uma nova fase O avanço também reforça uma tendência observada internacionalmente: a evolução das usinas renováveis para plataformas energéticas mais inteligentes, capazes de combinar diferentes tecnologias e responder de forma mais eficiente às necessidades do sistema elétrico. Na avaliação da Voltxs, essa transformação deve impulsionar novos modelos de negócios, ampliar a competitividade dos empreendimentos renováveis e acelerar investimentos em soluções de armazenamento nos próximos anos. “Os projetos pioneiros serão importantes para definir as melhores estratégias de utilização do armazenamento no Brasil. O aprendizado obtido nessa fase permitirá desenvolver modelos mais eficientes tanto do ponto de vista operacional quanto econômico. A tendência é que a gestão integrada dos ativos passe a ser um diferencial competitivo para o setor”, destaca o COO da Voltxs. Além dos benefícios operacionais, a integração entre geração fotovoltaica e armazenamento fortalece a discussão sobre a modernização da infraestrutura elétrica brasileira, criando condições para uma matriz energética mais flexível, resiliente e preparada para a expansão das fontes renováveis. Sobre a Voltxs Energia A Voltxs Energia atua no mercado de energia com soluções voltadas à gestão estratégica de ativos, eficiência energética e inteligência para o setor elétrico. A empresa desenvolve projetos que combinam tecnologia, análise de dados e conhecimento regulatório para apoiar empresas na otimização de custos, aumento da eficiência operacional e maximização do valor de seus ativos energéticos. artigo.texto: A Anthropic, criadora do assistente Claude, está em tratativas com a Nscale para um acordo de infraestrutura voltado à inteligência artificial que pode chegar a US$ 45 bilhões. A negociação envolveria uma segunda instalação da Nscale no empreendimento Monarch, na Virgínia Ocidental, conforme pessoas com conhecimento das conversas. A Nscale, apoiada pela Nvidia, já tem contratos de infraestrutura com a Anthropic que somam cerca de US$ 44,6 bilhões, conforme documentos regulatórios ligados ao seu IPO. O novo prédio no Monarch poderá ter capacidade computacional de 460 megawatts e usar chips Vera Rubin, da Nvidia. A Anthropic também pode ter preferência para contratar um terceiro edifício planejado no mesmo campus. As empresas podem fechar o acordo nos próximos dias, mas as negociações seguem abertas e ainda podem mudar. Anthropic e Nscale não quiseram se pronunciar. Quando estiver concluído, o complexo Monarch poderá superar 8 gigawatts de capacidade elétrica bruta, de acordo com os documentos do IPO. Num primeiro momento, a Microsoft ficaria com parte do espaço. Em março, a empresa divulgou o interesse em entrar no projeto por meio de uma carta de intenções. Ela desistiu da instalação na temporada de verão do hemisfério norte, o que abriu espaço para a Anthropic ampliar sua presença no complexo. O possível contrato surge enquanto a Nscale prepara sua estreia na Bolsa e busca avaliação próxima de US$ 30 bilhões. A empresa apresentou pedido de listagem em setembro, não começou a divulgar formalmente a oferta e responde a questionamentos da SEC. A Anthropic também amplia investimentos em infraestrutura para atender à demanda por IA, em meio a preocupações com o endividamento do setor.

artigo.texto: SK Nexilis, the copper foil business investment company of SKC for secondary batteries, said on the 20th that it has succeeded in developing "high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil," cited as a key material for next-generation batteries. The technology SK Nexilis developed this time is characterized by coating special carbon on the surface of copper foil to increase adhesion with the anode material. It suppresses "delamination," which can occur due to the volume expansion of silicon anode materials, enhances the structural stability of electrodes, and can help improve battery life and safety. This technology was developed in response to the recent trend in the battery industry of increasing the silicon content in anode materials to boost energy density. In particular, it focused on strengthening the adhesion between the anode material and copper foil, which becomes more important as silicon content rises. The copper foil developed in this way can also be applied to the dry-electrode process, known as a next-generation battery manufacturing process. The dry process is drawing attention as a manufacturing method that can reduce battery manufacturing expense and energy use. Because the dry process also requires stably securing adhesion between electrode materials and copper foil, the technology developed by SK Nexilis is expected to have high applicability. For mass production, SK Nexilis will build a pilot production system for high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil. It is currently verifying process stability and plans to secure technology for mass production and pursue commercialization in the second half of 2027. An SK Nexilis official said, "This development of high-adhesion carbon-coated copper foil is a result to respond to technological changes in the next-generation battery market, such as expanding high-content silicon anode materials and introducing the dry-electrode process," adding, "We will proceed with optimization for commercialization without a hitch and strengthen our competitiveness in the next-generation battery materials market through continuous technology development."

artigo.texto: Inner Mongolia leads world in energy storage Region forging master key for next industrial revolution, proving that whoever can best store electricity holds future of power For a long time, electricity has been a unique energy commodity, with production and consumption happening almost simultaneously. You use it the moment it is generated. But today, as solar and wind power have become China's largest sources of installed capacity, energy storage is quietly building "warehouses" for the power grid. These massive facilities store surplus green electricity during the day and deliver it to factories, shopping malls and millions of households at night. This time-shifting magic has found its grandest stage in North China's Inner Mongolia autonomous region. Driven by the massive deployment of new-type battery facilities designed to support its vast wind and solar power bases, Inner Mongolia has overtaken California to become the world's largest energy storage region. As of the end of 2025, the region's cumulative installed capacity of new-type energy storage exceeded 25 million kilowatts, ranking first in the nation. Under the blueprint of the 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-30), this figure is projected to break the 50 million kW mark, cementing the region's role as the most critical power "reservoir" for the country's renewable mega-bases in the Gobi Desert and other arid areas. The sheer scale of this deployment has triggered a profound industrial metamorphosis. In the past, Inner Mongolia's vast Gobi Desert served merely as an application ground for energy storage, with complete sets of equipment largely purchased from manufacturing clusters in China's eastern provinces. Today, the narrative has shifted from isolated breakthroughs to a multi-city synergy. Hohhot, Baotou and Ordos are firing on all cylinders, forming a differentiated energy storage equipment manufacturing cluster. This has created a new paradigm of "desert application plus multicity collaborative smart manufacturing" — a concentrated reflection of the region's upgrading new energy industry chain. Each city brings a unique strength to the table, but the regional capital, Hohhot, stands out for its specialized focus on system integration and custom solutions engineered for extreme environments. Operating at the forefront of grid resilience, Hohhot's manufacturing sector produces energy storage equipment uniquely designed to withstand the severe cold and punishing sandstorms characteristic of the northern frontiers. While Baotou boasts the most comprehensive industrial chain and Ordos combines equipment manufacturing with ultra-large application scenarios at sites like Envision's zero-carbon industrial park, Hohhot's tailored approach to hostile climate operations ensures these massive systems remain reliable year-round. "Deploying gigawatt-scale battery facilities in the Gobi Desert is fundamentally different from installing systems in temperate coastal plains," said Lin Boqiang, head of the China Institute for Studies in Energy Policy at Xiamen University. "Extreme sub-zero winters can degrade battery performance and discharge efficiency by double digits, while seasonal sandstorms pose severe risks to thermal management and air filtration systems." Hohhot's focus on hostile-climate customization addresses the industry's biggest operational bottleneck — ensuring that massive desert storage parks don't just get built, but actually run safely and reliably 365 days a year, he said. Inner Mongolia's regional triumph mirrors a broader national strategy. Entering 2026, the strategic importance of new-type energy storage has reached unprecedented heights. For the first time, it has been listed among the nation's six emerging pillar industries for the 15th Five-Year Plan. The China New Energy Storage Development Report 2026, released recently by the National Energy Administration, said China's cumulative installed capacity of new-type storage had reached 136 million kW/351 million kilowatt-hours by the end of 2025, representing a year-on-year surge of 84.3 percent. Accounting for roughly 50 percent of the global total, new-type energy storage has surpassed pumped-hydro storage to become China's largest regulating resource, it said. Yet, after years of rapid expansion, the fundamental logic of the industry is evolving. Experts agree that the sector has bid farewell to the era of simple policy-driven scale expansion. "The industry has formally entered a new phase characterized by market-oriented selection, value priority and a focus on quality," said Dai Hongcai, director of the new energy institute at the State Grid Energy Research Institute. While the "forced pairing" of storage with renewable projects drove early growth, future expansion will rely on sustainable business models.

artigo.texto: Huawei’s smart car business is signing on to CATL’s battery swap network, giving the world’s largest battery maker another heavyweight partner for a technology most of the industry wrote off a decade ago. Yinwang, the Huawei-controlled automotive unit also known as Newcool, signed a strategic cooperation framework with CATL and its swap subsidiary CAES on Monday. CATL’s Choco-swap network already counts 2,520 stations across about 200 Chinese cities. What Huawei and CATL agreed to According to Yinwang’s statement, reported by Reuters, the deal covers both swappable battery packs and the station network. CATL says the focus is on vehicles running Huawei’s Qiankun smart driving systems, which would be made compatible with Choco stations. The new partnership is betting heavily on automation. CATL wants to link the car, the station and the cloud so the vehicle works out when it needs energy, based on its battery status and the driver’s habits, then finds a station, drives in on its own and lines itself up for the swap. CATL quotes 99 seconds for the swap itself. CATL chairman Robin Zeng and Jin Yuzhi, Huawei senior vice president and Yinwang CEO, attended the signing. The new partnership looks serious, but the announcement left out a few key details. No vehicle models, launch date or service areas were announced. It’s a framework agreement, and those don’t always turn into products. Who’s behind Yinwang? Huawei owns 80% of it, with Seres and Changan’s Avatr holding 10% each. Seres builds AITO, the premium SUV brand Huawei’s software and retail network helped turn into a hit in China, and plenty of other Chinese automakers buy Huawei’s Qiankun systems. More than 200 new swap stations a month CATL first entered the battery swap market in 2022 with its EVOGO service, then relaunched the effort as Choco-swap around standardized packs at the end of 2024. The growth since has been fast. Choco-swap ended 2025 with 1,020 stations, passed 2,000 at the start of July, and hit 2,520 as of September 29. As we reported this summer, CATL is building more than 200 battery swap stations every month. It’s aiming for more than 3,000 by the end of the year and 30,000 long term. Huawei joins a growing list of Choco partners that includes GAC, BAIC and NIO. CATL is also pushing swapping for heavy trucks, including a joint venture with Octopus Energy for the UK and Europe. For comparison, NIO, which built the first big swap network on its own, hit its 100 millionth swap in February with 3,790 stations. It passed 110 million swaps by June. Electrek’s Take I’ve been skeptical of battery swapping for years, and I had good reasons to be. Tesla demoed a 90-second pack swap in 2013, opened a single pilot station at Harris Ranch in California, and quietly let it fade after owners showed little interest. Better Place raised about $850 million and still went bankrupt in 2013. And every year, chargers got faster, which shrank the one real advantage swapping had. My main argument was standardization. Swapping only works as infrastructure if lots of automakers share packs, and automakers don’t want to share the most expensive part of the car. NIO proved swapping can work for one brand. But one brand’s network is a perk, not infrastructure. CATL is the one company that can fix that problem, and it’s actually doing it. It supplies roughly 40% of the world’s EV battery cells, so when it shows up with a standard pack, automakers listen. 2,520 stations in under two years isn’t a pilot. Top comment by Mrvc I can see battery swapping and battery leases being big in the developing world. Possibly Europe. For the five eyes countries is probably a no. Getting people to buy a vehicle and lease a battery hasn't gone over well. The original smart evs were like that. I think the b class was too. But if someone had a lot of cash to burn building stations though out the us. Then offered a dirt cheap ev with lifetime price battery lease then maybe. Especially as there is a pretty irrational fear of battery replacement. Leased battery you change all the time takes that fear out of the equation. The vehicle would have to be sub $15k possibly under $10k. And battery lease would have to be under $80 a month probably with a cheaper under $50 tier. Even then could be a while to gain traction. Could be part of the solution to urban changing is the best solution for packs sized for real actual use. And Huawei brings autonomy. A car that drives itself into a station and leaves 99 seconds later doesn’t need anyone to plug it in. For robotaxis and commercial fleets, that solves a real problem. I still don’t think swapping replaces charging. Most EV owners charge at home, and the fastest chargers in China are now getting close to gas station times. So it’s a complement. But I’m surprised to be writing this: in China, battery swapping is starting to look like a permanent part of the EV mix rather than a gimmick. Will anyone build something like this outside of China? With electricity rates up almost 10% last year and expected to keep climbing, going solar is one of the best ways to protect yourself against rising costs. And with lease and PPA options, you can do it with zero upfront cost and start saving immediately. If you want to find the best deal, check out EnergySage. artigo.texto: In June, as public opinion on data centers soured, Gov. Greg Abbott took his first big swing at reining in the industry, issuing a round of regulatory recommendations to the Legislature that included his call to end a major tax break for the facilities. Donors with ties to the data center industry responded with cash. That same month, they gave Abbott’s campaign $1.5 million. Two months later, the third-term Republican governor toughened his stance by pausing approvals for data centers seeking to connect to the state’s electrical grid, pending a statewide audit. That same month, he said in an interview with ABC that data centers “dug their own grave” and “got the backlash they deserve” for not gaining community buy-in at the outset of projects. More money poured in. After announcing the pause, Abbott went on to receive another $2.8 million from data center-related donors, his biggest monthly haul from the industry over the course of this election cycle, an analysis by The Texas Tribune found. In total, Abbott has raised about $9 million from data center-related donors since July 2025, which accounts for about 13% of the donations he’s taken in during that time. The Tribune vetted the affiliations of every donor who contributed at least $25,000 to Abbott or his Democratic opponent Gina Hinojosa since July 2025. More than half of Abbott’s data center haul, or $4.9 million, came from people or companies (and their corporate political action committees) that develop, own or operate data centers. That group includes people like Rhett Bennett, the CEO of Black Mountain, a Fort Worth-based energy company building hyperscale data centers across Texas. Bennett and Black Mountain gave a combined $1 million to Abbott since last July. The group also includes people like Toby Neugebauer — the former CEO of Fermi America, the company behind the massive Project Matador data center campus in the Panhandle — who contributed $100,000 to Abbott. The other $4.1 million in donations came from donors the Tribune found to have indirect data center links: people and companies that invest in or have financial ties to data centers, are associated with companies that primarily develop AI, or whose business models involve, at least in part, serving or helping build data centers. That group includes people like Jeff Yass, a GOP megadonor best known for his interest in expanding school vouchers, but whose investment portfolio contains a number of companies that rely heavily on AI or data center technology. Yass’ investment firm Susquehanna International Group has stakes in Bytedance, the parent company of TikTok that also develops its own AI models; Broadcom, a company that supplies hardware and infrastructure to data centers; and Alphabet, Inc, the parent company of Google, which owns and operates data centers. This group also includes Edward Roski Jr., president of Majestic Realty Corp, a commercial real estate development company that counts data centers among its diverse list of tenants. They both gave Abbott $1 million. Identifying data center donors is imperfect because many people with ties to the industry also have other business interests or political motivations. For example, Abbott’s largest data center-related donor was Airbnb co-founder Joe Gebbia, who contributed $1.5 million. Gebbia is a board member of Tesla, which owns and operates its own data centers. Abbott has also received major data center-linked donations from megadonors Elon Musk and Harlan Crow, who are both active in advancing conservative politics. Musk, the CEO of Tesla, which operates AI data centers, gave Abbott $500,000 and Crow, who has been an Abbott donor long before the recent data center buildout, gave $250,000. Crow is the chair of the board and former CEO of Crow Family Holdings, which announced in January it was developing a data center campus in central Dallas with CleanArc Data Centers. “Mr. Crow has been a steadfast and long-standing supporter of Gov. Greg Abbott, dating back well over a decade and across several campaigns,” Crow’s office said to the Tribune. The affiliations have nonetheless proven to be a liability for Abbott this election year. As the explosion in data center development in Texas fuels bipartisan discontent, candidates up and down the ballot, on both sides of the aisle, have worked to distance themselves from the industry while weaponizing donations from data centers against their opponents. Staring down polling that has him neck-in-neck with Hinojosa, Abbott is for the first time fighting for his political life, trying to strike a balance between cracking down on the facilities while still holding onto his pro-business ethos. “Governor Abbott has made his position on data centers clear. Data centers must pay their own way, protect Texas’ electric grid, bring their own water, and not to disturb the communities where they operate,” said Abbott campaign spokesman Eduardo Leal to the Tribune. “The Governor also directed state agencies to issue no data center related permits until ERCOT completes its review and he has also called for ending outdated taxpayer-funded incentives. Those are the standards Governor Abbott has laid out, and those remain his priorities.” Leal also called the Tribune’s reporting a “disingenuous attempt to manufacture controversy out of information that is not new.” Hinojosa, meanwhile, has made connecting Abbott to data centers a central part of her attack. “Greg Abbott invited data centers into Texas with the richest tax breaks in the country, took millions of dollars in donations from the data center interests, and has spent months lying to Texans about his record to save his political career,” Hinojosa said. “Texans know I’ll fight for them – not the big corporations – and ensure they have a seat at the table to decide if and how data centers come into their communities.” In a campaign ad, Hinojosa accuses Abbott of taking $20 million from “data center executives and companies.” Th
