artigo.texto: Is Finland’s data center boom getting out of hand? In early September, Google announced that it would invest €13 billion in Finland and build data centers in several locations. It would be the largest investment in Finnish economic history. This was big news and politicians were grateful. The Finnish economy has been depressed for years and investments are needed. By October, the atmosphere had changed and Google’s construction site stood still. It had turned out that a forest on the site had been cut down and work had started — despite the fact that Google hadn’t yet secured permission or submitted the environmental impact assessment required by law. The company had been in a huge hurry, which appears to have backfired. In Finland, the debate surrounding the construction of data centers is getting increasingly heated. It is almost impossible to keep up with how quickly data center plans are appearing all over the country. Since Google, there have been other announcements of the same magnitude involving billions upon billions of euros. In mid-October, the number of data center plans was somewhere between 150 and 200. Different sources use different figures, and there is no exact up-to-date information available. Most of them were still just plans, but construction is going on in many locations. The news headlines are listing American giants like Google, Meta and Microsoft, but there are also Finnish or international companies that have emerged, suddenly announcing their intention to invest billions in remote corners of small municipalities. Decision-making on data centers is highly decentralised in Finland. Companies approach small municipalities one by one. These are often places where decision-makers are used to people and jobs gradually disappearing into large cities. Then, suddenly, someone appears at their door promising a huge investment in the municipality and a lot of new jobs. At that point, it is very difficult to say no. Finland’s new reality As a result, the whole thing has gotten out of hand. Finland is gradually waking up to a new reality in which excavators are roaring along the country’s outlying regions, and in some cities building data centers — the owners and users of which are typically somewhere far away. What are the benefits that remain in Finland, and what are the risks? Among decision-makers and the general public, the reactions have ranged from enthusiasm to horror, not to mention confusion. The Finnish economy has been depressed for a long time, and new investments have been desperately needed. But the data center boom is so big that it’s already raising suspicions. Where does all the electricity come from? Where would all the builders come from? Will Finland be made into a sort of colony of data centers, which after completion employ only a few people and consume a large part of Finland’s electricity production and whose benefits drain abroad? Companies are drawn to Finland by the northern climate, which helps to cool the data centers. Companies are also attracted by the fact that electricity is readily available, and its production is often emission-free thanks to nuclear power, hydropower or wind power. Finns, on the other hand, are beginning to worry about whether there really is electricity available for all this, while people also want to have low electricity prices. Many of the new data center plans are in northern Finland. For example, Google’s new locations are Kajaani, Vaala and Muhos. Of these, Kajaani is a small town with an industrial tradition. Vaala is deep in the country, and Muhos is located quite close to Oulu — the largest city in the region. Key locations All of these places have one thing in common: they are close to good electricity transmission networks. In each case, there are municipalities nearby where other companies are planning data centers of the same size. Locations in Northern Finland (but mainly outside Lapland, the northernmost region of the country) have to do with the structure of the electricity transmission network. There are large trunk lines in that area that can be joined. Especially in Northern Finland, it has been noticed that “green transition” often refers to the appearance of windmills on the landscape or some other activity where one’s own area is seen only as a source of resources or raw materials. In Eastern Finland, on the other hand, there is concern that due to the structure of the electricity transmission network, new investments won’t be made in the area whose economy suffers the most from the break-up of connections with Russia anyway. Looking at the bigger picture, this debate is also related to the strategic independence of Europe. The companies and users behind the data centers are primarily in America. How does this fit into Europe’s desire to reduce its technological dependence on the U.S.? In October, Finland hurriedly began to prepare a new law which would significantly slow down the connection of data centers to the electricity network and thereby slow down their construction. As a result, the Finnish data center boom appears to have reached a temporary limit, though no one knows the outcome of all this yet. Any opinions expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the views of Arctic Today. Markku Heikkilä is the Head of Science Communications at the Arctic Centre, University of Lapland, in Rovaniemi. As a former journalist at the Kaleva newspaper in Oulu, Heikkilä has followed Arctic cooperation from its early stages, and he received the State Award for Public Information for his work. He has written several books on these topics. The latest, Once We Had the Arctic – Journeys and Stories from the North, is available in English as an audiobook and e-book.

artigo.texto: “There are no more birds in the area,” Sterling, Virginia, resident Greg Pirio said at a public meeting of the Loudoun County Board of Supervisors in early July. “The sound has driven them away.” Pirio has lived in Sterling for more than a decade. Then, in 2025, Pirio and his neighbors began experiencing an “intolerable noise” stemming from the data centers that have swarmed their suburban community. Pirio said he and his neighbors, including children, suffer from headaches and sleep deprivation. Many have resorted to using mattresses and special plexiglass to keep the noise out, but this is only the beginning of the public health crisis they’re up against. “There’s a family up the street from me with four kids,” Pirio tells The Progressive. “All four children have come down with respiratory illnesses, and one had to be hospitalized.” Other residents of Pirio’s Northern Virginia suburb suffer from sinusitis and ringing in the ears as well as trouble breathing. Pirio himself says he has had to take sleeping pills to get rest amidst the noise and suffers from severely dry eyes due to the poor air quality. “I had to go to the emergency room twice in recent months,” he notes. “I have to keep my eyes lubricated all the time so I use eye drops every couple of hours along with a gel before bed.” As data centers transform the world through artificial intelligence (AI) connectivity, they are also transforming Black, brown, and working-class neighborhoods through strained infrastructure and depleted natural resources. These facilities are not hidden away in the middle of nowhere. More than half of all data centers in the United States are within a mile of a school, from Arizona and Texas to Georgia and Virginia. These data centers and the gas turbines that power them are not only looming over student playgrounds, they are also near parks, airports, office buildings, shopping malls, and even cemeteries. The epicenter of this global transformation, Northern Virginia, has been dubbed “Data Center Alley.” Three counties—Loudoun, Fairfax, and Prince William—are home to nearly 300 data centers and counting. Data centers in the region currently cover more than thirty million square feet, and more projects are proposed each year. A third of the world’s hyperscale data centers now sit in the backyard of our nation’s capital. Located near Dulles Airport, and with the greatest density of data centers on the planet, these Washington, D.C., suburbs have cashed in big time at 450,000 residents’ expense. “This issue felt distant initially,” says Bria Singleton, a Fairfax County resident who commutes into the capital five days a week for work. But the first time she heard that Northern Virginia had a data center problem, she was learning about towns like Ashburn and Sterling. “The metro line I take begins in Ashburn,” Singleton notes. Then, her Virginia town introduced a proposal to sell commercial property for a data center build-out. “As a health care consultant and Black woman, I knew what was coming and never supported data centers. There are no pros. Only cons,” she says. Now residents like her are demanding moratoriums and restitution, showing that the impacts of these centers are not tomorrow’s problem but today’s. When data centers first began popping up in the 1990s, residents were fairly out of the loop. Many of the initial data centers were no bigger than an average office building and seemed harmless enough while boasting of jobs and revenue that would benefit local residents. Data center developers often coordinate directly with local elected officials and invoke nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) in the name of “competitive interests.” By the time community members find out about a new data center, it’s because they’re seeing construction vehicles show up. After a series of tax incentives rolled out in the early 2000s, one approved data center proposal turned into two, which turned into ten, which quickly became more than 200 data centers statewide. The latest data centers are no longer mid-sized operations. They are what the industry calls “hyperscale”—meaning they are far bigger than earlier versions and create sprawling industrial parks. “In the NAACP’s People’s Report,” says Abre’ Conner, the NAACP’s director of environmental and climate justice, “we surveyed Virginians who expressed strong opposition to some existing infrastructure and new build-outs in the wake of a high concentration of data centers within the state.” Maryland’s Prince George’s County is the focus of the NAACP report, which found that residents of that county are “susceptible to air pollution from Data Center Alley located in Loudon [sic] County, Virginia” due to close proximity, cross-state wind patterns, and the sheer size of these facilities. With construction of the first beginning in 2018, the firm Vantage Data Centers built two data center campuses in the Ashburn-Sterling area. Within a few years, residents complained of incessant noise and fumes in the air. The first of the campuses was a massive fifty-two-acre compound with six data centers covering over 1.7 million square feet. The second sits on eighteen acres with three data centers, eight natural gas turbines, and fifty-one diesel generators. Gas turbines emit at least 188 different types of pollutants that increase the risk of asthma, pneumonia, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and stroke—and they do so loudly. Pirio lives 150 yards away from the second campus. “I feel it in my throat and lungs when they run the backup generators,” he says. “This data center has been a curse on our life here,” another homeowner told a 7News reporter. Hugh Kenny/The Piedmont Environmental Council A recreational trail takes pedestrians and bicyclists past a data center in Loudoun County, Virginia. artigo.texto: Energy storage manufacturer HiTHIUM has announced that its cumulative energy storage product shipments have surpassed 200 GWh. Having begun shipments in late 2021, the company reached the 100 GWh milestone in August 2025 and added another 100 GWh in just over a year. HiTHIUM said it ranked among the world's top 2 suppliers by energy storage battery shipments in 2025 and the first half of 2026. Looking ahead, the company said it would remain focused on energy storage, with long-duration energy storage (LDES) as a strategic priority. Recall that HiTHIUM started mass production at its integrated LDES industrial park in Heze, Shandong Province, in August (see China Solar PV News Snippets). It aims to promote large-scale global deployment of its first integrated long-duration energy storage solution, featuring 1,000 Ah-class cells, and to develop integrated solutions that cover the value chain from battery cells to the grid. In its earnings forecast, Chinese inverter and energy storage equipment manufacturer Deye expects a net profit of RMB 4.22 billion to RMB 4.32 billion in the first nine months of 2026, up 79.81% to 84.07% year-over-year (YoY). Net profit excluding non-recurring items is projected to be RMB 3.95 billion to RMB 4.06 billion, up 73.33% to 78.16% YoY. The company attributed the expected earnings growth primarily to rising overseas demand for energy storage. Supported by energy security policies and tighter electricity supply-demand conditions in several countries, sales revenue from its residential and commercial and industrial (C&I) energy storage products increased significantly YoY. Deye also cited its global sales network and supply-chain cost management as contributing factors. Deye released its earnings results for H1 2026, reporting that its revenue rose over 92% during the period (see China Solar PV News Snippets). Power equipment manufacturers CEEG and SINEXCEL have jointly developed a 13,800 kVA transformer for energy storage applications. The oil-immersed, self-cooled, dual-split transformer is designed for a 40-foot high-cube containerized AC/DC integrated energy storage system (ESS), enabling a rated continuous output of 13.8 MW per container. According to CEEG, the transformer achieves 99.66% efficiency, exceeding the EU Tier 2 benchmark of 99.645%. Its design reduces overall weight by ~10% and is intended to be maintenance-free. The product series now covers single-unit power ratings from 6 MW to 13.8 MW, with grid-side voltage options of 13.8 kV, 22 kV, and 33 kV. The products target GW-scale energy storage and renewable energy projects with integrated storage. Guangdong's provincial development and reform commission and energy administration have issued pricing rules for local renewable energy consumption projects, including direct green power supply, integrated source-grid-load-storage projects, and zero-carbon industrial parks. Under the policy, annual self-consumed renewable generation must account for at least 60% of total available generation and at least 30% of total electricity consumption. The minimum share of electricity consumption supplied by self-consumed renewable generation will rise to 35% for new projects from 2030. Projects connected to the public grid must pay capacity- or demand-based transmission and distribution charges. Electricity imported from the grid will no longer incur separate system reserve charges or energy-based transmission and distribution fees. Other applicable charges, including system operation fees, government funds, and surcharges, will continue to apply under the relevant rules. China's renewable energy price settlement mechanism will not cover electricity exported by these projects. Renewable energy projects already covered by the mechanism price that switch to local consumption arrangements will be deemed to have voluntarily withdrawn from the mechanism. Guangdong recently launched a mechanism price auction for 2026 renewable energy projects, with a volume of 7.934 billion kWh for distributed PV (see China Solar PV News Snippets).

artigo.texto: Union workers line up for data center jobs Electricians travel from as far as Idaho and Virginia for a chance at Mid-South data center work MEMPHIS, Tenn. (WMC) - Hundreds of people lined up along the streets outside the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers union office in Midtown, hoping to get hired for jobs at Mid-South data centers. Workers travel from out of state The crowd included electricians from across the country, with some traveling from as far as Idaho and Virginia. They camped out for hours outside the union office. Workers said the big turnout was no surprise given the pay for the jobs. “When you got a big paying money job, you got people paying money job. It’s going to show up like this, like heavy,” said Sam, who traveled in hopes of data center work. “Well, to be honest, Elon Musk is paying the most money in the country right now with this SpaceX little job that they got down there in Southaven, you know what I’m saying. It’s a killing,” said Ray Massey, who also traveled in hopes of data center work. Union workers said openings go to residents first, then to those who traveled from out of state following the job opportunities. Click here to sign up for our newsletter! artigo.texto: In recent days, a Ukrainian drone strike hit Russia’s largest data center, owned by bank and technology company Sberbank. The strike came after Ukraine hit three data centers belonging to the tech giant Yandex, which is often referred to as “Russia’s Google.” After those attacks, Yandex’s traffic dropped 94%. Its users experienced heavy disruption to features such as email, search, navigation, music, ride-hailing, marketplace and financial services. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the strikes had made it “easier to breathe on many social media platforms”, by reducing Russian disinformation and bot activity. Later reports have cast doubt on Zelensky’s claim. Either way, the incident highlights the role of physical communication infrastructure in the online world. It also raises questions over what “digital sovereignty” really means, and hints at a way to fight disinformation. Data in the line of fire Data centers are an unconventional military target. However, that may be changing as their importance grows. Attacking data centers may disrupt an enemy’s military operations, as well as the ordinary civilian services that rely on these facilities. In Russia, these disruptions may slow down the economy in the long term, undermining its ability to continue the war. Ukraine’s strikes came after Russian attacks on Ukrainian data centers and internet service providers. They also follow a precedent set by Iran earlier this year when it hit data centers in the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain in response to American attacks. The Middle East data centers were run by Amazon Web Services, the world’s biggest cloud computing company with facilities around the globe. Typically, data centres use redundancy and backups to make sure losing a single facility does not have permanent negative consequences. Even so, the Iranian strikes resulted in long-term degradation of services and irrecoverable loss of some data. Russian data centres may have less in the way of international redundancy options. This is due to a particular vision of “digital sovereignty”, which Moscow has actively championed over the past decade. The idea that nations should have autonomy and control over their own digital data and infrastructure is a sound one. However, Russia’s pursuit of “sovereignty” has enabled it to censor online information and isolate Russian users from global internet services. Russia passed laws requiring certain data to be stored locally in 2015. These were followed by international sanctions after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. As a result, Russia’s options for maintaining backup infrastructure abroad have been significantly limited. Disinformation and influence Disinformation is often considered as the strategic spreading of deliberate falsehoods. Governments have often tried to fight it by removing or debunking these falsehoods on the platforms where they circulate. However, influence operations work in many different ways. Not all of them propagate falsehoods. Most of them aim to undermine public trust and delegitimise democratic processes and institutions. In Australia’s 2023 referendum on an Indigenous Voice to Parliament, for example, campaigners generated plausible competing narratives to exacerbate political polarisation. In New Zealand, influence operations have involved avalanches of misogynistic abuse to derail public support for policy initiatives. Russia is known for its orchestrated interventions in democratic politics around the world. The goal of these interventions has often been to sow dissent, distrust and dismay. Supporting candidates with pro-Russian stances can also be a goal. Civil society and activist communities have developed creative approaches to tackling this problem. These have included debunking, prebunking (preemptively countering false claims), reporting misleading content to platforms, or strategically using humor and memes. Digital sovereignty can create points of weakness The data center attacks in Russia are a reminder that Russian internet services – including influence operations – depend on physical infrastructure. Whether or not the strikes have led to a significant reduction in disinformation bot activity this time around, targeting the physical sources of disinformation may still be an effective way to contain it. There are over 100 data centers operating on Russian territory. Few of them have backups and resilience plans in place. Concentrating all digital operations in a relatively small number of physical sites creates a vulnerability. Once this infrastructure is hit, rebuilding can be slow and challenging, especially as Russia is reliant on China to supply advanced semiconductors. Lessons for democracies What does this mean for efforts to counter Russian disinformation and influence operations more broadly? One set of solutions might involve imposing physical or regulatory limits (such as sanctions) on Russian-based platforms and services such as Telegram. Other solutions would require international cooperation to undermine Russia’s capability to inflict harm in the digital environments. This may include supporting Ukraine’s efforts on the battlefront through bilateral security agreements. In any case, the recent events have shown that Russia’s digital influence extensively relies on physical infrastructures: data centers, scarce semiconductor materials and a domestic platform ecosystem that has been splintered from the world wide web. As the Kremlin continues to isolate itself in the name of sovereignty, it is also becoming more vulnerable to attacks and disruptions. Democracies can draw lessons from these events. Digital sovereignty is not achieved through isolation and vertical control over digital infrastructures. Instead, it is constantly negotiated through geographically distributed backups, frameworks for risk and governance, and strategic alliances that keep critical systems running and make them resilient to attacks. Olga Boich

artigo.texto: China continues to dominate global clean-tech manufacturing in 2026, while the United States, Europe and India are investing billions of dollars in solar panels, electric vehicle (EV) batteries, energy-storage systems and wind equipment. Major manufacturing projects by CATL, BYD, First Solar, Qcells, Toyota, Volkswagen, Reliance Industries and Tata Group demonstrate the growing competition for industrial leadership. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), the global market for key clean-energy technologies reached nearly $1.2 trillion in 2025. However, annual manufacturing investment declined from nearly $220 billion in 2023 to below $200 billion in 2024. The competition is increasingly determined by factory output, manufacturing costs, supply-chain integration, technology and exports rather than investment announcements alone. China Leads Global EV Battery and Solar Manufacturing China remains the world’s largest clean-tech manufacturing hub, supported by integrated supply chains, extensive production capacity and competitive manufacturing costs. According to the IEA Global EV Outlook 2026, China manufactured approximately 16 million electric cars in 2025, representing nearly 75 percent of global production. Chinese electric-car exports exceeded 2.5 million vehicles. China also accounted for more than 80 percent of global battery-cell production, approximately 85 percent of cathode active-material production and more than 90 percent of anode active-material production. Major Chinese clean-tech manufacturing projects CATL – Lithium-ion battery manufacturing CATL operates major battery manufacturing facilities in Ningde, Yibin and other Chinese industrial locations. Its manufacturing network supplies batteries for electric vehicles, commercial transportation and stationary energy storage. CATL’s extensive production capacity and investment in lithium iron phosphate (LFP) technology strengthen China’s position in global battery supply chains. BYD – Integrated EV and battery manufacturing BYD manufactures electric vehicles, Blade batteries, power electronics and other automotive components. Its vertically integrated operations reduce dependence on external suppliers and support manufacturing efficiency. LONGi Green Energy – Solar manufacturing LONGi produces solar wafers, cells and modules, including high-efficiency photovoltaic technologies. Its integrated manufacturing capabilities support China’s domestic solar market and international exports. JinkoSolar – Solar cells and modules JinkoSolar operates large-scale solar manufacturing facilities in China and international markets, producing photovoltaic wafers, cells and modules. China’s main challenge is overcapacity, particularly in solar manufacturing, where aggressive pricing has weakened margins despite strong global demand. United States Invests Billions in Solar and Battery Factories The United States is expanding domestic clean-tech manufacturing through investments in solar modules, battery cells and advanced energy-storage technologies. First Solar: $1.1 Billion Alabama Solar Factory First Solar invested approximately $1.1 billion in its Alabama manufacturing facility, adding 3.5 GW of annual thin-film solar module capacity. The factory, commissioned in September 2024, directly employed approximately 855 workers during 2025. First Solar’s cadmium telluride technology differentiates its products from conventional crystalline-silicon solar modules manufactured predominantly in Asia. Qcells: 8.4 GW Solar Module Manufacturing in Georgia Hanwha Qcells expanded its manufacturing operations in Georgia, with its Cartersville facility beginning solar-cell production in June 2026. The company’s integrated manufacturing programme targets 3.3 GW each of ingot, wafer and solar-cell capacity. Together, Qcells’ Cartersville and Dalton facilities have approximately 8.4 GW of annual solar-module manufacturing capacity, supporting a workforce approaching 4,000 employees. The investment is intended to strengthen domestic solar supply chains and reduce dependence on imported photovoltaic components. Toyota: $13.9 Billion North Carolina Battery Factory Toyota began production at its $13.9 billion battery manufacturing facility in Liberty, North Carolina, in 2025. The factory covers approximately 7 million square feet and is designed to accommodate 14 battery production lines. The facility will manufacture batteries for hybrid, plug-in hybrid and battery-electric vehicles, with planned employment reaching approximately 5,100. Toyota’s investment demonstrates the growing importance of localized battery production for the US automotive industry. Tesla: Battery and Energy Storage Manufacturing Tesla operates battery manufacturing facilities in Nevada and Texas, alongside Megapack energy-storage system production in Lathrop, California. These operations support electric vehicle production and utility-scale battery storage, two important segments of the US clean-tech market. Europe Expands EV Battery Manufacturing Despite Cost Challenges Europe is developing domestic battery production to reduce reliance on imported cells and strengthen its automotive manufacturing industry. However, European manufacturers face higher electricity, labor and financing costs than many Asian competitors. The IEA estimates that manufacturing efficiency accounts for more than 40 percent of the battery-cell production-cost difference between China and Europe. artigo.texto: - The partnership will focus on vehicles using Huawei Qiankun solutions, aiming to deliver seamless energy replenishment for the autonomous driving era. - CATL has built 2,520 battery swap stations across 200 Chinese cities, with a long-term goal of expanding the network to 30,000 stations. Huawei's intelligent automotive business unit, Yinwang, or Newcool, has partnered with CATL (HKEX: 3750) on battery swapping, joining the battery maker's Choco ecosystem to further connect smart driving with energy replenishment services. Newcool, CATL and Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology (CAES) have signed a strategic cooperation framework agreement to jointly develop a smart battery swap ecosystem, according to a statement released by CATL on Monday. CAES operates CATL's battery swap business. The partnership will focus on vehicles using Huawei Qiankun intelligent automotive solutions, making them compatible with the Choco network and strengthening cooperation on swappable batteries and station networks. The 3 parties plan to integrate data and services across vehicles, swap stations and the cloud, using real-time battery status and users' travel patterns to anticipate energy needs and proactively schedule battery swaps. Under the proposed system, vehicles would independently determine when they need energy, locate and enter a station, align themselves for a fully automated 99-second battery swap, and drive away afterward. The partnership aims to extend assisted driving capabilities to battery swapping, creating a "seamless energy replenishment experience" for the autonomous driving era. However, the announcement did not identify specific vehicle models, a service launch date or initial coverage areas. This is similar to functionality Nio Inc (NYSE: NIO) already offers at some battery swap stations, where vehicles can automatically enter a station and complete a battery swap while using navigation-assisted driving. CATL chairman and CEO Robin Zeng, Huawei senior vice president and Newcool CEO Jin Yuzhi, and Yang Jun, co-president of CATL's marketing system, attended and witnessed the signing. For CATL, Newcool's participation provides a new avenue to expand vehicle partnerships for the Choco network as its station footprint extends from cities to highways. As of September 29, CATL had built 2,520 battery swap stations across 200 Chinese cities, according to the statement. Its long-term goal is to expand the network to 30,000 stations. Previously announced plans also call for building 1,000 highway battery swap stations in 2026 and 2027, creating a nationwide network spanning 11 north-south and 9 east-west highway corridors. Newcool grew out of Huawei's intelligent automotive solution business Unit, known as the car BU. It was formally established as a separate company in January 2024, initially wholly owned by Huawei. Huawei currently holds an 80% stake in Newcool, while Seres (HKEX: 9927) and Avatr, the EV unit of Changan Automobile (SZSE: 000625), each hold 10%. In April this year, Anhui Jianghuai Automobile Group Corp (JAC) announced plans to invest in Newcool without disclosing the proposed investment amount. Completion of the transaction has yet to be announced.

artigo.texto: The debate over data centers in Mason County has taken on a new wrinkle thanks to a report last week estimating the county’s schools could bring in $90 million a year — but only if residents renew a levy on the ballot in two weeks. That estimate — part of a report put out last week by Treasurer Larry Pack’s office — is based on projected property tax revenue from two new controversial data centers, the Monarch Compute Campus, currently under construction, and the proposed Project Tamarack data center. Last year, Mason County Schools brought in $10 million from the excess levy, according to data from the state Tax Division, meaning that the schools would get a 9-fold jump in levy revenue if the estimates are correct. However, Mason County Schools will only get the money if voters approve a renewal of the school excess levy on Nov. 3. Pack and some county officials are worried that may not happen. “We were hearing people say that Mason County is going to get all this tax money from the data center, so they don't need to pass this excess levy,” said Pack. “That’s not how the bill works, and that's not the impact.” Pack said he believes opposition stems from a misunderstanding about how the data centers are taxed. Under House Bill 2014, the controversial 2025 law that established state-wide regulations for high impact data centers, county boards of education do not immediately get access to data center property tax revenue. The money is contingent on voters passing the levy renewal. “If a county school board has no excess levy, they get zero money from the construction and operation of data centers in their county,” Pack said. Mason County officials have been trying to get the message out: The vote isn’t for or against the two data centers, which will stay either way. But if the levy fails, the data centers will, in effect, get a $90 million tax break and Mason County Schools will lose out on the extra tax revenue. “We’re talking not only academics, but band trips, athletic trips on busses. We're talking about helping out the extracurricular activities in the county as well as the academics,” said Rick Handley, president of the Mason County Commission. He said he supports the levy and is encouraging others to vote for it as well. Elaine Matheny is an advocate with Mason United, a group that has been fighting against the two data center developments. While she plans to vote for the levy, she said it hasn’t changed her opposition to the projects, and she’s skeptical about promises of how much money they will bring in. “Look at all the other extract industries that we've had in this state,” she said. “Look at the promises for the lottery and all the funds that were going to take care of the school system. Has that happened? No. We still have lots of problems funding our schools.” The levy question comes as Mason County — and West Virginia more broadly — debates how to handle the data center development. Proponents, including Gov. Patrick Morrisey and many Republicans in the Legislature, have argued that data centers will be an important economic boon for the state that will bring in money and growth. Opponents, however, have raised concerns about issues like water usage and pollution from the power plants needed to generate the enormous amounts of electricity the data centers require. Residents also worry about rising electricity prices and noise pollution created by the thousands of servers these centers house. In the background of it all is HB 2014. The law prevents local county zoning officials from blocking data center development and allows the developers to keep information about their projects from the public. It also spells out how the tax revenue from data centers will be split, with the state getting 50% while the local county keeps 30%. Regardless of how the vote shakes out, Pack expects lawmakers to reevaluate the law next year, especially when it comes to how revenue is split. “I do think that generally local folks know better how to spend the money than Charleston does,” he said. “So I think we'll have a spirited discussion about these allocations next session.” Election Day is Nov. 3. artigo.texto: Schneider Electric’s third quarter organic revenue jumped 17% to €11.5 billion euros ($12.9 billion US) — a record high for any quarter — the French multinational energy technology company said in an Oct. 16 earnings release. The company’s business associated with data centers “continues to be exceptionally strong with another quarter of triple digit demand growth in Q3, further improving our visibility into 2027 and 2028,” said Schneider’s CFO, Nathan Fast, during an earnings call. Schneider Electric has seen triple digit demand growth in orders associated with data centers for “three out of the last four quarters,” Fast said during the call. Morgan Stanley analyst Max Yates asked how much exposure the company has to neocloud businesses like CoreWeave. Fast said, “We do not break down exactly the impact or the split of hyperscaler, colo, neocloud, et cetera.” Schneider CEO Olivier Blum added, “We are extremely careful to select those companies that will be there in the long term.” Schneider Electric’s Energy Management segment made its most revenue in North America in the third quarter, but saw a higher organic growth rate of 32.4% in China and East Asia, compared to 20.3% That continues a trend in 2026, where North America led overall revenue volume but Asia saw a higher organic revenue growth rate. The sales growth in China was “led by everything to do with investment in AI infrastructure, driving growth in the data center and [semiconductor] segments, in particular,” said Fast during the call. “In our geographic trends, we add China alongside the U.S. and India in the countries we expect to drive growth. This is based on the strength of what we have seen over the recent quarters and which we believe is set to continue.” North American demand continues to grow, driven by momentum in data centers, “where we saw sustained high demand for prefabricated solutions and cooling,” Fast said. Blum said the company has also been bolstered in the European market by the “massive acceleration” of electric car adoption, as well as heat pumps. “We see very fast growth,” Blum said. “This fast growth is not only the growth of the EV charger, but every time you install an EV charger, you have to extend your electrical panel, so that creates a great opportunity, great synergy in a place where, for instance, in Europe, we have a very strong market share.”

artigo.texto: Vietnam Eyes Battery Storage to Unlock Rooftop Solar Potential Industry groups and policymakers identify energy storage infrastructure as critical bottleneck for distributed generation expansion across residential and commercial buildings. - ·Vietnam's rooftop solar expansion depends on battery storage deployment to address grid integration limits and intermittency challenges affecting distributed generation. - ·The Ministry of Industry and Trade is developing regulatory frameworks including time-of-use tariffs and capacity payments to incentivise storage systems alongside photovoltaic installations. - ·Lithium-ion battery costs fell 14 per cent globally in 2025 to USD 139 per kilowatt-hour, improving project economics for solar-plus-storage systems in Vietnam's industrial zones. Storage Gap Slows Distributed Generation Vietnam's rooftop solar sector faces a structural constraint that battery storage systems could resolve, according to industry stakeholders and government officials assessing the country's renewable energy transition. The Southeast Asian nation installed significant rooftop photovoltaic capacity during earlier subsidy programmes, but grid integration limits and the absence of storage infrastructure now restrict further expansion. Electricity demand in Vietnam grew 9.8 per cent year-on-year in the first eight months of 2025, driven by manufacturing export growth and rising household consumption. Rooftop solar offers a distributed generation pathway that reduces transmission losses and defers grid upgrade costs, yet the technology's intermittent output creates operational challenges for state utility Electricity of Vietnam without accompanying storage. Battery systems allow building owners to capture midday generation peaks and discharge during evening demand surges, smoothing supply curves and reducing strain on distribution networks. The technology also enables self-consumption models that improve project economics for commercial and industrial users facing higher tariff structures. Policy Framework Under Development Vietnam's Ministry of Industry and Trade is evaluating regulatory mechanisms to incentivise storage deployment alongside rooftop solar installations. Current feed-in tariff structures do not differentiate between solar-plus-storage projects and standalone photovoltaic systems, removing financial incentives for developers to add batteries despite grid benefits. Policymakers are examining time-of-use tariffs and capacity payment schemes that would reward storage operators for providing grid services. Such frameworks exist in Thailand and the Philippines, where battery systems participate in frequency regulation and peak shaving programmes. The ministry has not announced a timeline for new regulations, though industry participants expect pilot programmes to launch in major industrial zones during 2027. Manufacturing hubs in the southern provinces of Binh Duong and Dong Nai present logical test cases, given high daytime electricity consumption and existing rooftop solar penetration. Cost Trajectory Improves Economics Lithium-ion battery prices declined 14 per cent globally in 2025, reaching USD 139 per kilowatt-hour at the pack level. Analysts project further reductions as Chinese manufacturers expand production capacity and new chemistries enter commercial deployment. Vietnam imports most battery storage components, primarily from China and South Korea, with domestic assembly limited to a handful of renewable energy firms. Lower equipment costs improve payback periods for solar-plus-storage projects, though financing remains constrained for small and medium enterprises without access to green credit facilities. State-owned commercial banks have increased lending for renewable energy projects under central bank directives, yet loan terms typically require collateral exceeding project asset values. Development banks and multilateral lenders are exploring guarantee mechanisms to reduce perceived risks for rooftop solar storage investments. Grid Modernisation Parallel Track Energy storage deployment must proceed alongside broader grid infrastructure upgrades if Vietnam is to meet its 2030 renewable energy targets. The national power development plan calls for 47,000 megawatts of solar capacity by the end of the decade, with rooftop systems expected to contribute approximately one-third of that total. Transmission congestion in southern provinces already curtails utility-scale solar output during low-demand periods, a problem that distributed generation with storage could partially alleviate. However, distribution network operators lack real-time monitoring systems and advanced inverter controls necessary to manage high penetrations of behind-the-meter generation. International donors have committed funding for smart meter rollouts and grid management software, though implementation timelines extend beyond 2028 in most provinces. The sequencing challenge requires storage incentives to align with grid readiness, avoiding stranded assets or curtailment that undermines project viability. Vietnam's rooftop solar trajectory will depend on how quickly storage costs fall and whether policy frameworks create sufficient returns for combined systems. The country's manufacturing sector offers substantial demand for daytime generation paired with evening storage discharge, positioning industrial rooftops as the most viable near-term market segment.

The site plans for a 1-gigawatt Google data center and an accompanying electrical substation received final approval last week from the Van Buren Township Planning Commission. 🗳️ Civic Action Toolbox — see how you can get involved Why it matters The Van Buren Township data center could affect nearby residents' quality of life through noise, dust, and climate impacts. Who's making public decisions The Van Buren Township Planning Commission granted the site plan approval. The Michigan Public Service Commission oversees DTE's contracts and proposed gas plants, and EGLE regulates wetland and stream impacts. Upcoming Meetings Contact Your Representatives Civic Actions: What You Can Do What to watch for next Watch whether Van Buren Township adopts stricter data center zoning rules, and how regulators rule on DTE's proposed natural gas plants in Milan and Handy townships ahead of the planned December 2027 startup. Are you taking action? Let us know. Powered by Civic Action Toolbox Residents have said the “Project Cannoli” data center proposed by developer Panattoni could bring noise to the nearby Haggerty subdivision, harm water resources, and impact energy reliability and affordability. Project backers say it represents a boon for jobs and investment that will bring significant tax dollars to the area. The commission is compelled to approve the project because it’s a principal permitted use under the township’s zoning rules, Van Buren Township Planning Commissioner Jeffrey Jahr said Wednesday, Oct. 14. “I feel that the applicant has met all of the objective specific requirements for us to grant the request,” he said. Saline Township, in neighboring Washtenaw County, was sued by a data center developer that alleged exclusionary zoning in September 2025 after the township board denied the rezoning needed for Oracle and OpenAI’s 1.4 GW data center. Whether Van Buren Township places more restrictions on data centers will need to be evaluated, Jahr said, adding that he is leaning toward doing so. Residents say they’re already dealing with noise, dust Township residents said Wednesday they are already dealing with noise and dust from the project. Several people played recorded dump truck noise on their phones. Over 2,700 people have signed an online petition opposing the data center. Van Buren Township resident Tracy Osborne, who lives next to the data center site, said he’s concerned about the impact constant data center noise could have on his daughter with special needs. “My concern is not simply whether this facility meets a number on a noise report,” he said. “It is whether neighboring families will be able to enjoy their homes without continuous disruptive equipment noise.” A Panattoni spokesperson told Planet Detroit in a statement that the company takes resident concerns seriously, including noise and dust, and is committed to minimizing impacts. Multiple parties are working in the area, including utility providers, and not all work is associated with the project, the spokesperson said. Representatives for Panattoni said Wednesday that the I-94 Service Drive will be used for site access during construction — not Haggerty Road — to minimize resident impacts. Here’s how the data center could impact residents. How big will the project be? The project is set to occupy 282 acres north of I-94, east of Haggerty Road, west of Hannan Road, and south of Wayne County Community College. The project will permanently impact 13.55 acres of wetlands, require six culverts in regulated streams, and fill and abandon 573 linear feet of a stream, John Jones, an environmental quality analyst with Michigan’s Department of Environment, Great Lakes, and Energy (EGLE), said in June. Developers will offset wetland and stream impacts by purchasing wetland mitigation bank credits in the Huron River watershed and creating 1,174 feet of new stream channel on the property itself, Jones said. Forty-five percent of the acreage at the site will remain undeveloped under a conservation easement, Josh Capps, Panattoni’s director of data center delivery, said Wednesday. The data center will use roughly 1 GW of electricity, according to the township’s frequently asked questions document. One gigawatt is roughly equivalent to the power used by 800,000 homes. What are the economic impacts? The project represents a “generational investment from one of the best companies in the world,” Adam Kramer, president of data centers for Panattoni, said Wednesday. The data center will require 9.8 million labor hours for its construction and employ 50-200 employees on site, he said. Developers have already awarded $2 billion in contracts to Wayne County businesses, he said. The data center is projected to be the largest taxpayer in Van Buren Township and one of the top five taxpayers in Wayne County, Kramer said in February. How much noise will the project produce? Modeling shows the data center will comply with Van Buren Township’s noise limit of 67 dBA, Paul Kammer, an engineer with the consulting firm Fishbeck, said Wednesday. dBA is a weighted decibel scale for judging loudness, with 67 falling between the volume of a normal conversation and a vacuum cleaner, according to a Yale University decibel chart. Panattoni’s Capps said sound from the facility would largely fall below the area’s ambient nighttime noise. The loudest noise will be to the south and east of the facility, with anticipated dBA readings of 62.1 and 59.7, respectively, he said. Buildings are being used to block noise from leaving the site, Capps said. The Kimley-Horn noise study for the project says there are plans

artigo.texto: Leilão de baterias Aneel: transmissoras podem ficar de fora A área técnica da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) defende que a participação de transmissoras nos leilões de baterias depende da reversão de parte da receita da atividade para reduzir as tarifas. O entendimento consta de Ofício Conjunto enviado à diretoria da agência. A medida, se confirmada, pode impactar diretamente a competitividade das empresas do setor elétrico. Reversão de receitas para modicidade tarifária O ofício conjunto vincula a participação das empresas à destinação de parte ou total da receita dos projetos à redução das tarifas de transmissão. O documento cita: “Além disso, mantém-se a necessidade do benefício à modicidade tarifária, mediante reversão total ou parcial das receitas auferidas com a atividade da SPE para a concessão, em favor dos usuários do SIN [Sistema Interligado Nacional]”. Ainda segundo o ofício, os contratos firmados exigem autorização prévia para atividades estranhas ao objeto da concessão e estabelecem que parte ou toda a receita desses negócios contribua para a modicidade das tarifas de transmissão. No entanto, o ofício não define percentual, base de cálculo ou metodologia para a reversão. O texto usa a expressão “receitas auferidas com a atividade da SPE”, sem individualizar a receita fixa do CRCap (Contrato de Reserva de Capacidade para Potência). Essa lacuna gera insegurança jurídica para as transmissoras interessadas no leilão. Manifestação técnica, não deliberação da diretoria Vale destacar que a manifestação é das áreas técnicas; o documento não registra uma deliberação da diretoria colegiada da agência sobre os editais ou sobre a legitimidade dessa captura. Ou seja, o posicionamento ainda pode ser revisto ou ajustado pela instância superior da Aneel. A diretoria colegiada é responsável pelas decisões finais sobre regras de leilões e regulação do setor elétrico. Fontes ouvidas pela reportagem dizem que se o entendimento for mantido, as empresas transmissoras podem ficar de fora do leilão por perda de concorrência e desequilíbrio dos investimentos. A incerteza regulatória pode afastar players importantes e reduzir a competitividade do certame, com reflexos no preço final da energia para consumidores e empresas. Taesa contesta reversão da receita fixa “A Receita Fixa do CRCap não se sujeita a reversão à modicidade tarifária da transmissão”, sustenta a Taesa em um dos tópicos da contribuição enviada à Aneel. A transmissora argumenta que a receita fixa do contrato de reserva de capacidade tem natureza distinta e não deveria ser capturada para reduzir tarifas de transmissão. A empresa defende que a reversão comprometeria a viabilidade econômica dos projetos de armazenamento. Como os certames selecionam propostas de menor receita fixa, uma subsidiária de transmissora sujeita à reversão precisaria incorporar esse custo ao lance ou aceitar remuneração líquida inferior à de concorrentes com as mesmas obrigações contratuais. Isso criaria uma desvantagem competitiva clara para as transmissoras, que poderiam optar por não participar do leilão. Impacto no setor elétrico e na economia O leilão de baterias é visto como estratégico para ampliar a flexibilidade do sistema elétrico e integrar fontes renováveis intermitentes. A eventual exclusão das transmissoras pode reduzir o número de proponentes e elevar os custos dos projetos vencedores. Para o comércio e a indústria do interior paulista, como Araçatuba e região, tarifas de energia mais altas pressionam os custos operacionais e a competitividade das empresas locais. A definição sobre a reversão de receitas deve ocorrer antes da publicação do edital definitivo do leilão. Empresários e associações setoriais acompanham o tema de perto, pois a energia elétrica é um insumo essencial para a produção e os serviços. A fonte não detalhou se haverá nova rodada de contribuições ou audiência pública sobre o assunto. Perguntas Frequentes O que a área técnica da Aneel defende sobre a participação de transmissoras no leilão de baterias? A área técnica da Aneel defende que a participação de transmissoras nos leilões de baterias depende da reversão de parte da receita da atividade para reduzir as tarifas, conforme consta em Ofício Conjunto. Como a reversão de receitas das transmissoras no leilão de baterias afetaria a competitividade? Como os certames selecionam propostas de menor receita fixa, uma subsidiária de transmissora sujeita à reversão precisaria incorporar esse custo ao lance ou aceitar remuneração líquida inferior à de concorrentes, podendo ficar de fora do leilão por perda de concorrência e desequilíbrio dos investimentos. A Receita Fixa do CRCap está sujeita à reversão para modicidade tarifária da transmissão, segundo a Taesa? Não, a Taesa sustenta que ‘A Receita Fixa do CRCap não se sujeita a reversão à modicidade tarifária da transmissão’, conforme um dos tópicos de sua contribuição.

artigo.texto: It was as if Connie Lane were standing on the precipice of the Grand Canyon, she said, staring in disbelief at its enormity. The hyperscale data center near Milwaukee, where Lane had been visiting with friends from law school for a June reunion, left her incredulous. “I can’t begin to describe the scope. They brought in these huge lines to feed them electricity. I was stunned. It’s one thing when you read about it; it’s another thing to see it,” she said. Lane, a Democratic state representative, is running for reelection in Merrimack District 13, or Concord’s Ward 2. In her response to the Monitor’s general election survey, she cited energy policy and the feared effect of data centers on the power grid and ratepayers as one of the most salient issues facing the state of New Hampshire. There are currently ten data centers in New Hampshire, four of which are clustered in Manchester, according to the tracking platform Data Center Map. Proposals in Bow and Nottingham have spurred public outcry that, in the latter case, prompted the developer to withdraw his plan just hours before the town’s planning board was scheduled to review it. That opposition is hardly exclusive to the Granite State. Data centers have unified Democrats and Republicans, progressives and conservatives, in forceful resistance as local disputes over land use, municipal transparency, tax incentives and environmental impacts repeat themselves nationwide. “They’re going to come in, electricity is going to soar, and are we really ready for this vast use of our land? Is this the way we really want to develop acres and acres and acres?” Lane said. Earlier this year in New Hampshire, a group of Republican lawmakers inverted an effort to affirm municipalities’ ability to regulate data centers, amending the language of the bill, Senate Bill 439, to do the opposite: allow data centers by right in areas zoned for commercial or industrial development. The bill was ultimately tabled and didn’t advance further. Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican, told WMUR at the time that she opposed those alterations to the bill. In the months since, she’s stated she will impose a moratorium on new data center developments with the upcoming state budget, citing concern that, at an average energy consumption of 100 megawatts, even one hyperscale development could overburden the regional grid. “I’ve been clear that I oppose siting data centers in New Hampshire, including the proposed projects in Nottingham and Bow. Data centers would drive up our already too-high energy costs, and I share the concerns raised about their impact on our water and environment,” she said in a statement to the Monitor. Her gubernatorial challenger, Democrat Cinde Warmington, said she doubts the governor’s intentions based on her perceived lack of leadership on data center-related bills, like SB 439, and that she would like to see the state act more expediently. If elected, Warmington said she would impose a temporary moratorium on the permitting of new data centers on “day-one.” Her campaign’s “data center bill of rights” outlines some of the safeguards she’d push for in a regulatory framework: limits on noise pollution, requirements that construction draw on local labor through protected agreements and protections for clean air and water. “I think it is really hypocritical that Gov. Ayotte now suddenly is calling for a moratorium,” Warmington told the Monitor. “Now she says she’s for a moratorium in her budget next year — by next year we could have a massive data center in our state. We know there’s one proposed in Bow. So too little, too late, and pretty disingenuous.” Imagining how the legislature might devise more permanent regulations on data centers, Lane told the Monitor the state “would certainly want to do a lot of study” to inform the drafting process, but that “personally, I don’t want them at all.” The hyperscale data centers recently proposed in New Hampshire provide a window into the rabid acceleration of development to keep pace with artificial intelligence’s demand for computing power, and the imposing dimension of data centers being built in other parts of the country. One colossal data center development, imagined by technology company Fermi America for the Texas Panhandle and dubbed “Project Matador”, is expected to have a capacity of 17 gigawatts. The development’s first power-generating equipment, three 480,000-pound gas turbines, arrived on site near Amarillo last month, according to local reporting. By comparison, the proposal that public filings indicate is in the very early, exploratory stages of being permitted for development in Bow could draw between 200 and 350 megawatts of power — two percent of that capacity. William Lynch, the Democratic candidate for Merrimack District 10, which includes Hooksett and Dunbarton, said he worries not only about the unmistakable environmental consequences of such large developments but the possibility that, if the AI bubble bursts, today’s enormous investments will produce warehouses full of data storage no one uses tomorrow. “I’ve seen commitments to build out data centers that progress as far as building. But some data centers are not keeping pace with their commitments, and I’m concerned that it might come to a point, in two or three years, where the overall investment and use of the computing power won’t keep up,” he said. Lynch had an eight-year career with tech giant Oracle, a major cloud and AI data center operator. He described his work — first as a cloud applications engineer, then pivoting to health applications — as building the software infrastructure on top of which other software engineers iterate. His software could be adapted for use on websites like Facebook or the New York Times, or it could be deployed into traditional data centers. artigo.texto: Microsoft desiste de acordo para data center no Reino Unido em momento crucial para planos de IPO da Nscale Segundo o jornal The Telegraph, não foram apresentados os motivos para que a gigante americana abandonasse o acorfo referente ao empreendimento em Loughton, no condado de Essex A Microsoft desistiu de um acordo para um data center no Reino Unido com a britânica Nscale, especializada em infraestrutura de computação em nuvem para inteligência artificial, em um momento crucial para as perspectivas de abertura de capital da startup, informou o jornal The Telegraph. O jornal não apresentou uma razão específica para a decisão da gigante americana de tecnologia de abandonar o acordo referente ao empreendimento em Loughton, no condado de Essex, mas afirmou que o projeto vem enfrentando uma série de atrasos. Segundo a publicação, as autoridades informaram à Nscale que não esperam fornecer energia à instalação antes da década de 2030. O principal empreendimento da Nscale na Noruega também está seis meses atrasado, com apenas 6,4 megawatts dos 30 megawatts de capacidade previstos para o data center em operação. De acordo com um documento apresentado no âmbito dos preparativos para o IPO, a Nscale depende da Microsoft e da Anthropic para cerca de 85% de seus contratos. A Microsoft estava prestes a se tornar a principal cliente do primeiro data center britânico da Nscale, em Essex. A saída da Microsoft representaria um revés para a empresa, que pretende captar até US$ 3 bilhões em uma oferta pública inicial de ações (IPO, na sigla em inglês), possivelmente ainda neste mês, e que já vinha enfrentando a apreensão dos investidores em relação aos riscos da expansão mais ampla da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial. A Nscale é uma das empresas mais proeminentes do segmento conhecido como neocloud, formado por companhias que buscam construir enormes complexos computacionais voltados à inteligência artificial. Essas empresas querem aproveitar os centenas de bilhões de dólares que as gigantes de tecnologia se comprometeram a investir nessa área e representam um elo fundamental na cadeia de suprimentos que sustenta o boom da IA. Um porta-voz da Nscale disse ao The Telegraph: “Continuamos comprometidos com o projeto de Loughton e com o Reino Unido, e estamos estudando fontes alternativas de energia para o local, além de outros locais para expansão no país. “Nossa relação com a Microsoft continua sólida e é de longo prazo, e esse lamentável problema na rede elétrica de Londres não afeta nossos outros contratos.” A Microsoft não comentou o assunto ao The Telegraph e não respondeu imediatamente a um pedido de comentário da Bloomberg feito fora do horário comercial habitual. O cenário para os planos de abertura de capital da Nscale ficou mais desfavorável nos últimos dias. Na semana passada, a também neocloud CoreWeave ganhou destaque depois que seu cofundador afirmou que a empresa estava estudando formas de captar recursos nos mercados de dívida com grau de investimento, que oferecem amplos volumes de capital provenientes de investidores como seguradoras. Os investidores já vinham demonstrando cautela em relação aos fornecedores de capacidade computacional para IA, diante das dezenas de bilhões de dólares em empréstimos contraídos por essas empresas e por seus clientes para financiar a enorme expansão da capacidade dos data centers. As ações da CoreWeave despencaram nas três primeiras sessões da semana e depois se recuperaram parcialmente. Na sexta-feira, porém, as preocupações voltaram a pesar sobre os papéis, provocando a pior semana da empresa desde novembro, com uma queda de 25%. O episódio também ocorreu após a australiana Firmus, do setor de data centers, abandonar seus planos de abertura de capital porque a oferta não conseguiu atrair apoio suficiente ao preço das ações proposto ao mercado.

artigo.texto: Pittsylvania County’s Berry Hill megasite will eventually have 21 data center buildings, built in phases over 15 years, according to permits filed by Stack Infrastructure. The project, an AI data center campus, “represents the largest private single-investment commitment” on record with the Virginia Economic Development Partnership, according to permit information. When formally approved, the project will also be the largest economic development deal in Southside Virginia’s history. It’s expected to create up to $100 billion in investment and more than 2,500 jobs with salaries of more than $80,000 over a 20-year period. At full build-out, the campus — called Project Crossroads — will require about 3,000 megawatts of capacity power, mostly generated on-site, said the permit application. The application requests construction and environmental permitting from multiple agencies at once. It lays out project details, like power infrastructure, wetlands impact mitigation and community engagement for Project Crossroads. The project was first made public in March through a land sale between data center developer Stack Infrastructure and the Danville-Pittsylvania County Regional Industrial Facility Authority. Many of the details in the joint permit application were not available until now. Through the land sale and a local performance agreement, Stack claimed nearly 3,000 acres at the 3,528-acre megasite in Pittsylvania. According to the joint permit application, 1,715 acres of that land are developable. The 21-building data center campus, along with its on-site power and other infrastructure, would encompass those 1,715 acres, with a total of 1,733 acres disturbed during construction. The application also included expected property tax revenue for Pittsylvania County: up to $48 million per year at full buildout. That’s about $16.5 million in taxes per year on the first 1,000 acres and an additional $16,250 per acre for every developed acre after that. The county will also receive tax revenue on data center equipment at a rate of $1.62 per $100 of assessed value. This would almost certainly make the project the county’s largest taxpayer. The biggest chunk — about 42% — of the county’s revenue for fiscal year 2027 comes from real estate taxes. The project is not receiving any local discretionary monetary incentives. Though no formal announcement about the project has been made, Project Crossroads is expected to be the second tenant at the megasite, after lithium-ion battery separator manufacturer Microporous announced that it would build a facility on about 200 acres in 2024. The Berry Hill megasite was purchased jointly by Danville and Pittsylvania in 2008. Since then, over $217 million in public and private funds have been invested in grading, infrastructure and other preparations to ready the site for development. The megasite is now “shovel-ready,” meaning it has all the resources necessary for development. In January, the planning commission and board of supervisors in Pittsylvania County unanimously approved a fast-tracked zoning change to allow “special heavy industrial” developments, including data centers and power generation, at the megasite. On-site power generation Project Crossroads is expected to use on-site power generation for its massive energy needs, according to the application. A large part of the energy will likely be supplied by natural gas, via existing transmission pipelines to the megasite. Stack also plans to build a 150-megawatt substation at the megasite, which is expected to be operational by 2028, the application says. “The utilization of onsite power generation will reduce constraints on existing grid infrastructure, while providing reliability for operations,” the joint permit application says. “The project will also require backup and emergency power capabilities to maintain operational continuity during utility interruptions.” Specifics on the type, capacity and configuration of these systems will be determined later, based on requirements of future tenants, but they may include diesel generators, natural gas-fired generators, battery energy storage systems or a combination of these. The March performance agreement includes a condition on power use. It says that there will be a minimum load capacity of 299 megawatts for the project, provided by Appalachian Power by the end of 2028. There will be no restrictions on a load capacity higher than 299 megawatts, it says. The total projected capacity for on-site power at Project Crossroads is 3,000 megawatts. By comparison, a conventional nuclear power plant can deliver more than 700 megawatts, according to the International Atomic Energy Agency. For instance, Dominion Energy’s North Anna nuclear station’s two reactors supply, together, 1,890 megawatts. The joint permit application identifies two “energy generation campuses” as part of the facility — the 80-acre Southwest Energy Generation Campus and the 125-acre Northeast Energy Generation Campus. The combined 205 acres are the minimum acreage necessary to meet the project’s planned energy needs, the application says. The company is making efforts to minimize the on-site power’s environmental impact to streams and wetlands, according to the application. Where feasible, the energy generation facilities and infrastructure were consolidated to reduce environmental impacts, according to the document. Also released with the joint permit application were thousands of other pages of permitting information, submitted to the Virginia Department of Environmental Quality, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and other agencies. In an April community outreach meeting, Pittsylvania County Economic Development Director Matt Rowe said it’s a misconception that the project will raise electric bills for ratepayers. artigo.texto: Carbon market plan offers income opportunities — BBM Revenue from carbon credits could also help finance climate adaptation projects, including resilient infrastructure, water facilities and other essential services. President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has issued Executive Order (eo) 127, which seeks to create income opportunities for Filipinos through environmental protection activities, including tree planting, forest conservation and pollution reduction. The order mandates the formulation of the Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework to support the country’s climate commitments under the Paris Agreement, attract investments in green projects and establish rules for the trading of carbon credits. Executive Secretary Ralph Recto said communities, farmers, businesses and other groups that help reduce pollution or absorb greenhouse gases could earn additional income through qualified environmental projects. Under the framework, eligible projects could generate carbon credits that may be sold to companies or other buyers seeking to meet their climate commitments. Recto cited communities that plant and protect trees as potential beneficiaries, since trees absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. “In other words, people can earn from planting and caring for trees, using clean energy, and engaging in other activities that help protect the environment. You will be given carbon credits for every activity proven to have reduced greenhouse gases, which can be sold,” Recto said. He stressed, however, that projects must meet government standards and undergo proper verification before qualifying for carbon credits. Registry Recto said the initiative could encourage investments in reforestation, sustainable agriculture, renewable energy and waste management while creating livelihood opportunities, particularly in rural communities. “We’re hitting two birds with one stone. The President wants to protect the environment while helping people earn more,” he said. Revenue from carbon credits could also help finance climate adaptation projects, including resilient infrastructure, water facilities and other essential services, Recto added. Under EO 127, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) will develop rules on project eligibility, carbon credit measurement and verification, and the sharing of revenues and other benefits. The DENR will also establish a Philippine National Carbon Registry to monitor carbon credits and prevent double counting and other irregularities. An interagency committee chaired by the Climate Change Commission, with the Department of Finance as vice chair, will oversee the development and implementation of the policy.

artigo.texto: A battery that costs about $3 million could end up being nearly fully offset by stacked state and federal incentives in Illinois. Larger batteries can store electricity for later use, keeping homes and businesses powered through hot summer nights, winter storms, and stretches when solar and wind output dips. Here's what to know Richardson Electronics said on October 14 that it is increasing commercial-scale battery production at its La Fox plant and plans to build a 5-megawatt storage battery there in summer 2027. The Chicago Tribune reported that company officials said no Illinois company has connected a larger battery to the grid. Richardson has global ambitions for its battery business, but executives say Illinois could become one of its biggest markets because the state aggressively subsidizes storage. Scott DuBois, who directs the company's storage operations, said stacking state incentives on top of federal tax credits leaves little of a battery's cost left to pay. Rising electricity demand, including from artificial intelligence, is adding to concerns about whether the grid will remain dependable. Matthew Tomc, Ameren's vice president for regulatory policy and energy supply, warned, "We are depending on out-of-state resources to essentially keep the lights on." He added that consumers could face seasonal price spikes, especially in summer, if the company doesn't add more power sources and storage in time. More background Commonwealth Edison customers in northern Illinois now pay about $141 a month on average, a 4% increase since 2021, according to Heatmap News and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Ameren's downstate customers pay more, averaging $224 a month, a 51% jump over five years. Storage can help because it allows utilities and communities to store electricity generated during the day and use it later, including after sunset or during weather-driven disruptions. Gil Quiniones, ComEd's chief executive, said, "If the majority of our residential, commercial, and industrial customers put in batteries, that's going to be a big win for the state." He added, "It could increase the capacity utilization for the grid we've already paid for, and have a chance to really put downward pressure on prices for everybody." The technology affects climate goals, monthly bills, and resilience during outages. Illinois is also starting far behind. Cleanview, a market research company in Henderson, Colorado, said Texas has 18 gigawatts of utility-scale battery storage, California has 16 gigawatts, and Illinois has just 102 megawatts. What's being done? Richardson describes its approach as specialized engineering work rather than mass production. Instead of chasing the biggest utility projects, the company plans to focus on customized microgrid systems, local energy networks that can power nearby users directly or trade electricity with the regional grid. An early battery order came from an Alaska microgrid that serves seven remote communities. The company also said its railroad locomotive battery packs helped shape its utility-scale storage technology. Richardson also struck a deal in May to handle engineering and marketing for the batteries Gotion builds at both the utility and neighborhood scale. Gotion runs a $2 billion factory in Manteno, Illinois. For its largest systems, the two companies start with roughly 4,500 battery cells, sealed together with cooling and control equipment inside a container about the size of a 20-foot shipping container. State planning is moving in parallel. Consultants to the Illinois Power Agency and other state agencies said that by 2045, the ComEd service area would need 12 gigawatts of battery storage capable of running four hours, while the Ameren region would need 8 gigawatts. The agencies are set to release a draft Integrated Resource Plan on November 16 that will address how Illinois can meet growing demand while staying on track with its clean-energy goals. Illinois' challenge is getting much bigger, not smaller. Nathan Miller, a consultant working with regulators on the Integrated Resource Plan, said, "For Illinois to meet its broader decarbonization goals across sectors, we need to be in a growth mode here. The system needs to get bigger." Where can I learn more? As utilities and homeowners weigh battery storage, the economics and reliability picture is changing fast. The articles below cover home-battery incentives, large solar-plus-storage projects, grid-scale build-outs, and financing that cuts upfront costs. • In Connecticut, home batteries gained a major edge as rooftop-solar incentives hit new caps. • In Nevada, the Gemini project pairs vast solar generation with batteries outside Las Vegas. • Across the United States, grid batteries are reshaping when wind and solar power reach customers. • In Idaho, utilities are building the state's largest battery to steady the grid. • With Palmetto financing, homeowners can now get backup batteries installed without upfront payments.
