artigo.texto: O Google quer construir um data center de 780 megawatts em Pine Island, cidade de cerca de 4 mil habitantes a uma hora a sudeste de Minneapolis, e aposta que o projeto pode ajudar a financiar uma rede elétrica mais limpa e confiável. O modelo, apresentado pela empresa como a forma correta de atender à demanda da inteligência artificial, é tema de reportagem da CNBC, que ouviu especialistas e moradores céticos. O acordo proposto com a Xcel Energy prevê que o Google financie a adição de 1.400 megawatts de energia eólica, 200 megawatts de solar e 300 megawatts de armazenamento em baterias à rede da concessionária. O volume supera a capacidade do próprio data center porque eólica e solar não geram eletricidade o tempo todo. Segundo a Xcel, a nova energia atenderá todos os clientes da região, não apenas o Google, e ajudará a avançar no fornecimento local de energia livre de carbono. O contrato depende de aprovação da comissão de serviços públicos do Minnesota. O desenho inclui proteções para a concessionária: o Google pagará por pelo menos 75% da capacidade contratada mesmo se consumir menos e, em caso de rescisão antecipada, deverá arcar com até oito anos de cobranças mínimas de demanda. “Ninguém quer fazer uma grande expansão e depois não ter para onde mandar essa energia”, disse Amanda Rome, vice-presidente executiva da Xcel, à CNBC. O projeto também mira a meta do Google de operar com energia livre de carbono 24 horas por dia até 2030. A empresa diz que a área de nuvem, que sustenta seu modelo Gemini, teve receita de quase US$ 25 bilhões no segundo trimestre, alta de 82% em um ano. A corrida da tecnologia por capacidade computacional é o que vem impulsionando a demanda por eletricidade. Resistência dos moradores Pesquisa do Gallup feita em março mostrou que 71% dos americanos se opõem à instalação de um data center em sua vizinhança, com o consumo de energia no topo das preocupações. Levantamento do Pew Research Center de julho e agosto indicou que metade dos entrevistados avalia que os data centers serão majoritariamente ruins para o meio ambiente e para as contas de luz das famílias. Rede envelhecida e críticas A North American Electric Reliability Corporation, entidade sem fins lucrativos que atua como reguladora do setor, afirma que os novos data centers responderão pela maior parte do aumento projetado da demanda por eletricidade na próxima década. O Departamento de Energia, sob o governo de Joe Biden, informou que mais de 70% das linhas de transmissão e transformadores dos EUA têm pelo menos 25 anos. Para Amanda Peterson Corio, chefe global de energia do Google, o momento é ideal para usar capital privado na correção da infraestrutura envelhecida, segundo a CNBC. Jigar Shah, sócio da consultoria Multiplier, disse à CNBC que os operadores poderiam erguer instalações menores em locais onde a rede já tem capacidade ociosa, o que reduziria a necessidade de construir nova geração e transmissão. David Pomerantz, diretor-executivo do Energy and Policy Institute, afirmou que as concessionárias têm retornos em torno de 10% sobre novos investimentos — e por isso têm pouco incentivo para acomodar data centers na rede existente.

artigo.texto: O desenvolvimento dos mercados de carbono e das regulamentações sobre a divulgação de informações climáticas está a impor exigências crescentes à medição, ao controlo e à verificação dos dados de emissões. Na União Europeia (UE), as entidades abrangidas pelo Sistema de Comércio de Emissões da UE (SCE) devem monitorizar e reportar as emissões anualmente e submeter-se a verificações regulamentares para cumprirem as suas obrigações de quotas. Entretanto, o Mecanismo de Ajustamento de Carbono na Fronteira (MBCF) exige a comunicação das emissões contidas em determinados bens importados, obrigando as empresas não só a realizar inventários de emissões a nível local, como também a identificar dados para cada produto individualmente. No Vietnã, o roteiro para o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono está gradualmente concretizando os requisitos de gestão de emissões. A Decisão nº 232/QD-TTg, sobre o roteiro para o desenvolvimento do mercado de carbono nacional, fornece uma base para a implementação de mecanismos relacionados a cotas de emissão e negociação de carbono. Em particular, em 9 de fevereiro de 2026, o Primeiro-Ministro emitiu a Decisão nº 263/QD-TTg sobre as cotas piloto totais de emissão de gases de efeito estufa para 2025 e 2026 para 110 instalações nos setores de energia térmica, siderurgia e cimento. Esses desenvolvimentos significam que as emissões de gases de efeito estufa não são mais apenas uma questão de gestão ambiental, mas estão cada vez mais ligadas aos custos, obrigações e eficiência operacional das empresas. Nesse contexto, a contabilidade de carbono desempenha um papel crucial na conexão dos dados de emissões com os sistemas de informação contábil, auxiliando as empresas no controle de custos, na avaliação dos impactos financeiros e no aumento da transparência nos relatórios. Conectar os dados de emissão ao sistema de contabilização de carbono. O primeiro desafio da contabilização de carbono é garantir que os dados de emissões sejam completos, consistentes e verificáveis. Para atender a esse requisito, as empresas precisam identificar claramente a fonte das emissões, o escopo da medição, os métodos de cálculo e as responsabilidades de cada departamento no processo de coleta e agregação de dados. Se as informações entre produção, gestão ambiental e contabilidade forem inconsistentes ou carecerem de fundamento, as empresas enfrentarão dificuldades para determinar os custos de carbono, preparar relatórios e demonstrar a conformidade com as regulamentações pertinentes. No entanto, a contabilização de carbono vai além da simples medição e agregação de emissões. Os dados de carbono precisam ser comparados com informações sobre matérias-primas, consumo de energia, processos de produção e custos relacionados. Com base nisso, as empresas podem identificar processos que geram emissões significativas, avaliar a eficiência dos recursos e determinar estratégias adequadas de redução de emissões. Quando integradas a um sistema de contabilidade gerencial, as informações sobre carbono também auxiliam na análise de custos por produto, departamento ou processo, contribuindo para uma melhor tomada de decisão em relação a investimentos em tecnologia e organização da produção. Além da padronização de dados, o registro e a apresentação de transações relacionadas ao carbono também impõem novas exigências às práticas contábeis. Determinar como contabilizar cotas de emissão gratuitas, cotas de compra adicionais e obrigações de pagamento pode afetar o reflexo de ativos, despesas, passivos e resultados financeiros. Sem orientações adequadas ou com diferentes metodologias aplicadas pelas empresas, as informações financeiras podem apresentar inconsistências, reduzindo a comparabilidade entre empresas e entre períodos de reporte. Aprimorar a contabilização de carbono em conjunto com a transparência financeira. Para que a contabilização de carbono seja eficaz, as empresas precisam construir gradualmente um sistema de controle de dados de emissões integrado aos seus processos contábeis atuais. Isso inclui esclarecer as responsabilidades pela coleta, comparação e verificação de dados; estabelecer um mecanismo para armazenar registros rastreáveis; e fortalecer a coordenação entre os departamentos de produção, gestão ambiental, contabilidade e auditoria interna. Isso constitui a base para melhorar a confiabilidade das informações sobre emissões, minimizar discrepâncias na agregação de dados e facilitar a verificação quando necessário. Essencialmente, a contabilidade de carbono exige a integração de informações ambientais e financeiras. Enquanto os dados de emissões refletem o impacto ambiental das atividades de produção, as informações contábeis esclarecem os custos, as obrigações e as consequências econômicas associadas ao controle e à redução das emissões. Quando esses dois sistemas de informação são interligados com base em dados confiáveis e métodos de registro adequados, as empresas têm uma base sólida para melhorar a qualidade dos relatórios e desenvolver planos de produção sustentáveis.

artigo.texto: SHENZHEN, China, Oct. 19, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- BYD Energy Storage has built a comprehensive after-sales service network in a multi‑tier framework: station O&M, project centers, regional centers and global headquarters. BYD Energy Storage operates nine O&M centers globally, each spanning 2,500 square meters. Its after-sales service network covers China, Chile, South Africa, the UK, the US, Australia, Japan, Poland, and the Middle East. New service centers will open in South Africa and Bulgaria in 2027 to further expand its global service footprint. The centers deliver core functions including spare parts storage and management, batteries repair and maintenance, regional spare parts allocation, batteries recycling, and training for locally hired engineers. BYD Energy Storage's regional centers fully comply with local regulatory requirements, deliver structured workforce training and enable rapid on-site response. The professional service team comprises over 200 field engineers and more than 100 R&D specialists. The company enforces standardized service SLAs: response within 24 hours, on-site arrival within 48 hours, and fault troubleshooting within 7 days. The company's global service network has achieved widespread coverage. It forms a multi-point supply network that ensures rapid spare parts delivery worldwide. Furthermore, leveraging localized production lines, its O&M teams integrate regional resources to deliver local battery repair services, providing global customers with fast, convenient, and localized after-sales support. "Our global service footprint is tailored to our fast‑growing BESS deployments. Trustworthy after‑sales support underpins the long‑term stable operation of energy storage assets," commented Mr. He Dehong, Head of Global After-sales Service at BYD Energy Storage. Guided by its vision, empower global energy storage industry with digital and intelligent service, BYD Energy Storage's mature global O&M system strongly supports its expanding battery energy storage footprint. The company topped global BESS shipments at over 60 GWh in 2025, and has delivered more than 650 energy storage projects in total, supported by standardized, localized after-sales services for reliable asset operation. artigo.texto: O evento, presidido pela Associação Vietnamita de Energia Limpa (VCEA) e organizado em colaboração com a GG Power Joint Stock Company, teve como foco a discussão de oportunidades, desafios e soluções para o desenvolvimento de energia solar em telhados combinada com sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) no Vietnã. Em seu discurso de abertura na conferência, o Sr. Mai Duy Thien, Presidente da Associação Vietnamita de Energia Limpa (VCEA), enfatizou o papel da energia solar em telhados, combinada com sistemas de armazenamento de energia, no aumento da autossuficiência energética, e também levantou a questão do desenvolvimento da capacidade de pesquisa e produção de soluções de armazenamento de energia no país. A meta de alcançar uma taxa média de crescimento do PIB superior a 10% durante o período de 2026-2030 impõe exigências significativas ao setor energético: garantir um fornecimento de eletricidade suficiente, estável e seguro, reduzir as emissões e aumentar a autossuficiência da economia . A Resolução nº 70-NQ/TW sobre a garantia da segurança energética nacional até 2030, com uma visão para 2045, define claramente os requisitos para assegurar uma segurança energética nacional robusta; desenvolver fontes de abastecimento internas; promover energias renováveis; construir um sistema energético moderno e inteligente; e melhorar gradualmente a capacidade de produção nacional de equipamentos críticos para o setor energético. De acordo com o Sr. Thien, o desenvolvimento de capacidades tecnológicas e de produção nacionais não só contribui para a gestão proativa da cadeia de abastecimento, como também forma gradualmente um ecossistema da indústria energética vietnamita, criando uma base para o desenvolvimento a longo prazo do mercado de energia limpa. Do ponto de vista profissional e prático na indústria de eletricidade, o Dr. Vo Quang Lam, ex-vice-diretor geral do Grupo de Eletricidade do Vietnã (EVN), enfatizou a necessidade de desenvolver energia solar fotovoltaica autossuficiente em telhados, combinada com a tecnologia BESS (Building, Energy, and Service - Edifício, Energia e Serviços), ao mesmo tempo em que se aprimora a capacidade nacional de dominar a tecnologia de armazenamento de energia. Em relação aos requisitos para empresas que desejam entrar no mercado, o Sr. Lam enfatizou: "É crucial que as empresas também desenvolvam capacidades substanciais, garantindo a qualidade do produto, a segurança operacional, o serviço pós-venda a preços adequados e a competitividade a longo prazo." Na conferência, o Sr. Bui Xuan Binh, Presidente e CEO da GG Power Joint Stock Company, compartilhou sua visão, enfatizando o objetivo de aprimorar as capacidades tecnológicas, desenvolver soluções de energia limpa e consolidar gradualmente a posição das empresas vietnamitas no setor de armazenamento de energia. O Sr. Nguyen Quoc Dat, Diretor Geral Adjunto responsável pela Cadeia de Suprimentos e P&D da GG Power, apresentou as soluções de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS) da empresa e sua direção de pesquisa e desenvolvimento para aumentar a capacidade de produção nacional. Assim, a estratégia de desenvolvimento da GG Power para a solução BESS "Make in Vietnam" concentra-se não apenas na fabricação de equipamentos no país, mas também inclui pesquisa e desenvolvimento, controle de qualidade, integração de sistemas e serviços técnicos. Esses são elementos cruciais para agregar valor ao produto e atender aos requisitos operacionais práticos da rede elétrica do Vietnã, bem como às necessidades de eletricidade dos consumidores locais. O consenso na conferência foi que o desenvolvimento do mercado de energia solar em telhados, em conjunto com sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), requer mecanismos e políticas adequados, bem como capacidade real das empresas em pesquisa, produção, controle de qualidade, garantia de segurança e prestação de serviços técnicos. Os delegados concentraram suas discussões e soluções propostas em três grupos de questões: Em primeiro lugar, é necessário aprimorar os mecanismos e políticas sincronizados desde o nível central até o local, criando condições mais favoráveis para que pessoas e empresas invistam e implementem energia solar em telhados para autoprodução e autoconsumo, de acordo com as necessidades de uso de eletricidade e as condições reais. Em segundo lugar, é crucial promover o desenvolvimento de produtos de armazenamento de energia "Made in Vietnam" que atendam aos requisitos de qualidade, segurança operacional, estabilidade, fornecimento proativo e garantia de longo prazo e serviço pós-venda. O aprimoramento das capacidades tecnológicas nacionais é considerado um dos principais fatores para aumentar a competitividade das empresas vietnamitas. Em terceiro lugar, precisamos construir um ecossistema abrangente de soluções, desde energia solar e inversores até sistemas de armazenamento de energia balanceada (BESS), juntamente com políticas cooperativas e apoio ao desenvolvimento de mercado para a rede de distribuição. Isso fornecerá uma base para expandir o acesso a soluções de energia limpa, melhorar a eficiência dos investimentos e criar condições para que as empresas desenvolvam seus mercados de forma sustentável. Por meio das sessões de intercâmbio, a conferência "Desenvolvendo Energia Solar em Telhados - Autoprodução, Autoconsumo e Introdução de Novos Produtos" proporcionou aos participantes a oportunidade de compartilhar perspectivas práticas, identificar questões que necessitam de maior atenção e fortalecer as conexões entre agências, associações, empresas de tecnologia, distribuidores e organizações de investimento. As propostas apresentadas servem como base para o aprimoramento de soluções, a promoção da cooperação e o desenvolvimento do mercado de energia solar em telhados combinada com armazenamento de energia no Vietnã.

artigo.texto: Long County weighs temporary moratorium on data center development Long County leaders are considering a temporary moratorium on future data center development. The discussion comes as data centers draw increasing scrutiny nationwide and neighboring Liberty County recently paused new data center applications in unincorporated areas for 120 days. Although no project is currently proposed in the county, Long County’s Planning and Zoning Commission discussed Monday night whether to recommend a temporary moratorium to county commissioners, who have the final say. “My concern is that Long County has not touched on this subject at all, and it’s becoming a hot button item,” said Lisa Ruise, with Long County Planning and Zoning. Ruise also expressed concern about the potential community response to a proposed data center. “I don’t think our community can withstand the drama and the anger and outrage that a possible data center would bring,” she said. However, some planning and zoning commissioners were not on board. One commission member said they were not ready to support a moratorium without first exploring whether data center development could provide additional revenue for the county. “I’m not saying yes or no, but I’m not willing to just go and put that stop light on this right now without looking into it,” the commissioner said. Questions about the county’s ability to support a large-scale facility also have emerged. “I personally do not believe we have the infrastructure, power, water or ground to be able to hold such possibilities,” said Long County resident Ramsey Sleevar, who attended the meeting Monday. “I don’t think it needs to be dead in the water, but it definitely needs to be in place where people can be more educated." The Planning and Zoning Commission is scheduled to hold a public hearing and vote on a proposed data center moratorium at its next meeting, Nov. 16. If the measure advances, it will go to county commissioners for final approval.

artigo.texto: Pitt County to hold public hearing on data center moratorium GREENVILLE, N.C. (WITN) - Pitt County commissioners voted unanimously Monday night to schedule a public hearing on a proposed temporary moratorium on data centers. The hearing is set for Nov. 16. The vote followed a presentation by Pitt County Planning and Development Director Jonas Hill. Hill said a moratorium would give the county time to study the impact of data centers. He highlighted regulatory gaps including a lack of standards for electrical load infrastructure, low-frequency noise compliance and air quality from generators. “They use and consume a tremendous amount of water. There’s no standards for water usage in our current ordinance at all,” Hill said. Hill said current ordinances regarding data centers do not distinguish between small or hyperscale facilities. Hill said 24 counties in North Carolina currently have moratoriums on data centers, including Greene County and Wake County. Several residents spoke in favor of a data center moratorium at the meeting, saying it is important for county leaders to have enough time to make an informed decision. “Often it’s in community of color or working class communities because the billionaires impact these monstrous things. I think they can do that and get away with it because people might not know their rights,” Pitt County resident Don Cavellini said. Another resident, Zoey Dixon, said data centers pose environmental, social and employment threats. “I had nearly 10 years of tech experience. I am somebody who will not use AI, for example, and this has already cost me multiple job opportunities,” Dixon said. Copyright 2026 WITN. All rights reserved.

The battery swap partnership between Huawei's automotive business and CATL (HKEX: 3750) reportedly plans to introduce its first model in 2027 under Epicland, a brand jointly developed by Dongfeng and Huawei. Cailian reported the plan on Tuesday, without identifying the model. A day earlier, Huawei's intelligent automotive business, Yinwang, or Newcool, signed a strategic cooperation framework agreement with CATL and its battery swap operator. The report provides an initial product timeline for the collaboration between Huawei's intelligent automotive technology business and CATL's battery swap network. The previously announced agreement did not specify any models or a service launch date. Under the cooperation announced on October 19, Newcool formally joined CATL's Choco swap ecosystem. Newcool will work with strategic partners to make vehicles using Huawei Qiankun intelligent automotive solutions compatible with the Choco swap network and connect them to it, expanding access to battery swap services. The partnership also includes Contemporary Amperex Energy Service Technology (CAES), CATL's battery swap operator. The 3 parties plan to connect vehicle, battery swap station and cloud systems, using real-time battery status and users' travel patterns to anticipate energy needs and proactively arrange battery swaps. Under the plan outlined in the earlier statement, vehicles would autonomously locate a station, enter it and align themselves, then drive away after completing a fully automated battery swap in 99 seconds. These capabilities are part of the cooperation roadmap. Epicland launched its first model, the X9, on September 24 and began nationwide deliveries at Huawei's Songshan Lake campus on October 18. The X9 is a large, 3-row, 6-seat extended-range electric SUV, with Huawei Qiankun ADS 5 driver assistance fitted as standard across the lineup, along with the HarmonySpace 6 cockpit. The report did not identify the X9 as the battery swap model planned for 2027. Epicland is among the brands developed by Huawei's Qiankun business in partnership with domestic automakers. It is not part of the Huawei-led HIMA (Harmony Intelligent Mobility Alliance) business.

artigo.texto: At an Oct. 13 meeting on a proposed data center, more than 200 residents crowded into Elizabeth Forward Middle School's auditorium in Elizabeth Township, Pa. Opposition emerged, petitions circulated, and Elizabeth Township officers escorted one attendee out after a disturbance. Here's what to know Commissioners were first approached in June about locating a possible data center at a power plant site, and the gathering at Elizabeth Forward Middle School was the township's first public move since then, according to the Mon Valley Independent. About 330 questions were submitted beforehand, and township resident Eric Piper condensed them into roughly four dozen for the discussion. According to the Mon Valley Independent, Bucks County developer Tim Hendricks, who said he has 35 years in real estate, is looking at a 550-acre Henderson Road site in the Buena Vista area next to the Youghiogheny River. Preliminary concepts presented at the meeting included 20 two-story buildings and stormwater basins. Hendricks said the development might generate $125 million in tax revenue for the township and school district and create 200 to 300 permanent jobs with salaries ranging from $60,000 to $100,000, according to the Mon Valley Independent. He also said residents' energy service would stay the same and that the facility would not emit pollutants. Key details were still unavailable. Asked by Commissioner Jim Benedek about expected electricity and water use, Hendricks said he did not want to offer figures until he had dependable information, according to the Mon Valley Independent. Residents also disputed the claim that nearby homes would be about 2,000 feet away, saying some properties across the river sit closer than that. More background To illustrate the site's scale, Piper said the property is about 2.5 times the size of Kennywood Park, while Hendricks said, according to the Mon Valley Independent, "There's hundreds of acres proposed that would not be built on out of the total. This is an evolving process. Things change as we get more information. As I start to get answers, we can update the plan to make it more usable and hopefully better for the community." Hendricks said he learned about the property from a colleague's brother, who had been exploring it for a possible solar project. He added that existing utility lines and earlier environmental cleanup made the site more appealing for redevelopment, according to the Mon Valley Independent. The debate arrives amid broader concerns about data centers, artificial intelligence, and pressure on the electric grid. Hendricks told the audience that people often view data centers only through the lens of AI, but said they also support ordinary online activity such as texting and streaming movies. Data centers can add computing capacity that helps optimize cleaner energy systems. Residents and local officials often focus on the tradeoffs, including heavy electricity demand, significant water use, security concerns, and the possibility that large new loads could strain local infrastructure and utility bills. Residents pressed environmental and quality-of-life concerns. Resident Candy Woy raised questions about wildlife at the site and possible environmental effects, while Mary Jane Carnahan, who identified herself as a Terrytown Drive neighbor, said underground mines and prolonged construction could disrupt daily life and reduce property values, according to the Mon Valley Independent. What's being done? For now, Hendricks said, the proposal is still at a very early stage. As of Oct. 13, nothing formal had been filed, and he said the concept would need many permits and approvals before it could move ahead, according to the Mon Valley Independent. He added that if construction ever happens, the eventual company behind the site would step into his role. According to the Mon Valley Independent, Hendricks said he is trying to place any data center as far from homes as possible and is still talking with gas providers while deciding whether the project fits the community. He told residents the plans would be revised further if the process continues. Residents are organizing their own response. Attendees signed anti-project petitions on the way in, and Megan McDonough, state director at Food and Water Watch, questioned whether public opposition would matter if commissioners were later asked to change zoning, according to the Mon Valley Independent. Protect Elizabeth Township has another town hall set for 6:30 p.m. Oct. 29 at Butler's Golf Course on Rock Run Road, featuring a speaker panel and opponents of data centers from other communities. Piper said, "This community is my home. My family has been in this township for nearly 100 years. I care about this community just as I know everyone in this room does. And whether you support this proposed development, oppose it or simply want to learn more, I believe we all have something in common. We want what's best for Elizabeth Township, and the people that call it home." Where can I learn more? What's happening in Elizabeth Township echoes fights in other communities over proposed data centers. artigo.texto: Wisconsin regulators will conduct a full statewide review of the environmental impacts of data center development under a legal deal reached among environmental groups, a data center developer and the Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources. The settlement reached Friday stems from a lawsuit filed in July by Midwest Environmental Advocates, or MEA, on behalf of Sierra Club against the DNR in Ozaukee County Circuit Court. The DNR, Sierra Club and Denver-based Vantage Data Centers signed off on the deal. The groups sued over the agency’s decision to issue permits for the $15 billion Lighthouse data center campus in Port Washington without conducting an environmental impact statement. The project is being developed by Vantage Data Centers and tech companies Oracle and OpenAI to expand capacity for artificial intelligence, or AI. Under the deal, the DNR will conduct a strategic analysis of the anticipated build-out of AI data centers and associated infrastructure to power them under current plans and projections. The review will analyze the direct, indirect and cumulative effects of the buildout on the state’s agriculture, air and water quality, climate, energy, economy, cultural resources and more. MEA attorney Michael Greif said the DNR approached environmental groups about settling the lawsuit by either agreeing to an environmental impact statement for the Port Washington project or a broader statewide review of data centers. “That second option was really exciting to Sierra Club because it would provide a holistic, comprehensive look at the environmental impacts and the financial impacts of these AI data centers on the state and on communities, and that’s something that very few states have done across the country,” Greif said. In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul enacted the nation’s first statewide moratorium on data centers while the state reviews their effects on the environment and energy use. The deal reached Friday among the DNR, groups and Vantage does not pause permitting of data center projects while the state completes its review. “That’s something that the next governor certainly could put in place, and I think that’s something that would be the right approach for the state,” Greif added. Crowley supports ‘pause’ in development during yearlong review Democratic candidate for governor David Crowley said in a statement that he would support halting new data center projects while the environmental analysis is taking place. As governor, he will work with the legislature to pause development until the review is complete and the new guardrails are in place,” a Crowley campaign spokesperson said. Both Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany have called for new standards or guardrails before any new data centers move forward. A spokesperson for Tiffany’s campaign said Tiffany has consistently said there should be no new data centers without five standards that include ending subsidies for data centers and barring non-disclosure agreements. “Under my administration, the DNR will hold every proposed project to Wisconsin’s environmental standards before a permit is issued, ensuring our water, land, and natural resources are protected. If a project doesn’t meet these standards or the local community doesn’t support it, it will not move forward,” Tiffany said on his website. Tiffany’s spokesperson did not address the new statewide environmental analysis announced in the legal settlement. Vantage will pay all costs tied to the strategic statewide analysis A Vantage spokesperson said it supports a thoughtful, fact-based discussion about responsible data center development and has agreed to fund all costs tied to the strategic statewide analysis led by the DNR. “The analysis will examine the environmental and economic considerations associated with data center development, providing policymakers and communities with additional information as the state considers the industry’s continued growth,” said Mark Freeman, Vantage’s vice president of global marketing. The DNR will retain sole control over the review, and the agency will have full authority to determine whether any future application or project complies with state laws. The DNR must complete its strategic analysis by Jan. 31, 2028, according to the deal. The DNR must seek public comment and hold one or more public hearings on the analysis, and it will include summaries of the effects of data center development on energy bills. Under the settlement, permits for the Lighthouse data center campus will remain valid, and further environmental review of those approvals is not required. artigo.texto: O Google e sua parceira Xcel Energy afirmam que seu projeto de data center de 780 megawatts em Minnesota ajudará a modernizar a rede elétrica com fontes de energia mais limpas, sem transferir o ônus dos custos de infraestrutura para os clientes existentes. No entanto, especialistas dizem que grande parte dessa expansão poderia ser evitada e alertam que as empresas de energia têm um incentivo financeiro para construir continuamente mais infraestrutura. A corrida para fornecer energia a centros de dados com inteligência artificial está remodelando a rede elétrica dos EUA. Se há algo em que a maioria dos americanos concorda, é que eles não querem um centro de dados perto de onde moram. Uma pesquisa da Gallup realizada em março de 2026 revelou que 71% dos americanos se opõem à construção de data centers em suas localidades. A principal preocupação era o consumo de energia. Enquanto isso, de acordo com uma pesquisa do Pew Research Center realizada entre julho e agosto, metade dos entrevistados acreditava que os data centers teriam um impacto negativo no meio ambiente e nos custos de energia das famílias. Atualmente, o Google aposta que um centro de dados de IA em grande escala pode ajudar a financiar uma rede elétrica mais limpa e confiável. O acordo que está propondo com a Xcel Energy inclui a adição de capacidade proveniente de sistemas de energia eólica, solar e de armazenamento em baterias — totalizando mais energia do que o centro de dados deverá consumir. Nos termos deste acordo, o Google subsidiará o custo dessa energia adicional e continuará pagando mesmo que não utilize toda a eletricidade fornecida. Pine Island, uma pequena cidade com cerca de 4.000 habitantes, localizada a uma hora a sudeste de Minneapolis, é onde o Google espera que seu projeto de data center de 780 megawatts receba apoio da comunidade local. Ao mesmo tempo, este projeto também aproxima o Google de sua meta de operar inteiramente com zero emissões de carbono, 24 horas por dia, 7 dias por semana, até 2030. O Google, cujo negócio de serviços em nuvem dá suporte direto ao seu próprio modelo de IA Gemini, viu sua receita no segundo trimestre atingir quase US$ 25 bilhões (um aumento de 82% em relação ao ano anterior), afirmando ter encontrado o modelo certo para isso. O Google planeja financiar a adição de 1.400 megawatts de energia eólica, 200 megawatts de energia solar e 300 megawatts de armazenamento em baterias à rede da Xcel. A capacidade total dessas fontes adicionais supera em muito as necessidades do próprio data center; segundo o Google, isso ocorre porque a energia eólica e solar não conseguem gerar eletricidade continuamente. A Xcel Energy afirmou que essa nova fonte de energia atenderá a todos os clientes da região, não apenas ao Google. A Xcel também afirmou que essas melhorias contribuirão para aumentar o fornecimento de energia livre de carbono para a rede elétrica local. O acordo proposto entre o Google e a Xcel inclui cláusulas relativas a taxas mínimas de demanda e multas por rescisão. O Google afirma que esses termos garantem que a empresa continue responsável pelo pagamento da infraestrutura construída especificamente para ela, mesmo com a diminuição do interesse em inteligência artificial. O Google se compromete a pagar por pelo menos 75% da capacidade contratada, independentemente do consumo real; além disso, caso rescinda o contrato unilateralmente antes do prazo, deverá pagar uma multa equivalente à taxa mínima de demanda por até oito anos. Segundo Amanda Rome, vice-presidente executiva e chefe de relações com o cliente da Xcel Energy, ninguém quer investir em grandes obras de construção para depois se deparar com a falta de mercado para a eletricidade gerada e de quem a pagar. É exatamente por isso que essas medidas de segurança são necessárias. O acordo entre o Google e a Xcel Energy aguarda atualmente a aprovação da Comissão de Serviços Públicos do Estado de Minnesota. Os centros de dados estão impulsionando uma expansão sem precedentes da infraestrutura energética. De acordo com as previsões da North American Electric Reliability Corporation (NERC), os novos centros de dados serão responsáveis pela maior parte do aumento projetado na demanda de eletricidade na próxima década. Sob a gestão do ex-presidente Joe Biden, o Departamento de Energia declarou que mais de 70% das linhas de transmissão e transformadores nos EUA estão em operação há pelo menos 25 anos. O departamento também observou que, para atender à demanda futura com o custo mais otimizado, o sistema nacional de transmissão de energia precisa dobrar de tamanho até 2050. No entanto, os operadores de centros de dados de grande escala argumentam que podem fornecer o financiamento necessário para modernizar a rede elétrica, tornando-a também mais limpa e confiável. Amanda Peterson Corio, diretora global de energia e eletricidade do Google, acredita que o momento desta revolução industrial é particularmente oportuno, já que a empresa precisa de capital para modernizar sua infraestrutura obsoleta nos Estados Unidos. Será que os centros de dados podem utilizar a rede elétrica existente sem modificações? Jigar Shah, sócio da Multiplier, uma consultoria que auxilia startups de energia limpa em suas ofertas públicas iniciais (IPOs), sugere que os operadores de centros de dados poderiam construir instalações menores em locais onde a rede elétrica existente possui capacidade excedente. Essa abordagem minimizaria a necessidade de novas construções e os custos de investimento em novos equipamentos de geração ou transmissão de energia. Shah argumentou que a integração da crescente demanda por eletricidade dos centros de dados na rede elétrica existente reduziria significativamente os custos de eletricidade para todos os outros usuários. Ele citou a colaboração entre o Google e a Xcel em Minnesota como um excelente exemplo de como os centros de dados podem servir de catalisadores para novas tecnologias mais ecológicas. artigo.texto: Is battery storage the quick fix for apparel’s energy crisis? Battery energy storage systems could offer Bangladesh’s apparel industry a rapid path to energy security. However, the government must ensure affordable financing for factory installations If you ask anyone in Bangladesh's apparel industry what the sector needs most to survive and thrive in the years ahead, you will hear the same answer, almost without exception: energy security. The urgency is not hypothetical. A recent survey of 134 knitwear factories found that 55% had seen buyers cancel or cut orders because of gas and power shortages since late August. Across the sector, energy shortfalls are cutting output by as much as 25–30%, and the diesel needed to keep backup generators running now comes at a heavy premium. Let me be fair to those in charge. The government has been doing its best through careful rationing and prioritisation of available energy to keep the apparel industry, and industry at large, running without interruption. Entrepreneurs, for their part, are managing somehow. But managing somehow is not the same as operating smoothly. Flawless operations, the kind global buyers expect when they place their orders, require a steady supply of energy that is simply not available at the moment. So, what is the solution? The permanent answer is, of course, a long-term one. According to media reports, there has been little meaningful effort to explore domestic gas reserves over the past 17 years. Even if exploration began today, it would take a minimum of 10 to 20 years for that gas to reach our factories. We cannot ask the country's largest formal employer to wait two decades. Nor are we alone. The energy crisis is a global one, driven by turmoil in the Middle East, and the world's more forward-thinking economies are not waiting either. One quick solution they are turning to is the battery energy storage system, or BESS. What remains missing is access to finance. Few manufacturers, battered by falling orders and rising costs, can commit nearly a million dollars upfront. If the government were to extend financing directly to manufacturers — interest-free or at a low rate — installation could be completed within two to three months. No other measure on the table offers relief this quickly. The case for BESS has never been stronger. An all-inclusive turnkey system now costs around $135–165 per kWh globally, down from more than $380 per kWh as recently as 2022. A typical 5 MWh industrial system, suitable for a large apparel factory in Bangladesh, costs roughly $900,000, all-inclusive. The technology has matured, too. Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry now dominates industrial storage, valued for its safety and long cycle life. A system typically lasts 10–15 years, or 6,000 to more than 9,000 cycles. With periodic augmentation, it can continue delivering power for 15–20 years. I do not speak merely as an observer. At 4A Yarn Dyeing, we have never relied on a single energy source, and our rooftop solar and backup systems have helped us absorb rising costs. Even so, more expensive diesel has increased 4A's production costs by 2–3%. If a factory with multiple backup systems feels the squeeze, one can only imagine the strain on those without them. Here, the government deserves credit for a far-sighted move. The FY2026-27 budget has removed import duties, VAT and other taxes on BESS and solar equipment until 2031 and set the corporate tax rate at 0% for solar power generation until 2035. With diesel costly and outages frequent, these incentives have made the payback period shorter and the post-tax returns on BESS more attractive than they were even a year ago. What remains missing is access to finance. Few manufacturers, battered by falling orders and rising costs, can commit nearly a million dollars upfront. If the government were to offer financing directly to manufacturers, interest-free or at a low rate, installation could be completed within two to three months. No other measure on the table offers relief this quickly. We are well aware that the economy is currently facing a cash crunch. Nevertheless, since assuming office, the government has shown a clear willingness to support industry, and rightly so, because the only way to strengthen the economy is to help its industries grow. For example, Bangladesh Bank has rolled out a Tk60,000 crore stimulus package specifically aimed at reviving closed, sick and underutilised industrial and service-sector enterprises. It is a well-intentioned initiative. If even a portion of that fund were made available for BESS installation at existing, operational factories, the impact would be immediate. Reviving closed factories carries considerable risk, and the benefits will take time to materialise. By contrast, existing factories struggling to survive today could not only stay afloat by overcoming the energy crisis but also double or even triple their capacity in the years ahead. This is not an argument against long-term energy planning. Domestic exploration must begin in earnest, and renewable energy capacity must continue to grow. But the long term will mean little if our factories cannot survive the short term. Bangladesh's apparel industry has weathered far greater storms over four decades, and each time, it has come back stronger. With the right financial support at the right moment, it can do so again and, in doing so, give the wider economy the strength it needs to grow. Abdullah Hil Nakib is the Deputy Managing Director of Team Group. artigo.texto: Cincinnati residents voice data center concerns as city leaders provide zoning update City leaders are studying new zoning rules for data centers as residents raise concerns about their potential effects on local communities, utility costs and the environment. Dozens of people attended a public forum Monday in Walnut Hills to discuss how Cincinnati should regulate future development. While no large-scale facility has been proposed, officials said they want rules in place before an application is submitted. “Is that what Ohio wants to be known for? Is that what Cincinnati wants to be known for?” Over-the-Rhine resident Cayley Baker asked. Residents questioned where data centers could be built and how their heavy water and electricity use might affect ratepayers. Robert McCracken of Cincinnati’s Office of Environment and Sustainability anticipated increases costs but called for protections to keep costs down. “How can the state and Public Utilities Commission look at rules that pass on the costs to the end user, the data center, and not to us?” said Ohio ranks among the top states for data center facilities. About 28 are operating in the Greater Cincinnati area, including smaller-scale sites such as CyrusOne. Cincinnati has imposed a moratorium preventing data center construction within city limits until February 2027 while officials consider zoning regulations. Baker called the process an important first step but said residents must hold city leaders accountable. “Time will tell if the city will help developers feet to the fire," she said. "I think city members do a lot of talk but when it comes down to holding people accountable and making real changes, words are cheap."

artigo.texto: Sepco wins Saudi 500MW/2,000MWh BESS project contract The project is being developed by a consortium of French energy major Engie and Saudi group Haji Abdullah Alireza & Co The Saudi Arabia Group 1-KSB Independent Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project has been secured by Shandong Electric Power Construction Corporation (Sepco). The project is said to form part of the Kingdom’s first wave of large-scale battery energy storage projects. The Al Khushaybi Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) project has a planned capacity of 500MW/2,000MWh. It supports Saudi Arabia’s energy transition ambitions under Vision 2030, particularly the development of energy storage infrastructure to complement its expanding renewable energy capacity. The project is being developed by a consortium of French energy major Engie and Saudi group Haji Abdullah Alireza & Co. The Saudi Power Procurement Company (SPPC) is the offtaker for the project, which is mainly aimed at strengthening grid flexibility and supporting the integration of renewable energy into Saudi Arabia’s power system, said a report. Upon completion and commissioning, the BESS facility will help balance electricity supply and demand by storing energy during periods of lower demand and discharging it when demand increases, it added. The project is expected to improve grid stability, enhance the resilience of electricity supply, and support the integration of solar and wind power into the national grid.

artigo.texto: The training was attended by both representatives of enterprises and staff from the Environment Agency and the Environmental Protection Inspectorate. The former learnt about calculation and reporting rules, whilst the latter learnt methods for subsequently verifying the accuracy of the data submitted. The event was organised jointly with the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP) in Moldova as part of the project ‘Strengthening Capacity for Climate Action in the Republic of Moldova’, funded by the Green Climate Fund (GCF). How businesses are to report on emissions During the seminar, participants were introduced to the main stages of preparing annual reports: collecting the necessary information, conducting an internal check at the enterprise, having the report reviewed by an accredited verifier, and submitting the document to the Environment Agency. Particular attention was paid to identifying emission sources and the corresponding source streams, as well as selecting measurement equipment and monitoring methodologies. This data is essential for developing greenhouse gas monitoring plans. Participants were also introduced to current regulations and national guidelines explaining how to complete the documents. The seminar thus covered not only the preparation of reports but also the creation of a system for collecting and verifying data, which will enable the comparison of companies’ performance indicators and the verification of the accuracy of calculations. ETS: the next stage of climate regulation Preparing businesses is seen as one of the steps towards the subsequent introduction of an emissions trading scheme (ETS). Such schemes involve regulating greenhouse gas emissions within set limits and establishing a mechanism for trading emissions allowances. For industry, this means establishing emissions accounting processes in advance, designating responsible staff and ensuring the reliability of source data. In future, monitoring and reporting requirements may become a key part of compliance with climate legislation and the planning of production costs. Such preparation is of particular importance for energy-intensive sectors, including the cement, glass and sugar industries, as well as energy sector enterprises, as mentioned by the seminar organisers. For Moldovan businesses, the key issues are the timeline for implementing the future mechanism, the specific requirements for regulated enterprises, and the potential impact of climate regulation on production costs and competitiveness. artigo.texto: The prime ministers of Sweden, Finland and Denmark oppose plans to relax EU carbon market requirements, warning that the move could put industrial investment at greater risk and slow emissions reductions. A letter from the three Nordic leaders was sent to the Council of the European Union on October 14. The recipients were Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin, European Council President António Costa and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. Denmark’s Mette Frederiksen, Sweden’s Ulf Kristersson and Finland’s Petteri Orpo said the EU’s emissions trading system (ETS) must retain its ambition and credibility. The scheme requires the most polluting industries to pay for the carbon dioxide they emit. Diluting the rules, they warned, “would undermine the predictability on which investment decisions depend” and could hinder efforts to decarbonise industry. The three leaders also argued that easing requirements for heavy emitters would shift the burden to other sectors of the economy, forcing them to make steeper emissions cuts to ensure the EU meets its climate goals.

artigo.texto: (The Center Square) – Companies operating data centers should be the ones that pay for upgrades to the electric grid, most voters say according to a new poll. The Center Square Voters’ Voice Poll found that 66% of voters believe that data center companies should be paying for the increased power demand and infrastructure required to get that electricity to the data centers. Fourteen percent of those registered to vote say the costs of the upgrades should be shared by both data center companies and the public while 8% believe the upgrades are the responsibility of federal, state or local taxpayers and 6% believe that all electricity customers should pay for the upgrades. Another 6% said they were unsure who should pay. The results come from a survey conducted by Noble Predictive Insights from Oct. 5-7 that polled registered voters nationally via opt-in online panel and text-to-web cell phone messages. The sample included 2,527 respondents comprised of 1,011 Republicans, 1,011 Democrats, and 505 Independents. Among independent voters, 220 respondents were classified as true independents, which are individuals who do not lean toward either major party when given the choice. The margin of error is +/- 1.95%. The cost of electricity infrastructure to power data centers has been debated across the country as more energy sources are required as well as new transmission lines and power storage equipment. The U.S. House of Representatives nearly unanimously passed the Ratepayer Protection Act in September before it failed in the Senate on a 57-43 vote. The bill would have required state public utility commissioners “commence consideration” of implementing rules that would protect ordinary ratepayers within one year of the bill becoming law. President Donald Trump announced a Ratepayer Protection Pledge along with several hyper-scale data operators in 2025 with a goal of preventing Americans from paying for rising electricity costs associated with increased demand from data centers. The pledge states that companies including Amazon, xAI, Oracle, Microsoft, Meta, Google and OpenAI will pay for the new electricity generation and grid infrastructure needed to accommodate new data centers.

artigo.texto: ABDC pede corte de 90% no ICMS e cobra regulamentação do Redata Entidade relata projetos represados à espera das regras federais e defende ampliar os pontos de chegada de cabos submarinos. A Associação Brasileira de Data Center (ABDC) defende uma redução de 90% do ICMS sobre equipamentos de TI sem fabricação nacional e cobra a regulamentação do Redata para destravar investimentos. Segundo o presidente da entidade, Renan Alves, há operações com infraestrutura pronta que aguardam as regras do regime para importar hardware e ocupar a capacidade disponível. Em entrevista à TV Síntese, gravada durante o Futurecom, em 8 de outubro, Alves afirmou que a associação mantém conversas com governos estaduais sobre o benefício tributário. A proposta envolve uma deliberação no Conselho Nacional de Política Fazendária (Confaz) e a identificação dos equipamentos contemplados por meio da Nomenclatura Comum do Mercosul (NCM). “A ideia é você ter 90 por cento de redução do ICMS, nesses ativos de TI”, declarou. O dirigente ressaltou que o pleito se concentra no hardware que o país não produz. Segundo ele, a proposta não abrange todos os investimentos e despesas de um data center: construção, consumo de energia e outras atividades da cadeia continuariam sujeitos à tributação correspondente. Alves relatou receptividade de parte dos estados, mas também resistências. Lista de equipamentos condiciona decisão dos estados Na avaliação do presidente da ABDC, a definição dos produtos contemplados pelo Redata é necessária também para que os estados dimensionem o alcance de uma eventual redução do ICMS. O dirigente afirmou compreender a posição dos governos que aguardam a regulamentação federal antes de decidir sobre o benefício estadual. Sem a lista de NCMs, argumentou, faltam elementos para quantificar e qualificar os efeitos da medida. “Ninguém vai tomar uma decisão de olhos fechados”, afirmou. Além dos equipamentos elegíveis, Alves cobrou a definição dos critérios de habilitação das empresas, dos procedimentos de apresentação dos projetos e das eventuais exigências de auditoria. Estruturas prontas aguardam hardware A demanda imediata, segundo o executivo, inclui empresas que já operam no Brasil e precisam instalar equipamentos para ampliar seus negócios. Ele distinguiu esses investimentos dos projetos de novos entrantes, cuja implantação exige mais tempo. “O benefício é de quem já está com a estrutura pronta e você está fazendo só um crescimento orgânico”, explicou. Alves afirmou que existem projetos represados à espera do regime. Sobre a data limite para que as empresas conseguissem importar equipamentos ainda em 2026, diz que isso depende da complexidade das regras e da velocidade de aprovação dos pedidos. “O tempo que a gente perdeu, até agora ele não volta mais”, resumiu. Na avaliação do dirigente, o mercado brasileiro continuará crescendo para atender à demanda doméstica. A função do Redata seria ampliar a competitividade do país na disputa por investimentos que poderiam ser destinados a outras localidades, especialmente operações voltadas ao atendimento de clientes no exterior. Cabos submarinos para ampliar destinos dos investimentos Além da questão tributária, a ABDC defende ampliar os pontos de chegada de cabos submarinos para permitir que mais regiões disputem esses projetos. Alves argumentou que a conectividade internacional precisa integrar as políticas de infraestrutura, ao lado de estradas e linhas de transmissão. “Se você quiser que o data center venha, você precisa também fazer investimento em fibra”, afirmou. O executivo reconheceu que os empreendimentos dependem de operadores e de viabilidade econômica, mas defendeu participação do poder público na criação das condições para sua implantação.

artigo.texto: Marcos directs DENR to develop Philippine carbon market rules - October 19, 2026 - 0 President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. has directed the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to develop a national carbon market policy framework and submit it for inter-agency approval within 30 days of Executive Order (EO) No. 127 taking effect. Signed on October 13, the order seeks to establish rules for Philippine participation in domestic and international carbon markets, facilitate access to climate financing, technology and investments, and support projects that generate carbon credits. “There is a need to formulate a national carbon market framework aligned with international standards, through a whole-of-government approach, to support the achievement of the country’s NDCs (nationally determined contributions),” the EO stated. NDCs outline countries’ climate commitments under the Paris Agreement, including efforts to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and address climate change. Carbon markets allow companies and countries to buy and sell credits generated by projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. The Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework will establish requirements for participating companies, project approvals, carbon-credit trading, transaction monitoring and benefit-sharing arrangements. It will also provide safeguards to ensure compliance with national policies and international standards. The order designates DENR as the country’s national authority for carbon markets, responsible for overseeing and authorizing emission-reduction projects and ensuring compliance with environmental policies. DENR will also establish and maintain the Philippine National Carbon Registry, a digital system for tracking carbon credits and related transactions. To oversee the framework’s implementation, Marcos created the Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets (IACCM), chaired by the Climate Change Commission, with the Department of Finance as vice chair. Its members include DENR, the Department of Energy, Department of Agriculture, Department of Transportation, Department of Trade and Industry, and Securities and Exchange Commission. The committee will coordinate government policies, review implementation of the framework, and approve reasonable processing fees for carbon market applications and certifications. DENR must submit the proposed framework to the IACCM for review and approval within 30 days of the order’s effectivity. — How can the Philippines’ carbon market framework attract investment while ensuring credible emission reductions and fair benefit-sharing? artigo.texto: North Huntingdon officials are considering passing an ordinance to govern the development of data centers that would be permitted in 20 sites in the 27-square mile township. The township commissioners Thursday decided the proposed 16-page ordinance needs revisions regarding the size of data centers. They plan to revisit the issue in November. The proposed ordinance would permit the data centers on a 10-acre parcel with setbacks of 500 feet from the property line, as a conditional use on land zoned for industrial purposes, as well as parcels designated as planned economic development districts 1 and 2. The ordinance was developed by the township solicitor in conjunction with the municipality’s engineers. Township Commissioner Ron Zona said he would want language in the ordinance that would address smaller data centers, possibly those less than 20,000 square feet, as well as larger ones. Board Chair Commissioner Zachary Haigis said he is comfortable with the draft ordinance as proposed. Township Solicitor Ashley Puchalski said the language in the ordinance must not exclude the development of data centers. Any data center also would have to be 1,500 feet from any school, daycare center, hospital, nursing facility and place of worship. The developer would need the township’s approval of a land development plan, as well as all applicable building permits, Department of Environmental Protection permits, as well as any other state and local permits. The ordinance addresses the issue of how much power a data center would use by requiring a qualified professional to document electricity demand. An expert also must document water demand on an average daily basis and identify the source for water to address an issue regarding water usage that data center opponents have raised. Like data center ordinances passed by other municipalities, North Huntingdon’s regulations would set requirements for decommissioning a data center, including removing buildings when it becomes inactive. A bond must be obtained to cover the estimated decommissioning costs and the cost to restore the site. By passing the ordinance in November, a public hearing could be held in 2027, Puchalski said. If approved by the township commissioners, North Huntingdon would join East Huntingdon, Hempfield, Ligonier, Rostraver, Sewickley and South Huntingdon townships in setting rules to govern data center development. Upper Burrell already has a data center at the former Alcoa Technology Center that’s operated by TECfusions. The Upper Burrell supervisors are scheduled to vote on a data center ordinance Thursday, Oct. 22, but that ordinance would pertain to future development, not the data center currently in operation. A Department of Environmental Protection website on data centers shows the TECfusions data center, where a 3-gigawatt power plant is planned, is the only data center in the county that is under review by environmental regulators. In South Huntingdon, a Sewickley developer, TriEnergy Inc., has applied for a land use permit for a $25 million project that would contain a data center within a 1 million square-foot warehouse to be built on a former farm along Route 31, east of the intersection with Interstate 70. DEP has yet to approval a sewage permit for the project, so the township has not reviewed a land development plan submitted in May.

artigo.texto: Data center anxiety plays out in Senate campaign debates Democrats seek to capitalize on public sentiment over local impacts In debates and advertisements ahead of the midterm elections, Democratic candidates for Senate are consistently pressing their opponents on artificial intelligence data center policy, often as a proxy for voter fears about the economy and local impacts. In Ohio, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is fond of calling Republican incumbent Sen. Jon Husted “the face of data centers.” Sen. Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., tied the vote by opponent Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., for the Republican “One Big Beautiful Bill” health and tax cuts measure last year to data centers. And James Talarico is accusing his opponent in the race for the Senate, Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, of “selling off Texas” to data center firms. In addition to attacking each other’s policy positions on tech, candidates of both parties are attacking each other’s campaign donations from Big Tech groups and investments in data center companies. Both pro-AI and regulation-focused groups are spending millions on Republican and Democratic candidates. As Democrats have sought to put Republicans on the back foot by tying data centers to rising energy costs and the larger issue of affordability, polling data appears to support the choice. A Pew Research Center survey conducted in July and August found that 50 percent of U.S. adults think data centers are “mostly bad” for home energy costs, compared with 38 percent in January. Those polled have also gotten more pessimistic about data centers’ effects on the environment, jobs, tax revenue and quality of life for those living nearby. Dan Cassino, a professor of government and politics at Fairleigh Dickinson University, said because voters believe data centers are the cause of their higher electricity bills, the construction projects are part of affordability concerns. “President [Donald] Trump campaigned for office in 2024 saying he was going to make things more affordable, was going to break down inflation, and he hasn’t delivered on that,” Cassino said. “And that means it’s a real point of vulnerability for Republicans.” As a result, Cassino said, Democrats are “hitting Republicans really hard” on the need to regulate data centers. Pocketbook issues In a Georgia Senate debate earlier this month, Ossoff used last year’s budget reconciliation bill, which included tax breaks that Ossoff said are being used by data center companies, to criticize Collins. “Just think about this, when you are paying more for your health insurance, when a hospital in your community is closing down,” Ossoff said. “Mike Collins voted to take that money out of your pocket and out of your community and give it instead to data center developers.” Collins, in turn, said he favored “local control” over data center decisions. Data center attacks may work differently, however, against sitting members of Congress. Cassino posited that candidates like Collins who have already been on Capitol Hill may have an easier time on this issue than their counterparts coming from state and local government. “They might have been doing something indirectly, but they weren’t on zoning boards,” he said. Talarico’s race with Paxton highlights the local nature of the data center backlash, with ads tying data centers both to the cost of living and to accusations of corruption against Paxton. “The data centers bankrolled Paxton, they get tax breaks and you get stuck with the bill,” Talarico said in one ad. In another, he promised that if elected he would “take on the data centers raising our costs.” Husted, as well, is being challenged for actions during his time in state government. He served as lieutenant governor before his appointment to the Senate early last year when fellow Republican JD Vance became vice president. In an ad, Brown pointed to tax breaks his state agreed to for tech companies building data centers. Husted “gave away two and a half billion dollars to these out-of-state corporations and billionaires,” Brown said in the advertisement. “He gave up Ohio’s money, our tax money, to Meta, a company worth $2 trillion, to make sure they come to Ohio.” Other Brown ads connect data centers to rising residential electricity costs. He also pledged to “require the data centers pay the full cost of their electricity, not you.” While Husted’s own ads don’t seem to mention data centers, his work in the Senate has. He sponsored the Senate version of a bill, dubbed the “Ratepayer Protection Act,” that would encourage states to adopt standards to make data centers take on the cost of electrical grid upgrades needed to meet their new energy demand. The House-passed version stalled on a procedural vote last month on the Senate floor after Democrats said it wasn’t strong enough. In a debate last week between Sen. Susan Collins, R-Maine, and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson, Collins responded to Jackson’s data center attacks by pointing to her support for the Husted bill. She also said that “guardrails” on energy use are particularly important because of Maine’s high energy prices, which she blamed on Jackson, who previously served as state Senate president. Jackson agreed on the need for “real guardrails” to ensure that data centers don’t cause higher electricity costs for other consumers or hurt local water quality. Democrats’ data center arguments, while not the central issue of most campaigns, seem to be part of a successful strategy. Inside Elections rates Georgia as Lean Democrat, while Maine, Ohio and Texas, all seats currently held by Republicans, are rated as Toss-up. Effectiveness As sitting senators talk about the Ratepayer Protection Act bill, Cassino cautioned that voters may not care about Capitol Hill procedural votes. “Anything incumbents say about, ‘oh, this is what I’m doing to protect you,’ is going to ring hollow because everyone sees their electricity prices going up,” Cassino said. artigo.texto: À medida que empresas de inteligência artificial (IA) com infraestrutura de hiperescala e incorporadoras aceleram a construção de data centers, elas estão deixando de depender da rede elétrica e passando a construir, cada vez mais, sistemas privados de energia atrás do medidor (behind-the-meter, ou BTM, na sigla em inglês), que operam de forma independente das conexões com a rede pública. Isso ocorre porque as filas de espera para conexão à rede se transformaram em um gargalo estrutural. Desde 2017, o prazo entre a entrada na fila e o início da operação comercial aumentou aproximadamente 60%. Atualmente, esse período supera, em média, 2.100 dias para projetos que tinham como meta começar a receber energia em 2025. Esse é um dos fatores que fazem da geração de energia no próprio local uma solução que deixou de ser apenas temporária e vem se consolidando como uma alternativa amplamente adotada. A Bloom Energy estima que, até 2030, 38% das instalações de data centers utilizarão algum tipo de geração própria como fonte primária de energia. O percentual representa um aumento de 13% em relação ao ano anterior. A mesma fonte prevê que, dentro de quatro anos, aproximadamente 27% dessas instalações serão abastecidas integralmente por energia gerada no próprio local. No entanto, ao contornar as filas de espera de vários anos para garantir acesso à rede elétrica e resolver um problema, essas empresas se depararam com outras dificuldades que não haviam previsto. Um exemplo é o fato de que as cadeias de suprimentos de equipamentos não acompanharam o ritmo de expansão dos data centers. Os prazos de entrega de transformadores e turbinas a gás estão muito acima das estimativas iniciais, que variavam de 24 a 48 meses. Na prática, a Wood Mackenzie, empresa de pesquisa, análise e consultoria sediada em Edimburgo, na Escócia, informou que os prazos de entrega de turbinas a gás atualmente chegam a seis anos. Isso levou a consultoria a observar que o atraso “mudou fundamentalmente o mercado, que deixou de tomar decisões orientadas pela economia dos combustíveis e passou a priorizar estratégias de aquisição e a viabilidade dos produtos”. Cronogramas diferentes Há também outros problemas. A complexidade dessas instalações não tem precedentes, já que muitos projetos combinam diferentes tipos de tecnologia em uma única microrrede integrada. Ao mesmo tempo, as empresas responsáveis pela operação e manutenção precisam estruturar e operar as instalações conforme os equipamentos chegam, seguindo cronogramas escalonados. A disponibilidade inédita de equipamentos e a complexidade operacional resultante impuseram uma pressão inesperada sobre os responsáveis pela operação das usinas de energia. “Os incorporadores não estão mais esperando pela rede elétrica; eles não podem se dar a esse luxo”, afirma Doug Machon, vice-presidente de desenvolvimento de negócios da Kyuden Energy Partners, empresa de operação e manutenção de usinas de energia sediada em Aliso Viejo, na Califórnia. “A fila de espera para conexão à rede é um gargalo significativo, mas não é o único. O problema se ampliou e passou a abranger a cadeia de suprimentos da infraestrutura energética, desde turbinas e transformadores até sistemas de controle e equipamentos auxiliares das usinas. Como resultado, somos cada vez mais solicitados a estruturar uma capacidade operacional antes mesmo de todos os ativos físicos previstos para a instalação definitiva terem sido entregues e a colocar em operação sistemas integrados compostos por diferentes tecnologias, cujos equipamentos chegam em cronogramas distintos. Trata-se de um trabalho fundamentalmente diferente da operação de uma usina convencional.” A Kyuden Energy Partners, assim como empresas como Consolidated Asset Management Services (CAMS) e Ethos Energy, está entre os diversos fornecedores de serviços de operação e manutenção que ajudam os participantes do setor a superar esse desafio. Desafios de execução Embora cada projeto atendido por esses fornecedores tenha características próprias, determinadas complexidades se repetem. Entre elas estão a integração de diferentes tecnologias de geração em uma microrrede; o uso de fontes temporárias ou provisórias de energia até que a infraestrutura permanente esteja disponível; a contratação, integração e capacitação de grandes equipes técnicas e de manutenção para garantir operações presenciais ininterruptas; e a coordenação do comissionamento e da entrada em operação de diferentes fases do projeto, que ocorrem de forma escalonada. Em comparação com projetos tradicionais de geração de energia em grande escala, a Kyuden constatou que cada um desses obstáculos representa um desafio de execução. A CAMS, fornecedora de serviços de operação e manutenção (O&M) e gestão de ativos sediada em Houston, nos Estados Unidos, tem experiência em projetos que somam 70 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade de geração. A empresa oferece um programa que combina processos simplificados de licenciamento e gestão comercial com serviços diários de operação e manutenção. Sua resposta à demanda energética decorrente das cargas de trabalho de IA e da computação em nuvem está inicialmente concentrada na geração a gás natural e em fontes renováveis. Com experiência na gestão de mais de 100 instalações e de mais de 40 GW de capacidade de geração de energia em todo o mundo, a Ethos Energy desenvolveu seu Centro de Desempenho 24 horas por dia, sete dias por semana (24-7 Performance Center), para oferecer um modelo de operação remota voltado aos desafios dos sistemas BTM. Com o uso de monitoramento assistido por inteligência artificial, uma única equipe monitora, opera e gerencia remotamente várias usinas ao mesmo tempo. artigo.texto: The University of Illinois Springfield is hosting a presentation on Wednesday, Oct. 21, focused on the environmental impacts of artificial intelligence and data center development. The talk is free and open to the public. Mary Willis, assistant professor of epidemiology at the Boston University School of Public Health, “will investigate the local effects of data centers built in the United States and propose policy solutions to help mitigate environmental impacts and protect local communities,” according to a promotional annoucement. The event, at 6 p.m. in Brookens Auditorium, is a part the UIS Engaged Citizen Common Experience speaker series. Earlier this year, Willis, who previously studied fracking, told Illinois Times research on animals could reveal more information about the effects of hyperscale data centers on surrounding residents, animals and land. “The first study that really linked tracking to adverse health outcomes was on horse or cattle,” she said. “That’s how we kind of figured out that there was even something going on here, and so I would be 0% surprised if local animal studies are what help us actually figure out the effects of data centers faster than we will in humans.” The most immediate concern regarding the CyrusOne data center project planned for rural Sangamon County, according to Willis, is likely going to be the 420 backup emergency generators. While they will only need to run for 15 hours per year for maintenance, they would run for longer if the data center needed emergency power. “This fine, particulate matter can very quickly become a regional problem,” Willis said, though she noted it’s more of a concern for those near the site. “If you live near a coal-fired power plant, that’s probably a far more important source to consider than the data center if that’s not right near you – but this is likely contributing overall to regional air pollution.” Almost half of all Americans are living in areas with heavily polluted air, according to the American Lung Association. Sangamon County and the surrounding counties, according to the American Lung Association, rank middle of the road in particle pollution when compared to more than 200 more metropolitan areas. Polluted air is “associated with increased risks of mortality, asthma and preterm birth,” Willis said. She said she was surprised that CyrusOne plans to install that number of diesel-powered backup generators, a sentiment echoed by another researcher. In March, Max Zhang, a professor at Cornell University who researches air pollutants produced by diesel-powered generators, told Illinois Times that was the largest number of backup generators he’d ever heard of for a data center. Rising land temperatures Researchers at The University of Cambridge published a study in March that used remote sensors to observe temperature increases around active data centers. Data centers located in non-urban environments resulted in “heat islands,” where surface temperatures can rise as far as six miles away. Illinois Times asked CyrusOne about the study’s conclusions in July and whether the company had previously sampled land surface temperature around its data centers. “At CyrusOne, our facilities are designed, developed, and operated in accordance with applicable health, safety, environmental, and land-use requirements, while following established industry practices for site design, cooling, energy efficiency, and environmental performance,” wrote Blair Felter, vice president of communications. “We do not have surface-temperature data to share.” It’s unclear how nearby farmland might be impacted by the CyrusOne data center and the heat it gives off from running continuously; farmland is assessed by soil quality, which then affects the sale price and, ultimately, the tax assessment. Byron Deaner, the county’s chief assessment officer, told IT in July even if that study bears out in Illinois, farmland values wouldn’t change much until parcels of land are actually sold and the market potentially adjusts. “You really wouldn’t see any impact to those values until you started to see some farmland with those different productivity indexes sell at different rates,” he said. “Maybe that would force the Illinois Department of Revenue to revisit the values associated with those soils, if they could contribute the environmental impact of the heat to those particular soil types within the particular distance.”
