artigo.texto: Parcerias Colt DCS e RMZ iniciam a construção de data center de 64 MW em Mumbai, preparado para IA Adicione Unite.AI às suas fontes preferidas no Google A Colt Data Centre Services (Colt DCS), provedora global de data centers preparados para IA, hiperescaláveis e voltados a grandes empresas, e a RMZ, plataforma indiana de ativos reais de capital fechado, anunciaram em 15 de outubro de 2026 o início da construção do Mumbai 3, um data center de 64 MW preparado para IA no campus das parceiras em Navi Mumbai, na Índia. O primeiro cliente hiperescalável da instalação já foi contratado, e as empresas afirmaram que o data center está totalmente pré-alugado. A preparação do terreno começou em dezembro de 2025, e a construção está em andamento após a assinatura do contrato com o cliente. As empresas descreveram o início da construção como um marco que demonstra o ritmo de expansão da joint venture nos 18 meses desde sua assinatura. Investimento da joint venture e capacidade do campus O Mumbai 3 está sendo desenvolvido no âmbito da joint venture que a Colt DCS e a RMZ anunciaram em 2024 para investir US$ 1,7 bilhão no mercado indiano de data centers. Por meio da joint venture, as parceiras se comprometeram a desenvolver 250 MW de capacidade de data centers em Mumbai e Chennai. O Mumbai 3 será integrado às instalações existentes Mumbai 1 e Mumbai 2, no campus de Navi Mumbai, que atualmente atende a grandes empresas e cargas de trabalho em nuvem. O campus tem potencial para oferecer até 148 MW de capacidade quando estiver totalmente desenvolvido e, após a conclusão, o Mumbai 3 elevará a capacidade operacional do local para 86 MW, segundo as empresas. Projetado para cargas de trabalho de IA de alta densidade O Mumbai 3 foi projetado para atender a cargas de trabalho de IA e implantações de computação de alta densidade, com 64 MW de potência contratada garantida. A instalação usa uma arquitetura híbrida de refrigeração que combina o resfriamento a ar tradicional com o resfriamento líquido direto no chip. Uma subestação GIS de 220 kV localizada no campus oferece resiliência e escalabilidade, e o local dispõe de conectividade neutra em relação às operadoras, com acesso a rotas de fibra óptica de alta capacidade. Pratap Mane, responsável pela Colt DCS na Índia, afirmou que a demanda por data centers está evoluindo rapidamente, com clientes que precisam de implantações maiores, maior densidade de racks e infraestrutura capaz de atender a cargas de trabalho de IA cada vez mais intensivas. Ele disse que o Mumbai 3 foi concebido desde o início para estar preparado para IA, incorporando refrigeração líquida e infraestrutura elétrica reforçada para atender a implantações de alta densidade, e que isso permite aos clientes ampliar com eficiência as cargas de trabalho de IA de próxima geração e de computação de alto desempenho, mantendo a resiliência e a eficiência operacionais. Acrescentou que a instalação fortalece o campus de Navi Mumbai como uma plataforma escalável e preparada para o futuro de infraestrutura digital. Energia renovável e criação de empregos A instalação funcionará com 100% de energia renovável, afirmaram as empresas, e seu sistema de refrigeração em circuito fechado foi projetado para gerar quase nenhum efluente no processo de resfriamento. A expectativa é que o projeto crie mais de 700 empregos na construção e na operação, além de apoiar fornecedores, empreiteiros e prestadores de serviços locais. As empresas disseram que essas medidas refletem o compromisso conjunto de oferecer infraestrutura digital sustentável, que gere valor duradouro para as comunidades locais e a região como um todo. Deepak Chhabria, presidente da RMZ Infrastructure, afirmou que o campus foi projetado para permitir que provedores hiperescaláveis e de neocloud ampliem suas operações à medida que evoluem suas necessidades de capacidade e computação, reunindo escala, resiliência e rapidez de entrada no mercado. Ele disse que o investimento reforça o compromisso da RMZ com a construção de infraestrutura avançada de data centers e IA que atenda aos padrões globais e às demandas em rápida evolução da economia digital. A joint venture de 2024 A Colt DCS e a RMZ anunciaram a joint venture em 19 de novembro de 2024, como uma parceria em partes iguais voltada ao desenvolvimento de infraestrutura digital no mercado indiano. Na ocasião, as empresas disseram que o investimento se concentraria inicialmente em acelerar o desenvolvimento de locais existentes em Navi Mumbai e Ambattur, Chennai, com a inclusão de um terceiro local no futuro, e que os data centers teriam capacidade combinada de aproximadamente 250 MW após a conclusão de todas as fases. O anúncio de 2024 afirmou que a Colt DCS trazia 25 anos de experiência no desenvolvimento e na operação de data centers em mercados de primeira linha na Europa, no Japão e na Índia, e que a joint venture aceleraria a oferta de nova capacidade para clientes na Índia, aproveitando as relações de longo prazo da RMZ com parceiros da cadeia de suprimentos e seus clientes da lista Fortune India 500. Na assinatura, Niclas Sanfridsson, então diretor-executivo da Colt DCS, classificou a Índia como um país estratégico para os planos de crescimento da operadora, e Chhabria, então diretor-executivo da RMZ Infrastructure, descreveu a infraestrutura digital como um pilar do futuro econômico da Índia.

artigo.texto: Brasil e China buscam ampliar a cooperação na construção de mercados de carbono, com foco no intercâmbio de experiências, na medição das emissões de gases de efeito estufa e no desenvolvimento de mecanismos capazes de contribuir para a transição econômica de baixo carbono. A possibilidade de aprofundar essa parceria foi destacada por Cristina Reis, secretária extraordinária do Mercado de Carbono do Ministério da Fazenda, após sua participação na Conferência de Mercado de Carbono da China 2026, realizada em setembro, na cidade de Wuhan. O evento reuniu representantes de 27 países, regiões e organizações internacionais para compartilhar experiências sobre a criação e o funcionamento de mercados de carbono e discutir caminhos para a cooperação climática. Segundo Reis, a experiência chinesa oferece referências relevantes para o Brasil, especialmente na implementação gradual de mecanismos de precificação de emissões e na estruturação de sistemas de monitoramento, relato e verificação de gases de efeito estufa. A aproximação ocorre enquanto os dois países desenvolvem seus próprios instrumentos de política climática e participam de uma iniciativa internacional voltada à convergência entre mercados regulados de carbono. A cooperação pode contribuir para aprimorar metodologias, aumentar a transparência na contabilização das emissões e criar condições para uma maior compatibilidade entre os sistemas nacionais. Experiência chinesa pode orientar a estruturação do mercado brasileiro A China lançou seu mercado nacional regulado de comércio de emissões em julho de 2021. Desde então, o sistema passou por uma expansão gradual, com o objetivo de utilizar mecanismos econômicos para estimular a redução de gases de efeito estufa. Até o fim de agosto de 2026, o mercado regulado chinês havia acumulado negociações equivalentes a 961 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente, com movimentação financeira de 65,7 bilhões de yuans, aproximadamente US$ 9,71 bilhões, segundo os dados divulgados pela Xinhua. O país também desenvolve um mercado voluntário de redução de emissões. Até o mesmo período, 41 projetos haviam sido registrados nesse sistema, com volume acumulado de negociações de 21,71 milhões de toneladas e valor total de 1,74 bilhão de yuans. Os mercados regulados e voluntários têm características diferentes. No primeiro caso, o governo estabelece regras e obrigações para os participantes abrangidos pelo sistema. No segundo, projetos podem gerar créditos de carbono segundo metodologias específicas, que são adquiridos voluntariamente por organizações interessadas em compensar emissões ou apoiar iniciativas de redução e remoção de gases de efeito estufa. A secretária brasileira destacou a experiência da China na implantação progressiva desses mecanismos, começando por projetos-piloto, avançando para o mercado regulado e, posteriormente, fortalecendo o mercado voluntário. A troca de experiências, entretanto, não significa que o Brasil precise reproduzir o modelo chinês. As características econômicas, a estrutura produtiva e as prioridades ambientais de cada país exigem soluções próprias. O objetivo da cooperação é identificar práticas e metodologias que possam contribuir para o desenvolvimento dos respectivos sistemas, respeitando suas particularidades. Brasil implementa seu sistema regulado de carbono No Brasil, a estruturação do mercado regulado ganhou base legal com a Lei nº 15.042, sancionada em dezembro de 2024, que instituiu o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões de Gases de Efeito Estufa (SBCE). O sistema prevê a criação de regras para monitorar emissões, estabelecer obrigações para os agentes regulados e organizar a negociação de ativos relacionados às emissões e às reduções verificadas de gases de efeito estufa. Sua implementação está prevista em etapas. O processo envolve a regulamentação da lei, a preparação dos instrumentos de monitoramento e a definição de mecanismos para alocação e negociação de ativos de carbono. Em julho de 2026, o Ministério da Fazenda abriu uma consulta pública sobre uma proposta de cronograma para a implementação das obrigações de monitoramento, relato e verificação. A medida integra a preparação da infraestrutura necessária ao funcionamento do sistema. Esse processo torna a cooperação internacional particularmente relevante. A elaboração de metodologias confiáveis para contabilizar emissões é um dos requisitos para que os mercados funcionem com transparência e para que os resultados ambientais possam ser comparados de maneira consistente. Segundo Cristina Reis, Brasil e China podem aprofundar a colaboração justamente nessa área, compartilhando experiências sobre os sistemas de monitoramento, relato e verificação, conhecidos pela sigla MRV. Esses procedimentos permitem determinar a quantidade de gases emitidos por atividades econômicas, registrar as informações e verificar se os dados apresentados seguem critérios técnicos definidos. A confiabilidade dessas informações é fundamental para evitar a contabilização incorreta de emissões e preservar a credibilidade dos créditos de carbono. Coalizão internacional reúne Brasil, China e União Europeia A aproximação bilateral também está ligada à Coalizão Aberta para Mercados Regulados de Carbono, iniciativa lançada durante a COP30, realizada em Belém, em novembro de 2025, sob liderança brasileira. O mecanismo busca promover o diálogo entre países que adotam sistemas de precificação de carbono, com o objetivo de aproximar metodologias de contabilização, regras para créditos e procedimentos de verificação das emissões. Brasil, China e União Europeia ocupam posições de liderança na iniciativa. O Brasil exerce a presidência até 2027, enquanto China e União Europeia atuam como copresidentes. Em setembro de 2026, durante uma reunião de alto nível realizada em Wuhan, os participantes aprovaram um plano de trabalho até 2030 e definiram uma estrutura provisória para o secretariado da coalizão. artigo.texto: Premier Energies is advancing its planned 12 GWh BESS manufacturing agreement with RCT with a shareholders’ agreement The initial 6 GWh phase is expected to become operational in FY2027–28 RCT Nexor Energy can acquire a 15% stake in the JV in four tranches linked to project milestones, with an option to acquire an additional 5% India’s Premier Energies Limited has finalized a shareholders’ agreement for a joint venture (JV) to establish a 12 GWh battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturing facility in Telangana. The agreement was signed between Premier Battery Technologies Private Limited (PBTPL), a wholly owned subsidiary of Premier Energies; Premier Energies Storage Solutions Private Limited (PESSPL), the JV company; and RCT Nexor Energy Private Limited, part of Germany’s RCT Group. The facility is planned to come up in Seetharampur, Telangana, with an initial capacity of 6 GWh expected to be established in FY2027-28. The duo signed a binding term sheet for the facility in September 2026 (see India Solar PV News Snippets). The proposed facility will manufacture and assemble BESS for residential, small business, commercial, industrial, and utility-scale applications. Under the agreement, RCT Nexor Energy will have the right to acquire a 15% stake in the JV through four tranches linked to project milestones. It will also have the option to acquire an additional 5% equity stake for cash consideration at the end of the first phase, subject to the agreement’s terms. The JV’s board will comprise two nominees from PBTPL and one from RCT Nexor Energy. With this joint venture, solar cell and module manufacturer Premier Energies will enter BESS manufacturing, targeting both domestic and international markets. The company recently announced that it secured new orders worth INR 4,001 crore in Q2 FY2027 (July-September 2026). The orders cover 2,308 MW of solar cell and module supplies, along with EPC projects. It said the orders came from power producers, module manufacturers, EPC companies, and other customers, excluding the retail segment. Premier Energies’ module manufacturing capacity has nearly doubled to 11.1 GW, while its solar cell capacity has increased to 10.6 GW following the commissioning of a 7 GW TOPCon cell manufacturing facility in Andhra Pradesh (see Premier Energies Commissions India’s ‘Largest’ Solar Cell Fab).

artigo.texto: Na manhã de 18 de outubro, a Ucrânia lançou um ataque com drones em grande escala, visando uma instalação petrolífera, um centro de dados e uma ponte na cidade de São Petersburgo, localizada no noroeste da Rússia. A mídia russa noticiou que drones atacaram o porto petrolífero de São Petersburgo e o centro de dados do VKontakte, empresa que opera a maior rede social do país. O governador Aleksandr Beglov confirmou que um incêndio deflagrou na zona portuária do petróleo e em várias instalações civis em quatro distritos da cidade. As equipas de resgate atuaram imediatamente no combate às chamas e, até ao momento, não foram registadas vítimas. O incidente também afetou diversos voos no Aeroporto Internacional de Pulkovo. Na província de Leningrado, que circunda São Petersburgo, o governador Aleksandr Drozdenko anunciou que as defesas aéreas abateram 127 drones. Os destroços danificaram quatro carros em um estacionamento e causaram vários focos de incêndio. Fontes que monitoram o conflito disseram que o ataque começou por volta das 2h50 da manhã. Imagens registradas por moradores mostraram múltiplas explosões iluminando o céu noturno sobre São Petersburgo – uma cidade de 5,6 milhões de habitantes localizada a cerca de 856 km da fronteira com a Ucrânia. Alguns vídeos mostraram drones atingindo uma ponte de oito faixas e causando um grande incêndio na área portuária. O porto petrolífero de São Petersburgo tem capacidade para receber e transportar aproximadamente 12,5 milhões de toneladas por ano por via marítima, ferroviária e rodoviária, sendo um dos maiores centros de armazenamento e exportação de combustíveis da Rússia. A fabricante ucraniana Fire Point afirma ter utilizado seu avião de ataque FP-1 nessa operação. Diversos canais de notícias locais relataram que uma subestação de energia também foi danificada, causando cortes de energia localizados e redução da pressão da água em algumas áreas. Esses ataques fazem parte da operação de longo prazo da Ucrânia para pressionar intensamente o fornecimento de combustível e a infraestrutura digital da Rússia, em meio a uma complexa e contínua troca de ataques contra a infraestrutura energética entre os dois países. artigo.texto: The abandoned San Francisco Centre mall could find new life as a massive data center and artificial intelligence lab under a newly revealed proposal, though the idea faces immediate hurdles from city leadership and community members. The multistory shopping mall has been closed and boarded up since late January. According to a proposal confirmed by Jared Kreiger, CEO of the Maryland-based property development firm KG Growth Partners, a confidential client is exploring purchasing the entire property to convert the upper floors into a data center and AI lab. Watch NBC Bay Area News free wherever you are The plan would include public space on the ground level and water for a rooftop community garden that could be donated to nonprofits focusing on food insecurity. However, Kreiger declined to reveal the identity of the prospective buyer. The proposal comes at a complicated time for downtown San Francisco. Last week, Mayor Daniel Lurie approved a 45-day moratorium on City Hall approving any permits to build new data centers in the city. Addressing the proposal, Mayor Lurie said he was unaware of the plan and emphasized that the building remains on the market. "I am not aware of that proposal," Lurie said. "The building is still up for sale. There is not a buyer yet. I'm hopeful that we get someone in there that will bring a lot of people downtown." Communities across the country have increasingly raised concerns over data center developments, pointing to issues such as heavy water usage, environmental impacts, round-the-clock noise, and vibrations. Local reactions to the downtown San Francisco concept were mixed. Local "I've heard bad things about data centers," said San Francisco resident Paul Bodner. "By default I would not support it," added Guillaume Le Ster, also of San Francisco. Nicholas McNely, who lives a couple of blocks from the shuttered mall, questioned the motives behind such a project. "They're more trying to extract from whatever community they're trying to extract the resources from to enrich themselves so, I don't really see the reason for a data center here," McNely said. Conversely, some visitors saw potential upside. Janet Li of Burlingame noted, "If it's an AI center here, more people would work here so, I think it's good for the street." The proposal was first reported by the San Francisco Chronicle and confirmed to NBC Bay Area by development consultants.

artigo.texto: Ahead of iPhone Duo’s launch on Friday, accessory maker BMX is releasing what appears to be one of the first MagSafe batteries designed specifically for Apple’s foldable. The BMX Duo is available to order now and can wirelessly charge your iPhone Duo (or any other iPhone) at up to 15W. You can pick it up on Amazon for $79.99. The iPhone Duo supports MagSafe, but because it’s shorter than a standard iPhone, many existing MagSafe accessories likely won’t fit—or will hang awkwardly off the bottom. The BMX Duo 5000mAh Power Bank is designed to fit exactly on the iPhone Duo: A custom-size 5,000mAh cell is shaped to the iPhone Duo’s folded footprint, so it sits flush on the cover panel instead of hanging past the edges. It was built around the Duo, and it snaps onto the iPhone 12 through 18 series just as securely. In addition to attaching via MagSafe for 15W wireless charging, it also has a built-in USB-C cable that can charge at up to 20W speeds. The BMX Duo also features a built-in ring that rotates a full 360 degrees. The full-color display on the back shows the exact battery percentage and live charging wattage. It uses semi-solid-state cells, which BMX says “use significantly less liquid electrolyte than conventional lithium-ion cells, which helps reduce the risk of battery fires.” The BMX Duo 5000mAh Power Bank is available to order today for $79.99. artigo.texto: By Vũ Hoa HƯNG YÊN — Combining rooftop solar power with battery energy storage systems (BESS) could help Việt Nam strengthen energy security, improve electricity efficiency and ease pressure on the national grid, but policy gaps, high costs and technical requirements remain barriers to wider adoption, experts said. Speaking at a conference on self-produced and self-consumed rooftop solar power in northern province of Hưng Yên on October 16, Mai Duy Thiện, chairman of the Việt Nam Clean Energy Association (VCEA), said the country’s target of average annual GDP growth of more than 10 per cent in 2026-30 would require sufficient, stable and safe electricity supplies. Resolution No 70-NQ/TW on national energy security and Government Directive No 10/CT-TTg, issued on March 30, 2026, identify renewable energy development, electricity savings and rooftop solar power as priorities. The Government has also called for research into preferential credit mechanisms to support investment in rooftop solar and BESS. However, market development remains constrained by high initial investment costs, limited access to finance, gaps in technical standards, fire safety requirements and complicated implementation procedures. Thiện called for closer coordination among regulators, local authorities, power companies and businesses to improve the legal framework, facilitate grid connections, enhance product quality and expand financing options. He also stressed the need to strengthen domestic research, manufacturing and technical capabilities to reduce reliance on imported equipment. Storage capacity set to expand Võ Quang Lâm, former deputy general director of Vietnam Electricity (EVN), said the country’s installed power capacity reached 87,616MW at the end of 2025, ranking second in Southeast Asia. As of August 2026, Việt Nam had 134,410 rooftop solar systems with a combined capacity of more than 11,450MWp, while the number of self-produced and self-consumed installations equipped with BESS remained very limited. On larger storage projects, Hà Nội Power Corporation (EVNHANOI) had completed 50MW of BESS capacity, while Northern Power Corporation (EVNNPC) had completed 155MW and aimed to reach 305MW in October 2026, Lâm said. Electricity Project Management Board No 2 and Power Generation Corporation 3 (EVNGENCO3) were pursuing investment procedures for centralised storage projects in northern Việt Nam, with planned capacities of 550MW and 300MW, respectively. Lâm said factories, commercial buildings and industrial parks could combine rooftop solar, battery storage and smart energy management systems to optimise electricity consumption and reduce dependence on grid power. He called for technical standards, grid-connection requirements, fire safety regulations, testing procedures and pricing mechanisms for BESS services. He also proposed publishing the PVout coefficient used to estimate rooftop solar generation at ward and commune level to improve calculation accuracy and support investment decisions. Bùi Xuân Bình, chairman and general director of GG Power, said Việt Nam should build its capacity to research, manufacture and export energy technologies rather than remain primarily a consumer market for products developed elsewhere. GG Power is developing energy storage manufacturing capacity, targeting an annual scale of 5GWh to serve residential, commercial, industrial and large-scale projects. Bình said a competitive domestic industry would require a complete value chain covering research, design, manufacturing, installation, maintenance and battery recycling. Cooperation among businesses, research institutions, distributors and financial institutions would also be needed to improve technology and access to finance. He stressed that product safety, quality, customer protection and effective battery collection and recycling systems were essential to sustainable market development. Representatives from Goldwind Group, Cornex Group, SRNE Group, Đan Khuê Solar, Ngọc Long Energy and Solar Kinh Bắc, among others, expressed interest in cooperation with GG Power. At the conference, the company introduced its “Made in Vietnam” energy storage products and signed cooperation agreements with several businesses to strengthen industry links and expand distribution networks. Participants said the market had significant growth potential but needed more consistent policies, affordable products and reliable warranty and maintenance services to improve the competitiveness of domestic technologies. — VNS

artigo.texto: Microsoft (MSFT:NASDAQ) has pulled out of a planned AI data center in Loughton, Essex, that British cloud provider Nscale was building for it, Reuters reported on October 18, citing the Telegraph. Microsoft is one of Nscale's two largest customers. Reuters said the Telegraph did not specify why Microsoft withdrew, and Microsoft declined Reuters' request for comment. The site did have an obvious problem: power. The Telegraph reported that grid officials told Nscale they didn't expect to supply electricity until the 2030s. That matches a September report that UK Power Networks couldn't connect the site before the early to mid-2030s. Nscale says it remains committed to Loughton and is looking at other power sources. Loughton Was a Small Slice of Microsoft's Buildout Loughton was planned to house about 23,000 Nvidia (NVDA:NASDAQ) chips for Azure, starting at 50 MW. Nscale agreed to supply Microsoft with about 200,000 Nvidia chips across the UK, Norway, Portugal and Texas, so Loughton was about 11.5% of the program. Microsoft added roughly a gigawatt of capacity in the June quarter alone, which makes Loughton's starting load about 5% of one quarter. The spending shows no sign of a pullback. Cash capital expenditure reached $35.80 billion in the June quarter, more than double the $17.08 billion a year earlier. Fiscal 2026 cash capex totaled $115.95 billion, up about 80%. On management's broader measure including finance leases, June-quarter capex was approximately $41 billion, with more than $50 billion expected in the September quarter. Demand is keeping pace. Intelligent Cloud revenue hit $39.31 billion in the June quarter, up about 32% from $29.88 billion, and CFO Amy Hood said customer demand still exceeds available supply. Microsoft has the customers and the cash. What it can't buy quickly is electricity. Power First, Then Chips Microsoft has been picky with Nscale before. It signed a letter of intent for up to 1.35 GW at Nscale's West Virginia campus in March, then walked away over the summer, and Anthropic took the capacity. Meanwhile, it is paying up for sites with a power date. On October 16, two days before the Loughton report, NiSource (NI) announced a 20-year agreement with Microsoft, with service expected to begin in 2028 and approximately 1,100 MW of generation resources to be added in Indiana. The other workaround is making power on-site, which is where Bloom Energy (BE:NYSE) comes in. Nscale reportedly held talks with Bloom about fuel cells for Loughton. Bloom's revenue reached a record $1.065 billion in the June quarter, up 166% from a year earlier. Its last four quarters brought in about $3.12 billion, nearly double the $1.63 billion of the four before. Grid delays are already showing up in someone's income statement.

artigo.texto: Next Upcoming Virtual event Hold onto Your Tax Credits: How to Get Ahead of the 2027 Deadline By Canary Media Illinois has built out large amounts of renewables in the past decade to reach its mandate of 100% clean energy by 2050. So far, though, it has lagged on building battery storage, which advocates say is especially necessary now as data center development drives up energy demand. Last fall, Illinois passed an ambitious law requiring 3 gigawatts of batteries on the state’s grid by the end of 2030. In August, the Illinois Power Agency, which procures electricity on behalf of the state’s large utilities, ran an auction-type proceeding to hand out incentives for companies promising to develop these batteries. The results were mixed. Statewide, deals were made for 600 megawatts of storage — less than two-thirds of the target that the law set for the initial procurement. The state sought to get 588 MW of storage in the utility ComEd’s territory in northern Illinois, but the procurement ended with just one company planning to build an 80-MW battery project there. In utility Ameren Illinois’ territory, which stretches over much of the state, three developers’ bids were chosen to supply 520 MW. Advocates said that while they were disappointed in the outcome in northern Illinois, the results overall were encouraging. James Gignac, Midwest policy director for the climate and energy program at the nonprofit Union of Concerned Scientists, called it “a strong start” that indicates “there is interest in developing energy storage in Illinois.” He noted that the new deals will increase Illinois’ total energy storage manifold: The state currently has only 102 MW, according to energy data firm Cleanview. The Illinois Power Agency is collecting feedback from developers through Oct. 28, with the goal of improving the next procurement process. Already some important takeaways have emerged that Illinois can use to entice more developers to build battery storage over the next few years. “I believe storage developers see Illinois as a strong market for new utility-scale storage, especially with our policies in place and state agencies focused on expanding batteries’ role on the power grid,” Gignac said. Across the country, states are turning to battery storage to bank renewable energy that is abundant when the wind is blowing and the sun is shining. This helps meet clean energy goals and spiking demand. A few states — notably Texas with over 18 GW and California with over 16 — have already installed large amounts of energy storage on their grids. Indiana tops the list of Midwestern states with 587 MW, over five times Illinois’ capacity. Overall energy storage has increased dramatically on U.S. grids, from 4.7 GW total in 2022 to over 50 today, according to federal data, but that surge took time to ramp up. Massachusetts, for example, launched an energy storage initiative in 2015 and an official target in 2018, but progress was slow until an uptick the past couple years. The state passed legislation in 2024 and the governor issued an executive order this year to boost battery deployment. New York, like Illinois, has a goal of 3 GW of utility-scale storage on the grid by 2030, as part of its goal of getting off fossil fuel-fired electricity by 2040. New York has 288 MW of storage installed, according to Cleanview, and in September the state secured promises for 950 MW using the same incentive mechanism that Illinois has employed. Two of the four companies chosen in Illinois’ procurement are New York-based. In the regional grid known as the PJM Interconnection, which handles the flow of power in parts of 13 states, including New York and the ComEd territory in Illinois, long delays to connect batteries to the system have been a significant barrier to deployment. Brett Sproul leads regulatory work in Illinois for Advanced Energy United, a national industry organization whose members include renewable and battery storage companies. He said there are multiple developers that could build batteries in Illinois by 2030, “however because of the interconnection queue at PJM there’s a lot of uncertainty” as to whether those projects could actually start storing power by the deadline. “That uncertainty led to some cold feet,” he added. States like Illinois can have a hard time convincing developers to build batteries, because of the structure of their energy market. In states with vertically integrated energy markets, utilities can include batteries in their plans to meet energy demand, and with the approval of state regulators, charge customers for the cost. But in states such as Illinois, New York, and Ohio that have “restructured” markets where generators compete to get contracts to supply the grid, a different model is often needed to incentivize developers to invest in batteries and sell their storage services on the open market. In Illinois, that’s taken the form of an incentive program under the Clean and Reliable Grid Affordability Act signed into law in January that uses “indexed storage credits” to guarantee a certain amount of revenue to storage developers. During the bidding process that culminated Aug. 26, storage developers stated how much payment they would need in order to build batteries connected to the grid. If regional wholesale energy prices available to battery owners end up being below those amounts, the utilities will make up the difference — using customers’ funds to pay the storage companies. If wholesale prices are higher, the storage company will pay excess funds back to the utility. While the model means battery developers could feasibly earn less than they would without participating in the program, the guarantee of a certain revenue level is crucial to jumpstarting the state’s still-new industry, experts said. artigo.texto: The 15-Minute Space TPU: Why Orbital Data Centers Are a Radiator Problem Google's prototype can only run for 15 minutes before it has to cool down. The radiator, not the chip, explains the entire economics of space compute. Google's first Project Suncatcher prototype satellite has reached orbit on SpaceX's Transporter-18 rideshare mission. The spacecraft, built with Planet Labs and roughly the size of a refrigerator, carries four Google TPUs. Google says the ground team has made contact and that the satellite is operating as expected. The detail that traveled fastest was this: the TPUs can run for about 15 minutes, then must shut down while the radiator rejects the heat. That sounds like a thermal failure in orbit. It is not. The 15-minute window was written into the mission profile before launch. Google designed an intermittent operating cycle because, in vacuum, the radiator rather than the chip sets the long-run compute ceiling. That distinction matters. It moves the question from "can a TPU survive space?" to "what kind of system can run continuously in space?" A data center is judged by sustained average power, not by a 15-minute burst. On that measure, the radiator is the main character. Three problems, one still open Google's public test results divide the engineering risk into three buckets. Launch vibration: the TPU assembly passed three-axis vibration testing, with local loads of 50 to 100 g. Google's team described the result as better than expected. Radiation: at UC Davis, Google ran the Trillium TPU under a proton beam while it was executing workloads. The chip absorbed a total ionizing dose exceeding the cumulative dose of a five-year mission. That is a positive early signal for inference workloads. Training would face a higher risk profile. Heat rejection: Google tested the thermal path in a thermal vacuum chamber. The result was an intermittent operating mode. Vibration and radiation have fairly clear answers. Heat is being bypassed by duty cycle. Why the radiator sets average compute In space, there is no air convection and no atmospheric sink. Heat moves from the chip through heat pipes to a radiator, then leaves as infrared radiation. The radiator's continuous rejection rate is fixed by its area, its temperature, and its emissivity. The Stefan-Boltzmann relationship makes temperature the dominant term: rejection scales with the fourth power of absolute temperature. A rough estimate shows the scale. At a radiator surface temperature of 20°C (293 K) and emissivity 0.9, one square meter rejects about 376 W on one side. Two sides give roughly 750 W before accounting for Earth infrared and albedo inputs. The net figure is lower, around 600 W per square meter in a realistic low-Earth-orbit environment. A ground-based high-density AI rack now draws well over 100 kW. At 600 W per square meter net, one such rack maps to nearly 170 square meters of radiator area. That is one rack. This is why a space data center is a radiator-area project. The compute boards are a small part of the mass and volume. Most of the structure goes to radiators, heat pipes, and deployment mechanisms. Google's project lead has said the radiator is one of the heaviest components on the prototype. In an industry that charges by launch mass, the heaviest component also sets the compute ceiling. The economics follow the radiator. The design logic also flips. On the ground, cooling engineers push chip temperatures down: colder water, lower PUE, lower junction temperature, less leakage, longer life. In space, a hotter radiator is better. Raising the radiator surface from 20°C to 60°C (333 K) lifts single-side rejection from about 376 W per square meter to about 627 W per square meter, an increase of nearly 70%. A space-optimized compute chip should tolerate higher junction temperatures and accept a modest efficiency penalty in exchange for radiator mass reduction. Today's TPUs and GPUs are optimized for ground data-center temperature windows. Sending them up is a test under the wrong conditions. For a prototype, that is acceptable. For a scalable architecture, it is not. The long-run metric changes accordingly: from performance per watt to sustained performance per square meter of radiator area, or sustained performance per kilogram of launched mass. The duty cycle does not create extra compute The heat sink, heat pipes, and structure have thermal capacitance. During the 15-minute run, the chip's heat output exceeds the radiator's continuous rejection rate. The difference goes into thermal capacitance, and the temperature rises. When the chip shuts down, the radiator drains that stored heat. Averaged over a full run-and-cool cycle, the continuous heat rejection equals the radiator's capacity. The burst does not add a watt of long-run compute. It moves the radiator's capacity into a 15-minute window. For a single inference demo, one question and one answer, 15 minutes is enough. For a data center, the number that matters is the average. That number is set by radiator area and temperature. What the orbital test should measure Google says the satellite will run the Gemma open-weight model to observe how the chip behaves in space. The thermal chain matters more than the model output. Three measurements matter more than benchmark scores. First, whether thermal interface materials degrade under vacuum and repeated thermal cycling. Second, how far heat-pipe performance in microgravity diverges from ground measurements. Third, whether the 15-minute window shrinks over a year. A shrinking window would indicate thermal-path degradation. That is a more serious problem than radiation-induced bit flips, because it directly erodes average compute. Google plans to launch two more satellites in 2027 to test high-bandwidth laser inter-satellite links and formation flying. That work is as important as heat rejection. artigo.texto: Georgia candidates up and down the ballot are campaigning on an issue that has struck a nerve across the political spectrum: data centers. A wave of data center projects across Georgia has been met with outrage in many communities in the last year or so, causing state lawmakers from both parties to push a flurry of legislative solutions during the 2026 legislative session. But in the end, none of the bills passed. Since then, Georgia has become the leading state for data centers. Gov. Brian Kemp, a Republican who is term-limited and leaving office after this year, has welcomed the facilities, saying at a data center-related event in Washington this summer that "we cannot let China win this race, and that's what some people want," referencing the race between the U.S. and China to develop increasingly powerful artificial intelligence models. The November election will decide to what extent Georgia embraces the energy-hungry facilities in the future, with voters choosing a new governor, the lawmakers who shape the state's policies on data centers and other state leaders who play a role in carrying out those policies. At the top of the ballot, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the Democratic nominee for governor, has criticized Republican nominee Rick Jackson, a wealthy healthcare executive, for his investment in a data center in Texas through a company Jackson was the head of until recently. Though his campaign has tried to distance itself from that development, in his campaign financial disclosure, Jackson is listed as the CEO and president of Datahub Developers, the company that is advancing the data center in Texas that the local community is fighting. Bottoms and Jackson had a fiery exchange at a recent debate where they swapped accusations of being involved in advancing data centers. "There is a community asking him to not build a data center, a massive data center in their community, and he is moving forward. So, if he is an investor in data centers, if he builds data centers, he cannot be trusted on this," Bottoms said in the debate organized by Atlanta News First and Gray Media. Jackson fired back, accusing Bottoms of approving three data centers during her time as mayor of Atlanta, but Bottoms said that she was "not sure what data centers he's referencing," saying there was only one at Georgia Tech that wasn't one of the hyperscale data centers that cause concerns today. Attorney general candidate says family has 'moved on' from data center project once planned for their farmland At least one other candidate, Georgia state Sen. Brian Strickland, a McDonough Republican running for state attorney general, held a personal financial stake in a proposed data center as recently as the summer of 2025. But the proposal has since been shelved, according to public records and interviews. The Georgia Recorder examined financial disclosure documents for all candidates running for statewide office in November. The Recorder also reviewed other public records and reached out to all of the candidates and their campaigns to ask whether the candidate has a direct financial stake in a data center. In phone calls, text messages and emails with candidates and their campaign staff, all except those described in the story reported having no financial interest in data center projects. Public records show that Strickland, a lawyer who represents a suburban district southeast of Atlanta, was involved in advancing a $1.2 billion data center on his family's farmland in Henry County. On May 15, 2024, he authorized a real estate development firm focused on technology to pursue rezoning for the project. Strickland's personal financial disclosure statement shows that the state senator holds a greater-than-5% stake in Strickland Road Farms, which was a co-applicant in the rezoning application for the proposed 1.25 million-square-feet data center. The project came close to being finalized mid-2025 – about the same time Strickland launched his bid for higher office – but Strickland told reporters last week that his family backed out over concerns about the noise that would come from the data center and now says the project is "dead." A public hearing before the Henry County Board of Commissioners was scheduled to consider rezoning part of the farmland on June 17, 2025, but Carlotta Harrell, the commission's chair, said at the top of the meeting that the agenda item, along with other rezoning public hearings, "have all been removed at the request of the applicant and we will hear these items at a later time." County and local development officials confirmed the project is now inactive. The Democratic nominee for attorney general, state Rep. Tanya Miller, pressed Strickland on the project at last week's Atlanta Press Club debate. "It wasn't until days – and mind you, we're talking days – after he announced his run for attorney general, did he remove the agenda item from the public hearing. He didn't remove the data center application. He's playing with words. He's shape shifting," Miller said to reporters after the debate. Opponents of the data center project, like Connie Snow, a member of Conserve Henry County, a local advocacy group focused on zoning issues, say they're worried the project will be revived after the November election. "They've all told us that he's withdrawn and all this other stuff, but I don't think that it's going to go away," Snow said in an interview. "You have to also remember that all this happened coincidentally enough as it was getting close to election time." Snow also participated in a press call organized by the Democratic Party of Georgia. But Strickland said the decision to halt the project was not related to his decision to run for office and says the family now plans to add to an existing residence on the property and that his "parents decided to keep the entire farm intact." artigo.texto: City commission candidates split on data center restrictions at forum Incumbents and challengers divide over moratorium ahead of election What This Story Is About - City commission candidates at a forum discussed their positions on data center restrictions and a proposed moratorium. Why It Matters - The city’s handling of data center regulations has become a key dividing line between incumbents and challengers ahead of the election. For Context - Two city commission candidates, Don Langley and Sue Parrigan, did not attend the forum, though Parrigan provided a written statement defending the city’s existing data center ordinance. BOWLING GREEN, Ky. (WBKO) - Voters packed State Street Baptist Church Monday, Oct.19 for a candidate forum focused on city commission and contested magistrate races. Doors opened at 5:30 p.m. for a meet and greet. The forum started at 6:30 p.m., giving voters a chance to hear directly from candidates seeking to represent them on city issues and in county government. City commission candidates address data centers A central topic heading into the election is the ongoing debate over data centers. Candidates at the forum responded to questions on the issue. Incumbent Melinda Hill, who is running for re-election, voted against a proposed moratorium in June. She said restrictions already in place protect the community. “City commission voted five to zero with the strictest restrictions for data centers,” Hill said. “We’ve already put those in place. So yes, I know you’re mad there wasn’t a moratorium, or some of you are. But be thankful we put very strict restrictions for our community regarding data centers.” Fellow incumbent Carlos Bailey voted for the moratorium. He said he wanted a pause so outside experts could be brought in. “The reason why we wanted to have that is because we wanted to bring in the experts, because none of us on here were experts, to see how it is doing in other communities,” Bailey said. “We wanted to bring in people who actually are living with data centers, like Memphis and Gallatin, Tennessee. They could tell us how it affects their everyday life.” Thomas Morris said the data center debate is the main reason he is running. He said he supported a moratorium. “I went to Gallatin, Tennessee, talked to a city commissioner there,” Morris said. “I asked him what piece of advice do you have. He said, ‘take your time.’ In my opinion, we did not take our time. We rushed it through, and this is an issue that could come back to bite us.” Incumbent Dana Beasley Brown said she backed a moratorium because of transparency and unanswered questions about impact. “We haven’t done the research, like Commissioner Bailey said, about our unique karst topography and what a data center of that size, the impact it could have on it,” Beasley Brown said. “The fact that we have had a real long drought this summer, and thinking about our water usage, how we make sure we have enough for our kids and grandkids. It’s these concerns I have in mind, and the need to stop and make sure our whole community gets to give input about whether we want a data center in our future or not.” Two candidates absent from forum Two city commission candidates were not at the forum: Don Langley and Sue Parrigan. WBKO reached out to Langley for comment but has not yet heard back. Parrigan responded with a statement: “A pause does not stop a data center. A rule does! The city commission proactively voted unanimously to approve an ordinance to set rules to keep data centers off your street.” Voters react after forum Michael Trapasso was among those in attendance. He said data centers were his top concern heading into the forum. “My main issue was the data centers, of which I’m very much against,” Trapasso said. “I enjoyed hearing what people had to say, getting an idea about who these people are and how they feel about various issues. I thought it was quite enlightening.” Resident Sheila Downs said the forum was helpful for meeting the candidates, but it was difficult to draw lines between each candidate’s views. “I thought the forum was very nice. It was very informative,” Downs said. “One of the things that I noticed, and a couple of people did stand out to me, but they seemed to collaborate with each other and not a lot of them took the initiative to say, ‘this is what I’m going to do.’ So, I wasn’t able to differentiate between who was going to do what.” Both Downs and Trapasso say they’ll be heading to the polls Nov. 3. artigo.texto: Rising demand for energy storage systems driven by the spread of artificial intelligence data centers, coupled with expectations for the commercialization of next-generation batteries, has pushed a Shinhan Asset Management exchange-traded fund investing in solid-state battery companies to the top of three-month return rankings. The SOL Solid-State Battery & Silicon Anode ETF posted a 22.76% return over the three months through Oct. 16, according to the Korea Exchange on the 19th. That was the highest return among domestically listed equity ETFs, excluding leveraged and inverse products. It also exceeded the KOSPI's return of minus 16.90% over the same period by 39.66 percentage points. The fund's main holdings include next-generation battery companies such as Samsung SDI, LG Energy Solution, EcoPro BM, Isu Specialty Chemical, Lotte Energy Materials and Daejoo Electronic Materials. The product focuses on competitiveness in next-generation technologies such as solid-state batteries and silicon anode materials, rather than short-term shifts in demand in the existing electric vehicle market. With the recent rally in domestic semiconductor shares losing momentum, secondary battery ETFs have moved into the top tier of returns. Analysts attribute the shift to improved investor sentiment as the battery industry, long weighed down by slowing EV demand, secures a new growth driver centered on ESS. Growing electricity demand from AI data centers and the expansion of renewable power generation are cited as the main drivers of ESS market growth. LG Energy Solution posted preliminary third-quarter operating profit of 756 billion won ($528 million), beating market expectations. The expansion of its North American ESS business and the conversion of production facilities are seen as supporting the earnings recovery. Expectations are also building for the commercialization of next-generation battery technology. Samsung SDI is pursuing technology development and cooperation with customers with the goal of mass-producing solid-state batteries in 2027. The government also plans to provide about 400 billion won for next-generation battery research and development over five years starting in 2027. Solid-state batteries replace conventional liquid electrolytes with solid ones to improve safety and energy density, and their applications are expected to expand beyond electric vehicles into areas such as humanoid robots and aerospace. "The secondary battery industry is securing a new demand base through ESS, and growth drivers are diversifying as the commercialization of next-generation technologies such as solid-state batteries and silicon anode materials comes into view," said Kim Jung-hyun, head of the ETF business group at Shinhan Asset Management. "Going forward, the earnings recovery through ESS and competitiveness in next-generation technologies such as solid-state batteries will be key factors determining corporate value."

artigo.texto: Green credit joins forces with the carbon market: A way to unlock capital for businesses. (Dan Tri Newspaper) - Reducing emissions is no longer a cost burden when carbon credits can generate real revenue, helping businesses have more cash flow to repay loans and unlock large-scale green credit packages. In many industrial zones, the challenge of investing in clean technology used to be a major concern for many business owners due to the high cost of machinery and the long payback period. Now, the mindset regarding green investment is fundamentally changing. Reducing emissions is no longer just about complying with environmental standards, but has become a concrete source of financial revenue through the sale of carbon quotas and credits. Businesses sell emissions reductions to repay loans. According to the Government Newspaper, at the workshop on Credit Policy and Carbon Market: Unlocking Green Capital Flows on October 14th, Deputy Governor of the State Bank of Vietnam (SBV) Nguyen Ngoc Canh stated that achieving the goal of net-zero emissions by 2050 requires significant resources for technological innovation and energy transition. Decree No. 29/2026 on the domestic carbon exchange, along with the pilot phase in 2025-2026 with a scale of over 511 million tons of CO2 equivalent across three sectors—thermal power, iron and steel, and cement—has established a clear legal framework. Green credit and the carbon market thus form a natural synergistic link. Specifically, banks provide capital for businesses to install energy-saving equipment and low-emission technologies. In return, the carbon market helps convert the reduced emissions into cash. This revenue improves cash flow, enhances debt repayment capacity, and directly reduces the risk of bad debt for the banks. The Measurement, Reporting, and Verification (MRV) system for emission reduction results will provide transparent data for credit institutions to monitor capital utilization and manage loan risks more effectively. You may also like The thirst for hundreds of billions of USD in capital and the legal challenges. Capital flows into sustainable sectors have shown significant progress. As of the end of June, outstanding green credit across the system reached over VND 856,000 billion, an increase of 9.87% compared to the end of 2025. The period from 2017 to 2025 recorded an average growth rate of over 20% per year. The largest concentration of capital flows is in agriculture , forestry, fisheries, and biodiversity conservation (accounting for over 31%), followed by green energy (accounting for nearly 28%). Nevertheless, the need for green transition capital in Vietnam remains very high. Mr. Bui Minh Giap, Chief Economist of the Asian Development Bank (ADB) in Vietnam, estimates that by 2040, Vietnam will need approximately US$368 billion for climate change adaptation and emission reduction, equivalent to 6.8% of GDP annually. Specifically for the electricity sector, the investment needs for power generation and transmission networks in the 2026-2030 period, according to the revised Power Development Plan VIII, are approximately US$136 billion. Mr. Giap noted that banks need to carefully assess the likelihood of credit approval, production volume, selling price, verification costs, and collection timing before calculating carbon revenue into the debt repayment plan. From the perspective of lending institutions, Dr. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Director of the Training School for Cadres and Deputy Head of the ESG Steering Committee of Agribank , stated that Agribank's green credit outstanding reached nearly 30,000 billion VND by the end of March 2026. Dr. Ha suggested clarifying ownership, disposal, and benefit-sharing rights from carbon credits, perfecting the legal framework for secured transactions, accounting, taxation, and foreign exchange, and reducing verification costs for cooperatives and small businesses. Adding channels for mobilizing international financial resources. You may also like Alongside domestic efforts, opportunities to expand access to foreign capital through carbon trading mechanisms are being promoted. According to Carbon Herald, the Climate Vulnerable Countries Forum and the V20 Finance Ministers Group (CVF-V20), along with the Voluntary Carbon Integrity Initiative (VCMI), recently published a guide on implementing Article 6 of the Paris Agreement in Bangkok, ahead of COP31. This document was developed for 77 countries facing an estimated $490 billion annual development finance shortfall, aiming to mobilize an additional $20 billion in carbon finance annually by 2030. Previously, developing countries' participation was quite limited, with the 45 least developed countries accounting for only 1.5% of projects under the Clean Development Mechanism (CDM). Several practical examples have emerged. For instance, Ghana and Switzerland implemented an agreement expected to generate 8 million tons of carbon credits, bringing in $300 million in carbon revenue and attracting $1.1 billion in investment. The Philippines entered into bilateral partnerships with Japan and Singapore, while Bhutan established its own climate fund. Ms. Usha Rao-Monari, Chair of VCMI, emphasized that the handbook helps policymakers make decisions based on accurate data, thereby obtaining higher economic value when undertaking international carbon projects. Simultaneously opening up bank credit channels and the carbon market promises to unlock a stable flow of funds for the energy transition in the coming period.

artigo.texto: Ecobiz.asia – The Philippines will develop a national carbon market policy framework to regulate carbon credit projects and transactions, as the government seeks to attract climate investment and strengthen implementation of its emissions-reduction commitments under the Paris Agreement. President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr. ordered the development of the framework through Executive Order No. 127, signed on Oct. 13, directing the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to establish rules for the country’s participation in domestic and international carbon markets. The order, announced by the Presidential Communications Office on Saturday (Oct. 17), designates the DENR as the Philippines’ national authority for carbon markets and establishes an Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets to coordinate government policy and oversee implementation. The proposed Philippine Carbon Market Policy Framework will set requirements for carbon credit projects, project approvals, transaction monitoring and benefit-sharing arrangements. It will also establish safeguards to ensure that carbon market activities comply with national policies and international standards. The government aims to use carbon markets to expand access to climate finance, technology and investment while supporting projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. “There is a need to formulate a national carbon market framework aligned with international standards, through a whole-of-government approach, to support the achievement of the country’s NDCs,” the executive order states. The Philippines’ nationally determined contribution (NDC) sets out its climate commitments under the Paris Agreement. Carbon markets can help finance emissions-reduction activities by allowing eligible projects to generate credits that can be traded, subject to applicable rules and safeguards. Under the order, the Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets will be chaired by the Climate Change Commission, with the Department of Finance as vice chair. Other members include the DENR, Department of Energy, Department of Agriculture, Department of Transportation, Department of Trade and Industry, and Securities and Exchange Commission. The committee will coordinate policies across government agencies, review implementation of the framework and approve reasonable processing fees for carbon market applications and certifications. The DENR will also establish and maintain the Philippine National Carbon Registry, a digital system intended to track carbon credits and related transactions. The agency is required to submit the proposed framework to the inter-agency committee for review and approval within 30 days of the executive order taking effect. The order will take effect upon publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation. The framework is expected to provide a coordinated basis for the Philippines’ participation in carbon markets, including mechanisms for international cooperation under the Paris Agreement and voluntary carbon markets. Its detailed rules, however, remain to be developed. ***

artigo.texto: Trontek to Unveil 5-MWh BESS, Targets 12 GWh Capacity by 2028 Trontek Electronics will unveil its 5-MWh EKOM battery energy storage system at The Battery Show India 2026 as it plans to scale manufacturing capacity from 3 GWh to 12 GWh by 2028. October 19, 2026. By News Bureau Trontek Electronics, an Indian battery and energy technology company advancing the future of energy storage, will unveil its 5-MWh EKOM containerised Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at The Battery Show India 2026, marking a step in its evolution from mobility batteries to large-scale energy storage. With active manufacturing capacity of 3 GWh and plans to scale to 12 GWh by 2028, the company is building capabilities to address India’s expanding energy storage needs. Trontek will showcase EKOM at Stall C16, Hall 18, from October 22–24, 2026, at India Expo Mart & Centre, Greater Noida. The launch expands Trontek’s presence into large-scale energy storage, bringing its battery expertise to applications beyond electric mobility. Designed for industrial and utility-scale requirements, the EKOM platform addresses the growing role of energy storage in renewable energy integration, power management and the evolving needs of India’s energy infrastructure. The unveiling comes as energy storage gains strategic importance in India’s energy transition. As renewable energy capacity expands and electricity demand evolves, BESS is emerging as a critical enabler of greater flexibility in how power is stored, managed and deployed. Trontek’s move into this segment reflects its ambition to participate in this expanding market through locally developed and manufactured solutions. Building on more than two decades of experience in battery technology and manufacturing, Trontek is extending its capabilities across a broader range of energy applications. The company is targeting 12 GWh of manufacturing capacity by 2028. Speaking ahead of the unveiling, Samrath S. Kochar, Founder & CEO, Trontek, said, “Energy storage is becoming central to how India powers its next phase of growth. With EKOM, we are taking Trontek’s two-decade battery expertise into large-scale energy storage, building capabilities in India for the country’s evolving industrial and energy needs. Our ambition is to contribute to a globally competitive Indian energy storage ecosystem.” The unveiling of Trontek’s 5-MWh EKOM containerised Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) marks the company’s expansion into large-scale energy storage, extending its battery technology expertise to industrial and utility-scale applications. At The Battery Show India 2026, Trontek will showcase its portfolio across electric mobility, energy storage, and power and critical infrastructure solutions. Its electric mobility segment includes battery solutions for two-wheelers, three-wheelers and other mobility applications. Under energy storage, the company offers POWERCUBE for residential applications, NOVARA for commercial facilities and EKOM for industrial and utility-scale storage, including the newly unveiled 5-MWh system. Its power and critical infrastructure portfolio includes inverters and solar solutions for distributed energy applications, along with battery systems for telecom infrastructure and backup power requirements. The portfolio reflects Trontek’s expansion from a mobility-focused battery business into a broader energy technology company, with Made-in-India solutions spanning mobility, distributed energy and large-scale energy storage. A key pillar of Trontek’s expansion is the development of energy storage solutions suited to Indian market requirements, supported by local engineering and manufacturing capabilities. As demand grows across residential, commercial, industrial and utility applications, the company sees an opportunity to build scale while contributing to the development of India’s domestic energy storage ecosystem. please contact: contact@energetica-india.net.

artigo.texto: Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos, Jr has ordered the creation of a national carbon market policy framework to attract climate investments and support domestic emissions cuts, the Presidential Communications Office announced on 17 October. To continue reading, subscribe to Eco‑Business. Access all our exclusive content and archive — with a 7-day free trial. Then just US$5/month. Cancel anytime. - Exclusive access to training across business and policy topics - Direct access to industry leaders at Eco-Business events - A seat among the decision makers shaping the region's sustainable development The executive order, signed on 13 October, directs the Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) to develop rules governing participation in domestic and international carbon markets, which enable trading in credits generated by projects that reduce or remove greenhouse gas emissions. The framework will cover voluntary carbon credits, bought by choice rather than legal obligation, as well as credits under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, which sets government approval and accounting rules for international carbon trading. The categories can overlap, but voluntary credits do not automatically meet Article 6 requirements. Under the order, the DENR will provide technical, policy and regulatory inputs for nature-based solutions, forestry and waste, while the Department of Energy will cover the energy sector. The Department of Agriculture and Philippine Statistics Authority will handle agriculture-related inputs, and the Department of Transportation will cover transport-related carbon credit projects. The Department of Finance will address fiscal policy, investment promotion, climate finance and the fiscal implications of carbon market transactions. “There is a need to formulate a national carbon market framework aligned with international standards, through a whole-of-government approach, to support the achievement of the country’s NDCs,” the order stated, referring to the Nationally Determined Contribution, a country’s climate action plan under the Paris Agreement. The Philippines submitted its updated pledge in September, seeking to strengthen its net sink status but without committing to a fossil fuel phase-out or net zero. John Leo Algo, national coordinator of the 40-member civil society network Aksyon Klima Pilipinas, said the order signals that the framework could be completed by COP31 or early 2027, potentially attracting investors awaiting clearer rules. But its contribution to stronger climate ambition remains uncertain, he told Eco-Business. “While the 2026 NDC has been finalised, it is missing a 1.5°C-aligned decarbonisation pathway and, subsequently, how much of its conditional target is planned to be achieved through carbon markets.” Algo urged meaningful consultations in the coming weeks, including with communities whose lands are being considered for carbon projects, rather than only prospective market participants. Jonathan Joson, Philippine operations head at Singapore-based carbon solutions firm Kennemer Eco Solutions, welcomed the order’s multi-agency approach. “I am more confident that this executive order resolves the fragmentation. There is higher regulatory certainty leading to investor confidence,” he told Eco-Business. Joson previously warned that carbon credit rules released last year, covering only clean energy projects, could divert investment from nature-based solutions, agriculture and blue carbon without an overarching framework. The order follows a Philippine-Singapore Article 6 agreement signed in May, establishing a legal framework for transferring emissions reductions between the countries. Observers cautioned that credible benefits would depend on robust rules for measuring and approving those reductions. Other Southeast Asian countries have also pursued such agreements before establishing comprehensive domestic carbon markets. Vietnam, which plans to make its carbon market fully operational around 2028, signed an agreement with Singapore last year allowing credits generated by Vietnamese projects to be transferred to the city-state. Thailand also signed an Article 6 agreement with Singapore last year. It operates voluntary crediting schemes and is exploring an emissions trading system, but has yet to introduce a nationwide compliance carbon market.

artigo.texto: Russia’s Rosatom and Egypt’s Telecom and Technology Co. (Teletech) have signed an agreement to establish local battery energy storage system (BESS) assembly facilities in Egypt, with a potential annual production capacity of 500 megawatt-hours (MWh). The agreement, signed during the Egypt Energy 2026 Exhibition and Conference, covers personnel training and the gradual expansion of production capacity, according to a press release by Rosatom. “Teletech’s partnership with Rosatom represents a timely step toward strengthening Egypt’s energy infrastructure: we are combining advanced lithium-ion battery storage technology with local implementation capabilities,” said Ihab Saad, Chief Technology Officer of Teletech. The partnership aims to support the deployment of energy storage solutions across several sectors, including electricity, telecommunications, data centers, oil and gas, and other industries. “Egypt’s energy transition increasingly depends on the ability to combine a diversified energy mix with resilient infrastructure and stronger local industrial capabilities. Building local capacity for energy storage systems can support grid stability as renewable energy expands, reduce dependence on imported technologies and external supply chains, and develop domestic technical expertise,” said Murad Aslanov, Director of Rosatom’s Country Office in Egypt. Rosatom’s Energy Storage business unit develops lithium-ion energy storage systems for backup power supplies, renewable energy applications, and electric vehicles. Teletech is an Egyptian technology and telecommunications company specializing in technology design and implementation, procurement, logistics, and project execution. Egypt is rapidly expanding its battery energy storage systems (BESS) to stabilize its grid, shift daytime solar power to evening peaks, and achieve its updated target of 42% renewable energy generation by 2030. In August, Egypt laid the foundation stone for China’s Sungrow’s $50 million energy storage assembly plant in the Suez Canal Economic Zone (SCZONE), with a planned annual capacity of 10 gigawatt-hours (GWh) and operations expected to begin in April 2027. The project, which spans an area of 50,000 square meters (m²), is expected to have an annual production capacity of 10 gigawatt-hours (GWh) at full operation. In July, the Cabinet granted golden licenses for two BESS projects operated by Nefertiti Energy Storage Batteries Company and Horus Energy Storage Batteries in the Benban area in Aswan Governorate.

artigo.texto: Crédito verde une forças com o mercado de carbono: uma forma de desbloquear capital para empresas. (Jornal Dan Tri) - Reduzir as emissões deixa de ser um fardo financeiro quando os créditos de carbono podem gerar receita real, ajudando as empresas a terem mais fluxo de caixa para pagar empréstimos e desbloquear pacotes de crédito verde em larga escala. Em muitas zonas industriais, o desafio de investir em tecnologia limpa costumava ser uma grande preocupação para muitos empresários devido ao alto custo das máquinas e ao longo período de retorno do investimento. Agora, a mentalidade em relação ao investimento verde está mudando fundamentalmente. Reduzir as emissões não se trata mais apenas de cumprir as normas ambientais, mas tornou-se uma fonte concreta de receita financeira por meio da venda de cotas e créditos de carbono. As empresas vendem reduções de emissões para pagar empréstimos. Segundo o jornal oficial do governo, durante o workshop sobre Política de Crédito e Mercado de Carbono: Desbloqueando Fluxos de Capital Verde, realizado em 14 de outubro, o vice-governador do Banco Central do Vietnã (SBV), Nguyen Ngoc Canh, afirmou que alcançar a meta de emissões líquidas zero até 2050 exige recursos significativos para inovação tecnológica e transição energética. O Decreto nº 29/2026 sobre o mercado interno de carbono, juntamente com a fase piloto em 2025-2026, abrangendo mais de 511 milhões de toneladas de CO2 equivalente em três setores — energia térmica, ferro e aço e cimento — estabeleceu um quadro legal claro. O crédito verde e o mercado de carbono formam, assim, uma ligação sinérgica natural. Especificamente, os bancos fornecem capital para que as empresas instalem equipamentos de economia de energia e tecnologias de baixa emissão. Em contrapartida, o mercado de carbono ajuda a converter a redução das emissões em dinheiro. Essa receita melhora o fluxo de caixa, aumenta a capacidade de pagamento da dívida e reduz diretamente o risco de inadimplência para os bancos. O sistema de Medição, Relato e Verificação (MRV) dos resultados de redução de emissões fornecerá dados transparentes para que as instituições de crédito monitorem a utilização de capital e gerenciem os riscos de empréstimo de forma mais eficaz. Você também pode gostar A sede por centenas de bilhões de dólares em capital e os desafios legais. Os fluxos de capital para setores sustentáveis têm apresentado progressos significativos. No final de junho, o crédito verde em circulação em todo o sistema atingiu mais de 856 trilhões de VND, um aumento de 9,87% em comparação com o final de 2025. O período de 2017 a 2025 registrou uma taxa média de crescimento superior a 20% ao ano. A maior concentração de fluxos de capital está na agricultura , silvicultura, pesca e conservação da biodiversidade (representando mais de 31%), seguida pela energia verde (representando quase 28%). Contudo, a necessidade de capital para a transição verde no Vietname permanece muito elevada. O Sr. Bui Minh Giap, Economista- Chefe do Banco Asiático de Desenvolvimento (BAD) no Vietname, estima que, até 2040, o Vietname necessitará de aproximadamente 368 mil milhões de dólares para a adaptação às alterações climáticas e a redução das emissões, o equivalente a 6,8% do PIB anualmente. Especificamente para o setor elétrico, as necessidades de investimento para a geração e transmissão de energia no período de 2026-2030, de acordo com o Plano de Desenvolvimento Energético VIII revisto, são de aproximadamente 136 mil milhões de dólares. O Sr. Giap observou que os bancos precisam avaliar cuidadosamente a probabilidade de aprovação do crédito, o volume de produção, o preço de venda, os custos de verificação e o cronograma de cobrança antes de incluir a receita de carbono no plano de pagamento da dívida. Do ponto de vista das instituições de crédito, a Dra. Nguyen Thi Thu Ha, Diretora da Escola de Formação de Quadros e Vice-Chefe do Comitê Diretivo de ESG do Agribank , afirmou que o saldo de crédito verde do Agribank atingiu quase 30 trilhões de VND no final de março de 2026. A Dra. Ha sugeriu esclarecer os direitos de propriedade, alienação e compartilhamento de benefícios dos créditos de carbono, aperfeiçoar o arcabouço legal para transações garantidas, contabilidade, tributação e câmbio, e reduzir os custos de verificação para cooperativas e pequenas empresas. Criar canais para mobilizar recursos financeiros internacionais. Você também pode gostar Paralelamente aos esforços nacionais, estão sendo promovidas oportunidades para ampliar o acesso ao capital estrangeiro por meio de mecanismos de negociação de carbono. De acordo com o Carbon Herald, o Fórum de Países Vulneráveis às Mudanças Climáticas e o Grupo de Ministros das Finanças do V20 (CVF-V20), juntamente com a Iniciativa Voluntária para a Integridade do Carbono (VCMI), publicaram recentemente um guia sobre a implementação do Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris em Bangkok, antes da COP31. Este documento foi desenvolvido para 77 países que enfrentam um déficit estimado de US$ 490 bilhões em financiamento para o desenvolvimento, com o objetivo de mobilizar US$ 20 bilhões adicionais em financiamento de carbono anualmente até 2030. Anteriormente, a participação dos países em desenvolvimento era bastante limitada, com os 45 países menos desenvolvidos representando apenas 1,5% dos projetos no âmbito do Mecanismo de Desenvolvimento Limpo (MDL). Surgiram diversos exemplos práticos. Por exemplo, Gana e Suíça implementaram um acordo que deverá gerar 8 milhões de toneladas de créditos de carbono, arrecadando US$ 300 milhões em receitas de carbono e atraindo US$ 1,1 bilhão em investimentos. As Filipinas firmaram parcerias bilaterais com o Japão e Singapura, enquanto o Butão criou seu próprio fundo climático. A Sra. Usha Rao-Monari, Presidente da VCMI, enfatizou que o manual ajuda os formuladores de políticas a tomarem decisões com base em dados precisos, obtendo assim maior valor econômico ao empreenderem projetos internacionais

artigo.texto: For once, I have to agree with Cooper Freeman regarding putting a data center in the middle of Cook Inlet. One has to wonder why Louis Wolfson, representing Deep Green, would come to Alaska from Massachusetts and think building a massive data center in Cook Inlet was a good idea. The 32-foot tide alone would be a serious engineering concern! Why would one want to try and permit such a beast? One would have to do a huge number of studies in a very inhospitable environment to be able to convince scientists, permitting experts and the public that your submarine heat pump wouldn’t harm the environment. This will likely be a long process, cost millions of dollars and may or may not be successful in the end (assuming the engineers could design such a thing). Why build at the bottom of Cook Inlet when we have so much land in Alaska? Wolfson should have looked out the window while flying into the Anchorage International Airport and seen all that open land. Here’s a suggestion — why not build a data center on land, far enough away from neighborhoods (since many people aren’t that thrilled about having a data center nearby), but close enough to use the waste heat from the data center to either heat homes or, better yet, grow fresh, hydroponically grown produce? Having a large land-based anchor customer should lower everyone’s power bill if structured properly (much like the Kinross Fort Knox mine’s large baseload power consumption lowers everyone’s monthly electric bill in Fairbanks). If approached this way, a data center would bring real benefits to the general public — Alaskans would certainly welcome lower energy bills and more farm-to-table fresh produce! — Rick Van Nieuwenhuyse, GeoMetallica Inc., Fairbanks Have something on your mind?
