artigo.texto: Why Should Delaware Care? Government works best when its citizens are knowledgeable and engaged. Delaware’s government has scores of commissions, working groups, agencies and legislative committees. All must hold meetings that are open to the public. Below we highlight a few of those meetings that are happening this week. Below you will find information about the most important or interesting public meetings happening in Delaware this week. - Hospital cost review board to discuss charity care - State opioid commission to review grants for approval - Wilmington to host an early season budget town hall - Sussex County to consider a slate of new solar fields - Harrington to discuss a data center ban Will hospitals become more charitable? Delaware’s controversial hospital oversight board will meet Tuesday morning to discuss a new law that goes into effect early next year, compelling hospitals to widen the net of patients eligible for free or discounted care. The Diamond State Hospital Cost Review Board is set to discuss regulations that will guide how hospitals will be held accountable for the new codified standards in the years to come. The law requires hospitals to expand eligibility for free and discounted care, usually called charity care. In order to qualify for their tax-exempt nonprofit status, hospitals must offer a “community benefit,” according to the IRS. Historically, that benefit has been charity care. Earlier this month, financial leaders from Delaware’s hospital systems flooded a small government meeting room to voice concerns with the drafted regulations. The regulations are also being crafted with input from the state’s hospital lobbying group, the Delaware Healthcare Association, which expressed support for the legislation but asked state leaders to target other healthcare sectors that also earn money from patients, such as insurers and pharmaceutical companies. 📍 The Diamond State Hospital Cost Review Board is set to meet at 10 a.m. on Tuesday, Oct. 20, at the Herman M. Holloway Sr. Campus – DHSS Chapel, located at 1901 N. Dupont Highway in New Castle. More information, including about virtual attendance, can be found here. State to approve new opioid dollars The Delaware commission charged with appropriating dollars secured from state settlements with opioid manufacturers and distributors will meet Monday to review grant applications submitted by local governments and nonprofits. The meeting comes a year after lawmakers reformed how the commission grants dollars to organizations. Those reforms followed reports of mismanagement and potential fraud within the program that emerged the previous year. The Delaware Opioid Settlement Commission is expected to receive $250 million from opioid settlements through 2038. Spotlight Delaware previously reported that Delaware has the only state government that directly distributes money from opioid settlements to various organizations, rather than leaving it up to counties, cities, and towns. 📍 The Delaware Opioid Settlement Commission will meet Monday from 1 to 3 p.m. at the Springer Building, located at 203 Mitchell Lane, in New Castle. For information about virtual attendance and other meeting details, click here. Wilmington to get a head start on its budget The Wilmington City Council on Tuesday will host its first budget town hall as part of an early start to next year’s budget negotiations. Last week, the council announced plans to hold four town halls covering the city’s eight districts, giving residents an opportunity to learn about the budget process, discuss financial priorities or concerns and raise questions. The town halls come after a budget season earlier this year that was marked by debate between the mayor and City Council over how to address housing needs in the city. The city did not hold similar public meetings early in the process last year. 📍 Wilmington’s first-of-four budget town halls is scheduled for Tuesday from 6 to 7 p.m. at the NOMA Library, located at 3905 North Market Street in Wilmington. For more information, click here. Solar fields in Sussex County The Sussex County Council on Tuesday will consider plans for four solar fields – two in Seaford, one in Laurel and one in Delmar. Together they would cover almost 170 acres of farmland, equal to over 100 football fields. They would also have the capacity to produce 11 megawatts of electricity, enough to power about 9,000 homes. The proposals come as Gov. Matt Meyer has encouraged solar development as a way to produce more power in the state. Earlier this year, he fast-tracked permits for some solar projects. He also signed a bill that guarantees power bill discounts for those who sign up for community solar projects. At the same time, some residents feel the arrays are covering too much farmland and could harm local ecosystems. The county’s Planning and Zoning Commission recommended approval for all the proposals. 📍 The Sussex County Council will meet Tuesday at 1 p.m. at the Sussex County Administrative Office Building, located at 2 The Circle in Georgetown. The public hearings for the solar projects will begin at 1:30 p.m. For additional details, including information about virtual attendance, click here. Harrington data center ban Harrington on Monday will do a first reading of an ordinance that would ban any data center projects within its borders. The city council recently rejected a proposal to build a data center on the site of a former cold storage warehouse. Residents packed into the meeting room for the vote, overwhelmingly in opposition to the plan. That opposition came despite the developer behind the proposal offering the city of about 4,000 people contributions totaling $1 million. The council will hold its official hearing for the ordinance at a later date, but Monday’s meeting will be the first time the ordinance will be publicly discussed. 📍 Harrington City Council will meet Monday at 6 p.m. at the Harrington Public Library, located at 101

artigo.texto: FAYETTEVILLE, N.C. (WTVD) -- The future of a proposed data center in Fayetteville remains uncertain after a special City Council session Monday morning drew a crowd of concerned residents demanding transparency and answers. Dozens filled the council chamber, some holding signs reading "Moratorium now, do the right thing," as city leaders debated next steps for a project that has been the subject of heated discussion in the community for the past eight months. After nearly two hours, the council scheduled another public hearing to further discuss the draft moratorium and agreed to consult an attorney to revise the proposed ordinance language, leaving many attendees frustrated by the lack of clear resolution. "They're flying the plane while they're building it," said Christi Davis, an Eastover resident who lives just 1.1 miles from a proposed data center site. "The deal, it's got to go through a bunch of hoops to get passed. But Fayetteville, if the landowner requests annexation, then Fayetteville's rules apply. Right now, Cumberland County's rules apply, and it's agricultural land at the moment." The council's deliberations come after a 120-day study, launched in April, which included tours of data centers in North Carolina and Virginia and consultations with industry experts. According to city officials, three community sessions have been held, with water use, noise, and power emerging as residents' top concerns. Councilmember Shaun McMillan voiced frustration about the lack of preparedness and transparency: "I would love to understand why we didn't have the advanced materials both in text and in PowerPoint form prior to this meeting," he said. Despite a lengthy presentation, many residents left the meeting feeling their questions had gone unanswered. Nubian "King" Holmes, a Fayetteville resident, said, "They were unprepared, nor did they have answers to simple yes or no questions. How do you vote on something like that? There are too many things at stake. There are too many people's livelihood and health at risk." Davis echoed the sentiment, expressing dissatisfaction with the council's approach. "They should have gone on and voted the moratorium because all this stuff is taking time and they're seeing it. And this they can't even agree," she said. "They're jumping the gun. They're flying the plane while they're building it. And that's why we need the moratorium to give us time to set this stuff in motion." The City Council plans to draft a moratorium ahead of its next work session, scheduled for November. The conversation is far from over as residents and officials continue to debate the project's effects and the city's path forward.

artigo.texto: Huawei automotive unit joins CATL network with 2,520 stations — Electrek In China, Huawei’s automotive unit Yinwang, also known as Newcool, has entered into a framework agreement on strategic cooperation with battery manufacturer CATL and its subsidiary CAES. The agreement provides for the use of swappable batteries and vehicle compatibility with CATL’s Choco-swap network, which has 2,520 stations in around 200 Chinese cities. As Electrek reports, CATL plans to adapt vehicles with Huawei’s Qiankun intelligent driving systems for Choco-swap stations. The company wants to connect the vehicle, station and cloud services so that the system determines a car’s energy needs based on battery condition and driver habits, finds a station and independently directs the vehicle for a battery swap. Battery swap in 99 seconds According to CATL, the battery swap itself at a station can take 99 seconds. CATL Chairman Robin Zeng and Huawei Senior Vice President and Yinwang CEO Jin Yuzhi took part in signing the agreement. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. Huawei owns 80% of Yinwang, while Seres and Changan-affiliated Avatr hold 10% each. Seres produces premium SUVs under the AITO brand, while Qiankun systems are also used by other Chinese automakers. Expansion of the Choco-swap network CATL entered the battery-swapping market in 2022 with the EVOGO service and relaunched this business under the Choco-swap brand with standardized battery packs at the end of 2024. At the end of 2025, the network had 1,020 stations; in early July, the number exceeded 2,000, and as of September 29, it reached 2,520. CATL is building more than 200 battery-swap stations per month and aims to increase their number to more than 3,000 by the end of the year. Other network partners include GAC, BAIC and NIO. At the same time, the agreement with Yinwang is a framework agreement: specific vehicle models, launch timelines and service regions have not been announced.

artigo.texto: Hitachi Global Life Solutions (Hitachi GLS) will begin accepting orders for its AIXROSS air-cooled chiller units for data centers in April 2027. The new system is designed to address increasing server density and heat generation associated with generative AI, combining cooling capacity with energy efficiency. It also aims to reduce water consumption, support stable operation, and accommodate future cooling infrastructure expansion. AIXROSS will be available in a 2450 model with a rated cooling capacity of 245 kW (approximately 836,000 BTU/h), based on planned specifications. The lineup includes a standard version without refrigerant pumps, a Hybrid-M version with one refrigerant pump, and a Hybrid-H version with two refrigerant pumps. Each configuration is available with or without an integrated chilled-water circulation pump. The rated capacity is specified at an outdoor air temperature of 40°C (104°F), chilled-water inlet temperature of 30°C (86°F), and outlet temperature of 20°C (68°F). The newly designed refrigeration cycle improves cooling capacity and coefficient of performance (COP) at outdoor temperatures of 40°C (104°F). Hybrid configurations automatically switch between compressor and refrigerant pump cycles according to ambient temperature and operating conditions, with the aim of reducing electricity consumption during low-temperature operation. Hitachi GLS expects these features to contribute to lower annual energy consumption. For installation flexibility, AIXROSS supports bottom air intake to reduce space requirements. Hitachi GLS also offers engineering services covering modular configurations that integrate chillers with piping, pumps, tanks, and other peripheral equipment. A high-speed startup mode reduces the time required to return to rated-capacity operation following a power outage. Integrated chilled-water pumps can also be connected to an external uninterruptible power supply (UPS). The modular system adjusts the number of operating modules according to thermal load, supporting stable operation under low-load conditions. AIXROSS supports remote monitoring through Hitachi GLS’s exiida HVAC IoT solution, which requires a separate paid contract. The company also plans to introduce predictive fault detection and energy-saving controls using physical AI. The chiller will form part of Hitachi’s HMAX Data Center solution portfolio, which integrates AI-based operation, maintenance, and optimization across data center power, IT, and cooling infrastructure.

artigo.texto: Battery banks are (rightfully) getting a bit of a reputation on planes these days, so safer, more stable options are needed. Enter the LASER ChargeCore Powerbank range using new semi-solid state battery tech, offering enhanced battery safety and stability. LASER has been at the forefront of powerbanks, even introducing the newer LiFePO4 batteries to their battery banks last year, and are now introducing semi-solid state batteries with a focus on safety and peace of mind. Chris Lau, Managing Director of LASER said “We’ve been closely following semi solid state battery development for some time, since first visiting an EV factory several years ago, and advancements since that time mean that it can now move into smaller, more compact options. Simply put, I believe that Semi Solid State chemistry makes this the safest powerbank technology available in Australia today. We are focused on safety and peace of mind, and we know that it is a huge concern for Australian consumers these days when buying powerbanks.” The new ChargeCore PowerBanks come in three capacities, 10,000mAh, 20,000mAh and 27,000mAh offering a USB Type-C and two USB-A ports giving you versatile charging for your phones, tablets and more. The 10k and 20kmAh PowerBanks are able to deliver 20W of power across the three ports, while the 27,000mAh option can charge devices at up to 35W. All three models include an easy-to-read digital battery display showing how much is left, as well as including integrated protection against overcharging, overcurrent, short circuits and overheating. The new ChargeCore PowerBanks are available now in Black, with LASER also announcing Galactica, Grey, and Dark Cherry colour options are coming soon for their 10K and 20K ChargeCore PowerBanks. While the ChargeCore range is arriving now, LASER is also looking ahead, with Magnetic Charging and Waterproof options also using the semi-solid state battery tech coming soon. You can find the new ChargeCore Everyday Semi Solid State Series at Harvey Norman and Laser Online. The 10,000mAh with 20W USB-C PDis priced at .95, while the 20,000mAh with 20W USB-C PD is priced at .95. Lastly, the 27,000mAh ChargeCore PowerBank with 35W USB-C PD charging is priced at .95. artigo.texto: Promovido pelo fundo Aura Capital, através da Aura Technologies, que se apresenta como uma plataforma europeia de investimento e desenvolvimento focada em infraestrutura digital, o projeto prevê a instalação, no Parque Empresarial do Sorraia, do primeiro de uma rede de centros de dados “compactos” para treino e inferência de inteligência artificial (IA). A rede deverá estender-se a Espanha e ao sul de França, avançou o ECO. Com 6,4 MW, a capacidade ficará quase ao nível da do centro de dados da Covilhã. O objetivo é que a nova infraestrutura entre em funcionamento no final de 2027, empregando cerca de 30 pessoas. Segundo a informação publicada pelo SAPO, a empresa veículo para este projeto é a Nextgen AIDC Coruche, com sede na incubadora de empresas de Coruche, que pediu à Câmara Municipal que retirasse os ónus e encargos associados a um terreno no Parque Empresarial do Sorraia, avaliado em cerca de 180.000 mil euros. A proposta já foi aprovada em reunião do executivo, com os votos favoráveis dos três eleitos do PS e a abstenção dos quatro vereadores da oposição, do Movimento Volta Coruche e do PSD. O anúncio surge numa altura em que a associação ambientalista Quercus contabiliza 46 centros de dados já existentes em Portugal, 25 em Lisboa e 11 no Porto. O Governo admite poder vir a somar mais 44, quatro deles de grande dimensão, o que elevaria para 90 o número de infraestruturas deste tipo em território nacional.

artigo.texto: Professor David S. Levine discusses trade secret protections, nondisclosure agreements and proposed federal legislation to improve public access to information around data centers. As Congress considers legislation to increase transparency in data center development, Elon University School of Law Professor David S. Levine recently discussed how trade secret protections and nondisclosure agreements can prevent the public from learning how taxpayer resources are used and how projects affect local communities. An Oct. 14 article published by MLex, “Trade secrets could constrain US legislative push to open data center deals,” examines the bipartisan No Secrets for Data Centers Act BILL, which would restrict non-disclosure agreements between data center developers and public officials. MLex, a LexisNexis news service, covers legal and regulatory developments for attorneys, businesses and government agencies. “The public expects transparency and accountability when it comes to allocation of taxpayer funds … NDAs piled on top of robust trade secret protection leaves the public largely blind. Given this compounded secrecy, the likelihood of corruption increases,” Levine told MLex. Levine, who studies trade secrecy and information law, also discusses how existing trade secret protections could continue to limit public access to information even if non-disclosure agreements were prohibited, preventing access to information about environmental, health, and safety risks and where public money is going. an area of focus, Levine was consulted by then-vice president Joe Biden’s staff regarding NDAs and trade secrecy during the second Obama administration. Read the full article at MLex. A subscription is required.

artigo.texto: A Microsoft (MSFT) desistiu de um planejado data center de IA em Loughton, Essex, que o provedor britânico de nuvem Nscale estava construindo para ela, informou a Reuters em 18 de outubro, citando o Telegraph. A Microsoft é um dos dois maiores clientes da Nscale. A Reuters disse que o Telegraph não especificou o motivo da retirada da Microsoft, e a Microsoft declinou comentar o pedido da Reuters. O local realmente tinha um problema óbvio: energia. O Telegraph informou que os oficiais da rede disseram à Nscale que não esperavam fornecer eletricidade até a década de 2030. Isso corresponde a um relatório de setembro de que a UK Power Networks não conseguiria conectar o local antes do início a meados da década de 2030. A Nscale diz que permanece comprometida com Loughton e está analisando outras fontes de energia. Loughton Era uma Pequena Fatia da Expansão da Microsoft Loughton foi planejado para abrigar cerca de 23.000 chips da Nvidia (NVDA) para o Azure, começando com 50 MW. A Nscale concordou em fornecer à Microsoft cerca de 200.000 chips da Nvidia no Reino Unido, Noruega, Portugal e Texas, então Loughton representava cerca de 11,5% do programa. A Microsoft adicionou aproximadamente um gigawatt de capacidade apenas no trimestre de junho, o que faz com que a carga inicial de Loughton seja cerca de 5% de um trimestre. Os gastos não mostram sinais de recuo. Os gastos de capital em caixa atingiram US$ 35,80 bilhões no trimestre de junho, mais que o dobro dos US$ 17,08 bilhões de um ano antes. O capex em caixa do ano fiscal de 2026 totalizou US$ 115,95 bilhões, um aumento de cerca de 80%. Na medida mais ampla da administração, incluindo arrendamentos financeiros, o capex do trimestre de junho foi de aproximadamente US$ 41 bilhões, com mais de US$ 50 bilhões esperados no trimestre de setembro. A demanda está acompanhando o ritmo. A receita da Nuvem Inteligente atingiu US$ 39,31 bilhões no trimestre de junho, um aumento de cerca de 32% em relação aos US$ 29,88 bilhões, e a CFO Amy Hood disse que a demanda dos clientes ainda excede a oferta disponível. A Microsoft tem os clientes e o caixa. O que ela não consegue comprar rapidamente é eletricidade. Energia Primeiro, Depois os Chips A Microsoft já foi exigente com a Nscale antes. Ela assinou uma carta de intenção para até 1,35 GW no campus da Nscale na Virgínia Ocidental em março, depois desistiu durante o verão, e a Anthropic assumiu a capacidade. Enquanto isso, ela está pagando mais por locais com uma data de fornecimento de energia. Em 16 de outubro, dois dias antes do relatório sobre Loughton, a NiSource (NI) anunciou um acordo de 20 anos com a Microsoft, com o serviço previsto para começar em 2028 e aproximadamente 1.100 MW de recursos de geração a serem adicionados em Indiana. A outra solução alternativa é gerar energia no local, e é aí que entra a Bloom Energy (BE). A Nscale supostamente conversou com a Bloom sobre células de combustível para Loughton. A receita da Bloom atingiu um recorde de US$ 1,065 bilhão no trimestre de junho, um aumento de 166% em relação ao ano anterior. Seus últimos quatro trimestres renderam cerca de US$ 3,12 bilhões, quase o dobro dos US$ 1,63 bilhões dos quatro anteriores. Os atrasos na rede já estão aparecendo na demonstração de resultados de alguém. A saída prejudica muito mais a Nscale do que a Microsoft. O prospecto de IPO da Nscale lista acordos com a Microsoft no valor de até US$ 43,8 bilhões, e Loughton era seu principal local no Reino Unido. O Número que a Microsoft Divulga em 28 de Outubro A Microsoft divulga os resultados do primeiro trimestre fiscal após o fechamento em 28 de outubro. O capex incluindo arrendamentos financeiros é o número a ser verificado em relação à previsão de US$ 50 bilhões. Um valor acima de US$ 50 bilhões seria consistente com a orientação de gastos da Microsoft, mas não estabeleceria se os compromissos relacionados a Loughton foram redirecionados para outro lugar. Um valor mais baixo precisaria ser avaliado juntamente com a contabilidade de arrendamentos, o cronograma de entrega e a perspectiva de demanda da administração antes de concluir que a expansão está desacelerando. Não interpreto Loughton como a Microsoft perdendo o apetite por capacidade de IA, principalmente porque o trimestre de junho é difícil de conciliar com isso: o capex em caixa mais que dobrou ano a ano, a receita da Nuvem Inteligente cresceu cerca de 32%, e a Microsoft já tem 1.100 MW garantidos em Indiana a partir de 2028. O que ela parece ter perdido a paciência é com a data de conexão à rede de um local, não com a expansão. Até que 28 de outubro diga o contrário, estou tratando isso como uma história sobre energia. artigo.texto: MHI partners with Ingeteam to advance power solutions for data centers The alliance combines MHI’s expertise in integrated power, cooling and energy management with Ingeteam’s expertise in rotating electrical machines, power electronics, control and automation and digital technologies. Japan’s Mitsubishi Heavy Industries (MHI) and Spanish company Ingeteam have announced an MOU forming a strategic partnership to distribute, integrate and jointly develop advanced energy infrastructure solutions for US data Centers. The alliance combines MHI’s expertise in integrated power, cooling and energy management with Ingeteam’s expertise in rotating electrical machines, power electronics, control and automation and digital technologies, helping data center operators address power quality and grid-integration challenges created by next-generation AI workloads, according to a press release. MHI Group brings a systems integration approach to AI data center infrastructure with decades of experience delivering large-scale energy systems, industrial cooling systems and complex infrastructure projects. Ingeteam brings more than five decades of industrial and technological experience, combining engineering and manufacturing capabilities in power conversion systems for power generation, grid integration, control and automation, and energy management. Its technology portfolio encompasses electrical generators, advanced power electronics architectures, battery energy storage solutions, power quality and grid stability technologies, and EMS/SCADA control platforms, the press release said. Through this alliance, MHI and Ingeteam intend to collaborate on expanding the availability of Ingeteam's power conversion solutions and related software for the U.S. data center market through MHI Group, while exploring opportunities to integrate selected technologies into advanced energy infrastructure architectures and solutions developed by MHI Group for its customers. “Ingeteam's depth in power electronics and power conversion strengthens our ability to deliver complete, reliable solutions for our U.S. data center customers developing AI Data Centers,” said Shin Gomi, Senior General Manager, Data Center & Energy Management Department at MHI. “This alliance lets Ingeteam bring our power electronics and grid expertise to U.S. data centers alongside a partner with deep systems-engineering capability,” said Adolfo Rebollo, Chief Executive Officer, Ingeteam. “Together, we can provide a bridge between the electric grid and next-generation AI infrastructure, enabling customers to scale computing capacity while maintaining reliability and efficiency.”

artigo.texto: A Microsoft (MSFT) desistiu de um planejado data center de IA em Loughton, Essex, que o provedor britânico de nuvem Nscale estava construindo para ela, informou a Reuters em 18 de outubro, citando o Telegraph. A Microsoft é um dos dois maiores clientes da Nscale. A Reuters disse que o Telegraph não especificou o motivo da retirada da Microsoft, e a Microsoft declinou comentar o pedido da Reuters. O local realmente tinha um problema óbvio: energia. O Telegraph informou que os oficiais da rede disseram à Nscale que não esperavam fornecer eletricidade até a década de 2030. Isso corresponde a um relatório de setembro de que a UK Power Networks não conseguiria conectar o local antes do início a meados da década de 2030. A Nscale diz que permanece comprometida com Loughton e está analisando outras fontes de energia. Loughton Era uma Pequena Fatia da Expansão da Microsoft Loughton foi planejado para abrigar cerca de 23.000 chips da Nvidia (NVDA) para o Azure, começando com 50 MW. A Nscale concordou em fornecer à Microsoft cerca de 200.000 chips da Nvidia no Reino Unido, Noruega, Portugal e Texas, então Loughton representava cerca de 11,5% do programa. A Microsoft adicionou aproximadamente um gigawatt de capacidade apenas no trimestre de junho, o que faz com que a carga inicial de Loughton seja cerca de 5% de um trimestre. Os gastos não mostram sinais de recuo. Os gastos de capital em caixa atingiram US$ 35,80 bilhões no trimestre de junho, mais que o dobro dos US$ 17,08 bilhões de um ano antes. O capex em caixa do ano fiscal de 2026 totalizou US$ 115,95 bilhões, um aumento de cerca de 80%. Na medida mais ampla da administração, incluindo arrendamentos financeiros, o capex do trimestre de junho foi de aproximadamente US$ 41 bilhões, com mais de US$ 50 bilhões esperados no trimestre de setembro. A demanda está acompanhando o ritmo. A receita da Nuvem Inteligente atingiu US$ 39,31 bilhões no trimestre de junho, um aumento de cerca de 32% em relação aos US$ 29,88 bilhões, e a CFO Amy Hood disse que a demanda dos clientes ainda excede a oferta disponível. A Microsoft tem os clientes e o caixa. O que ela não consegue comprar rapidamente é eletricidade. Energia Primeiro, Depois os Chips A Microsoft já foi exigente com a Nscale antes. Ela assinou uma carta de intenção para até 1,35 GW no campus da Nscale na Virgínia Ocidental em março, depois desistiu durante o verão, e a Anthropic assumiu a capacidade. Enquanto isso, ela está pagando mais por locais com uma data de fornecimento de energia. Em 16 de outubro, dois dias antes do relatório sobre Loughton, a NiSource (NI) anunciou um acordo de 20 anos com a Microsoft, com o serviço previsto para começar em 2028 e aproximadamente 1.100 MW de recursos de geração a serem adicionados em Indiana. A outra solução alternativa é gerar energia no local, e é aí que entra a Bloom Energy (BE). A Nscale supostamente conversou com a Bloom sobre células de combustível para Loughton. A receita da Bloom atingiu um recorde de US$ 1,065 bilhão no trimestre de junho, um aumento de 166% em relação ao ano anterior. Seus últimos quatro trimestres renderam cerca de US$ 3,12 bilhões, quase o dobro dos US$ 1,63 bilhões dos quatro anteriores. Os atrasos na rede já estão aparecendo na demonstração de resultados de alguém. A saída prejudica muito mais a Nscale do que a Microsoft. O prospecto de IPO da Nscale lista acordos com a Microsoft no valor de até US$ 43,8 bilhões, e Loughton era seu principal local no Reino Unido. O Número que a Microsoft Divulga em 28 de Outubro A Microsoft divulga os resultados do primeiro trimestre fiscal após o fechamento em 28 de outubro. O capex incluindo arrendamentos financeiros é o número a ser verificado em relação à previsão de US$ 50 bilhões. Um valor acima de US$ 50 bilhões seria consistente com a orientação de gastos da Microsoft, mas não estabeleceria se os compromissos relacionados a Loughton foram redirecionados para outro lugar. Um valor mais baixo precisaria ser avaliado juntamente com a contabilidade de arrendamentos, o cronograma de entrega e a perspectiva de demanda da administração antes de concluir que a expansão está desacelerando. Não interpreto Loughton como a Microsoft perdendo o apetite por capacidade de IA, principalmente porque o trimestre de junho é difícil de conciliar com isso: o capex em caixa mais que dobrou ano a ano, a receita da Nuvem Inteligente cresceu cerca de 32%, e a Microsoft já tem 1.100 MW garantidos em Indiana a partir de 2028. O que ela parece ter perdido a paciência é com a data de conexão à rede de um local, não com a expansão. Até que 28 de outubro diga o contrário, estou tratando isso como uma história sobre energia. artigo.texto: Africa’s ambition to turn carbon credits into a major source of climate finance faces a fundamental obstacle: investors want projects that are ready for financing, but developers often lack the money needed to prepare them. Teddy Mugabo, Chief Executive Officer of the Rwanda Green Fund, raised the concern during the Carbon Markets Africa Summit in Kigali, where she joined a panel discussion titled “What Are Investors Actually Funding and Why?” “If we want more investable African carbon projects, someone must invest in making them investable,” Mugabo said. Her argument highlights a financing gap affecting African climate projects. Before a project can attract commercial investment, developers must often finance feasibility studies, establish emissions baselines, prepare technical documentation and demonstrate that the expected carbon reductions can be independently verified. These preliminary activities require capital, yet investors frequently prefer to commit funding only after such requirements have been met. Mugabo called for patient capital and shared financial risks involving governments, development partners, project developers and private investors. The challenge is particularly significant given Africa’s ambitions in the global carbon market. The Africa Carbon Markets Initiative has outlined an ambition to generate 300 million carbon credits annually by 2030, potentially unlocking $6 billion in revenue and supporting 30 million jobs. These figures represent targets and projections, not realised market outcomes. The summit, held at the Kigali Convention Centre from October 13 to 15, brought together more than 500 participants, including investors, project developers, government representatives and carbon credit buyers. Organisers showcased more than 40 projects and programmes, including at least 8 opportunities presented as investment-ready. Rwanda has already established a National Carbon Market Framework under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, providing procedures for developing, approving and trading carbon credits. In March 2025, Rwanda also launched an $854,859 programme with the Global Green Growth Institute to strengthen its readiness for international carbon markets. The country has experience in carbon credit generation. Government figures show that more than 2.25 million credits had been issued by December 2020, with improved cookstove projects accounting for 87% of certified emission reductions reported in its historical portfolio. However, expanding the market beyond established activities into larger forestry, agriculture, energy and industrial projects requires credible project pipelines and financing mechanisms that can absorb early-stage risks. For Mugabo, the immediate priority is therefore not simply attracting more investors, but ensuring that promising African projects receive the preparation funding needed to meet investment standards. Without that support, Africa risks having substantial carbon market potential on paper while too few projects reach the stage where investors are willing to finance them.

artigo.texto: Área técnica da Aneel quer repasse de transmissoras no leilão de baterias Ofício conjunto vincula participação das empresas à destinação de parte ou total da receita dos projetos à redução das tarifas de transmissão A área técnica da Aneel (Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica) defende que a participação de transmissoras nos leilões de baterias depende da reversão de parte da receita da atividade para reduzir as tarifas. O entendimento consta de Ofício Conjunto obtido pela reportagem que também exige autorização prévia da agência para participação nos certames e separação contábil, financeira e contratual entre os negócios. A orientação se apoia em um parecer da Procuradoria Federal junto à Aneel. O documento corrobora o entendimento da procuradoria de que estaria sendo prestado um serviço de engenharia pelas Transmissoras. O ofício responde a uma consulta apresentada pela Taesa sobre a participação de concessionárias de transmissão no leilão de baterias, previsto para ocorrer em dezembro. A Taesa apresentou contribuições na Consulta Pública instaurada pela Aneel sobre o leilão afirmando que condicionar a participação de transmissoras nos eventos à reversão de receitas para reduzir as tarifas de transmissão torna a entrada desses agentes economicamente inviável e impõe uma retenção ilegítima de receita autorizada em outra modalidade de atuação (armazenador). A companhia sustenta que a exigência cria uma desvantagem na disputa e pode encarecer a contratação de armazenamento, custeada pelos geradores de energia. O ofício, contudo, diz que a obrigação de beneficiar as tarifas de transmissão permanece quando o armazenamento é explorado por uma SPE (Sociedade de Propósito Específico) da transmissão, ainda que juridicamente independente da concessionária. “Além disso, mantém-se a necessidade do benefício à modicidade tarifária, mediante reversão total ou parcial das receitas auferidas com a atividade da SPE para a concessão, em favor dos usuários do SIN [Sistema Interligado Nacional]”. Ainda segundo o ofício, os contratos firmados exigem autorização prévia para atividades estranhas ao objeto da concessão e estabelecem que parte ou toda a receita desses negócios contribua para a modicidade das tarifas de transmissão. O ofício não define percentual, base de cálculo ou metodologia para a reversão. O texto usa a expressão “receitas auferidas com a atividade da SPE”, sem individualizar a receita fixa do CRCap (Contrato de Reserva de Capacidade para Potência). Vale destacar que a manifestação é das áreas técnicas; o documento não registra uma deliberação da diretoria colegiada da agência sobre os editais ou sobre a legitimidade dessa captura. A Aneel já autorizou a ISA Energia Brasil a oferecer serviços de eficiência energética com baterias diretamente a empresas, com compartilhamento de receitas para reduzir as tarifas de transmissão, segundo ao portal MegaWhat. Nesse caso, os serviços são contratados por clientes privados. Nos leilões, o pagamento será pela disponibilidade de potência para atender o sistema elétrico, com custos divididos entre os geradores. Transmissoras podem ficar de fora Fontes ouvidas pela reportagem dizem que se o entendimento for mantido, as empresas transmissoras podem ficar de fora do leilão por perda de concorrência e desequilíbrio dos investimentos. Nas contribuições à Consulta Pública do leilão, a Taesa afirma que a autorização adicional e a reversão de receitas não constam das minutas dos editais nem das notas técnicas que embasam os certames. Na avaliação da companhia, o tema precisa ser definido de forma geral, isonômica e transparente antes da aprovação dos editais, porque todos os empreendedores interessados no certame devem competir em igualdade. “A Receita Fixa do CRCap não se sujeita a reversão à modicidade tarifária da transmissão”, sustenta a Taesa em um dos tópicos da contribuição. Como os certames selecionam propostas de menor receita fixa, uma subsidiária de transmissora sujeita à reversão precisaria incorporar esse custo ao lance ou aceitar remuneração líquida inferior à de concorrentes com as mesmas obrigações contratuais. A reportagem procurou a Abrate, associação que representa as empresas transmissoras. Em nota a entidade disse que apresentou contribuições às Consultas Públicas nº 22 e 23/2026, relativas aos Leilões de Reserva de Capacidade para Sistemas de Armazenamento de Energia (SAE), com foco em apenas três aspectos: Área de Desenvolvimento da Subestação (ADS); Riscos de Escoamento e Conexão à Rede; e Inadimplência Intrasetorial. No que diz respeito à referida regra de captura de receitas de SPEs de armazenamento controladas por transmissoras no leilão de baterias, “a Abrate informa que, até o momento, esta não é uma agenda setorial da entidade, tratando-se de uma demanda específica de algumas associadas, e portanto, não emite manifestações sobre o tema, mas segue acompanhando”, diz o comunicado.

artigo.texto: Nscale Loses Microsoft Deal as Power Delays Threaten AI The cancellation highlights the financial risks developers face when grid connections fall behind project schedules and customers cannot wait for capacity. Microsoft has terminated its contract for Nscale’s planned AI data center in Loughton, England, after delays to the site’s expected power connection. The cancellation highlights a growing challenge for data center developers: customer demand and financing commitments do not guarantee that electricity will be supplied in time to meet commercial schedules. For developers, delayed power can leave construction and financing costs running while revenue remains out of reach. For cloud operators, it can mean scrambling for replacement capacity when a planned facility misses its delivery schedule. The risk can be especially acute for neocloud providers, which often depend on a small number of large customers and finance GPU deployments against specific contracts. Nscale announced the Loughton project in 2025 as a 50 MW campus that could scale to 90 MW, with plans to deploy 23,040 Nvidia GB300 GPUs for Microsoft Azure. A company spokesperson confirmed that Microsoft terminated the contract. Nscale remains committed to the site and is exploring alternative power sources as well as other UK expansion opportunities, according to the spokesperson. The company also said the issue does not affect its other contracts with Microsoft and that the broader relationship between the companies remains strong. The Guardian reported that UK Power Networks told Nscale it could not supply enough electricity for the site until the early to mid-2030s, well after the project’s planned opening. The companies have not disclosed any financial consequences tied to the termination. “Capacity that isn’t energized generates no revenue, but the costs keep running,” said Alex Cordovil, research director at Dell’Oro Group. Power Timing Remains a Core Risk AI infrastructure projects depend on three elements aligning at the same time: a creditworthy customer, financing supported by that customer commitment, and available electricity, Cordovil said. Developers generally have more control over winning customers and arranging financing than they do over the timing of utility power delivery. Grid operators can revise connection commitments by six months or a year, and in some cases longer, Cordovil said. Permitting processes that depend on third parties can also push projects off schedule. “The problem isn’t necessarily that AI demand disappears,” said Neil Osnato, founder of Persistence Analytics Group. “It’s that capital can become committed long before the physical and financial assumptions supporting its recovery are proven.” How severe those consequences become depends on the underlying contracts, including missed-milestone provisions, termination rights, and equipment commitments. Nscale has not publicly detailed how much it spent on the Loughton project, whether any termination payments apply, or what contractual protections were in place. Neocloud May Be More Exposed Than Hyperscalers A delayed site can create a larger financial shock for neoclouds than for hyperscalers, Cordovil said. Neoclouds often operate with more concentrated customer bases, higher capital costs, and GPU financing tied to specific deployments. “A hyperscaler can absorb one delayed site across a large, diversified fleet and balance sheet,” Cordovil said. “A neocloud typically has more concentrated customers and a higher cost of capital.” If an anchor customer walks away, the provider can be left with equipment and financing structures built around a deployment that no longer has a buyer. A replacement customer may recover part of the investment, but not necessarily the original economics. “The issue with neoclouds is that the debt and financing is colossal, and the demand they’re betting on is not assured,” said Owen Rogers, senior research director of cloud computing at Uptime Institute Intelligence. Nscale’s September IPO filing reported $103.4 billion in active and contracted total contract value as of Aug. 31, 2026, compared with $2.6 billion in active contract value. The filing said Microsoft’s agreements with the company provided for payments of up to $43.8 billion through December 2033, subject to delivery and service-availability requirements. Separate agreements with Anthropic provided for up to $44.6 billion. Nscale also said in the filing that, as of the prospectus date, it had not secured binding financing commitments for the GPU equipment and infrastructure needed to fulfill the Anthropic agreements. The filing does not specify how much financing or equipment spending, if any, was tied specifically to Loughton. Contracted Capacity Is Not the Same as Operating Capacity For analysts tracking AI infrastructure build-outs, the Loughton cancellation is a reminder that announced capacity, contracted capacity, and operating capacity are not interchangeable. “Contracted capacity is meaningless until it’s energized capacity,” Cordovil said. “Backlog only turns into cash if the neocloud can actually build and power the capacity on time,” Rogers said. He added that customer commitments must remain in place long enough for providers to recover their investments. Power Delays Can Reshape GPU Economics Power delays can also compress the window developers have to earn returns on expensive accelerators before newer hardware generations change the economics. “Nvidia is now releasing new generations roughly every year, so today’s best GPU won’t be top-end for long,” Rogers said. Older hardware can still be used for inference and less demanding workloads, he added. Osnato said providers can lose money even when their GPUs remain commercially useful. artigo.texto: O mercado de carbono e as oportunidades para empresas estarão em pauta no Circular Connect: Práticas Sustentáveis para o Planalto Norte, que será realizado entre segunda-feira (19) e quarta-feira (21), no auditório da Univille, em São Bento do Sul. A programação é gratuita e reúne especialistas para discutir práticas sustentáveis, inovação e os impactos das novas regras brasileiras sobre emissões de gases de efeito estufa. A programação de terça-feira (20) será dedicada ao mercado de carbono e às implicações do Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE). O tema ganha relevância diante das mudanças na legislação e da necessidade de as empresas compreenderem como as emissões podem influenciar suas estratégias e operações. A mesa será mediada pela vice-reitora da Univille, Therezinha Maria Novais de Oliveira. Entre os participantes estão Fernanda do Nascimento Stafford, professora de Engenharia Ambiental da Univille, que abordará a compra e venda de créditos de carbono; Charles Leber, da área de Tecnologia Ambiental do Senai, que falará sobre emissões atmosféricas; e Fernando Cuzinsky, que apresentará uma plataforma de gestão de gases de efeito estufa. O encontro faz parte do Circular Connect, iniciativa promovida pelo Centro de Inovação do Planalto Norte, com a participação de instituições da região. O evento busca aproximar empresas, profissionais, pesquisadores e representantes do poder público para discutir soluções sustentáveis, inovação e novas oportunidades de negócios. A programação também inclui debates sobre economia circular, gestão de resíduos, reciclagem, logística reversa e estratégias para o desenvolvimento de negócios sustentáveis. Inscrições A participação é gratuita, mediante inscrição pela plataforma Sympla, por meio da busca pelo nome Circular Connect: Práticas Sustentáveis para o Planalto Norte. Mais informações podem ser obtidas com o Centro de Inovação do Planalto Norte pelo telefone ou WhatsApp (47) 9633-3992.

artigo.texto: Portland, Westbrook look to tighten regulations on potential data centers The two Cumberland County cities held meetings on Monday where the city councils voted to advance restrictions on data center construction. Portland, Westbrook look to tighten regulations on potential data centers The two Cumberland County cities held meetings on Monday where the city councils voted to advance restrictions on data center construction. On Monday, Portland and Westbrook held separate city council meetings to discuss restrictions on data centers. Right now, no data centers have been proposed, but each council took actions to change land use codes. PORTLAND: The city council voted to ask Planning and Urban Development to develop recommendations to present to the city council. Those recommendations will center around land use as it relates to data center noise, placement and environmental concerns. The city council is also worried about the placement of potential data centers and the proximity to neighboring buildings in Maine's largest city. This was not a ban or moratorium on data centers in Portland. WESTBROOK: In June, the city council proposed a moratorium on data centers, with an exception for "server rooms" as part of businesses. Under it, no data centers can be built on land in the city. Monday's comments also focused on land near Rock Row where the city does not want data center construction. No proposals have been submitted, according to Mayor David Morse. The city council is expected to vote to finalize that moratorium at its next meeting after public comment. "Westbrook welcomes thoughtful investment, always. Part of thoughtful planning includes determining which uses are appropriate for our community and ensuring development serves the people who live here. The prospect of investment must be weighed against the use of our resources and the effects on residents' quality of life," Morse said. Back in April, Gov. Janet Mills vetoed a moratorium on data centers in Maine.

artigo.texto: Cincinnati launches zoning study to guide data center growth, seeks public input CINCINNATI (WKRC) - Cincinnati is taking steps to get ahead of the growing demand for data centers, and it held a public meeting about its zoning study aimed at understanding their potential impacts and how the city should regulate them. The city began its data center zoning study in February at the direction of the city manager. City research presented at Monday's meeting said there are 240 data centers in Ohio, giving the state the sixth-most data centers in the country. Cincinnati officials also said the city currently has eight data centers. Sophia Ferries-Rowe, a city planner with the Department of City Planning and Engagement, said the study is intended to give the city time to determine long-term rules for data centers. “The purpose of the IDC [Interim Development Control Overlay #89 "Data Centers" and Zoning Study] is to give us, as a city, time to study data centers and figure out how we want to regulate them permanently in our zoning code,” Ferries-Rowe said. A primary goal of the study is to define what a “data center” is for zoning and regulatory purposes. The study is also examining what regulations other cities across the country are putting in place. During the meeting, the Metropolitan Sewer District of Greater Cincinnati and Greater Cincinnati Water Works discussed how data centers use water and addressed common concerns. Scott Bessler, superintendent of the Metropolitan Sewer District of Greater Cincinnati, said the city has a lot of high-water-use customers, and generally, data centers are under the same regulations as other high-use customers. “Our primary concern is protecting our treatment plant performance and public infrastructure,” Bessler said. "So, construction and start-up activities of data centers have been known to create wastewater containing chemicals, metals, or other elevated nutrient levels." The meeting also included information about the energy data centers use. One slide in the presentation compared the energy a certain size of data center uses with a city that uses the same amount of energy. It showed that a medium-sized data center uses between 43.8 and 438 gigawatts annually, which is equivalent to a city with a population between 3,500 and 34,000. The slide used Mason as an example of a city, residences and businesses, that would use the same amount of power a medium-sized data center uses. "It requires a lot of energy," Rob McCracken from the city's Office of Environment & Sustainability said. "Electric utilities are allowed to recoup their investment. So, any investment in infrastructure they make, all the ratepayers pay." That is one concern Manny Addo had, who attended the meeting. "If we can find a way where we could shave that cost and let it go where it belongs, it would be a great idea," said Addo. Attendees were able to ask questions. One attendee raised concerns that data centers vary widely, particularly those used for artificial intelligence, and asked whether zoning should consider not only size but also reusability, citing a lack of plans for reuse for some facilities. Addo said he found the presentations helpful, and is happy the city is trying to get ahead of things. “The rapid growth of data centers may pose a challenge, because we may not be able to grapple with the growth and to anticipate or cover all the disadvantages that it might come with,” Addo said. The team working on the study hopes to have zoning recommendations by February, though the study could be extended if necessary. City officials said Cincinnati currently has no building permit applications for data centers. If an application is submitted before zoning code changes are adopted, it would have to be approved by the Planning Commission.

artigo.texto: Is Front-of-the-Meter Power the Next Data Center Play? Front-of-the-meter power could help data centers ease grid strain, expand capacity, and address growing concerns over energy demand. Behind-the-meter power has become a popular strategy as data center operators look for ways to expand capacity in regions where grid constraints are slowing growth. Some data center operators – especially large hyperscalers – are now exploring a reverse approach: front-of-the-meter power. Instead of building generation solely for their own use, they help add power capacity that feeds into the grid itself. That distinction could matter as electricity availability becomes one of the defining constraints on data center expansion. What Is Front-of-the-Meter Power? In the data center context, front-of-the-meter power refers to arrangements in which a data center operator develops or supports power generation capacity that delivers electricity to the grid, rather than reserving that energy exclusively for its own campus. For example, instead of relying only on on-site backup generation or dedicated behind-the-meter assets, a company could build or back a power project that supplies electricity to the broader grid. In return, the operator may gain more reliable access to power in the market where it is expanding. That is what separates front-of-the-meter power from behind-the-meter strategies. Behind-the-meter generation serves a specific facility or campus. Front-of-the-meter generation contributes to overall grid supply. How New Is the Concept? The idea is new in one sense and familiar in another. Large technology companies have been involved in energy infrastructure and grid-related partnerships for years. Hyperscalers like Meta and Apple have worked with utilities and developers on projects intended to support broader power availability, renewable procurement, or grid expansion. What makes front-of-the-meter distinct is the possibility that data center operators themselves take a more direct role in developing generation assets that serve the grid. That would go beyond simply financing projects or signing power agreements; it would represent a deeper operational stake in energy infrastructure. This model is also distinct from grid-interactive or “grid-supportive” data center designs, in which on-site generation can sometimes help stabilize the grid. In those cases, the primary purpose of the asset is still to support the data center. A front-of-the-meter project is designed from the outset to add supply to the grid. Why Would Data Center Operators Pursue It? The clearest benefit is capacity. If a company helps bring new generation online, it may improve the odds that enough electricity will be available to support future data center development. That is especially important in markets where utilities are warning of long interconnection queues, delayed energization timelines, or broader supply constraints. It’s also worth noting that front-of-the-meter power can involve developing entire power plants, potentially supplying more energy than on-site, behind-the-meter infrastructure, which is usually smaller in scale. Front-of-the-meter strategies could also offer political and regulatory advantages. Data centers are drawing scrutiny over the impact on local power systems, land use, and electricity prices. A company that is seen as adding grid capacity rather than just consuming it has a stronger response to concerns that new facilities strain public infrastructure. At the same time, front-of-the-meter power is unlikely to be the simplest or most financially expedient route to expansion. Building or backing generation assets is capital-intensive, operationally complex, and subject to regulatory hurdles. For many operators, behind-the-meter infrastructure or utility partnerships may remain more practical in the near term. Who Is Actually Doing It? So far, front-of-the-meter power appears to be more of an emerging strategy than an established industry norm. Amazon has been linked to a possible front-of-the-meter arrangement tied to a large AI data center facility it’s building in Texas. However, public statements suggest the company is still exploring its options rather than committing to a final model. If Amazon moves forward with a structure that directly adds generation to the grid, it could set an important precedent for other hyperscalers. For now, however, the concept remains in its early stages. Most data center operators are still relying on a mix of utility partnerships, long-term power procurement, energy storage, and behind-the-meter generation rather than directly building grid-serving power plants themselves. Will Front-of-the-Meter Power Catch On? That will depend on how severe grid constraints remain, how quickly grid utilities can expand service, and whether hyperscalers see a strategic advantage in taking a more direct role in power development. If interconnection delays persist and AI-driven demand continues to rise, front-of-the-meter projects may become more attractive, particularly for the largest operators with the capital to support them. If grid conditions ease or public opposition softens, the business case may be less compelling. Either way, the idea is worth watching. As power becomes a gating factor in digital infrastructure growth, companies seeking to build the next generation of data centers may need to think less like pure real estate developers and more like energy infrastructure partners.

On October 16 of this year, the delivery ceremony for the 90,000th Firefly unit was successfully held in Zhengzhou. artigo.texto: Empresas de transporte pagarão indenização por ônibus que atingiu casa e carros TJ-SP manteve condenação de R$ 14,4 mil por danos materiais e morais após acidente com coletivo desgovernado Tecnologia Especialista explica por que ampliar a infraestrutura de dados é estratégico para o país diante do avanço da inteligência artificial O Brasil está criando condições para acelerar a instalação de data centers, estruturas responsáveis por armazenar e processar os dados utilizados por serviços digitais, sistemas de inteligência artificial e computação em nuvem. Sancionada em setembro, a Lei nº 15.504/2026 criou o Regime Especial de Tributação para Serviços de Datacenter (Redata), que prevê incentivos fiscais para estimular investimentos no setor. Para o advogado especialista em LGPD e professor de Direito Constitucional Newton Moraes, os incentivos previstos na legislação contribuem para fortalecer a soberania tecnológica brasileira. “Sem data centers no Brasil, o armazenamento de dados e a própria operação de sistemas de IA teriam de ser realizados em outros países. Isso significa que uma infraestrutura que será cada vez mais estratégica para a economia e para a sociedade ficaria fora do nosso território”, afirma. Segundo o Ministério de Minas e Energia, o Brasil possui 205 data centers em operação, enquanto os projetos em construção representam mais de R$ 114 bilhões em investimentos. Os pedidos de conexão de novos empreendimentos cresceram 330% entre 2024 e 2025. Apesar desse avanço, o país ainda tem participação reduzida no mercado mundial, ocupando a 10ª posição em participação relativa, atrás de países como Japão e Holanda. O Ministério da Fazenda também aponta uma elevada dependência nacional de serviços digitais prestados no exterior, que atendem cerca de 60% das cargas digitais brasileiras. A expectativa é que a nova legislação contribua para ampliar a infraestrutura instalada no país e, consequentemente, reduzir a dependência de estruturas localizadas no exterior. O avanço, no entanto, traz também desafios relacionados à segurança das informações processadas e armazenadas nesses ambientes. Newton chama atenção para a necessidade de que a expansão ocorra acompanhada de mecanismos adequados de proteção. “Quanto maior a quantidade de informações concentradas nesses centros, maior também é a responsabilidade em relação à segurança e à proteção de dados pessoais”, explica. Os incentivos previstos pelo Redata estão vinculados ao cumprimento de uma série de requisitos. Poderão se habilitar ao regime pessoas jurídicas que implementem projetos de instalação, modernização ou ampliação de serviços de data center no Brasil. Os serviços abrangidos serão estabelecidos em ato do Poder Executivo federal, de acordo com a Nomenclatura Brasileira de Serviços (NBS). A habilitação ao Redata exige compromissos relacionados à sustentabilidade, ao desenvolvimento tecnológico e à oferta de capacidade ao mercado brasileiro. Entre as exigências estão: disponibilizar ao mercado interno, no mínimo, 10% do fornecimento efetivo de capacidade de processamento, armazenamento e tratamento de dados a ser instalada com os benefícios do ReData; cumprir critérios de sustentabilidade a serem definidos em regulamento; atender à totalidade da demanda de energia elétrica por meio de contratos de suprimento ou autoprodução provenientes de fontes renováveis ou de baixa emissão, conforme disposto em regulamento; apresentar Índice de Eficiência Hídrica (WUE) igual ou inferior a 0,05 L/kWh, com aferição anual; investir no país 2% do valor dos bens adquiridos com os benefícios do ReData em projetos de pesquisa e desenvolvimento (P&D), em parceria com instituições científicas, tecnológicas e de inovação (ICTs), universidades, empresas públicas ou organizações sociais. Será o primerio nó de uma rede descentralizada que deverá estender-se a Espanha e ao sul de França. Um grupo de investidores pretende construir no Parque Empresarial do Sorraia, em Coruche, o primeiro de vários centros de dados "compactos" para treino e inferência de inteligência artificial (IA). Deverá entrar em operação no final de 2027 e empregar cerca de 30 pessoas. O promotor é o fundo Aura Capital, mais especificamente a Aura Technologies, que se assume como "uma plataforma europeia de investimento e desenvolvimento focada em infraestrutura digital". artigo.texto: (KNSI) — The St. Cloud City Council voted 5-0 Monday night to set a November 16th public hearing on proposed data center rules. Council Member Tami Calhoun pulled the item from the consent agenda for discussion, mainly to thank city staff for their work preparing the proposal. “I was so appreciative that [Community Development] Director [Matt] Glaesman had given us all this background information because that’s what we need. We need the information going forward.” No developer has brought a specific project to the city. Calhoun told KNSI data centers are relatively new and the city’s planning rules haven’t caught up. “So we need to be sure, be proactive, and be sure that we get exactly what we want in there before we’re ever approached to ask if we want a data center.” Calhoun says energy use, noise and what happens to a building if a data center operator leaves are among the concerns she’ll be weighing before the hearing. In a memo to the council and Planning Commission, Glaesman says adopting standards ahead of a site-specific proposal is the best practice. The city’s code currently has no data center category and allows a broad “communication facility” use by right in the I3 planned industrial district, with no design standards. The proposal has two parts. A comprehensive plan amendment would call data centers a valuable part of the city’s economy and tax base, while saying the city must limit effects on residential areas and address noise, public resources and the environment. A land development code amendment would create two categories. Smaller enterprise data centers, with 2,000 servers or fewer, 10,000 square feet or less of building area and 50 megawatts or less of peak electrical use, would be allowed by right in the C3 Central Business and C5 Highway Commercial districts. Larger hyperscale facilities would need a conditional use permit in the I3 district and would have to stay a quarter mile from residential zoning. All data centers would have to submit studies on noise, environmental impacts, community impact, backup power, sustainability and decommissioning. Projects of 450,000 square feet or more also require a state environmental review, and the memo says findings from that review could be grounds to deny a permit. The Planning Commission recommended approval of both items on a 4-2 vote October 13th. In a September 8th letter to the city, Pipefitters Local 539 voiced support for responsible data center development and asked for clear, objective standards with no arbitrary geographic restrictions. ___ Copyright © 2026 Leighton Media. artigo.texto: Premier Energies Limited’s wholly owned subsidiary, Premier Battery Technologies Private Limited (PBTPL), has executed a share allotment cum shareholders agreement with RCT Nexor Energy Private Limited, part of Germany’s RCT Group, to formalise Premier Energies Storage Solutions Private Limited (PESSPL) as a joint venture (JV) company of PBTPL and RCT Nexor Energy. The agreement formalised the joint venture announced in September 2026 between PBTPL and RCT Nexor Energy. PESSPL will establish a 12 GWh battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturing facility at Seetharampur in Telangana, with the first 6 GWh phase expected to be set up in FY 2027-28. The facility will manufacture and assemble BESS products for residential, small business, commercial, industrial and utility-scale applications. PESSPL is currently a wholly owned subsidiary of PBTPL. Under the agreement, RCT Nexor Energy will receive a 15 per cent equity interest in PESSPL through four milestone-linked allotments and will have the option to acquire an additional 5 per cent stake after completion of Phase I.

Our global service footprint is tailored to our fastgrowing BESS deployments. Trustworthy aftersales support underpins the longterm stable operation of energy storage assets, commented Mr. He Dehong, Head of Global After-sales Service at BYD Energy Storage. Guided by its vision, empower global energy storage industry with digital and intelligent service, BYD Energy Storages mature global O&M system strongly supports its expanding battery energy storage footprint. artigo.texto: Chery pairs 12C liquid battery cells with 400 Wh/kg solid-state technology Chery outlined its Rhinoceros Battery roadmap at the 2026 Chery Global Innovation Conference on October 20, including a dedicated Rhinoceros S solid-state battery pilot line scheduled to enter operation in 2027, reports IT-Home. The schedule adds a manufacturing milestone to Chery’s existing development plan. The company previously targeted solid-state battery applications in vehicles as early as 2026, while chairman Yin Tongyue said in September that vehicle-level testing would begin in 2027. Pilot-line operation and vehicle validation are separate stages, and neither establishes a date for customer deliveries. The manufacturing timeline also needs context. Chery completed construction of a 0.5 GWh pilot line for 60 Ah-class solid-state cells in February 2026 and issued equipment procurement tenders in early October. Chery has not clarified whether the line scheduled to enter operation in 2027 is that facility, a separate installation, or a further stage of commissioning. Rhinoceros S specifications and development challenges Chery lists the Rhinoceros S solid-state battery at 400 Wh/kg, with an operating temperature range of -40°C to 100°C. The company also reported an internal thermal-box test at 200°C. Still, it did not disclose the test duration, state of charge, or sample configuration needed to compare the result with standardised battery-safety tests. The 400 Wh/kg figure is not new in itself. Chery previously presented solid-state technology targeting 600 Wh/kg. Its development programs use different electrolyte and cathode formulations: earlier reporting identifies a sulfide-based electrolyte and high-nickel ternary cathode for the 400 Wh/kg cell, compared with an in-situ polymerised electrolyte and lithium-rich manganese cathode for the 600 Wh/kg route. The figures therefore describe different technical approaches and should not be treated as directly comparable versions of the same cell. Chery identified material-interface contact, battery-pack integration, and its proprietary Dedicated Management System (DMS) as engineering priorities. In solid-state cells, maintaining stable contact between the solid electrolyte and electrodes during repeated charging and discharging remains a key technical challenge. The timing places Chery among several Chinese automakers and battery manufacturers targeting solid-state battery trial production or vehicle validation around 2027. CATL and BYD have both targeted small-scale solid-state battery production for that year. Their plans are at different development stages and do not indicate that any of the companies will reach mass production in 2027. Liquid cells, sodium-ion storage and ammonia-fueled SOFC The Rhinoceros portfolio also covers liquid-electrolyte cells and sodium-ion batteries for energy storage. Chery lists a peak charging rate of 12C and a sustained average above 8C for its liquid cells; these figures do not apply to the Rhinoceros S solid-state battery. Its sodium-ion storage cells are rated for up to 15,000 cycles in commercial, industrial, and residential applications. For vehicles, Chery has outlined a long-term solid-state battery range target of up to 1,500 km. This remains a development target, not a confirmed range for a production vehicle. Chery also presented an ammonia-fueled solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) system for stationary power generation. The conference slides identify ammonia as the fuel and describe green ammonia produced using wind and solar power. They list electrical efficiency of 60%, combined heat and power (CHP) efficiency of 90%, adjustable output from 30% to 100%, and a 90-day deployment window. Ammonia can serve as a hydrogen carrier for fuel-cell systems, but fuel processing and ammonia production affect overall efficiency and emissions. Using renewable electricity to produce ammonia does not, by itself, establish zero lifecycle emissions. An independent assessment of the stated efficiency figures would require more operating details. Proposed applications include decentralised power generation and remote charging infrastructure. Their viability would depend on fuel supply and transport, installation requirements, electricity demand, and operating costs.

artigo.texto: SHENZHEN, China, Oct. 20, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- A BYD Energy Storage desenvolveu uma rede abrangente de serviços pós-venda em uma estrutura de vários níveis: operação e manutenção de estações, centros de projetos, centros regionais e sede global. A BYD Energy Storage opera nove centros de O&M de 2.500 metros quadrados em todo o mundo. Ela conta com uma rede de serviços de pós-venda em diversos países como China, Chile, África do Sul, Reino Unido, Estados Unidos, Austrália, Japão, Polônia e Oriente Médio. Novos centros de serviços serão inaugurados na África do Sul e na Bulgária em 2027 para expandir ainda mais sua presença global de serviços. Os centros desempenham funções essenciais, como armazenamento e gestão de peças de reposição, reparo e manutenção de baterias, alocação regional de peças de reposição, reciclagem de baterias e treinamento de engenheiros contratados localmente. Os centros regionais da BYD Energy Storage estão em total conformidade com os requisitos regulamentares locais, oferecem treinamento estruturado para a força de trabalho e viabilizam uma resposta local rápida. A equipe de serviços profissionais é composta por mais de 200 engenheiros de campo e mais de 100 especialistas em P&D. A empresa aplica SLAs de serviço padronizados: resposta em até 24 horas, chegada ao local em até 48 horas e solução de problemas em até 7 dias. A rede global de serviços da empresa alcança uma ampla cobertura. Ela forma uma rede de suprimentos multiponto que garante a entrega rápida de peças de reposição em todo o mundo. Além disso, com suas linhas de produção locais, as equipes de operação e manutenção integram recursos regionais para oferecer serviços locais de reparo de baterias, fornecendo aos clientes globais um suporte pós-venda rápido, conveniente e localizado. "Nossa presença global de serviços é adaptada às nossas implementações de BESS em rápido crescimento. "O suporte pós-venda confiável sustenta a operação estável de longo prazo dos ativos de armazenamento de energia", comentou He Dehong, Chefe de Serviço Pós-Venda Global da BYD Energy Storage. Guiado por sua visão de capacitar o setor global de armazenamento de energia com serviços digitais e inteligentes, o sistema global maduro de O&M da BYD Energy Storage apoia fortemente sua crescente presença no armazenamento de energia em baterias. A empresa liderou as remessas globais de sistemas de armazenamento de energia em baterias (BESS), superando 60 GWh em 2025, e entregou, ao todo, mais de 650 projetos de armazenamento de energia, contando com serviços pós-venda padronizados e localizados que garantem a operação confiável dos ativos. artigo.texto: From Pilot to Production: Mastering Liquid Cooling Deployment Moving liquid cooling from pilot to production brings new challenges. Explore eight critical considerations for deploying DLC at scale. October 19, 2026 Sponsored by Schneider Electric The reality of AI infrastructure has arrived: the power-hungry chips of today, such as the NVIDIA Blackwell, have rendered traditional air cooling obsolete. With rack densities soaring from 20 kW to over 140 kW, and the 1 MW milestone looming, the industry is transitioning from speculative planning to an urgent, high-stakes deployment phase. Direct liquid cooling (DLC) has become the IT industry’s preferred cooling method for extreme chip power densities, but the jump from a small-scale pilot to a full production environment is fraught with technical traps. Here we detail 8 common DLC deployment challenges and tips for overcoming them. Specification Challenges 1. Material incompatibility between the CDU and connected components increases the risk of galvanic corrosion, which can create debris that clogs cold plates and damages servers. Operators must minimize the difference in the anodic index between the materials used for all wetted surfaces. Strictly follow IT manufacturer guidelines for compatible materials. 2. Opposing liquid and air-cooling requirements force a tradeoff between operating energy savings and the capital costs of chilled water plants. When you cool your IT equipment with water, you can set your chilled water temperature higher compared to air. For every 0.6°C (1°F) increase in chilled water temperature, the chiller efficiency increases 1%-2%. The best path forward is to perform a total cost of ownership (TCO) analysis over a 10-year period or more to decide whether to share an existing low-temperature chiller or build a dedicated high-temperature chiller. 3. Direct coupling between servers and DLC infrastructure complicates specification because the cooling pipes are physically connected to the IT equipment, introducing new variables related to space, leak risks, and specific coolant flow needs. Collaborate closely with IT and infrastructure vendors to specify compatible quick-connect couplings and dedicate a single cooling loop to a single server model to avoid uneven cooling. 4. A lack of CDU system efficiency standards makes it very difficult to compare the capacity and efficiency ratings of different CDUs. Variables including fluid types, flow rates, fluid temperatures, and ambient temperature influence a CDU’s efficiency or capacity rating. The standards exist for air cooling, but not liquid cooling. Until official ASHRAE testing standards are finalized, request vendors to provide performance ratings based on draft test points. 5. Provisioning IT space for unknown liquid-cooled IT creates the risk of overpaying for oversized piping or stranding cooling capacity, as the system must be prepared for unknown maximum and minimum rack densities. To mitigate these variations, size the main loop piping diameter for the bulk CDU capacity, ensuring the piping is long enough to accommodate the maximum number of racks (lowest density). However, size the branch piping and manifolds for the highest potential rack density. Installation Challenge 6. The complexity of preventing TCS contamination drastically increases the risk of server damage through fouling, microbial growth, corrosion, or scaling. Combat these risks by taking proactive steps in the design and installation process. Limiting the size of individual cooling loops will help to contain any contamination. During installation, assemble components in clean environments, add biocide before the initial system fill, and thoroughly flush the loop while purging all air before connecting any IT equipment. Operational Challenges 7. A lack of clarity between cooling and server vendor warranties creates undue stress, often leading to finger-pointing if a leak or component failure occurs. You can help set boundaries by getting your IT vendors on the same page by having agreement on a common TCS supply temperature, flow rate and pressure. Clarify operations and maintenance responsibilities between installers, cooling vendors, and IT vendors early in the specification process. Review all warranties to ensure that required maintenance steps (like filter replacements) do not void another vendor’s warranty. 8. Slow DLC system response to GPU power transients poses a risk of expensive GPUs overheating during sudden power spikes common in AI training workloads. You can use software to power cap the GPUs, although this negatively impacts AI training times. A better operational approach is to implement a strict test plan, starting servers at a low utilization percentage and monitoring GPU temperatures as workloads increase. If temperatures approach dangerous levels (e.g., 90°C), decrease the chilled water supply temperature (e.g., by 5°C) to increase the rate of heat transfer, or increase the coolant flow rate. Where the Liquid Meets the Chip Moving from a conceptual pilot to a robust, production-ready liquid cooling environment requires a fundamental shift in how data center life cycles around specification, installation and operation are managed. The complexity of AI-ready infrastructure leaves no room for silos. With the right technical framework, it becomes the foundation for sustainable, high-performance AI growth. Want to learn more? Book a design workshop with our team today. His passion lies in innovation and sustainability, and he is known for challenging traditional mindsets to accelerate conservation and drive meaningful progress.
