artigo.texto: Crédito de carbono de alta qualidade sobe 75%, diz MSCI AGÊNCIA DE COMUNICAÇÃO Conteúdo de responsabilidade da empresa 7 de outubro de 2026 Os créditos de carbono classificados como de alta qualidade pela MSCI tiveram valorização de 75% em 12 meses e chegaram a US$ 14 por tonelada, enquanto os de menor qualidade são negociados abaixo de US$ 2. Os dados foram apresentados por Guy Turner, diretor-geral da área de mercados de carbono da companhia, durante a Climate Week NYC, realizada em Nova York em setembro de 2026, e indicam avanços em três frentes: ampliação dos sistemas regulados, diferenciação de preços por qualidade e mobilização de capital. Segundo a apresentação, foram registrados US$ 5,5 bilhões em investimentos em contratos futuros e projetos, distribuídos em mais de 200 transações, com um quarto dos recursos destinado a iniciativas de remoção de carbono. Os contratos de compra antecipada de créditos de restauração da natureza monitorados pela MSCI, com entrega prevista para 2035, alcançaram US$ 45 por tonelada, alta de 10% em relação ao primeiro semestre de 2025. Sistemas regulados ganham escala No período analisado, a União Europeia passou a incluir integralmente as emissões do transporte marítimo no comércio de emissões do bloco, o EU ETS. A Indonésia avançou em normas para dar clareza e amplitude às negociações de carbono, e o México se comprometeu a lançar um sistema nacional em 2027, com cobertura de 40% de suas emissões. Na Ásia, a Índia colocou em operação um portal para administrar registros e transações do período de conformidade de 2025 a 2027, que abrange 740 entidades e mais de 700 milhões de toneladas de dióxido de carbono equivalente (CO₂e). O Vietnã contabilizou as primeiras operações de seu sistema, referentes ao ciclo 2025 a 2026, e o Japão tornou obrigatório o GX-ETS, que cobre 40% das emissões nacionais de gases de efeito estufa e reúne entre 300 e 400 empresas. Para Laura Albuquerque, co-CEO da Future Climate e membra do Comitê da Ambição Net Zero da Rede Brasileira do Pacto Global da ONU, durante cerca de duas décadas a defesa desses mercados se apoiou em estudos sobre seu potencial para reduzir o custo de cumprimento das metas climáticas. “A lógica econômica permanece: direcionar recursos para oportunidades de redução e remoção de emissões que permitam alcançar essas metas com maior eficiência. A diferença é que, hoje, a experiência acumulada oferece dados concretos para orientar decisões de política pública e investimento”, afirma. Demanda corporativa e integridade No segmento de créditos, os números da MSCI mostram atividade consistente. Cerca de 4 mil empresas definiram metas pela Science Based Targets initiative (SBTi), o equivalente a 4 bilhões de toneladas de emissões, e um quarto delas assumiu compromissos de emissões líquidas zero (net zero). Em 12 meses, mil novos projetos foram registrados, outros 1.150 entraram na carteira em preparação e empresas aposentaram créditos provenientes de 2.850 projetos. A projeção da MSCI indica que as aposentadorias globais de 2026 devem ficar próximas do volume de 2025, em torno de 200 milhões de toneladas. Na leitura da co-CEO, o sinal mais relevante está na distância de valor entre projetos, que torna a avaliação de qualidade parte central da decisão de alocação de recursos para compradores e investidores. A executiva observa ainda que a convergência em torno dos Core Carbon Principles, definidos pelo Conselho de Integridade para o Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (ICVCM, na sigla em inglês), cria uma linguagem comum sobre integridade, mas exige que preços e financiamento reconheçam os custos de desenvolvimento. Capital antes da receita Para as desenvolvedoras, o cenário evidencia a necessidade de recursos antes da geração de receita. “Projetos exigem recursos para estruturação, implantação, monitoramento, ratings para a verificação ao longo de anos. A valorização dos créditos de qualidade precisa se traduzir em condições de financiamento que permitam produzir essa oferta”, diz Laura. Segundo ela, os contratos futuros podem contribuir nesse processo ao conectar a demanda dos compradores ao ciclo de investimento dos projetos. O Brasil tem diferentes vias de demanda em construção: o mercado voluntário; o Sistema Brasileiro de Comércio de Emissões (SBCE), instituído pela Lei nº 15.042, de 11 de dezembro de 2024, com os Certificados de Redução ou Remoção Verificada de Emissões (CRVEs); os mecanismos do Artigo 6 do Acordo de Paris; o programa de combustível sustentável de aviação (SAF, na sigla em inglês) previsto na Lei nº 14.993; e o Esquema de Compensação e Redução de Carbono para a Aviação Internacional (Corsia). Na avaliação da executiva, são caminhos com regras e escalas distintas, que precisam ser considerados na estruturação dos investimentos. Laura pondera que preços, investimentos e aposentadorias não substituem a mensuração dos resultados climáticos, embora demonstrem uma base observável de atividade econômica, demanda e alocação de capital. “Para o país, a oportunidade está em usar essa experiência para desenvolver um mercado capaz de financiar projetos de qualidade, e o próximo avanço dependerá de transformar os sinais de demanda em capital disponível para quem entrega reduções e remoções verificáveis”, conclui a executiva. artigo.texto: Trontek Electronics will unveil its 5 MWh EKOM containerised Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) at The Battery Show India 2026, marking the company’s entry into large-scale energy storage for industrial and utility applications. The company will showcase the system at Stall C16, Hall 18, at India Expo Mart & Centre in Greater Noida from October 22 to 24, 2026. The launch extends Trontek’s battery technology and manufacturing experience into applications beyond electric mobility. The EKOM platform is designed to address larger energy storage requirements as India expands its renewable energy capacity and seeks greater flexibility in power management. Battery energy storage systems can help manage variations in electricity supply and demand, support renewable energy integration and improve the use of stored power across industrial and utility operations. Trontek has more than two decades of experience in battery technology and manufacturing. The company currently has an active manufacturing capacity of 3 GWh and plans to increase this to 12 GWh by 2028. The proposed expansion is intended to support its growing presence across mobility, distributed energy and large-scale storage markets. Samrath S Kochar, Founder and CEO of Trontek, said energy storage would play an important role in meeting India’s future power requirements. He said the EKOM launch would extend the company’s battery expertise into large-scale applications while supporting the development of domestic energy storage capabilities. At the exhibition, Trontek will present its products across three business areas: electric mobility, energy storage, and power and critical infrastructure solutions. Its electric mobility portfolio includes battery solutions for two-wheelers, three-wheelers and other mobility applications. Under energy storage, the company offers POWERCUBE for residential applications, NOVARA for commercial facilities and EKOM for industrial and utility-scale requirements. The newly unveiled 5 MWh system will form part of the EKOM range. The company will also display inverter and solar solutions for distributed energy applications, along with battery systems for telecom infrastructure and backup power requirements. Trontek’s expanded portfolio reflects its move towards a broader energy technology business, supported by Indian engineering and manufacturing capabilities. The company aims to develop products for residential, commercial, industrial and utility customers as demand for energy storage increases. The EKOM unveiling marks a new phase in Trontek’s business development as it seeks to build manufacturing scale and expand its participation in India’s changing energy landscape. Its planned capacity increase to 12 GWh by 2028 forms a key part of this strategy.

artigo.texto: - Nigeria has commissioned a 1MW solar mini grid with 2.4MWh of battery energy storage in Tallasse, Balanga Local Government Area, Gombe State, serving 6,028 active connections. - The facility powers productive-use businesses, including electric groundnut oil processing, rice milling, flour grinding and electric tricycles, linking clean electricity directly to rural enterprise and job creation. - The project forms part of the US$750 million Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up programme, which targets 1,350 mini grids and electricity access for 17.5 million Nigerians. The Federal Government, through the Rural Electrification Agency, has commissioned the Tallasse solar mini grid in partnership with the Gombe State Government and a private sector developer. The facility combines 1MW of solar generation with a 2.4MWh battery energy storage system to improve supply reliability for households, commercial users and productive enterprises. The project serves 6,028 connections, comprising 5,929 residential customers, 84 commercial connections and 15 dedicated productive-use nodes. Its design moves beyond household electrification by supporting agricultural processing, local logistics and small business growth in a community that had lacked a national grid connection for more than 17 years. The Tallasse installation includes electric groundnut oil processing equipment, modular rice milling machinery, flour grinding facilities and electric tricycles. These assets are intended to help farmers process produce locally, reduce operating costs, create income opportunities and strengthen rural value chains. Officials said the battery storage component is central to the economic case for the project, because reliable power is required to sustain milling, processing and transport activities. The approach reflects a wider policy shift from measuring installed capacity alone to measuring the commercial and social value created by electricity access. The Tallasse project is being delivered under the Distributed Access through Renewable Energy Scale-up programme, a US$750 million World Bank funded initiative managed by the Rural Electrification Agency. DARES aims to provide new or improved electricity access to more than 17.5 million Nigerians through private sector led distributed renewable energy solutions. The programme targets the deployment of 1,350 mini grids, including 250 interconnected systems, alongside more than one million standalone solar home systems. It is also expected to support more than 237,000 micro, small and medium enterprises and replace more than 280,000 polluting petrol and diesel generator sets. DARES is designed to mobilise more than US$1 billion in private capital, with additional parallel financing from development partners, including US$100 million from the Global Energy Alliance for People and Planet and US$200 million from the Japan International Cooperation Agency. The commissioning of the Tallasse facility coincided with the flag-off of four interconnected mini grid projects in Dukku, Bajoga, Kumo and Kaltungo, with a combined planned capacity of 16MW. The wider Gombe programme is expected to deepen off-grid electricity penetration and support commercial activity across the state. The Rural Electrification Agency said the initiative forms part of a broader national strategy to expand mini grids, embedded generation, solar home systems and dedicated clean power solutions for universities, markets and agricultural clusters. The agency is also working to unlock domestic and international financing to accelerate private sector participation in Nigeria’s distributed energy market. artigo.texto: 0 a 100% na bateria do iPhone 18 Pro: a pegadinha O iPhone 18 Pro finalmente carrega rápido de verdade, mas a Apple jogou bem baixo um detalhe na hora da compra. A fonte de energia do smartphone dobrável iPhone Duo, primeiro aparelho da Apple na categoria teve novos detalhes técnicos revelados. Um deles envolve a bateria do aparelho e uma comparação inevitável com dispositivos rivais. Ao todo, o conjunto de baterias do iPhone Duo tem 4.883 mAh. Outro dobrável com o mesmo formato de tela, chamado de passaporte, é o Galaxy Z Fold 8 da Samsung — que fica apenas logo atrás, com 4.800 mAh de bateria. Nesse quesito, a Maçã vence também o iPhone 18 Pro (4.288 mAh) e o dobrável Google Pixel 11 Pro Fold (4.806 mAh), mas fica atrás do Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra (5.000 mAh) e do Motorola Razr Fold (6.000 mAh). Porém, a quantidade de mAh não significa necessariamente que a bateria de um dispositivo dura mais em qualquer condição. Esse valor envolve a capacidade da fonte de bateria em armazenamento de energia (medido em mAh, ou miliamperes-hora), mas o consumo depende de outros componentes do hardware e otimização do sistema operacional. Mais detalhes do iPhone Duo A Apple não costuma detalhar todas as especificações dos seus celulares, incluindo a quantidade de RAM e o tamanho da bateria. Porém, desta vez ele acabou fazendo isso de forma acidental. Os valores foram revelados em documentos submetidos pela empresa no EPREL, um órgão regulador da União Europeia que obriga a divulgação desses dados para eletrônicos de consumo. Como aponta o Tom’s Guide ao analisar o documento, outros detalhes revelados pela submissão incluem detalhes como: - a certificação IP68 de resistência contra água e poeira; - a duração garantida de 1.000 ciclos de recarga para a bateria (ou seja, para manter ao menos 80% da capacidade total); - a durabilidade de 140 quedas em um teste de resistência até quebrar (quando fechado) e somente 35 quedas (no modo aberto); - uma resistência contra riscos na tela parecida com a do iPhone 18 Pro Max no display externo; - um grau de reparabilidade (facilidade e possibilidade de conserto) de 2.65, número inferior aos rivais da Samsung e ao iPhone 18 Pro Max. Por que o iPhone Duo só está com previsão de entrega de fevereiro de 2027 no Brasil? Entenda nesta matéria! /Com informações de Tom’s Guide.

artigo.texto: EPRI Research: Li-Ion Battery Storage Failure Risk Down 98% Since 2018 As battery storage deployment accelerates across the U.S., a new report by the Electric Power Research Institute highlights that safety performance is significantly improving in newer systems than in vintage lithium-ion battery energy storage system (BESS) designs. According to EPRI’s “Risk Factors and Failure Statistics of Lithium-Ion BESS” white paper within its Battery Energy Storage System Failure Incident Database, annual BESS failures per deployed GWh declined 98% between 2018 and 2025. The analysis found that BESS safety risk overall is comparable to oil-filled transformers, which reportedly maintain a 0.1% annual failure rate as a long-established power grid technology. EPRI attributes these lessons learned from early failures that caused destructive fires to having been incorporated into the latest designs and best practices. The institute explained that some of its incident research dates back to 2011. Still, drawing on more than a decade of cumulative incident data, the institute urges operators to conduct safety reviews and retrofits for early-vintage systems to mitigate fire risks. These concerns are underscored by previous incidents at high-profile facilities. The fires at Moss Landing, Morris and Surprise Vistra Corp.’s battery energy storage facility at the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, serves as an early example of these early-vintage risks. A major lithium-ion battery fire in January 2025 damaged over half of the site’s 300-MW system. The Moss Landing facility suffered a second fire in September 2026 due to leftover, damaged batteries that reignited during ongoing cleanup efforts. In 2021, another major fire incident took place at the Superior Battery Inc. warehouse in Morris, Illinois, which contained roughly 180,000 to 200,000 pounds of lithium batteries. While the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency conducted extensive air quality testing around the incident, investigators determined that the blaze was triggered by a water reaction from a severe roof leak. Rainwater reportedly dripped onto the batteries, sparking an initial reaction. Before those disasters, a thermal runaway event in Surprise, Arizona, severely injured eight firefighters in 2019. An internal cell defect within the utility-sized lithium batteries used on-site for storage and distribution of solar energy at the APS McMicken substation triggered the failure, according to an Arizona Public Service analysis. As these batteries fail, technical safety flaws, such as escaping gases, create intense and potentially devastating fire dangers to utility-scale BESS made up of lithium-ion chemistry. BESS advancements driving down failure rates All of these incidents occurred during the period of EPRI’s research, which highlights that while the rate of battery storage failures is becoming less frequent relative to massive-scale deployment, they can still be severe. EPRI noted that the 2019 BESS failure incident in Arizona was part of a wider BESS safety research effort, initiated to inform energy storage industry stakeholders and the public. Residential energy storage system failures were not tracked in this research. Managing these risks, however, remains a critical focus as BESS installations accelerate nationwide, driven by utilities dealing with grid constraints and the growing power demands of AI data centers. Currently in the U.S., installed capacity has passed 52 GW and has grown at an average rate of 70% per year over the last three years, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Lakshmi Srinivasan, principal team lead of Energy Storage at EPRI, told EnergyTech that key aspects evaluated that weren’t known before include statistical analysis on the impact of indoor versus outdoor BESS architecture. Srinivasan noted that the data “demonstrates that modularization and spacing can limit the amount of a system that is damaged in an incident, also limiting first response needs and environmental and public health impacts.” These latest BESS advances have reportedly yielded major benefits in California, where utility-scale storage capacity grew to 13 GW by the end of 2024. According to EPRI, this has directly reduced the state's reliance on “Flex Alerts,” which are voluntary calls for residents to reduce consumption during peak demand periods, typically on hot summer days. “The number of Flex Alerts has dropped to zero (in 2023 and 2024) from 11 in 2022, due to the use of energy storage to reduce supply constraints,” said Srinivasan. Safely scaling future storage deployments EPRI aims to help power operators apply these standards to accelerate large-scale renewable integration. This guidance is particularly critical as operators navigate thermal risks for lithium-ion BESS across various project types, including behind-the-meter installations. To mitigate these risks, Srinivasan explained that conducting safety analyses of older systems can “help ensure the latest safety designs and practices are being implemented for all systems operating today.” While safety improvements are a continuous process, Srinivasan emphasized that dedicated research and development efforts are actively reducing risks in both existing and new BESS deployments. These advancements ultimately aim to deliver tangible benefits to the grid and local communities. “These benefits include supporting grid flexibility, reliability and resilience through applications such as renewable integration and peak demand reduction,” she added. Although lithium-ion remains a dominant mix for energy storage due to its high energy density and quick discharge, the industry is actively seeking alternatives to mitigate foreign supply chain risks and thermal safety concerns. artigo.texto: Beyond Colossus: 5C Advances $575M Memphis AI Factory Expansion Key Highlights - 5C Data Centers is converting a former Fred's distribution complex in Memphis into a high-density AI computing facility, with a $575 million fourth-phase construction permit application. - 5C plans to expand available power at MEM01 from approximately 20 MW to 84 MW, using fuel cell technology to supply additional capacity rather than relying on a corresponding increase in utility power. - The project's announced AI architecture includes NVIDIA GB200 and newer GB300 NVL72 systems, liquid cooling, high-bandwidth networking and integrated storage to support large-scale AI training and inference. - Memphis is considering a data center moratorium and new zoning standards while conducting a 90-day policy review addressing electricity demand, water resources, air quality and community impacts. - 5C has secured more than $1.4 billion in financing for its North American AI infrastructure platform, supporting development in Memphis and other markets as questions remain about execution, infrastructure capacity and local economic benefits. Memphis has emerged as a major center of AI infrastructure development, driven largely by the extraordinary scale of xAI's Colossus supercomputing operations. But the city's growing AI computing market extends beyond Elon Musk's flagship project. At the former headquarters and distribution complex of discount retailer Fred's, 5C Data Centers is developing another substantial AI computing facility, combining industrial adaptive reuse with a phased expansion strategy and plans for behind-the-meter power generation. On October 6, 2026, a $575 million commercial alteration permit application was filed for the fourth phase of 5C's MEM01 data center at 4300 Getwell Road. The application covers approximately 504,000 square feet of the property's 1.1 million-square-foot building, representing the largest construction phase yet proposed at the site. MEM01 is already operating. According to September reporting from The Daily Memphian, 5C had established operations in approximately 200,000 square feet of the former Fred's property, leaving substantial additional space available for conversion. The latest permit application marks a significant escalation in the scope of the development. The expansion also introduces a major new element to 5C's power strategy. On October 11, 5C Group Chief Revenue Officer Brad Nimri told The Daily Memphian that the company plans to increase available power at MEM01 from approximately 20 MW to 84 MW over the next six months, using fuel cell technology to supply the additional capacity rather than relying on a corresponding increase in electricity from Memphis Light, Gas and Water (MLGW). Like Colossus, which began with the conversion of a former Electrolux manufacturing facility, 5C's development reflects the growing role of industrial adaptive reuse in AI infrastructure. The projects differ considerably in scale and their approaches to on-site power generation, but both illustrate the challenge of transforming existing industrial properties into high-density computing environments with substantial electrical requirements. As Memphis considers tighter oversight of data center development, 5C's expansion underscores a broader industry challenge: bringing new AI computing capacity online while navigating power constraints, regulatory scrutiny and mounting concerns over the environmental and community impacts of large-scale infrastructure. From Retail Distribution to AI Infrastructure The MEM01 development occupies a property with a long history in Memphis commerce. Fred's operated hundreds of discount retail and pharmacy locations across the southeastern United States before declaring bankruptcy in 2019. Its former headquarters and distribution complex on Getwell Road, near Memphis International Airport, served as a major logistics hub for the regional retail chain. In June 2026, 5C acquired the 1.1 million-square-foot complex and its approximately 58-acre property from Olymbec USA for $25 million, according to Shelby County property records, securing ownership of a site where data center construction and infrastructure modifications were already underway. The project's development history reflects a rapid escalation in scale. Plans submitted in late 2024 and reported in 2025 contemplated converting the property into a data center supporting an initial 15-MW IT load. An April 2025 construction permit, valued at $25 million, described a more limited initial deployment of 2.5 MW, together with infrastructure designed to support future expansion. Additional permits issued in early 2026 included $100 million for interior construction and $8 million for accessory structures. The October phase-four application, valued at $575 million, represents a substantial increase in the scope of planned construction, although permit valuations do not necessarily represent completed capital expenditures or the project's total investment. The expansion also illustrates the distinction between announced capacity and operational computing infrastructure. According to 5C's published data center portfolio, the Memphis facility's 20-MW capacity for 2026 is fully committed, with additional capacity listed for subsequent years. That commercial designation does not establish how much electrical capacity has been energized or how much IT load is currently supporting customer workloads. The company has not publicly disclosed a complete inventory of installed and operating AI accelerators at the site, leaving the precise scale of its commissioned computing infrastructure unclear. artigo.texto: From robotic gloves to safer batteries, CUHK puts research to work Summary CUHK researchers are developing technologies for use beyond the laboratory in Hong Kong. A robotic glove uses air-powered artificial muscles to help stroke survivors and people with spinal injuries open and close their hands for rehabilitation and daily tasks. Researchers also developed a sulfur-based flow battery with water-based electrolytes, while a startup is commercializing the technology for solar installations, electric vehicle charging and artificial intelligence data centers. Key Facts - The robotic glove was developed by a team led by Raymond Tong, a CUHK professor of biomedical engineering. - The glove can respond to signals associated with a patient’s intention to move, and clinical trials involve people with strokes and spinal injuries. - The sulfur-based flow battery was developed by a team led by CUHK professor Yi-Chun Lu, and Luquos Energy has installed a demonstration system on campus. - Luquos Energy estimates that the battery’s electrolyte could remain usable for more than 15 years, although that is not a verified real-world service life. - The company is building a production line in Shenzhen and has developed battery systems for projects including electric vehicle charging. Wearable device helps patients regain hand movement as university-developed battery technology targets energy storage HONG KONG — From helping stroke patients perform everyday tasks to developing safer ways to store electricity, researchers at The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) are developing technologies for use beyond the laboratory. During a visit to the university on Sept. 1, a reporter tried on a robotic glove that moved the fingers with noticeable force, but without jerking them. For stroke survivors who cannot move their hands, that movement could help them do something as ordinary as holding a spoon or picking up a phone. The device uses air-powered artificial muscles developed by a team led by Raymond Tong, a professor of biomedical engineering at CUHK. Unlike conventional motor-driven rehabilitation equipment, the lightweight system uses a small pump to help patients open and close their hands. “Nowadays, you can see those exoskeletons are very rigid. They are very heavy,” Tong said, inviting the reporter to try the device. Patients can use it both for rehabilitation exercises and everyday tasks, including gripping objects, writing and eating. Tong said the system can also respond to signals associated with a patient’s intention to move. “They can use the brain to control it,” he said. “I just imagine moving the hand and the hand moves.” Tong said the team was conducting clinical trials involving people with strokes and spinal injuries, with plans to expand use in hospitals. He also described work with children who have difficulty standing or walking. Elsewhere on campus, researchers showed a battery designed to reduce the fire risks associated with conventional lithium-ion batteries. Developed by a team led by CUHK professor Yi-Chun Lu, the sulfur-based flow battery uses water-based electrolytes. Luquos Energy, a startup founded to commercialize the research, has installed a demonstration system on campus. “This is a completely different technology compared to lithium,” said Luquos Energy CEO Simon Zengyue Wang. “We do not use lithium. We use sulfur.” “The battery electrolyte is water, so it never catches fire,” Wang said. The company estimates its electrolyte could remain usable for more than 15 years, although that is not a verified real-world service life. Wang said the technology could serve solar installations and power-hungry artificial intelligence data centers because it can discharge electricity for “over eight hours, even 12 hours, even longer.” He said Luquos Energy was building a production line in Shenzhen and had already developed battery systems for projects including electric vehicle charging. artigo.texto: BYD Energy Storage Expands Global After-Sales Network With Nine Operations and Maintenance Centers BYD Energy Storage operates nine operations and maintenance centers of 2,500 square meters each. The company plans two new sites in 2027 and reports contractual response times for its battery systems. BYD Energy Storage has built an after-sales service network in four tiers: station-level maintenance, project centers, regional centers and global headquarters, according to the company. The group operates nine operations and maintenance (O&M) centers worldwide, each covering 2,500 square meters. The announcement comes in a sector where several players are expanding their capacity, such as Saft, which inaugurated its first solid-state battery production lines in Bordeaux, or Grenergy, which secured $457 million for 446 MW of solar and storage in Chile. A geographic footprint set to widen The after-sales network covers China, Chile, South Africa, the UK, the US, Australia, Japan, Poland and the Middle East. BYD Energy Storage says new service centers will open in South Africa and Bulgaria in 2027. The sites perform several functions: spare parts storage and management, battery repair and maintenance, regional spare parts allocation, battery recycling and training of locally hired engineers. According to the company, its regional centers comply with local regulatory requirements and enable rapid on-site response. The service team includes more than 200 field engineers and more than 100 research and development (R&D) specialists. BYD Energy Storage says it applies standardized service level agreements (SLAs): response within 24 hours, on-site arrival within 48 hours and fault troubleshooting within 7 days. Localized spare parts supply and repairs The company says the network forms a multi-point supply chain intended to ensure rapid delivery of spare parts worldwide. It adds that its O&M teams rely on localized production lines and integrate regional resources to carry out battery repairs locally. "Our global service footprint is tailored to our fast-growing BESS deployments. Trustworthy after-sales support underpins the long-term stable operation of energy storage assets," said Mr. He Dehong, Head of Global After-sales Service at BYD Energy Storage. The company cites a vision of empowering the global energy storage industry with digital and intelligent service. Shipment volumes reported by the company BYD Energy Storage says it topped global battery energy storage system (BESS) shipments in 2025, with more than 60 GWh. It reports having delivered more than 650 energy storage projects in total. artigo.texto: Advait Energy unit signs 1 GWh LFP cell supply deal with Hithium - ABEPL, a subsidiary of Advait Energy Transitions, signed a Master Supply Agreement with Hithium. - The deal covers the purchase of up to 1 GWh of 314 Ah LFP prismatic battery cells over one year. - Initial pricing is fixed at $49.5/kWh for the first 350 MWh tranche. - The agreement supports Advait's 2.5 GWh BESS assembly facility in Gangad, Gujarat. *this image is generated using AI for illustrative purposes only. Advait Battery Ecosystem Private Limited (ABEPL), a step-down subsidiary of Advait Energy Transitions Limited , has entered into a Master Supply Agreement with Hithium for the purchase of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) prismatic battery cells. The agreement, executed on September 18, 2026, structures cell offtake of up to 1 GWh over the next year. This partnership anchors the supply chain for Advait’s upcoming 2.5 GWh annual capacity cell-to-container Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) assembly facility in Gangad, Gujarat. Deal Structure and Pricing Under the terms disclosed in the exchange filing under Regulation 30 of the SEBI (Listing Obligations & Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2015, Hithium will supply 314 Ah LFP prismatic cells. The contractual value is set at $49.5/kWh for the initial tranche of up to 350 MWh. Pricing for volumes beyond this threshold will be determined based on future project receipts. Strategic Context Hithium is recognized as a BloombergNEF Tier 1 global energy storage manufacturer. For the first half of 2025 (H1 2025), Hithium reported net profit exceeding RMB 100 million ($14 million USD) and operating cash flow surpassing RMB 1 billion ($140 million USD). ABEPL, incorporated on April 27, 2026, is building an integrated BESS supply chain. The company has previously collaborated with Adaptive Engineering for engineering design and Energy Management System (EMS) architecture. The Hithium agreement addresses the critical cell sourcing component of this ecosystem. What the Numbers Show The pricing structure reveals a tiered approach to volume scaling. With a fixed rate of $49.5/kWh applied only to the first 350 MWh, approximately 65% of the potential 1 GWh annual offtake remains subject to future price negotiations. This suggests that while the initial supply chain risk is mitigated for the first third of the year's capacity, long-term cost certainty depends on subsequent project wins and market conditions for LFP cells. What is the timeline for Advait's 2.5 GWh BESS assembly facility in Gujarat to reach full operational capacity, and how does this align with the 1-year supply agreement? Given Hithium's strong H1 2025 financials, how does their current production capacity compare to Advait's potential future scaling beyond the initial 1 GWh commitment?

artigo.texto: Carlsquare advised diveo GmbH on the sale of three agri-PV and BESS co-location projects to an established German energy provider Carlsquare advised diveo GmbH (“diveo”) on the sale of three agri-PV and BESS co-location projects to an established German energy provider. The three projects are located in Southern Germany, are spread across different medium-voltage grid areas and have a grid connection capacity in the double-digit megawatt range. diveo, a spin-off of the Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE, is an independent developer of agri-PV and battery storage projects in Germany. The company focuses on commercially viable co-location concepts that combine long-term agricultural use with renewable power generation and flexible storage operation. Its goal is to create economically attractive solutions for landowners, farms and asset operators that last for decades. The buyer is an established German energy provider that is active in, among other areas, the development, construction and long-term operation of renewable energy assets. The projects combine agricultural use with solar power generation through single-axis tracker agri-PV systems and high-capacity battery storage. The co-location concepts enable flexible trading of the energy generated, as well as operation of the battery storage systems as hybrid or grid-charged storage that can draw power from the public grid and market it. In this way, the projects combine long-term, economically viable agricultural management with efficient use of grid connection capacity. As the share of renewable energies grows, so does the need for flexibility in the power system. Combining yield-optimized agri-PV systems with flexibly marketable battery storage opens up additional revenue potential and creates attractive investment opportunities. The transaction underlines the interest of established energy providers in integrated agri-PV and BESS projects. “The successful sale of the three projects shows that agri-PV combined with battery storage is an attractive business model for large energy providers as well. What matters is the interplay between farmers who want to unlock new economic prospects for their land, efficient project development and asset operators with a long-term focus. This creates projects from which agriculture and the energy sector benefit equally. We would also like to thank Carlsquare for their professional support throughout the transaction.” – Kai Klapdor, Managing Director, diveo GmbH Carlsquare acted as exclusive financial advisor to diveo.

artigo.texto: Taunton weighs one-year data center freeze as developer warns deal is at risk TAUNTON, Mass. (WJAR) — Taunton officials are considering a one-year freeze on new data centers, but an industrial property owner warns the delay could jeopardize a multimillion-dollar development deal. The Taunton Municipal Council is scheduled to discuss the proposed 365-day moratorium Tuesday. City leaders say the pause would allow them to review zoning rules and assess the infrastructure, electrical and environmental demands of data centers. VMD Companies, which owns an industrial building at 50 John Hancock Road in the Myles Standish Industrial Park, urged Mayor Shaunna O’Connell in a letter to exempt certain existing industrial buildings. The company said a yearlong delay would derail a pending agreement with a confidential technology tenant. According to VMD’s filings with the Taunton Municipal Lighting Plant, the proposed project would require 24 megawatts of electricity across two phases: 13 megawatts for the first phase and an additional 11 megawatts for the second. While acknowledging the city’s need for caution, VMD is asking officials to exempt existing industrial buildings that are already approved, comply with building codes and generate property tax revenue. Some area residents have raised concerns about data centers’ potential effects on the environment, water resources and surrounding communities. “We need to really look at the impact,” said Peggy Hall, of Easton. “And not just let these big businesses and billionaires just roll over these small-town communities where they think that they can just come in and suck up our land and not have any repercussions.” Jackson Isenstadt, of Norton, said a pause could give officials more time to evaluate potential concerns. “All these other data center lawsuits that are happening now, other things could come out in the next year about them,” Isenstadt said. “So maybe a one year pause would be a good thing.” The council is scheduled to meet at 7 p.m. Tuesday in the Chester R. Martin Municipal Council Chambers at City Hall.

Coloque a eixos nas suas fontes preferidas do Google Veja nossas notícias com mais destaque nas suas buscas. NESTA EDIÇÃO. Fundo de Inovação da UE destinará € 3,4 bilhões a 77 projetos de tecnologias de emissão líquida zero. Entre os selecionados, 27 são ligados ao transporte e receberão € 1,3 bi para combustíveis sustentáveis e eletrificação, entre outras soluções. EDIÇÃO APRESENTADA POR: EDIÇÃO APRESENTADA POR: Combustíveis sustentáveis de aviação (SAF, em inglês), navegação (e-metanol e amônia), biometano e tecnologias de eletrificação serão financiados na Europa com recursos do mercado regulado de carbono, em uma estratégia que busca reduzir emissões e garantir independência energética. A Comissão Europeia divulgou nesta segunda (19/10) a seleção de 77 projetos de tecnologias de emissão líquida zero para receber apoio financeiro de € 3,4 bilhões, dos quais, 27 estão relacionados à descarbonização do setor de transportes, com € 1,3 bilhão em subvenções. A chamada do Fundo de Inovação foi lançada em dezembro de 2025, e usará as receitas do Sistema de Comércio de Emissões da União Europeia (EU ETS) para financiar tecnologias consideradas inovadoras, com foco na indústria de baixo carbono. A próxima rodada está prevista para dezembro de 2026, com uma categoria de € 1 bilhão para a fabricação de tecnologias limpas que reduzam riscos com cadeias de suprimentos, em linha com o RESourceEU. Dos projetos relacionados ao setor de transportes, oito dos selecionados tratam exclusivamente da produção de combustíveis sustentáveis, enquanto cinco abastecerão também outros segmentos da economia. Cinco propostas para SAF receberão € 367 milhões em subvenções. Três delas estão na França. A lista divulgada pela Comissão Europeia menciona o projeto BELair, de produção de combustíveis sintéticos (e-SAF), na Normandia, com capacidade para produzir até 13 mil toneladas por ano. Outro é o H4 Marseille Fos, que pretende construir uma cadeia de valor integrada de e-SAF na zona portuária industrial de Marselha-Fos, para produzir até 75 mil toneladas/ano de combustível sintético a partir de hidrogênio de baixo carbono, e-metanol e CO2 capturado. Já o projeto L’Ardoise prevê a construção e operação de uma planta integrada de conversão de eletricidade em combustíveis líquidos (Power-to-Liquid, PtL), em Laudun-L’Ardoise. A previsão é que a unidade produzirá 70 mil toneladas anuais de querosene sintético e 40 mil toneladas anuais de e-metanol para o transporte marítimo. Os outros dois projetos estão na Espanha e nos Países Baixos. Localizado na fábrica de cimento da Holcim em Villaluenga de la Sagra, na província de Toledo, o ECO2FLY quer estabelecer uma cadeia de valor totalmente integrada de captura, utilização e armazenamento de carbono (CCUS, em inglês) industrial para a produção de e-SAF. Enquanto no Porto de Roterdã, o projeto EFR está apostando na rota metanol-para-combustível de aviação (MtJ, na sigla em inglês). A instalação terá capacidade para produzir aproximadamente 280 mil toneladas de e-SAF por ano, utilizando e-metanol importado. No horizonte da navegação Além do SAF, dez dos projetos selecionados para desenvolver tecnologias inovadoras para o transporte, com investimentos totais de € 277 milhões, aplicadas em três segmentos: transporte marítimo (6), transporte rodoviário (6) e aviação (2). Um deles é o GAFF, na Itália, cuja ambição é implantar a primeira frota europeia de navios gaseiros de médio porte equipados com sistemas de propulsão tricombustível. Desenvolvidas pela empresa norueguesa Færder Tankers, as embarcações transportarão amônia verde e realizarão operações de abastecimento de navios a navios (ship-to-ship bunkering) em rotas intercontinentais entre a Índia, a costa do Golfo dos Estados Unidos e o noroeste da Europa. A principal inovação do projeto é o motor capaz de operar com amônia, gás liquefeito de petróleo (GLP) e óleo diesel marítimo. O projeto estima que a nova frota de embarcações terá capacidade para transportar até 1 milhão de toneladas de amônia verde por ano, com potencial de evitar a emissão de mais de 1,2 milhão de toneladas de CO2 equivalente ao longo de dez anos. O bloco também está colocando a eletrificação como uma área prioritária. Prova disso, é que quatro projetos receberão, ao todo, € 539 milhões em financiamento para apoiar a fabricação de baterias e de seus componentes. Pilotos de SMR e captura de carbono Pela primeira vez, a lista do fundo financiado pelo ETS europeu incluiu um projeto de reator nuclear modular (SMR, em inglês) e a captura direta de carbono do ar com armazenamento (DACCS). Ambos pilotos. Chamado NetZeroHeat, o primeiro reator modular europeu mira a produção de calor para o aquecimento urbano em larga escala, com um módulo de 30 MWh. O SMR deve fornecer 131 GWh de calor de baixo carbono por ano à rede de aquecimento urbano de Pierrelatte, na França. E promete evitar a emissão de mais de 221 mil toneladas de CO2 equivalente nos primeiros dez anos de operação. Em outra frente, o Projeto Furu quer ser uma referência europeia para a captura direta de CO2 do ar com armazenamento permanente. A unidade-piloto em Øygarden, na Noruega, será conectada ao sistema de armazenamento geológico da Northern Lights e projeta a remoção de cerca de 4 mil toneladas de CO2 por ano. Ao todo, os 16 projetos projetos-piloto selecionados vão demandar cerca de € 394 milhões. Além dos SMRs e DACCS, as propostas estão atreladas aos setores de aviação, energia eólica, energia oceânica e transporte marítimo, hidrogênio, produtos químicos e refino. Cobrimos por aqui Curtas Terras raras e privatizações no debate presidencial. artigo.texto: India’s Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) is a historic milestone. Specific obligated entities across nine notified sectors—iron and steel, aluminium, cement, chlor-alkali, pulp and paper, petroleum refining, petrochemicals, textiles and fertilizers—are required to reduce their greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions below the assigned intensity target, for which they will be issued carbon credit certificates (CCCs). A CCC, representing 1 tonne of CO2 emission, could be sold on power exchanges or banked for future compliance needs. Projects in non-obligated sectors can also generate credits for sale to obligated entities. Trading in CCCs, which is expected to commence soon, will establish an explicit and observable carbon price in India, help drive investment in emissions reduction and influence policy. CCC pricing will also help exports to markets such as the EU and UK, whose carbon border adjustment mechanisms (CBAMs) require the price differential of embedded emissions to be paid as a price for market access. The UK has recognized that the CCC price can be treated as a deductible for eligible products. But its immediate significance must not be overstated. Exporters will still bear the brunt of a carbon price gap with the UK market, estimated at $70-80 per tonne. CBAM frameworks in both the EU and UK are also expected to expand their reach to downstream products of steel and aluminium, other sectors like organic chemicals, and to transport and indirect emissions. What we need beyond CCTS: Industrial decarbonization requires a more complex policy mix beyond price signals for the deployment of emerging technologies, support infrastructure and access to affordable finance. India has already demonstrated the value of targeted support in building clean-technology ecosystems through its production-linked incentive scheme for solar PV modules and its Sight programme for green hydrogen production and electrolyser manufacturing. Similar dedicated frameworks are needed for carbon capture utilization and storage (CCUS), hydrogen-ready industrial equipment, industrial electrification, advanced recycling and other low-carbon process technologies. A Niti Aayog report earlier this year on Scenarios Towards Viksit Bharat and Net Zero estimates that we need $22.7 trillion in cumulative investment by 2070 and recommends strengthening transition finance for hard-to-abate sectors through verified transition plans, wider use of transition and sustainability-linked bonds, expanded guarantees and blended-finance mechanisms to de-risk investments, etc. Similarly, Niti Aayog’s MSME Green Transition Roadmap calls for dedicated green-finance mechanisms, credit enhancement and risk-sharing instruments along with common technology, testing, certification and advisory infrastructure to reduce the cost and complexity for smaller firms. Global experience is informative. Low-carbon industrial clusters such as the UK’s East Coast Cluster and HyNet programmes have lowered costs through shared infrastructure, risk-sharing mechanisms and coordinated public support. Sweden’s Hybrit is an example of a state-supported, industry-led integrated value chain initiative linking green hydrogen—produced using fossil-free wind and hydropower—to iron and steelmaking processes to eliminate carbon emissions. The Reserve Bank of India’s (RBI) Priority Sector Lending Directions also need expansion beyond renewable energy projects to recognize industrial decarbonization investments. Tax policy can reinforce this shift. India currently provides accelerated depreciation for specified energy-saving, waste-heat recovery, pollution-control, recycling and renewable-energy equipment. As industrial decarbonization technologies evolve, the eligible list could be periodically updated to include emerging low-carbon technologies needed by hard-to-abate sectors. A national decarbonization fund could also play a crucial role in supporting technology deployment and prioritizing sectors with the highest abatement costs and greatest strategic importance. As for the question of where the resources will come from, here are some thoughts: First, a range of implicit carbon costs already exists in the form of coal levies, fuel taxes and electricity duties that influence behaviour but are not explicitly linked to financing decarbonization. Channelling a portion of these revenues into a dedicated fund would recycle resources from carbon-intensive activities into cleaner alternatives while improving coherence across instruments that operate in silos. Second, India can leverage opportunities under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to mobilize finance and technology to enhance bilateral cooperation. Credible carbon accounting methodologies, institutional capacity and a pipeline of investable projects can accelerate the scaling up of such initiatives. Most importantly, the finance ministry’s draft Climate Finance Taxonomy of 2024 urgently needs to be finalized. A credible taxonomy will serve as a foundational enabler for our climate-finance architecture by providing a common basis for identifying genuine green-transition investments and channelling finance consistent with India’s climate goals. CCTS provides a price signal. India must now build the rest of the ecosystem that would enable industry to translate climate ambition into industrial reality. The authors are, respectively, partner, Clarus Law Associates and a Mumbai-based economist.

artigo.texto: Premier Energies and Germany's RCT Nexor Formalise 12 GWh Battery Storage Manufacturing Joint Venture Premier Energies has signed the shareholders agreement for its joint venture with RCT Nexor. The project plans a 12 GWh plant at Seetharampur, Telangana, with a 6 GWh first phase in FY2027-28. Premier Energies Ltd has formalised its battery energy storage system (BESS) manufacturing joint venture with Germany's RCT Group. Its wholly owned subsidiary, Premier Battery Technologies Pvt Ltd (PBTPL), signed a share allotment-cum-shareholders agreement on October 15, 2026. The other signatories are RCT Nexor Energy Pvt Ltd, formerly RCT Energy India Pvt Ltd, and Premier Energies Storage Solutions Pvt Ltd (PESSPL), the joint venture company. The storage market already counts large players: HiTHIUM has surpassed 200 GWh of cumulative deliveries from Chongqing, while GIGA Storage has declared its Albatross project ready to build, with 350 MW of storage in Lower Saxony. A 12 GWh plant planned in Telangana The joint venture plans to establish a 12 GWh BESS manufacturing facility at Seetharampur, in the Indian state of Telangana. According to Premier Energies, a first phase of 6 GWh is expected to be set up in FY2027-28. The site is intended to manufacture and assemble products for residential, small-business, commercial, industrial and utility-scale applications. The agreement follows a binding term sheet signed on September 10, 2026 by PBTPL and RCT India. Premier Energies says the joint venture would address demand for energy storage solutions across multiple market segments. The group, already active in solar cells and modules, also identifies BESS, inverters and transformers as areas for expanding its portfolio. Ownership and governance structure PESSPL is currently a wholly owned subsidiary of PBTPL. The agreement gives RCT Nexor Energy the right to subscribe to equity representing 15% of the joint venture's issued and paid-up capital, in four tranches linked to project milestones. It also grants the option, but not the obligation, to acquire an additional 5% for cash at the end of Phase I, subject to the agreement's terms. The board will comprise two nominees of PBTPL and one nominee of RCT Nexor Energy. Premier Energies states that no immediate share issuance is proposed under the agreement. RCT's technology contribution Germany-based RCT Group operates across several renewable technologies, including photovoltaic manufacturing engineering and energy storage. Its RCT Power arm has developed residential, commercial and grid-scale solutions, including systems designed for applications of up to 5 MWh per unit. It has also reported a 2.1 GWh order for grid-connected battery storage projects in Australia. These capabilities could help support the Indian joint venture's technology development and market reach. The Premier Energies stock-exchange filing does not, however, detail the specific technology-transfer and manufacturing responsibilities under the agreement with RCT Nexor. - Gas44.1 % - Nuclear16.1 % - Coal15.7 % - Solar10.6 % - Wind8.3 % - Hydro3.5 % - Bioenergy0.9 % - Other fossil0.5 % - Other renewables0.4 %

artigo.texto: MCEE, a South Korea-based ministry for climate, energy and the environment, has issued a national guideline that could cut up to 3 months from the permitting of an outdoor BESS. Until now, each local government had used its own policy, so the same unit could be a building in one district and a structure in the next. That distinction has mattered, because a building has required a permit process of about two to four months. A structure, on the other hand, has required only about half a month to one and a half months. The guideline adds human access, structure and use as tests, and a sealed enclosure that cannot be entered will therefore be classed as a structure. MCEE has described energy storage as core infrastructure for the expansion of renewable energy. Land permits and fire safety rules, however, still apply to each site as before. South Korea guideline cuts outdoor BESS permit time by up to 3 months A sealed outdoor BESS in South Korea will be classed as a structure under a guideline from MCEE, and its permit could take up to three months less. artigo.texto: MOUNT PLEASANT, Wis. — Mount Pleasant’s proposed Microsoft data center is reducing the number of buildings while increasing the project’s overall square footage. According to Village of Mount Pleasant Planning Commission documents, the number of buildings has been reduced from nine to seven. The project originally encompassed 5.2 million square feet at 12023 Durand Ave. Under the revised design, the total square footage will increase to 5,878,080 square feet, Village of Mount Pleasant Communications Director Sean Ryan said. Samuel Schultz, Mount Pleasant’s community development director, said the square footage will “likely fluctuate” as Microsoft continues refining its site plans. The documents also show plans for 10 parking lots, internal roads, stormwater ponds, sound walls and perimeter security fencing. “We continue to refine the design and layout of our expansion parcels in the Village of Mount Pleasant. The changes in no way reflect a reduction in our ambition, they have been made to ensure faster development, allowing us to access this increased capacity quicker. We will continue to evolve our design and keep the community updated prior to beginning any vertical construction,” a Microsoft spokesperson said in an email. The development’s total taxable value is projected at $6,095,690,000, which would generate $103,148,899 in incremental tax revenue, according to the documents. Schultz said the preliminary projections are based on a 40-year period. The documents also estimate the data center project would generate $7,694,420 per acre. The Village of Mount Pleasant Planning Commission met Thursday at 1 p.m. and unanimously approved the site plan modifications. The changes will now go to the Mount Pleasant Village Council for approval. The council’s next meeting is scheduled for Oct. 19 at 6 p.m. “These (plans) will continue to be refined over time as they both go to pull building permits, but also look at site plans, so this is just kind of the next step in their refinement of the site plan approval process,” Schultz said during the Planning Commission meeting. The traffic impact analysis for the data center project indicated it could take up to 10 years for the site to be fully completed, Schultz said. In July, Microsoft was sued by Sturtevant residents over noise complaints related to the data center. The Planning Commission requested that Microsoft add sound mitigation measures along the west side of the project.

artigo.texto: ORLANDO, Fla. – Election Day 2026 is just days away. Voters in Orange County will be choosing a new mayor for the first time in eight years. Chris Messina and Tiffany Moore Russell are running to replace Jerry Demings. [ELECTION 2026: Make sure you’re eligible to vote|How to vote by mail|Election Myths] It comes as AI and data centers are becoming hot-button political issues. News 6 anchor Lisa Bell asked both Messina and Moore Russell their views on data centers moving into Orange County. MOORE RUSSELL: So I think that’s a very general term, right? Because data centers vary based upon the size and their purpose, right. So at the clerk’s office, there’s a smaller version of that that houses our data, because we’re now in the cloud. We don’t have paper anymore in the courthouse, right, so someone is housing our digital court records. But I do not support the big data centers, the AI data centers that is being proposed today. And so I did commend the county for pushing for a moratorium just to pause. Allows for us to study the issue and determine what is the best fit for Orange County and so I do not believe the large AI data centers are appropriate for our community for what we’re trying to do moving forward. BELL: What are your biggest concerns about those large data centers? MOORE RUSSELL: It’s the water usage, it’s the demand on our power sources, whether it’s going to impact our water supply and the quality of our water, right, what’s feeding into our aquifer. And so it’s all of those environmental concerns that’s an issue for me, as well as is it a right fit for our community? Right? Where are you going to put a data center? No one wants a data center next to their home or next to a school. And so I just doesn’t think, I don’t think it matches the brand of Orange County and will fit in our community. MESSINA: Small ones we need. I’m sure you have a data center here (at News 6), right, running your operations. It’s the hyperscale data centers, the ones that are football fields in size, those I don’t feel are right for Florida. And the reason I don’t feel they’re right is not necessarily energy because they can make their own energy with solar and other small power, associated power generation plants, it’s the impact on water. So I’ve seen personally first-hand what happens when you have a problem with a water supply to a data center. It’s pretty scary and the temperature goes way up. Systems fail and then you have discharge of water and the problem is what’s in the water in order to run those data centers. They have to add biocides and basically bacteria killers, but they will kill things out in the environment. BELL: So if we shouldn’t have data centers here in Florida, where should we have them? MESSINA: So, I really like Elon Musk’s idea to put it in space. And the reason I think that’s such a good idea is because space is near absolute zero. And we are, right now, we’re on the cusp of being the space tech center of the country." BELL: That seems like it would take decades to build enough data centers in space to power AI needs here on Earth. MESSINA: I’m not sure it would. When you think about the pace of technology and who thought at one point that you could recapture a rocket booster landing or have a self-driving electric car or a watch where you can make phone calls, the pace in technology is pretty significant. So I would not bet against that. We also asked each candidate their views on other issues such as Flock license plate reader cameras. To see their responses and our full interview, watch below. artigo.texto: O mercado nacional de comércio de direitos de emissão de carbono da China acumulou mais de 930 milhões de toneladas em transações até o final de julho de 2026, segundo dados apresentados nesta quinta-feira, 13 de agosto, pelo ministro da Ecologia e do Meio Ambiente, Huang Runqiu. O sistema chinês de comércio de emissões iniciou suas operações em 2021 e passou a desempenhar um papel importante na estratégia ambiental do país. Segundo Huang, o mecanismo tem ajudado setores industriais a reduzir suas emissões de carbono com custos menores e contribuído para a transição para uma economia de baixo carbono. A expansão do mercado está entre as medidas previstas no 15º Plano Quinquenal para a Construção de uma China Bonita, divulgado recentemente pelo país. O plano estabelece a ampliação gradual da cobertura do mercado nacional de emissões, além do aumento do número de empresas participantes. A meta também inclui reduzir em aproximadamente 3% as emissões de carbono por unidade de produto dos setores abrangidos pelo sistema. A China pretende ampliar o alcance do mercado de carbono para incluir outras atividades industriais de elevada emissão. Segundo Li Gao, vice-ministro de Ecologia e Meio Ambiente, a expansão deverá incluir setores como petroquímica e indústria química, que se somarão às áreas atualmente abrangidas, como geração de energia, siderurgia, produção de cimento e fundição de alumínio. Com a ampliação, aproximadamente 80% das emissões de dióxido de carbono da China deverão ficar sob controle efetivo do sistema nacional de comércio de direitos de emissão, de acordo com o vice-ministro. A estratégia busca utilizar mecanismos de mercado para estimular empresas a reduzir a intensidade das emissões e investir em tecnologias mais eficientes e menos poluentes. As autoridades chinesas também destacaram os avanços realizados nos últimos anos no enfrentamento das mudanças climáticas. Segundo o Ministério da Ecologia e do Meio Ambiente, as estruturas energética, industrial e de transporte do país vêm passando por transformações voltadas à melhoria da eficiência e à redução das emissões. Além da expansão do mercado de carbono, o governo pretende continuar promovendo a transição verde em áreas consideradas estratégicas, incluindo energia, indústria, transporte e desenvolvimento urbano e rural. Outra frente será o controle de gases de efeito estufa diferentes do dióxido de carbono. Entre eles está o metano, que também deverá receber maior atenção nas políticas ambientais chinesas. A ampliação do mercado nacional de carbono representa, assim, uma das principais ferramentas econômicas utilizadas pela China para estimular a redução das emissões e apoiar suas metas de desenvolvimento de baixo carbono. artigo.texto: The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources and a group of environmental organizations announced a settlement agreement Monday that would require stricter environmental impact assessments of future data center developments and initiate a statewide review of how data centers use the state’s resources. In June, the Sierra Club and Midwest Environmental Advocates sued the DNR in Ozaukee County court, arguing that the agency approved the permits for Vantage’s massive data center currently under construction in Port Washington without conducting a proper environmental impact statement. “AI data centers are massive, thirsty, energy hogs and have popped up all over Wisconsin,” Elizabeth Ward, director of the Wisconsin chapter of the Sierra Club, said in a statement. “They could completely change our landscape and use unprecedented amounts of water and energy. Wisconsinites and our regulators need to understand the impacts and opportunities to reduce harm before allowing data centers to move forward. Wisconsinites deserve an informed, transparent process for decisions that could shape their communities and environment for decades. A report this summer by the state Public Service Commission found that the Port Washington data center and data centers being built by Microsoft in Mount Pleasant and Meta in Beaver Dam are set to be responsible for a 40% increase in statewide energy demand over the next six years. As part of the settlement agreement in the lawsuit, the DNR will conduct full environmental impact statements of individual data center proposals moving forward and complete a statewide strategic analysis of how data centers consume resources. State law and the DNR’s administrative rules allow the agency to conduct such an analysis when conflicts arise over resource demands for a “complicated or complex issue; an issue that is new to the state; an issue or policy that will likely lead to future department actions that will require an environmental impact statement; issues for which there is a high potential for legislation or new department policy and the planning and development of controversial resource-oriented projects.” “What started as a lawsuit over the environmental review of one data center has become an opportunity to address the data center issue on a much bigger scale,” MEA attorney Michael Greif said. “Looking at these impacts holistically is important because the impacts of data centers are statewide. State regulators will now have to examine the cumulative impacts of data center development across Wisconsin.” Wisconsin will become one of a few states assessing the statewide impacts of data centers on their resources. In July, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed an executive order that initiated a similar analysis and last December, the Maryland Legislature enacted a law that requires a number of state agencies to study “the likely environmental, energy, and economic impacts of data center development.” Originally published by Wisconsin Examiner, a nonprofit news organization.

Pepco has approved ConnectDER's meter collar products for solar, battery storage and electric vehicle charging installations across its service territory in Washington, D.C., according to a report by Billy Ludt. The approval extends ConnectDER's reach to a national footprint of 54 utilities serving nearly 40 million households, with additional utility expansion underway. ConnectDER's adapters connect directly to the existing meter socket on the exterior of a home. By creating a safe connection point at the meter, the devices remove the need for main panel upgrades, service upsizing, circuit relocations or added backup load panels and system controllers, which the company says can raise labor costs and extend project timelines. Ivo Steklac, ConnectDER's president and chief executive, said demand for residential solar, battery backup and electric vehicles in the District continues to grow, while older electrical infrastructure poses a physical obstacle that slows installations. He said approval of the adapters for exterior meter-socket installation means installers can avoid re-engineering entire panels and home wiring, allowing them to deliver clean energy resilience more efficiently while saving homeowners thousands of dollars in total costs and days of labor. Steklac added that this translates into greater installation capacity and fewer barriers, which he described as important for the District's electrification goals. The District's clean energy market is driven by its Clean Energy DC mandates, which include a renewable portfolio standard with a dedicated 15% local solar carve-out. Its urban building stock, largely historic row homes with aging electrical infrastructure, often has 100-ampere electrical panels that require main service upgrades costing thousands of dollars before solar, battery storage or EV charging equipment can be interconnected. Robin Dutta, executive director of the Chesapeake Solar and Storage Association, said the approval by Pepco DC is a significant win for District residents and installation companies, following dedicated work by several association members to pass enabling regulations. Dutta said the change makes solar and battery storage more accessible for everyday homeowners. ConnectDER's IslandDER MSA is designed specifically for whole-home backup and battery storage. It integrates a Microgrid Interconnect Device, current transformers, voltage sensing and real-time grid disconnect capability into a single compact device mounted outside at the meter. artigo.texto: From robotic gloves to safer batteries, CUHK puts research to work Wearable device helps patients regain hand movement as university-developed battery technology targets energy storage HONG KONG — From helping stroke patients perform everyday tasks to developing safer ways to store electricity, researchers at The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) are developing technologies for use beyond the laboratory. During a visit to the university on Sept. 1, a reporter tried on a robotic glove that moved the fingers with noticeable force, but without jerking them. For stroke survivors who cannot move their hands, that movement could help them do something as ordinary as holding a spoon or picking up a phone. The device uses air-powered artificial muscles developed by a team led by Raymond Tong, a professor of biomedical engineering at CUHK. Unlike conventional motor-driven rehabilitation equipment, the lightweight system uses a small pump to help patients open and close their hands. “Nowadays, you can see those exoskeletons are very rigid. They are very heavy,” Tong said, inviting the reporter to try the device. Patients can use it both for rehabilitation exercises and everyday tasks, including gripping objects, writing and eating. Tong said the system can also respond to signals associated with a patient’s intention to move. “They can use the brain to control it,” he said. “I just imagine moving the hand and the hand moves.” Tong said the team was conducting clinical trials involving people with strokes and spinal injuries, with plans to expand use in hospitals. He also described work with children who have difficulty standing or walking. Elsewhere on campus, researchers showed a battery designed to reduce the fire risks associated with conventional lithium-ion batteries. Developed by a team led by CUHK professor Yi-Chun Lu, the sulfur-based flow battery uses water-based electrolytes. Luquos Energy, a startup founded to commercialize the research, has installed a demonstration system on campus. “This is a completely different technology compared to lithium,” said Luquos Energy CEO Simon Zengyue Wang. “We do not use lithium. We use sulfur.” “The battery electrolyte is water, so it never catches fire,” Wang said. The company estimates its electrolyte could remain usable for more than 15 years, although that is not a verified real-world service life. Wang said the technology could serve solar installations and power-hungry artificial intelligence data centers because it can discharge electricity for “over eight hours, even 12 hours, even longer.” He said Luquos Energy was building a production line in Shenzhen and had already developed battery systems for projects including electric vehicle charging.

artigo.texto: Fairfield leaders discuss C-PACE financing tool that could help businesses, proposed data center FAIRFIELD, Ala. (WBRC) - Fairfield city leaders are looking into a new financing tool that could help business and property owners pay for upgrades on commercial buildings, including the proposed Patmos data center. The tool is called C-PACE, or Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy. Monday, the Fairfield City Council discussed considering the program, but tabled the issue for now. What is C-PACE? C-PACE lets businesses seek private financing for upgrades such as LED lighting, heating and cooling systems, and water-saving fixtures. A new state law allows cities to offer this kind of private financing locally. Mayor Herman Carnes Jr. said the city is not taking out a loan to build a data center. He said the program is about letting businesses and property owners tap into private money to fix up their buildings. Carnes called C-PACE a “help” mechanism and said it is not a financial liability for the city. “If we are saying we’re open for business, that means we need to do everything possible and legally tactical so that we can make sure that people be able to come in, purchase a building, not run out of money once they do the electrical system and then you have a building sitting,” Carnes said. Protest outside city hall Before the meeting, members of the Fairfield Environmental Justice Alliance protested outside city hall. They want more transparency around the Patmos data center project. Patmos wants to build a colocation data center and technology campus inside the former Walmart supercenter in Fairfield. Neighbors are asking city leaders to release all documents so they can see the potential impact. “A project with major effects on our community should be presented openly, examined carefully and discussed with the people who will live with the results,” said Gilda Walker of the Fairfield Environmental Justice Alliance. City says program not limited to Patmos The mayor said C-PACE is not just about Patmos and is available to businesses looking for financial help. A Patmos spokesperson sent WBRC this statement: “Fairfield taxpayers are not on the hook. Tonight (Monday) the City is only considering whether to adopt the C-PACE program; it is not issuing a loan, lending City money, or taking on any debt, guarantee or liability. Under Alabama law, C-PACE is private financing that a property owner voluntarily repays through an assessment on its own property, public funds cannot be used to fund or repay it, and billing, collection and enforcement are handled entirely by the private lender. Once adopted, the program is open to a wide range of property owners, including commercial properties such as office buildings and hotels, industrial, agricultural and multifamily properties. Patmos is one of several parties interested in using it, and others aren’t even in our industry.”- Patmos spokesperson, Kyler Schmitz City leaders discussed a possible work session on the issue and a town hall before any final vote.
