artigo.texto: As preocupações com a localização, a procura de água e de electricidade levaram a apelos para uma maior supervisão da construção de centros de dados no estado de Cowboy, mas não para um alinhamento sobre como o conseguir. CODY, Wyoming. — Em uma noite quente de outubro, em um bar no centro de Cody, os habitantes de Wyoming se reuniram para refletir sobre o futuro do que alguns esperam que seja a próxima indústria em expansão do Estado Cowboy: os data centers. Neste verão, o governador cessante, Mark Gordon, assinou uma ordem executiva intitulada “Data Centers the Wyoming Way” que, segundo ele, “orientaria o desenvolvimento responsável no Wyoming”, ao mesmo tempo que manteria o estado um ponto de aterrissagem atraente para os enormes armazéns de servidores que alimentam a indústria de IA. Os potenciais impactos dos centros de dados no precioso abastecimento de água do Wyoming, nos já crescentes preços da electricidade e nas valiosas terras públicas têm irritado muitos cantos do estado. Gordon reconheceu essas preocupações numa declaração que acompanha a divulgação da ordem, que não é vinculativa. Grupos ambientalistas no Wyoming concordam que é necessário haver mais barreiras de proteção no desenvolvimento de data centers, mas não estão totalmente alinhados sobre como atingir esse objetivo. O capítulo do The Sierra Club do Wyoming acredita que uma moratória sobre data centers poderia ser útil em certas circunstâncias, mas o grupo não tomou posição sobre a utilidade de interromper o desenvolvimento em todo o estado. O Wyoming Outdoor Council vê uma oportunidade tangível para avançar em novas políticas de data center com a chegada de legisladores e um novo diretor do Departamento de Qualidade Ambiental. Mas uma moratória, na sua opinião, não garantiria essas barreiras de protecção e é, portanto, uma forma arriscada de gastar o capital político limitado dos grupos ambientalistas. “Por sua própria natureza, uma moratória é temporária, e um pedido de moratória sobre data centers seria realmente um paliativo”, disse Jocelyn Wulf, gerente de campanha de data center do Wyoming Outdoor Council, a algumas dezenas de residentes de Cody este mês na prefeitura do data center que a organização hospedava. Representantes de ambas as organizações disseram ao Naturlink que acreditam que a nova safra de legisladores tem apetite para mudar a forma como o Wyoming gerencia a construção de data centers. Nem todos em Cody pareciam convencidos de que os data centers seriam um resultado positivo para o Wyoming. “Qual é o benefício?” perguntou Anne Trosper, uma residente do Wyoming que trabalhou nas indústrias de petróleo e gás e de conservação. “Onde o Wyoming consegue dinheiro com isso?” Os data centers pagam impostos sobre a propriedade e impostos sobre vendas de eletricidade no Wyoming, além de hospedar trabalhos de construção na fase de construção das instalações e empregar um pequeno número de trabalhadores permanentes quando estiverem em funcionamento. Mas os data centers poderiam fornecer receitas fiscais ao Wyoming de outra forma familiar, embora indireta. Com os centros de dados a exigir enormes quantidades de energia – o Projecto Tembo da Google, anteriormente conhecido como Project Jade, poderia consumir até 10 gigawatts de electricidade, mais de cinco vezes o consumo de electricidade em todo o estado do Wyoming – muitas empresas estão a optar por satisfazer essa procura no Wyoming com combustíveis fósseis. Grande parte da base tributária do Wyoming provém de royalties pagos pelas indústrias do carvão, petróleo e gás, e o estado tem defendido o apoio da administração Trump aos combustíveis fósseis. Para alimentar o crescimento da indústria, alguns condados do Wyoming estão a zonear parcelas de terreno como parques industriais, isentando as empresas de centros de dados de obter licenças ao abrigo da Lei de Localização Industrial do Wyoming. O Wyoming Outdoor Council descreve este acordo como uma “brecha” que as empresas utilizam para construir mais rapidamente e evitar alguma supervisão pública. “Isso significa que não há um processo de revisão abrangente por parte das agências estatais”, disse Wulf na reunião de Cody, para que as comunidades não recebessem os pagamentos de assistência de impacto associados a alguns projectos que passam por esse processo. “Isto não quer dizer que ainda não estejam sujeitos às leis estaduais e federais, mas estamos a perder esse processo de revisão como um todo (porque) os governos locais devem então rever estes projectos da melhor forma possível. Apesar das suas melhores intenções, os governos locais têm uma capacidade mais limitada para uma revisão completa.” Cheyenne, capital do Wyoming, passou anos cortejando o desenvolvimento de data centers com sucesso misto. Embora a nova construção tenha criado muitos empregos temporários e alguns permanentes, a escala, a dimensão e os impactos dos novos projectos geraram controvérsia. Em 2025, WyoFile relatou que a Microsoft solicitou uma licença aérea para operar 128 geradores a diesel de backup para um complexo de data center ao sul da cidade. Em julho deste ano, o Conselho de Serviços Públicos de Cheyenne descobriu que um empreiteiro que trabalhava em um projeto de data center para a Meta, empresa-mãe do Facebook, introduziu acidentalmente uma bactéria rara no sistema de tratamento de águas residuais da cidade. Esse incidente ocorreu depois que os membros do conselho municipal de Cheyenne votaram contra uma proposta de moratória de 12 meses sobre o desenvolvimento de data centers em maio deste ano. “Guardrails são a direção que deveríamos seguir”, disse Emma Jones, organizadora associada da filial de Wyoming do Sierra Club, ao Naturlink. “Muitos membros da comunidade querem ver grupos defendendo moratórias porque (o desenvolvimento do data center) está avançando muito rápido.” Mas pedir uma moratória seria imprudente sem um plano sobre o que realizar durante a pausa, disse ela. artigo.texto: European independent power producer (IPP), R.Power, has energised its first standalone energy storage project in Poland and is now supporting grid stability. The 5 MW/10 MWh Herby battery energy storage system (BESS) is the IPP’s first standalone energy storage project to be energised and serves as a precursor to an extensive rollout of operations across the company’s European BESS pipeline. Herby BESS has secured an optimisation agreement with Entrix, a European leading energy trader. Entrix is now managing the trading and optimisation across all relevant electricity markets, while the qualification process for balancing services provision is ongoing. The partnership provides a blueprint for integrating innovative optimisation approaches across R.Power’s wider European BESS operations. Herby began construction in 4Q25, having secured its long-term contract in Poland’s capacity market auction in December 2024 and also a supplementary capacity market contract organised in September 2026. The project paves the way for R.Power’s advanced utility scale BESS projects – Jedwabno, Dziegielewo, Gdansk, Scornicesti, and Studina – to follow in suit as R.Power scales up its battery energy storage capacity across Europe. Rafał Hajduk, Chief Commercial Officer at R.Power, commented: “Herby is the first standalone BESS in R.Power’s portfolio to reach the market. We look forward to working together with Entrix on this interesting asset with capacity market contracts and asymmetrical battery design. With a combined capacity of 1.6 GW/5.8 GWh across several large BESS assets in the pipeline today – including Jedwabno, Dzięgielewo, Gdańsk, Scornicesti, and Studina – we’re taking the next step on the journey to deliver the storage capacity Poland and Europe needs.”

(CNN Brasil) Terras raras e privatizações no debate presidencial Minerais críticos e privatizações foram os temas de energia do primeiro debate entre Lula (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL), no domingo (18/10), na Band. Lula perguntou se Flávio pretende “entregar” aos EUA as terras raras e os minerais críticos do país e disse que o adversário prometeu aderir ao Escudo das Américas. Flávio chamou a acusação de “mais uma fake news” e disse que foi aos EUA defender as empresas e os produtos brasileiros contra o tarifaço. artigo.texto: A landmark permitting reform bill has united U.S. senators from both parties, but it is dividing the artificial intelligence data center sector. Some industry leaders say it would make data centers easier to build, while others worry it would make them substantially more expensive. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act is being called “the most significant permitting reform bill in years” — intended to accelerate the build-out of major infrastructure and other large-scale projects across the U.S. The bill enjoys support on both sides of the aisle and is expected to clear the Senate during the lame-duck session following November's midterm elections. If it is signed into law, BAAJA would likely have significant implications for the data center industry, potentially rewriting the federal rulebook on how data centers purchase electricity and connect to regional grids. But industry insiders are split on whether the legislation would ultimately be a net positive for the sector or usher in disaster for at least some firms pursuing large-scale digital infrastructure projects. Some within the industry — and some critics of the sector — say BAAJA is poised to fuel further acceleration of the AI data center boom by flattening permitting hurdles and codifying a clear pathway to acquiring power. But others say consumer protection provisions in the bill will make acquiring power much more expensive, adding significant development costs early in projects that could push smaller operators to the sidelines. “Upfront capex, especially speculative, is a death knell,” said Harmol Samra, CEO of AI data center provider Host Digital. “This is just going to slow everyone down.” BAAJA is centered on measures intended to speed up the construction of energy assets, power transmission and other infrastructure, plus other major industrial projects for industries like manufacturing and mining. To do so, the bill would impose firm deadlines for permit approvals, exempt more projects from lengthy reviews, limit how long approvals can be challenged and give previously approved projects greater legal protection. Controversially, it would also make significant changes to the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act. Those provisions have drawn vocal opposition from some environmental groups, with the Center for Biological Diversity calling it a “back-door deal” meant specifically to accelerate data center development. “This would be a golden ticket for huge AI data centers and tech billionaires. Gutting environmental safeguards means opening the floodgates for more gas-powered data centers fouling the air and draining communities’ water supplies,” said Camden Weber, senior climate and energy policy specialist at the Center for Biological Diversity. While other environmental groups have been more receptive — particularly to provisions aimed at accelerating transmission infrastructure that could bring more renewable generation onto the grid — there is truth in the notion that data centers will benefit from faster permitting. Large campuses can face federal delays when projects affect wetlands or trigger environmental or historic preservation reviews. More consequentially, faster approvals for new transmission and generation could shorten the wait for electricity in markets where developers can wait years for grid connections. Yet beyond its permitting reforms, BAAJA also contains a separate set of provisions aimed squarely at data centers, specifically at one of the sector’s most contentious issues: who ends up paying for the billions of dollars of new power infrastructure needed to provide them with electricity. The measures, which apply to data centers larger than 20 megawatts, are intended to ensure that regular electricity customers don’t get stuck with the bill for new power plants and infrastructure for electric transmission built specifically for data centers. Concerns that homeowners, businesses and other existing customers are effectively subsidizing grid improvements driven mainly by data center demand have become a central talking point in a rising wave of opposition to data center development. And lawmakers from both parties have been eager to show they are taking these concerns seriously. The Trump administration’s Ratepayer Protection Pledge, announced in March, aimed to address the same concern, with major tech firms committing to cover the full cost of power delivery and grid updates needed to serve them. But what constitutes “full cost” has remained a matter of interpretation. A report released this month by four Democratic senators found that tech giants generally accept responsibility for the cost of infrastructure built exclusively for them, such as a substation serving a single data center campus. But the answer is murkier when the new infrastructure also benefits other customers, such as a transmission line built primarily to deliver power to a new campus that also improves reliability elsewhere on the grid. Consumer advocates have argued that in such a case, the data center should bear all costs that would not have existed “but for” its arrival. Tech giants and other developers, according to the report, have generally only been willing to cover, at most, a portion of such shared costs and have fought with state regulators to shoulder as few of such shared grid costs as possible. “There is a significant gap between data center developers and the public regarding how much data centers should pay for shared infrastructure, and particularly for infrastructure built primarily, but not exclusively, for their benefit,” the report’s authors wrote. The standards for what constitutes a data center’s fair share of grid costs vary significantly across the balkanized U.S. grid system. artigo.texto: NTPC Renewable Energy Limited (NTPC REL) invites bids for an EPC package with land to develop up to 600 MW of solar capacity. The EPC project developer is required to arrange land for the solar project and the BESS project owner This comprises a (300 MW + 300 MW) ISTS-connected ground-mounted solar project near the Dhule Solar Project in Maharashtra. Bids have been invited until November 13, 2026. Brief Scope of Work Under the scope of work, the developer is require to handle design, engineering, manufacturing, supply, packing, forwarding, transportation, unloading, storage, and installation of the solar project. The bidders are expected to provide a 300 MW solar project under Block 1 for a minimum net worth / turnover threshold of Rs. 192 Crores. Under block 2, the bidder is expected to provide a 300 MW for a minimum financial requirement of Rs. 192 Crores, bringing the combined (Block 1 + Block 2) requirement to Rs. 384 Crores. The scope also requires the commissioning as well as the operation and maintenance (O&M) of the grid-connected solar PV project located near NTPC REL’s Dhule Solar Project. This includes the power evacuation system from the solar project to NTPC REL’s Dhule Solar Project PSS / ISTS substation, as well as the development of a terminal bay at NTPC REL’s Dhule Project PSS. Additionally, the scope includes identifying, acquiring, and completing the total transfer of ownership or lease of encumbrance-free land (including land for BESS) in favor of NTPC Renewable Energy Limited. The developer is required to supply, erect, and commission new 220 kV terminal line bays at NTPC REL’s Dhule Solar Project PSS. The EPC developer must develop a dedicated 220 kV transmission line, including Right of Way (ROW), from the solar plant to NTPC REL’s Dhule Solar Project PSS. The project comprises two blocks of 300 MW each. The evacuation scheme may involve either a single common PSS or two separate PSSs.

artigo.texto: Industrial Manufacturing U.S. Data Center Construction Starts Still Soaring Despite Some Bumps in the Road News reports about data centers being delayed or cancelled, or states and municipalities enacting or considering moratoria on data-center construction, are real, but are not the whole story, according to Industrial Info Resources data tracking. Released Tuesday, October 20, 2026 Reports related to this article: Written by John Egan for IIR News Intelligence (Sugar Land, Texas) Summary News reports about data centers being delayed or cancelled, or states and municipalities enacting or considering moratoria on data-center construction, are real, but are not the whole story, according to Industrial Info Resources data tracking. In fact, the pace of data-center construction starts in the U.S. is growing much faster than the pace of cancellations, delays, or moratoria being considered or enacted, meaning the drive to build data centers in the U.S. is still growing robustly. High Profile Announcements Obscure More Complex Picture Recent high-profile announcements that Big Tech firms or data-center developers have delayed or abandoned planned data centers, or that a growing number of communities are considering or enacting pauses on new data-center construction, may give a casual observer the idea that the drive to build data-centers in the U.S. is slowing, perhaps significantly. But data tracked by Industrial Info Resources tell a different story. While project abandonments and moratoria efforts are real, they constitute only a small part of the overall picture, the proverbial tail of the dog. The bigger picture is that U.S. data-center construction starts are continuing to grow far more rapidly. Project Activity Continues to Surge "Delays are real, but they are not the story that some headlines suggest," said Shane Mullins, IIR senior vice president for energy market solutions. "What we are seeing is developers prioritizing sites that already have power, or that can be powered with less risk of a delay--for example, at a location where a permit that is already in hand, or land that is not under a local or state moratorium. The pie is still growing fast. Even a sharp rise in moratoria is small next to the volume of projects moving into construction." "Weak, grid-dependent, early-stage projects are falling out and the projects that can get power are moving," he continued. "Construction activity still is ramping." New U.S. data-center project value entering Industrial Info Resources coverage has risen every half-year since late 2023, from about US$27 billion a month to about US$350 billion a month since April 2026. Monthly construction kickoffs have roughly doubled over the past year, though they have leveled off since an April 2026 peak of US$48.5 billion. The value of delayed projects was near zero until late 2025 and reached US$29.9 billion in July 2026 and US$27.6 billion in August 2026, he noted. In Industrial Info Resources' U.S. Behind the Meter Data-Center Power Development platform, monthly project activity has gone from US$10 billion to US$30 billion through 2023, to US$100 billion to US$250 billion in 2025, and US$220 billion to US$360 billion so far in 2026. Through early October, about $2.9 trillion has been added to that dataset this year. IIR's data showed that about $425 billion of data-center projects are under active construction in the U.S. now (part of roughly $643 billion globally), with substantially more value in earlier stages of development. By the Numbers - 5.1: Total investment value (TIV), in trillions, of U.S. data-center projects that have been proposed or under construction in the U.S. - 48.5: The US dollar value of data-center projects that began construction in April 2026 - 220-360: The monthly average value, in US billions, of data projects that have entered Industrial Info Resources coverage in 2026 - 27.6: The dollar value, in US billions, of data-center projects that were delayed in August 2026 What Factors Affect Data-Center Construction Decisions? "I'm not going to say moratoria aren't real, because they are," Mullins continued. For more on the data-center moratoria, see June 8, 2026, article - New York Lawmakers Pass One-Year Permitting Ban for New Data Centers. But, he said, "the data-center pie is growing so fast that even a surge of delays and moratoria this year is relatively small potatoes compared to projects that are moving into construction." For more on that, see September 22, 2026, article -- As Data-Center Construction Plans Soar, U.S. Electric Utilities Race to Serve Once-in-a-Lifetime Load Growth. Non-moratoria factors, including rising interest rates, can affect a developer's decision to begin constructing a data center. The interest rate on 10-year and 30-year U.S. Treasury securities is higher now than it has been in nearly two decades. And that's for bonds guaranteed by the U.S. government, which carry a AA+ rating by the major rating agencies. For issuers with lower credit rating, interest rates would be higher, potentially significantly higher, depending on their credit rating. Other factors affecting data-center construction decisions are the local conditions, including: - What is the cost of land? - Is a proposed location close to major fiber-optic routes, internet-exchange points and cloud-provider networks? - Are tax credits available, or are they in the process of being limited or withdrawn? - Is there a surplus, or a shortfall, of electric generation? - Is there an adequate supply of affordable skilled craft labor locally? Regarding the Electric Power situation, a growing number of electric utilities and regional grid managers have enacted a "bring your own generation" policy In which developers and Big Tech firms need to supply their own generation. Companies are doing that because the alternative, waiting for a utility to build the generation or infrastructure to supply a planned data center, takes too long. For more on that

artigo.texto: Coral Energía, an Argentine renewable energy developer and power marketer, is entering a key phase of operational growth driven by solar projects under construction, new battery energy storage systems (BESS) and the exploration of new commercial opportunities in the country"s evolving electricity market. The company expects to finish 2026 with around 260 MW of renewable capacity built within its contracted portfolio, while advancing several parallel developments that will define its position among Argentina"s renewable energy suppliers. "This is a year of growth and consolidation for Coral. Our goal is to strengthen our position among the key players in renewable electricity sales. Once all projects are operational, we will evaluate where the market is heading and where we should position ourselves," said Marcelo Álvarez, Director of Planning and Institutional Relations at Coral Energía, during an interview at Future Energy Summit (FES) Argentina. Coral Energía currently operates four solar parks built under the Generfe program in Santa Fe province, totalling 20 MW of installed capacity. At the same time, the company is advancing projects awarded under RenMDI, a national renewable energy auction designed to promote distributed and regional generation across Argentina. In addition, Coral Energía will soon begin construction of two battery energy storage systems (BESS) awarded through the AlmaGBA program, which aims to improve power system reliability in the Buenos Aires metropolitan area. The projects include: Project Capacity Grid connection Payment BESS Pilar 50 MW Edenor distribution grid USD 11,461 per MW/month BESS Parque 50 MW Edenor distribution grid USD 11,979 per MW/month Overall, the company currently accumulates around 400 MW between contracted renewable capacity and projects under development. Coral Energía"s strategic roadmap targets 1 GW of renewable energy contracts by 2030, reflecting the growing diversification of contracting mechanisms and business models in Argentina"s electricity market. The company"s strategy includes expanding its participation in several segments of Argentina"s energy market, including: - Standalone battery storage projects are expected under the upcoming AlmaSADI tender, which could allocate around 700 MW of BESS capacity across the country. - Renewable projects connected to distribution networks, where available grid capacity may allow new developments. - Corporate power purchase agreements (PPAs) within Argentina"s Mercado a Término de Energías Renovables (MATER). - New demand segments, such as mining operations and data centres, are increasingly seeking a renewable electricity supply. SIn storage, we are evaluating projects between 100 MW and 200 MW, although smaller systems could also emerge," Álvarez explained. Regarding renewable projects connected to distribution networks, the executive highlighted that grid node capacity determines the feasible project size. "We want to build the largest projects possible within each node"s technical limits. Today we have many developments between 10 MW and 20 MW, and the next step is increasing that range to 3050 MW projects, he said. This approach reflects growing congestion in Argentina"s high-voltage transmission system, which is encouraging developers to pursue generation projects connected directly to distribution networks. Álvarez also noted that mergers and acquisitions (M&A) could become part of the company"s growth strategy. "There may also be opportunities to acquire renewable parks already developed for the MATER market, particularly those with dispatch priority, he added. Potential role in transmission infrastructure projects Beyond renewable generation and storage, Coral Energía is also evaluating participation in electric transmission expansion projects in Argentina. The government is expected to launch tender documents this year for AMBA I, a major transmission project aimed at reinforcing the Buenos Aires metropolitan grid. Two additional high-voltage transmission projects could follow in late 2026 or 2027: Project Voltage Route Río Diamante Charlone O"Higgins 500 kV Central-west Argentina Puerto Madryn Choele Choel Bahía Blanca 500 kV Patagonia to the Buenos Aires region SCoral Energía could participate as part of a consortium. Our parent group, Corven, is actively evaluating involvement in some of these projects, Álvarez said. However, he noted that from a generator"s perspective, the economic participation in transmission projects is often relatively limited. As a result, developing new transmission infrastructure typically requires multi-stakeholder consortia involving different actors in the power system with aligned interests.

artigo.texto: ACCURE AI-based platform to provide analytics for Fidra's 1.4GW Thorpe Marsh BESS Germany-headquartered ACCURE will use its AI-driven software to provide independent analytics from factory testing through to commercial operations. Fidra Energy has selected ACCURE Battery Intelligence to provide battery analytics for its 1.4GW/3.1GWh Thorpe Marsh battery energy storage system (BESS). Germany-headquartered ACCURE will use its AI-driven software to provide independent analytics from factory testing through to commercial operations. At factory testing and commissioning, it will support the verification of battery performance against project requirements. Once the Thorpe Marsh project in Doncaster comes online, ACCURE’s predictive analysis will track battery health, state of charge (SOC) and rack availability. Construction at the project began in July this year, and it is due to enter commercial operations in 2027. Approved in early 2025, the 1.4GW project is the largest of its kind in the UK and represents over £1 billion in funding, including finance from the state-owned National Wealth Fund. In September last year, EDF was selected to provide long-term optimisation for 560MW of the project’s capacity, providing route-to-market (RtM) services. Statkraft has a power purchase agreement (PPA) with Fidra to optimise 280MW. ACCURE, for its part, is already onboarded at several Gore Street Energy Storage Fund’s UK sites, including the 80MW Stony project, which was energised last summer and is also optimised in the market by EDF; and Lower Road, a 10MW project that went online in 2020 and is optimised by Arenko. Notably, Gore Street’s collaboration with ACCURE at the time was a UK-first agreement that improved the insurance terms for projects in its portfolio. Read more about:

artigo.texto: Portland City Council considers putting new limits, regulations on data centers PORTLAND (WGME) -- Portland leaders discussed possible new restrictions on data centers Monday. It comes after the city's Housing and Economic Development Committee wrote a memo outlining potential holes in the existing ordinances. It says the ordinances “do not adequately address” the infrastructure demands as well as environmental and neighborhood impacts of data centers. Some of their concerns include land and water usage, noise pollution, and potentially higher electricity costs. "I'm opposed to data centers and want them to be regulated completely out of Portland, Maine," one Portland resident said. Scarborough, Gorham, Saco, Sanford, Westbrook, and other towns have approved temporary moratoriums on these centers to allow more time to address community concerns and update local zoning ordinances. Portland is considering doing the same, but no final decisions have been made.

artigo.texto: Norway's sovereign wealth fund is still avoiding battery storage, fearing a decline in returns Norway's sovereign wealth fund, the largest of its kind in the world, is not yet investing in battery storage. The reasons are the insufficient scale of available projects and the risk of so-called market cannibalization, in which a growing number of batteries gradually narrows the price spreads on which their operators make money. The fund nevertheless considers energy storage a potentially suitable complement to its investments in wind and solar power. “We see significant risk of market cannibalization from batteries,” said Borge Rygh Sivertsen, portfolio manager for new energy at Norway's sovereign wealth fund, at the Energirike conference in Haugesund, Norway. According to him, the economics of battery storage are based primarily on the differences between high and low electricity prices. Batteries buy electricity when prices are low and then sell it when electricity is more expensive. However, as the number of storage facilities grows, more operators compete for the same opportunities. If many batteries buy electricity during cheap hours and feed it into the grid when prices are high, the price spreads gradually narrow. This reduces the potential returns of individual projects and makes their future revenues less predictable. According to Sivertsen, this uncertainty is a significant obstacle to investment. The fund is therefore waiting for now, even though it considers storage a technology that could complement its portfolio of wind and solar power plants. Available projects are not large enough Another obstacle is the size of the investments. The Norwegian fund typically considers projects worth around 500 million euros, or approximately 5 billion Norwegian kroner. According to Sivertsen, it cannot invest in smaller projects on sufficiently competitive terms. The fund already invests in renewable energy in Europe. Through partnerships with RWE, Ørsted, Iberdrola and EnBW, it has acquired stakes in projects with a total installed capacity of 3.3 GW. The fund's investment mandate allows it to invest in renewable energy in Europe and North America, across the energy value chain from generation to electricity distribution. Energy storage is also covered, but its economic attractiveness must meet the fund's requirements. Investment environment clouded by uncertainty According to Sivertsen, geopolitical uncertainty, fluctuations in natural gas prices and higher inflation are also making energy projects harder to finance. These factors increase the cost of capital and make it harder for buyers and sellers to agree on project prices. The fund representative also noted that investors have recently been placing greater emphasis on energy security, while some have partially scaled back their financing of renewable energy. Uncertainty about future electricity supply and demand is therefore another risk that must be taken into account in investment decisions. Renewables currently account for approximately 1% of the value of Norway's sovereign wealth fund. According to Sivertsen, this share could rise to 2% under its investment mandate. artigo.texto: ‘No data centers’: Fairfield residents question possible Patmos data center, C-PACE financing Chants of “No data centers” echoed outside Fairfield City Hall as residents protested a proposed Patmos data center and demanded more transparency from city leaders. The project has been under consideration for months, even though the Fairfield City Council passed a moratorium on future data centers. Questions surrounding a potential $150 million C-PACE financing arrangement are now adding to residents’ concerns. Some residents fear the financing could be used to help construct the Patmos facility and leave the city responsible for the debt. Mayor Herman Carnes strongly disputes that claim and said C-PACE is a financing option available to eligible businesses — not money the city would borrow to build the data center. Gilda Walker, with the Fairfield Environmental Justice Alliance, said residents have not received clear information about the project’s status or what actions city officials may have taken. “People should not have to rely on rumors or to piece together answers on their own,” Walker said. “We also need clear information about the financial side. The city is considering a resolution of intent that could help the project secure financing before the city takes that step. Residents deserve to understand what the resolution does, what commitments it could involve, and whether public resources or incentives are part of the proposal.” Carnes said residents are misunderstanding the purpose of the C-PACE program and insisted it is separate from the Patmos project. C-PACE, which stands for Commercial Property Assessed Clean Energy, is generally used to finance eligible energy, water and property-resilience improvements. Carnes described it as one tool in Fairfield’s effort to attract investment and revitalize the city. “Fairfield has a lot of buildings that are in real need of a lot of things roofs, electrical planning — you name it — before they can move in,” Carnes said. “The city is not tied to whatever amount the citizens are thinking. Those are accusations that are not factual. It's just to try to help bring business to the city of Fairfield. The citizens elected us to revitalize and try to find out ways to be creative. We're doing our job. Huntsville, [Texas] — as a matter of fact — they're using C-Pace. Instead of being behind, we are progressively finding new ways to bring business here in the city of Fairfield.” Questions about transparency intensified during Monday’s protest when Carnes handed reporters a document explaining how C-PACE financing works. A resident called out, “Mayor! Mayor! May I have one of those?” but her request went unanswered. Protesters said the exchange strengthened their concerns about access to information. Carnes, however, maintained that the city has been open with the public and that its actions are documented. “It's a good fit is what's needed,” Carnes said. “The city has been idle for two decades. That’s too long for nothing. City funds will not be used at all. Period. The city has nothing to do with that. That's a that's misleading for the citizens that don't know — putting this out. That's not true.” Walker said residents want information before any decisions are made, not after the fact. “A project with major effects on our community should be presented openly, examined carefully, and discussed with the people who will live with the results,” Walker said. “Today, we're asking city leaders to release the relevant documents and studies, explain the project's cost and expected benefits, and whole accessible public meetings where residents can ask questions and get direct answers.” A public town hall is expected to be part of the process before the C-PACE program can move forward. During its latest meeting, the Fairfield City Council voted to first hold a dedicated work session to discuss the program in its entirety. No date has been announced for either the work session or town hall.

artigo.texto: As concessionárias de transmissão de energia elétrica podem participar dos leilões de reserva de capacidade com sistemas de armazenamento em baterias (BESS), desde que obtenham autorização prévia da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) e cumpram condições previstas nos contratos de concessão. Entre elas está a demonstração de benefícios para os consumidores, com a possibilidade de reversão total ou parcial das receitas obtidas com a nova atividade para a modicidade tarifária. O entendimento é da Procuradoria Federal junto à Aneel, que analisou a possibilidade de atuação das transmissoras no segmento de armazenamento a partir de uma consulta envolvendo a Taesa. A companhia solicitou à agência a ratificação de seu entendimento de que poderia disputar futuros leilões de reserva de capacidade na forma de potência (LRCap) com sistemas de armazenamento autônomos. A Procuradoria concluiu que não há proibição legal para que transmissoras desenvolvam atividades fora do objeto de suas concessões, diferentemente das restrições expressas impostas às distribuidoras. A participação nos certames, contudo, não é automática e depende das condições estabelecidas nos contratos de transmissão. A Taesa discorda de parte desse entendimento. Em posicionamento enviado à MegaWhat, a companhia afirmou que o marco regulatório já dispõe de mecanismos suficientes para permitir a participação dos agentes, sem a necessidade de uma exigência adicional de autorização contratual prévia. A transmissora também contesta a classificação das receitas fixas dos contratos de armazenamento como receitas acessórias da transmissão. Segundo a empresa, os empreendimentos possuem patrimônio, contabilidade, financiamento, obrigações e outorgas próprios, o que justificaria o tratamento independente dessas receitas. Em agosto, a Aneel autorizou a ISA Energia Brasil a explorar atividades atípicas relacionadas à prestação de serviços de eficiência energética e uso racional da energia para clientes B2B, utilizando sistemas de armazenamento de energia por baterias (BESS). O aval contemplo uma atividade econômica diferente daquelas diretamente previstas nos contratos de concessão de transmissão da empresa. Como não havia regulamentação específica da agência sobre a prestação desse tipo de serviço, foi necessário solicitar anuência. Transmissoras poderão atuar por meio de subsidiárias O parecer considera juridicamente admissível que concessionárias de transmissão participem dos leilões de baterias por meio de subsidiárias ou sociedades de propósito específico (SPEs) com objeto social próprio. Essa estrutura, no entanto, não dispensa a autorização regulatória. Segundo a Procuradoria, o exercício de atividades fora do objeto da concessão depende de anuência prévia da Aneel, independentemente de ocorrer diretamente pela transmissora ou por meio de outra empresa controlada. A análise tomou como referência cláusulas do contrato de concessão nº 05/2023 da Taesa, que permitem o desenvolvimento de outras atividades empresariais, desde que observadas as exigências regulatórias. Entre as condições apontadas estão a manutenção de registros contábeis, demonstrações financeiras, fluxos de caixa, contratos e relatórios gerenciais individualizados, de forma a impedir a confusão patrimonial entre a concessão de transmissão e os negócios de armazenamento. A fiscalização dessas condições caberia à Superintendência de Fiscalização Econômica e Financeira (SFF) da Aneel. O parecer também destaca que, em regra, a responsabilidade da transmissora como sócia ou controladora de uma SPE de armazenamento ficaria limitada à sua participação e à integralização do capital social da subsidiária. Receitas de baterias podem ser revertidas O parecer também descreve a necessidade de que a participação das transmissoras em atividades de armazenamento poderá produzir benefícios econômicos para a concessão e, consequentemente, para os usuários do Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN). A Procuradoria aponta que a autorização deverá estar condicionada à preservação da modicidade tarifária, mediante reversão total ou parcial das receitas obtidas com a nova atividade, conforme as disposições do contrato de concessão analisado. Para o órgão, o pedido poderá ser deferido caso fique demonstrado, de maneira objetiva e juridicamente vinculante, que a exploração do armazenamento por meio de uma subsidiária produzirá benefícios econômicos concretos para a concessão. A avaliação caberá à Aneel, que deve considerar as circunstâncias específicas de cada pedido e o interesse público, especialmente a continuidade da prestação do serviço de transmissão e a modicidade tarifária. Taesa contesta exigências para participar dos leilões A Taesa afirmou à MegaWhat que vem desenvolvendo estudos para avaliar oportunidades de negócios relacionadas aos sistemas de armazenamento de energia. A companhia considera que a tecnologia é necessária para o avanço da transição energética e para aumentar a resiliência e a confiabilidade das redes de transmissão e distribuição. Segundo a empresa, o mercado brasileiro de armazenamento ainda está em desenvolvimento e parte das regras permanece em construção. Nesse contexto, a transmissora entende que o posicionamento sobre a necessidade de anuência prévia e sobre a classificação dos contratos de armazenamento como receitas acessórias ocorreu em caráter preliminar e precisa ser aprofundado à luz do arcabouço regulatório aplicável. Na avaliação da Taesa, os mecanismos de controle e as salvaguardas já existentes são suficientes para assegurar a participação dos agentes, sem a imposição de um requisito adicional de autorização contratual prévia. A companhia também sustenta que as receitas fixas provenientes dos contratos dos leilões de reserva de capacidade são juridicamente independentes das receitas da transmissão. artigo.texto: Stellenbosch solar and battery storage: Wine harvest shows why timing counts Stellenbosch’s procurement of up to 41.9 MW of solar photovoltaic capacity and 14.8 MWh of battery storage, awarded, 22 May 2026, comes as new data from Vergenoegd Löw shows how sharply electricity demand can rise during the wine harvest. The two developments point to a broader local energy issue: whether new solar and storage can help meet the needs of Stellenbosch’s commercial customers when demand is highest, beyond adding lower-cost power over the course of a year. At Vergenoegd Löw, an August 2026 PV-monitoring report provided to Cape Business News earlier this month shows what that seasonal demand looks like at an individual commercial operation. Harvest drives the electricity surge In February, the estate used more than twice as much electricity as it did in June. Its solar system generated the equivalent of 63% of that demand, so its grid electricity was only about a third higher. Compared with June, the estate’s reported load was 40 318 kWh higher in February. Grid electricity was only 6 603 kWh higher. Of interest is the coinciding timing of peak solar potential and the harvest season. February falls within the Cape wine harvest, when electricity demand rises sharply, while solar production is also strong. March followed the same pattern, with solar again covering more than half of the estate’s demand. January, the estate’s heaviest month for electricity, relied more on the grid and also drew on a generator. The estate still draws on the grid every month. What changes is the balance between on-site generation and grid electricity as demand and solar output rise and fall. For a seasonal commercial operation, generating more electricity on site during its busiest period can limit the increase in power that has to be bought from the grid. That matters as tariffs climb. Eskom’s tariff increases this year were close to 9%, from April for its direct customers and from July for municipalities. Almost half the load from PV Between January and August, the estate’s solar system generated the equivalent of almost half its electricity use. The monitoring report records 183.17 tonnes of CO₂ avoided over the same period. The harvest figures are more revealing than that average. In every other month, solar covered less than half of the estate’s demand. For a seasonal business, that timing is the central feature of the data: the harvest months, when demand climbs, are also the months in which solar covers the largest share of it. Stellenbosch is adding generation and storage The municipal project is on a very different scale, but its combination of solar and battery storage points to a wider change in Stellenbosch’s electricity system. The municipality’s tender, BSM 89/25, called for 41.9 MW of solar PV and 14.8 MWh of battery storage, procured through an independent power producer model. The RFP was issued in 2025, and the project was awarded in May 2026. For commercial electricity users, storage can address the gap between when solar is generated and when power is needed. At Vergenoegd Löw, the harvest provides a favourable match because its demand rises during a period of strong solar generation. The municipal buildout is also being accompanied by network investment. Stellenbosch has tendered for two 20 MVA, 66/11 kV transformers to replace three existing 7.5 MVA units at its main substation.

artigo.texto: LITTLETON, Colo. - The City of Littleton is considering a six-month moratorium on any future data center projects. Denver7 confirmed there are no current data center proposals within Littleton city limits that have been filed; the proactive move follows several communities across Colorado considering similar moratoriums. WATCH: City of Littleton considers six month moratorium on data centers The proposed ordinance acknowledges that demand for data centers has grown across the country, and the data centers require large amounts of electricity, water-intensive cooling systems and may create continuous noise and emissions. The moratorium directs City staff to study the land use, energy, water, noise, air quality, infrastructure, fiscal and economic impacts of data centers and proposed changes to the land use code for any potential future projects. Denver7's South Metro Reporter Danielle Kreutter heard from Littleton neighbors about their thoughts on data centers. "What would you like to see as far as restrictions or things that City Council should consider before they allow those kind of projects?" Kreutter asked long time Littleton resident, Paul Bingham. "Well, I can't think of anything beyond: simply not having any," said Bingham. Bingham has lived in Littleton for more than 60 years and has seen his fair share of changes and is hopeful data centers stay out of the city. "[They're] 10-15 football fields in size, a gigantic amount of water and electricity, it all sounds pretty bleak as far as I'm concerned," he said. He believes the space required for a data center will be a logistical challenge in Littleton regardless. "We don't have any land available for a data center. Not a great amount of it. It's all being taken up with, well, right now, a gigantic Costco," Bingham said of construction of the 159,000-square foot Costco project at the Mineral Place mixed-use development. Another Littleton resident, Billy Gooch, also noted how built out Littleton already is. "You need a lot of land, a lot of power, a lot of water. I'm not sure Littleton has any, much less all of those," said Gooch. Gooch worked in telecommunications for 14 years. "I've worked in and around data centers. There are ways to do it responsibly," he said. He's hopeful, if passed, the moratorium requires any possible future projects to follow that requirement. "What would you like to see, generally, included in those considerations?" asked Denver7's South Metro Reporter Danielle Kreutter. "At the very least, they need to pay their own way. No public subsidies. We need to make sure rate payers' electricity is not being impacted and that water is not being impacted," he said. The first hearing on the ordinance is Tuesday night, with a public hearing currently scheduled for November 3. A final vote will happen after the public hearing, however a date has not been set. artigo.texto: The increasingly contentious national debate over data centers moved into Mesa last week as Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes told a town hall that their explosive growth threatens to leave communities with higher utility bills, a range of health and environmental problems and inadequate government oversight. Addressing over 250 people at a Mesa community center Oct. 14, Mayes questioned whether Arizona has done enough to protect residents as developers rush to build the enormous facilities needed to support artificial intelligence, cloud computing and other digital services. The setting was particularly appropriate. Mesa has become a major data center hub, with over 7.5 million square feet of existing and proposed facilities. Yet roughly three-quarters of those attending the meeting had traveled from Ahwatukee, where residents have organized against a 1-million-square-foot facility currently being constructed amid neighborhoods with thousands of homes. Phoenix officials contend California-based Menlo Equities was allowed to build the five-building data campus because the site had been rezoned since the mid-1990s. Critics contend that when data centers were included in that zoning category 30 years ago, no one could envision the mammoth facilities that have torn apart communities across the country. Like Mesa, Phoenix last year adopted a more targeted set of guidelines for data centers, but projects like Menlo’s were not covered because they had already been approved under the older zoning standards. Mayes, a Democrat seeking reelection, has called for a moratorium on data center construction “to get our house in order to determine the principles that should guide this build-up, if it happens, and to decide what’s needed to protect our communities in Arizona. “This issue is too important to let data center developers themselves decide what is right for our state and our communities,” Mayes told the audience. She then put data centers’ explosive growth into perspective for Arizonans: “The Phoenix area is now the second largest U.S. data center hub. … My office has identified more than 180 operating or planned data centers across Arizona.” Of those, 110 are operating, 10 are under construction and almost 40 more are planned, according to Mayes. The Legislature and Gov. Katie Hobbs agreed in June to impose a three-year moratorium starting July 1 on millions of dollars in tax incentives that data centers have been getting from the state. The state Commerce Authority reportedly received 113 applications for those incentives in the second half of June before the moratorium took effect. In the last 10 years, 123 applications were filed. Mayes said her office’s research has found that data center growth in Arizona poses especially dire circumstances amid the state’s unfolding water crisis. “If all planned data centers in the Phoenix area are built,” she said, “stress on our local water supplies will increase by 32%. That would occur at the same time that Arizona loses 30% of our Colorado River water supplies.” She also asserted that data centers’ demand for electricity would drive up customers’ utility bills. Ironically, just hours before her town hall, Chris Bauer, vice president and treasurer for Pinnacle West Capital Corporation and its primary subsidiary, Arizona Public Service Company (APS), told the audience at the East Valley Partnership’s Statespersons’ Luncheon his company intends to “make growth pay for growth. The attorney general currently is suing APS’ proposed 14% rate hike. Mayes also cited noise and even temperature impacts of data centers. She said data centers “regularly generate 94 decibels of noise.” Mesa’s noise ordinance has a 24-hour average sound limit of 60 decibels for residential zones and 65 for commercial zones. She also cited a recent Arizona State University study that says data centers can add 4 degrees to a neighborhood’s temperature downwind from a facility. Mayes outlined a series of demands she wants Arizona to develop for data centers, starting with transparency. She said some data center companies have required municipalities to enter nondisclosure agreements “which limit the ability of local governments … to discuss the project with their constituents.” She said she is currently suing unidentified municipalities over such agreements. She also said data centers should be forbidden from creating nuisances, that natural resources must be protected, that developers be required to pay fully for their power, and that the facilities “must give back.” “In Arizona, it is a tradition that any large development project gives back to the community it inevitably impacts, whether this is through taxes, fees, assessments, or even water storage credits,” she said. “We must ensure that communities that host data centers and that choose to host data centers indeed all Arizonans benefit from their development.” Mayes conceded her office is studying a major issue that has developed when municipalities in Arizona try to deny a data center from being built. Proposition 207, passed by an overwhelming majority of voters in 2006, requires any government level in Arizona to compensate a property owner if zoning or other restrictions lower the fair market value of the property. Earlier this year, Phoenix City Council reversed a denial of a permit for a data center after the property owner filed a claim for over $50 million. “We’re hearing a lot about Prop 207 from cities,” Mayes told the audience – well, mainly from the city of Phoenix, and we are analyzing that issue. So I’m not going to opine yet on Prop 207. But what I will say very clearly is that Prop 207 does not prevent me as your attorney general from filing a nuisance lawsuit against the AI data center.” She added, “I am certain that there are data centers that are being plopped in the middle of new neighborhoods that would meet the classical definition of a nuisance.” Mayes’ Republican opponent, Senate President Warren Pe

artigo.texto: A ISA Energia Brasil pediu à Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel) orientação sobre os critérios de prioridade para conexão de grandes consumidores à Rede Básica de transmissão, diante de casos em que pareceres de acesso emitidos pelo Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS) indicam viabilidade sistêmica, mas não garantem espaço físico suficiente nas subestações para todas as conexões solicitadas. Em carta, a companhia relatou dificuldades para conciliar a emissão de múltiplos pareceres de acesso com a disponibilidade física das instalações. Segundo a empresa, o problema tem se tornado mais relevante com o crescimento dos pedidos de conexão de consumidores de grande porte, especialmente empreendimentos voltados à implantação e operação de data centers. Subestação Anhanguera tem espaço para apenas duas conexões A ISA Energia apresentou como exemplo a subestação Anhanguera, em 345 kV, sob sua concessão. O ONS emitiu quatro pareceres de acesso à Rede Básica para empreendimentos que pretendem se conectar à instalação: Odata Sampa (Matriz), Odata Sampa 08 (Filial), Data Center Rodoanel e Data Center Anhanguera. As solicitações foram protocoladas entre 27 e 29 de maio de 2026. Durante as consultas sobre a disponibilidade de espaço, a ISA Energia informou que havia capacidade física para instalar dois novos módulos de conexão no barramento existente, considerando a configuração da subestação naquele momento, além de reforços e ampliações já indicados no Plano de Outorgas de Transmissão de Energia Elétrica (Potee) e pareceres de acesso anteriormente emitidos. Após a emissão dos quatro pareceres, porém, os estudos realizados pela transmissora confirmaram que a subestação comportava apenas dois novos módulos de conexão com tecnologia GIS (sigla em inglês para Gas Insulated Switchgear, equipamento de manobra isolado a gás). A capacidade física, portanto, era insuficiente para viabilizar todas as conexões contempladas nos documentos emitidos pelo ONS. ISA Energia propõe ordem cronológica para priorizar acessos Diante da ausência de uma regra regulatória específica para situações desse tipo, a ISA Energia adotou a ordem cronológica de protocolo dos pedidos de acesso ao ONS como critério para definir a prioridade entre os empreendimentos. A empresa, no entanto, solicitou à Aneel que avalie se esse procedimento é adequado para determinar a prioridade dos processos de conexão e da assinatura dos Contratos de Conexão à Transmissão (CCTs). A transmissora também questionou como deve ser definida a prioridade quando dois ou mais pedidos são protocolados na mesma data. Outro ponto levantado é se uma consulta prévia à concessionária sobre a existência de espaço físico na subestação deve conferir prioridade ao interessado, mesmo que o pedido formal de acesso tenha sido apresentado posteriormente ao de outros empreendimentos. Por fim, a ISA Energia perguntou se um consumidor que não conseguir prioridade na conexão pode propor e custear, por sua conta e risco, soluções alternativas para viabilizar o acesso, passando à frente de outros interessados que também tenham sido preteridos.

artigo.texto: GRIDCO Limited, Odisha’s renewable energy nodal agency under the Odisha Renewable Energy Policy 2022, has issued a Request for Proposal (RFP) to appoint an experienced consultant for conducting an Environmental and Social Impact Assessment (ESIA) for the proposed 225 MW Upper Indravati Floating Solar Photovoltaic and Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Project. The project, including its associated power evacuation infrastructure and transmission lines, is located across the Nabarangpur and Kalahandi districts of Odisha. The consultancy assignment aims to evaluate the potential environmental and social impacts of the proposed floating solar and battery storage development. The assessment will follow applicable Indian regulations, the International Finance Corporation (IFC) Performance Standards 2012, and the World Bank Group Environmental, Health, and Safety (EHS) Guidelines. The selected consultant will be responsible for undertaking detailed technical, physical, biological, and socio-economic assessments to identify potential risks and recommend appropriate mitigation measures. The scope of work includes evaluating the project footprint over the Indravati reservoir and examining its potential effects on water quality, aquatic ecosystems, biodiversity, and surrounding communities. The consultant will also conduct a Critical Habitat Assessment to identify ecologically sensitive areas that may require special protection. Hydrodynamic water quality modelling and oil spill modelling for synthetic transformer oils will be undertaken to assess potential environmental risks associated with project operations. Battery energy storage safety will be another important component of the assignment. The consultant will evaluate risks associated with fire incidents, thermal runaway, hazardous waste management, and other potential environmental and operational hazards linked to BESS installations. A Climate Change Risk Assessment will also be prepared to examine the project’s vulnerability to climate-related risks and identify suitable adaptation measures. In addition to the technical assessments, the selected consultant will prepare several environmental and social management documents. These will include an Environmental and Social Management Plan (ESMP), Stakeholder Engagement Plan (SEP), Livelihood Restoration Plan (LRP), and Indigenous Peoples Development Plan (IPDP). These plans are intended to establish appropriate procedures for managing environmental impacts, engaging affected stakeholders, addressing livelihood-related concerns, and protecting vulnerable communities. GRIDCO issued the RFP document on October 16, 2026. The pre-bid meeting is scheduled for October 30, 2026, at 11:00 AM at the GRIDCO Conference Hall, with video conferencing facilities also available. Responses to queries and the publication of any corrigendum are scheduled for November 3, 2026. The last date for online bid submission is November 17, 2026, until 3:00 PM, while techno-commercial bids will be opened at 5:00 PM on the same day. Technical proposal evaluation and declaration of qualified bidders are scheduled for November 20, followed by price bid declaration on November 25. GRIDCO plans to issue the Letter of Award on December 2 and sign the contract agreement on December 23, 2026. The tender document costs ₹10,000 plus 18% GST, bringing the total fee to ₹11,800. Bidders must furnish an Earnest Money Deposit of ₹1 lakh, while the selected consultant will be required to submit a Performance Bank Guarantee of ₹2.5 lakh within 20 days of the work order. The guarantee must remain valid for 12 months, with an additional six-month claim period. Proposals must remain valid for at least 180 days from the submission deadline. Em entrevistas, Flávio e Lula citam propostas econômicas que não cabem nas contas do governo, dizem analistas
Candidato do PT minimiza necessidade de moderar despesas e fala em novas benesses. Candidato do PL defende ajuste, mas sem explicar como chegar ao corte de gastos sem mexer em benefícios
O presidente Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, candidato a reeleição pelo PT, e o senador fluminense Flávio Bolsonaro, candidato do PL, reforçaram contradições de suas propostas para a economia nas entrevistas que concederam à Globo, quinta e sexta-feira, a pouco mais de uma semana do segundo turno da eleição presidencial, marcado para o próximo domingo.
- Contas que não fecham: Plano genérico de Flávio Bolsonaro e gradualismo de Lula deixam dúvida sobre Orçamento
- Flávio Bolsonaro ou Lula: Quem foi melhor nas entrevistas da Globo? Veja notas e avaliações dos colunistas do GLOBO
Ao tratarem de temas econômicos nas entrevistas à jornalista Renata Lo Prete, ambos candidatos citaram medidas que não cabem nas contas do governo, como especialistas já vêm apontando.
O presidente Lula voltou a minimizar a necessidade de moderar as despesas públicas, embora tenha se dito preocupado com o crescimento da dívida pública, mas acrescentou, no rol de medidas e benesses que o atual governo vem anunciando na reta final da campanha, a ideia de oferecer passe livre no transporte público de todas as cidades do país aos fins de semana.
- Do salário mínimo ao Bolsa Família: Lula e Flávio apresentam divergências sobre benefícios sociais e trabalho
Já Flávio Bolsonaro reafirmou a necessidade de fazer ajustes na condução da economia, criticou o governo Lula, mas repetiu propostas contraditórias para equilibrar as contas, garantindo que, em caso de vitória nas eleições, uma gestão liderada pelo PL não mexerá em alguns dos mais importantes itens para segurar os gastos públicos de forma estrutural, como a regra de reajuste do salário mínimo e a vinculação dos benefícios previdenciários ao piso salarial, segundo a avaliação de diversos especialistas.
Para o economista-chefe da gestora de recursos ARX Investimentos, Gabriel Leal de Barros, as contradições em torno das propostas econômicas nas entrevistas refletiram a campanha até aqui, marcada menos por debates em torno de programas e mais por discursos eleitorais para conquistar votos, ao mesmo tempo em que um ajuste nas contas do governo é urgente.
— Veio dentro do esperado. Não achava, nesta altura do campeonato, que o Lula fosse prometer alguma coisa diferente do que ele está fazendo no curto prazo ou que Flávio fosse (citar medidas que pudessem) dar armas para o PT para bater nele. Então, é uma estratégia de tocar a bola de lado, dos dois candidatos — afirmou Leal de Barros.

A matemática criou a IA, mas agora a IA pode destruir a matemática
Máquinas solucionam problemas em 'idioma' que só elas entendem e reforçam temor de fuga ao controle humano
A matemática criou a inteligência artificial (IA). Os chatbots e agentes que hoje impressionam foram erguidos sobre uma base com séculos de raciocínio humano, que inclui conceitos como descida do gradiente, derivadas parciais e jacobianas, espaços vetoriais e inferência bayesiana. Porém, após anúncios recentes da OpenAI, a IA pode estar perto de destruir a matemática — ao menos, a matemática que atravessou a história entre a Grécia antiga e os tempos atuais.
- Tecnologia com visões distintas: Flávio propõe ‘liberdade para inovar’; Lula defende soberania e regulação
- Receita da Anthropic salta para US$ 16,8 bilhões no trimestre que antecede IPO, diz agência
No começo do mês, a empresa do ChatGPT anunciou que um de seus modelos internos solucionou 377 problemas matemáticos complexos em áreas como álgebra, teoria dos números e topologia — alguns desafiavam pesquisadores havia décadas. Antes disso, a OpenAI já havia surpreendido ao afirmar que resolveu as equações de Navier-Stokes, um dos problemas do milênio, aberto havia 90 anos.
Para quem sofria com as provas de matemática na escola, que focam exclusivamente em resultado e velocidade, parece um avanço espetacular. Mas, para quem vive de pensar o campo da matemática, o apetite das máquinas por respostas se apresenta mais como uma maldição do que como uma bênção.
No filme Gênio Indomável (1997), o personagem Will Hunting (Matt Damon) não é considerado um grande talento da matemática apenas por chegar ao resultado de problemas complexos na lousa do professor Gerald Lambeau (Stellan Skarsgård). Ele provou a solução, deixando claro como estruturou seu raciocínio lógico. É isso que os sistemas de IA estão prestes a usurpar dos matemáticos.
— O que fez a matemática avançar até hoje é muito mais fazer perguntas do que respondê-las. No processo, você pega ideias anteriores, interpreta e entende em profundidade. Assim, cria pontes para novas ideias. É um processo enriquecedor. A IA não faz nada disso. Ela produz um código que prova a todo custo que você resolveu o problema. Mas o que você pensou? — diz Marcelo Viana, diretor-geral do Instituto Nacional de Matemática Pura e Aplicada (IMPA).
- Carta assinada por mais de 220 cientistas pede 'mudanças imediatas' para evitar incidentes graves com a IA; entenda
Um dos exemplos clássicos de que, na matemática, o que vale é a jornada, e não o destino final, é o Último Teorema de Fermat, proposto em 1637 e solucionado apenas em 1994, por Andrew Wiles — que passou sete anos criando e implementando a estratégia. Ao longo dos 357 anos, o processo gerou ramos inteiros da matemática, incluindo a base para os algoritmos de criptografia moderna que hoje protegem suas mensagens no WhatsApp e todas as transações bancárias do mundo.

Quem é Gabriella Wilde, atriz de ‘Mulher-Maravilha 1984’ que se tornou 'doula da morte'
Aos 37 anos, britânica conhecida por ‘Poldark’ e ‘Carrie, a Estranha’ passou a acompanhar pessoas no fim da vida
Conhecida por trabalhos em produções como “Mulher-Maravilha 1984”, “Doctor Who” e “Poldark”, a atriz britânica Gabriella Wilde, de 37 anos, encontrou um novo caminho profissional fora dos sets de filmagem. Além da carreira artística, ela atua como doula da morte, profissional que oferece apoio emocional e acompanhamento a pessoas em fase final da vida e a seus familiares.
- Entrevista: Ronaldo Fraga fala sobre a chegada aos 60 anos: 'Cada vez mais safado'
- 'Exercícios, alimentação saudável e bons produtos na pele': os hábitos de beleza de Elizabeth Hurley
A mudança começou enquanto Wilde trabalhava na série histórica “Poldark”, exibida pela BBC entre 2016 e 2019. Durante esse período, ela iniciou uma formação em psicoterapia e passou a estudar a relação das pessoas com o luto e a mortalidade. Em entrevista recente ao programa britânico “This Morning”, a atriz contou que o contato com esses temas mudou sua maneira de compreender a morte e a própria vida.
— Comecei a me capacitar à noite enquanto ainda trabalhava em “Poldark” — disse.
Segundo Wilde, o interesse surgiu quando percebeu como a morte continua sendo um assunto pouco discutido socialmente. A formação levou a atriz a aprofundar suas reflexões sobre o luto e a buscar uma maneira de oferecer apoio a pessoas que enfrentam o fim da vida.
A artista contou que, inicialmente, sentiu a chamada síndrome do impostor ao assumir a nova função. Com o tempo, porém, compreendeu que o trabalho não depende necessariamente de encontrar respostas para todas as perguntas, mas de oferecer presença e acolhimento a quem está passando por um momento delicado.

Em jogo dominante, Flamengo vence o Bahia fora de casa e segue na liderança do Brasileirão
Rubro-negro balançou as redes três vezes no segundo tempo e chegou a 67 pontos na competição
Por O Globo
Atualizado
Pressionado após a vitória do Palmeiras, no sábado, o Flamengo visitou o Bahia, neste domingo, fora de casa, e conseguiu o resultado positivo para se manter na liderança do Campeonato Brasileiro. O time rubro-negro dominou os mandantes durante quase os 90 minutos e venceu por 3 a 0, com gols de Jorginho, Plata e Lucas Paquetá.
No primeiro tempo, o Flamengo parou em grande atuação do goleiro Ronaldo, que fez oito defesas, e não conseguiu balançar as redes do Bahia. O Tricolor de Aço, mandante, pouco fez e não incomodou tanto como o rubro-negro. O placar de 0 a 0 não traduzia o jogo.
Por outro lado, na segunda etapa, o Flamengo conseguiu ser eficiente e balançou as redes três vezes. Jorginho abriu o placar após pênalti sofrido por Carrascal, Plata, de cabeça, fez o segundo, e Lucas Paquetá marcou um golaço para fechar o placar. Com o resultado, o time carioca chegou a 67 pontos, um a mais do que o vice-líder Palmeiras.
Agora, o time rubro-negro vira a chave para a semifinal da Copa Libertadores e encara o Estudiantes, na quinta-feira, no Maracanã, precisando de uma vitória simples para avançar à final. No Brasileirão, o Flamengo recebe o Atlético-MG, na segunda-feira, dia 26, no Maracanã, às 20h.

Saiba quando a GDA Luma deve assumir oficialmente o comando da SAF do Botafogo
Associativo aguarda fim do prazo da Eagle para compra de novas ações enquanto diretoria do clube-empresa negocia aprovação da Recuperação Judicial
“Quando a GDA Luma vai, de fato, assumir o Botafogo?”. Essa é a pergunta que mais circula entre torcedores desde junho, quando a empresa assinou acordo que prevê a conversão de empréstimos financeiros em participação societária e, consequentemente, a transferência de 90% das ações da SAF. Ainda não há uma data definitiva para a conclusão do processo, mas os próximos passos nos bastidores podem aproximar uma resolução.
Atualmente, o Botafogo social detém 51% das ações da SAF e já iniciou o processo para assumir também a parcela de 49% que pertence à Eagle Football Holdings Bidco.
Em 24 de setembro, uma Assembleia Geral Extraordinária (AGE) aprovou a emissão de 200 milhões de novas ações ordinárias da SAF, ao preço de R$ 0,01 por ação. Desse total, o clube associativo ficou com 102 milhões de ações, mantendo sua participação proporcional, enquanto a Eagle Bidco teve preferência para adquirir as outras 98 milhões.
A diretoria do clube social aguarda o fim do prazo concedido à Eagle, que termina ainda em outubro. Com a confirmação de que a holding não comprou todas as ações a que tem direito, o associativo poderá adquirir as restantes. Com isso, o Botafogo social passaria a deter praticamente 100% da SAF, enquanto a participação da Eagle Bidco ficaria abaixo de 0,1%.
Com o controle de quase todas as ações, o associativo poderá transferir 90% da SAF para a GDA Luma. Dos US$ 105 milhões previstos no acordo, cerca de US$ 50 milhões já foram repassados. Além disso, as partes estão nos trâmites finais para a entrada de outros US$ 7 milhões, cujo depósito é esperado entre a última semana de outubro e a primeira de novembro. O CEO Eduardo Iglesias conduz as tratativas com os executivos da futura investidora, entre eles o empresário Gabriel de Alba.
A transferência das ações, porém, não deve ocorrer imediatamente após a conclusão dessa etapa societária. Nos bastidores, há o entendimento de que o melhor caminho é aguardar o avanço das negociações da recuperação judicial antes de oficializar a entrada da GDA Luma na SAF. A avaliação da diretoria alvinegra é que a mudança de controle poderia dificultar as conversas com os credores sobre o deságio das dívidas — isto é, a possibilidade de pagar um valor menor do que o originalmente devido.
Interlocutores envolvidos nas negociações afirmam que o Botafogo já obteve a adesão de credores que representam entre 35% e 40% dos créditos necessários para aprovar o plano, cujo percentual mínimo é de 51%. O principal obstáculo está nas tratativas com outros clubes, que também concentram algumas das maiores dívidas.

artigo.texto: Few rideshares come with a theme, but SpaceX’s Transporter-18—which launched Thursday from Vandenberg—had one: getting power to compute in orbit. Three of its payloads are each testing a different piece of the ODC puzzle. - Cowboy Space’s Reason-1 will attempt to beam solar power to Earth via laser—a test run for the optical links its future data centers will need. - Google’s Project Suncatcher will run AI chips on traditional solar power to see how they hold up in orbit. - Star Catcher’s Protostar will try to beam power between two spacecraft, with orbital data centers among its customers. “We passed the point of saying, ‘Will there be people doing AI computing in space?'” Cowboy Space COO and Chief Legal Officer Joseph Yaffe told Payload. “We’re focused on building the infrastructure for that.” cowboy like me: Cowboy Space began as Aetherflux—a power-beaming startup—before rebranding in May to focus on orbital data centers and rockets. Reason-1 is the stepping stone that brings the two efforts together. - Cowboy hopes to attempt to beam as soon as late October, sending solar power via infrared laser to a 10–20 m spot at a ground test facility and aiming to deliver 30–100 W. Cowboy calls it the first commercial kilowatt-class laser in space designed to deliver energy to Earth. - The same laser technology will form the backbone of the data link on Reason-2, which is slated to fly H200 GPUs in the first half of 2027—this time beaming data instead of power. - Longer term, Cowboy is building its own rocket, whose upper stage doubles as a 1 MW data center, targeted to launch in December 2028. “We’re an orbital energy infrastructure company that’s delivering power, computing power, and the ability to connect all of those things through laser infrared technology,” Yaffe said. Hot N Cold: While Cowboy is testing the laser, Google is testing out chips. Its Project Suncatcher MVP—built with Planet Labs—was announced last year as a research “moonshot” to run AI in orbit. The fridge-sized satellite carries four Trillium TPUs—roughly one server’s worth of compute—using about 1kW of solar to run Gemini queries in short bursts. On Thursday, Google also released an updated, peer-reviewed version of its Suncatcher paper in the energy research journal Joule, sketching the company’s long-term vision: - The constellation: Satellites that could eventually hold a data-center rack’s worth of compute, roughly 50–100 kW each, flying in tight, laser-linked clusters. One illustrative example packs 81 satellites within a 1 km radius. - Radiation: In ground tests, the TPUs survived a radiation dose equivalent to five years in orbit. Radiation still caused occasional silent errors—about one per three million queries—which is manageable for answering questions but may be a problem for training models. - Heat: The paper calls thermal management a major challenge. MVP’s chips will have to power down every 15 to 20 minutes to avoid overheating. Google says its two follow-up satellites in 2027 will run continuously. If launch costs fall to $200/kg, Google estimates the cost of launching a kilowatt of solar power to orbit would be about $810 per year, comparable to what US data centers spend on electricity. Its learning-curve analysis suggests that price is possible by the mid-2030s, if Starship flies about 180 times a year. Pocketful of Sunshine: The final piece is power. Star Catcher’s Protostar will be the company’s first end-to-end in-space demo. - Protostar will deploy a cubesat and beam measurable power to its off-the-shelf solar panels—aiming to validate commercial power-beaming operations. - Orbital computing companies Starcloud and Aethero are among Star Catcher’s publicized customers. As Yaffe put it, the “if” of AI compute in space may be settled. The next few weeks will give a glimpse into how far along the “how” is.

Gelion takes step closer to commerciality with latest lab result
Published: 02:24 19 Oct 2026 EDT
Gelion PLC (AIM:GELN, OTC:GELNF, FRA:X0S) told investors it has taken another step towards commercialising its next-generation battery technology after independent US laboratory testing confirmed its ability to deliver high power without sacrificing much of its capacity.
The National Laboratory of the Rockies (NLR), part of the US Department of Energy, found that cells using Gelion's Nano-Encapsulated Sulfur (NES) technology retained 92% of their reference capacity despite a 20-fold increase in cycling rate.
The laboratory also independently manufactured electrodes and assembled battery cells, reproducing key performance characteristics previously demonstrated in Gelion's own facilities. The results provide evidence that the technology can be transferred to third-party manufacturers.
The findings build on earlier testing by UK defence technology group QinetiQ, which demonstrated sustained high-power performance under conditions representative of drone flight, including repeated rapid-discharge pulses.
NLR's Matthew Keyser described the results as "very encouraging", highlighting both the reproducibility and high-rate performance of the material.
Gelion chief executive Matt Wood said the findings strengthened the case for deploying NES in drones, defence and aerospace applications, where batteries must combine high energy capacity with rapid power delivery.
"We're incredibly pleased with these preliminary results from our program with NLR. Having independent validation of both our internal capacity results and such exceptional rate performance supports the already-strong case for deploying Gelion's NES in applications that require both high energy and high-power delivery, such as drones, defence, and aerospace.
"It also demonstrates the value of working with a partner as capable and credible as NLR."
The next phase of the US collaboration will focus on developing and validating larger commercial pouch-cell prototypes, with the longer-term aim of qualifying the technology for US government and defence procurement.
